title: ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning
authors: Chaehyun Kim,Chi-Pin Huang,Jisoo Kim,Min-Hung Chen,Yu-Chiang Frank Wang,Seungryong Kim,Fu-En Yang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made substantial progress in robotic manipulation, but their generalization remains constrained by the diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Human videos provide much broader behavioral and environmental experience, while learning from them faces a fundamental trade-off between scalable data and explicit action grounding. We introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and strengthens it through reinforcement learning with world imagination. ThinkWorld represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures the intermediate dynamics connecting the current world to a future state and serves as a common action representation across embodiments. We first initialize CoD with action-labeled demonstrations, then predict the future induced by each CoD and reinforce those whose predictions better match the observed outcome. This enables videos without action annotations to provide direct supervision from observed state transitions, allowing human and robot experience to refine the same reasoning space. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate effective human-to-robot transfer and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments.
introduction:
Building general-purpose action models that transfer across tasks, objects, environments, and embodiments is a central goal of robot learning. Recent vision-language-action models (VLAs) (Brohan et al., 2023; O’Neill et al., 2024; Team et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024a; Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025) have made substantial progress by transferring pretrained vision-language knowledge and scaling across heterogeneous robot demonstrations. Nevertheless, their policy learning and behavioral coverage remain largely tied to action-labeled robot trajectories, whose collection requires physical platforms, embodiment-specific interfaces, and substantial human effort. Human videos offer a complementary source of experience with far greater behavioral and environmental diversity, but do not provide directly executable robot actions.

Existing approaches seek to extract actionable supervision from human videos along two main directions. Latent action models (Ye et al., 2025; Bu et al., 2025; Dai et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026a) infer transition variables from pairs or sequences of frames and use them for representation or policy learning. While naturally scalable to action-unlabeled videos, these inferred variables are underconstrained and may capture appearance changes or camera motion rather than controllable behavior. In contrast, fully supervised approaches recover hand poses, object interactions, or retargeted trajectories to provide explicit motion supervision (Kareer et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026c). Such supervision provides direct physical grounding, but relies on accurate pose estimation and human-to-robot correspondence. Human-video learning therefore yields a trade-off between stronger action grounding from explicit supervision and broader behavioral coverage from unlabeled videos.

Future observations provide a natural supervisory signal to bridge this gap as every video records the consequences that follow a behavior, regardless of embodiment. Predictive world models (Agarwal et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2024; Assran et al., 2025) and foresight-based VLAs (Zhang et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026a; Cai et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026c) exploit this signal by forecasting future pixels, visual features, or trajectories, providing a direct account of what changes in the world. However, inferring the intermediate dynamics that result in these changes remains challenging, particularly from large-scale human videos without action annotations. Recent reasoning-augmented VLAs offer a useful perspective by introducing intermediate tokens, such as textual plans (Zawalski et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2026b), visual guidance (Lee et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2026), continuous latents (Huang et al., 2026a), or coarse action trajectories (Zhong et al., 2026), to structure action generation. This raises a natural question of whether such intermediate representations can instead be grounded in the dynamics they induce in the world, providing a shared action interface across embodiments.

Motivated by this perspective, we introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that formulates action thoughts as Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD) and reinforces them through world imagination. CoD represents an action as a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures how the world evolves over time, providing a common reasoning interface across human and robot behaviors. We first initialize this space with action-labeled demonstrations, grounding CoD in physically meaningful behavior. ThinkWorld then predicts the future world representation induced by each CoD and compares it with the future observation, using their alignment to reinforce action reasoning. As a result, videos even without motion annotations provide a learning signal, allowing large-scale human videos and robot trajectories to jointly refine the same CoD space. This training objective propagates through the shared VLM, enriching the representations for action prediction with knowledge of how motion transforms the world. Across simulation benchmarks and real-robot evaluations, we demonstrate that ThinkWorld enables human-to-robot skill composition and generalization to unseen scenarios.

Our contributions are as follows:

We introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that couples a common VLM-native action-reasoning interface for both human and robot with internal world imagination.

We propose consequence-grounded reinforcement learning, which rewards CoD according to its consistency with observed future consequences and thereby enables action reasoning to improve from videos without action labels.

We show that ThinkWorld benefits from scaling action-unlabeled human video and enables human-to-robot skill transfer, allowing robots to execute complete tasks demonstrated in human videos while receiving robot supervision only for the constituent atomic skills.

1. We introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that couples a common VLM-native action-reasoning interface for both human and robot with internal world imagination.

2. We propose consequence-grounded reinforcement learning, which rewards CoD according to its consistency with observed future consequences and thereby enables action reasoning to improve from videos without action labels.

3. We show that ThinkWorld benefits from scaling action-unlabeled human video and enables human-to-robot skill transfer, allowing robots to execute complete tasks demonstrated in human videos while receiving robot supervision only for the constituent atomic skills.

title: Pushing Dexterity and Safety for In-Hand Object Pose Reaching That Works Remarkably Well
authors: Ian Chuang,Hiya Shah,Vamsi Chilamkur,Iman Soltani,Claire Tomlin
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands is the next frontier of robotics, yet learned hand skills remain limited to simple grasps or basic repeated motions, such as rotating an object. As robots attempt more demanding in-hand maneuvers, safety, such as not dropping the object, becomes critical, yet it is rarely measured. We study in-hand object pose reaching, a task that demands diverse and difficult grasps: moving an object to almost any position and orientation within reach of the fingers, at any wrist orientation, through long sequences of consecutive goals. We present a recipe for training such policies for a LEAP hand in simulation without human data, built on a range of insights, from diverse resets and goals via generated grasp datasets to an adaptive friction curriculum. With careful system identification, the policies transfer zero-shot to the real hand, using either motion capture or a single wrist-mounted depth camera, and prove remarkably capable and robust. On top of the task policy, we add a learned residual safety filter with adjustable conservativeness, letting us tune the balance between performance and safety and greatly reduce object drops. In 13.3 hours of real-robot evaluation over 4,800 unseen goals across 4 objects and diverse wrist orientations, the state-based policy reaches 95.2 % of goals within 2 cm and 0.4 rad, and the filter cuts its drops by 75 % while still reaching 91.5 % of goals. The policies can also spin a lightbulb held in an arbitrary pose, reach out-of-distribution goals, withstand fast arm motion and perturbations, and, needing only a wrist camera, serve as portable skills such as screwing in a lightbulb. We release the full recipe as a platform for studying performance, reliability, and safety in high-dimensional dexterous systems. Videos and more are available at https://ian-chuang.github.io/dexsafe/.
introduction:
Multi-fingered robot hands promise human-like dexterity, but these high-dimensional, contact-rich systems are very difficult to control and leave little margin for error. Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) and imitation learning have produced increasingly capable hand controllers, for in-hand reorientation, grasping and everyday manipulation tasks [1, 2, 3, 4]. Yet the current landscape of in-hand skills remains narrow. Most systems operate at a single wrist orientation, often palm up, where the palm supports the object from below, and perform simple, repetitive motions such as object rotation [5, 6, 7]. Many of these works also report performance only over short, limited trials and treat reliability and safety as an afterthought, handled implicitly, e.g., through reward shaping, or not at all. Human in-hand dexterity is far broader: a person can move an object into a difficult grasp at almost any position and orientation in the hand, through diverse finger and wrist motions, and rarely drop it. Achieving such grasps reliably over long sequences of goals remains an open challenge. As robots move outside the lab, where objects can be fragile or hazardous, reliability (how long the system runs without failing), safety (how often it violates a constraint, such as dropping the object) and robustness (to different wrist orientations, scenes and external disturbances) matter as much as success rate. How far a dexterous system can be pushed while staying safe therefore becomes a central question.

To study this question, we consider in-hand object pose reaching: moving an object to any position and orientation relative to the hand, at any wrist orientation, over long sequences of consecutive goals (Fig. ). Beyond rotation or reorientation [1, 5, 8], the task demands precise translation, so the hand must often hold the object at the tip of its fingers, in hard-to-reach positions and without the palm to support it. Its difficulty makes the task both a frontier for sim-to-real dexterity and a natural testbed for pushing performance and safety together.

We share a complete recipe for training a pose-reaching policy in simulation and transferring it zero-shot to a 16-DoF LEAP hand [9]: goals and initial states drawn from large generated grasp datasets, an adaptive friction curriculum, a simple reward of a few dense goal-reaching terms and regularizers, careful system identification of the actuators [10], and teacher–student distillation into policies that track the object with either motion capture (the state policy) or only a wrist-mounted stereo depth camera (the depth policy). To improve the policy’s safety, we train a residual safety filter, adapted from ResSafe [11], that sits on top of the frozen policy and corrects its actions to keep the hand from dropping the object. It trains in a few hours, and a single dial, the correction weight ww, makes it easy to tune how conservative it is at deployment.

We evaluate the system extensively on a real robot hand: 13.3 hours of robot run time over 4,800 unseen, randomly drawn goals, four objects, some of highly nonconvex shape (a knife, a wineglass, a lightbulb and a rubber duck), and six wrist orientations, with and without the safety filter. The state policy reaches 95.2 % of goals within 2 cm and 0.4 rad, and the filter cuts its drops by 75 % (from 16 to 4) while still reaching 91.5% of goals. Using only the wrist camera, the depth policy still reaches 72 % of goals (95 % and 88 % on the lightbulb and rubber duck), and the filter nearly halves its drops (from 88 to 46). In further experiments, the system reaches out-of-distribution goals, spins a lightbulb held in difficult poses, withstands fast arm motion and physical perturbations, and, since the depth policy needs no external cameras or motion capture, it can easily be deployed with a robot arm as a skill for multi-step tasks, such as screwing in a lightbulb until it lights up, or picking up and reorienting objects.

In summary, our contributions are:

A sim-to-real recipe for robust in-hand object pose reaching with a LEAP hand at any wrist orientation, trained without human data, including a novel adaptive friction curriculum. We ablate the main design choices and will release the code and trained checkpoints.

An adaptation of the learned residual safety filter ResSafe [11] to dexterous manipulation, as a simple add-on for learning safety in high-dimensional systems that is quick to train and easy to tune, balancing safety and performance.

An extensive real-robot evaluation of performance and safety: 13.3 hours of robot run time and 4,800 unseen goals, in which our state policy achieves 95.2 % of goals and the safety filter cuts its drops by 75 %, and further experiments that stress-test our system with difficult goals and external disturbances and showcase its use as a skill in dexterous arm-and-hand tasks.

1. A sim-to-real recipe for robust in-hand object pose reaching with a LEAP hand at any wrist orientation, trained without human data, including a novel adaptive friction curriculum. We ablate the main design choices and will release the code and trained checkpoints.

2. An adaptation of the learned residual safety filter ResSafe [11] to dexterous manipulation, as a simple add-on for learning safety in high-dimensional systems that is quick to train and easy to tune, balancing safety and performance.

3. An extensive real-robot evaluation of performance and safety: 13.3 hours of robot run time and 4,800 unseen goals, in which our state policy achieves 95.2 % of goals and the safety filter cuts its drops by 75 %, and further experiments that stress-test our system with difficult goals and external disturbances and showcase its use as a skill in dexterous arm-and-hand tasks.

title: RESPLE2: Inertial-Informed Recursive Non-Uniform Spline Estimation for Multi-Sensor Odometry with Global Refinement
authors: Ziyu Cao,William Talbot,Song Li,Pakpong Chirarattananon,Fredrik Gustafsson,Marco Hutter,Kailai Li
abstract: We present RESPLE2, a recursive multi-sensor state estimation framework using non-uniform B-splines for 6-DoF motion representation. By exploiting the knot-clamping boundary property, we propose a theoretically grounded mechanism for exact control-point prediction directly informed by inertial kinematics along the trajectory, with knot placement adapted to motion and measurement availability. Within an iterated extended Kalman filter, we perform this prediction using a subset of inertial measurements. A subsequent reset step preserves trajectory consistency as the knots extend. The update step further incorporates heterogeneous sensor measurements at their native timestamps through continuous-time observation models, supporting flexible combinations of LiDARs, cameras, inertial measurement units, and leg kinematics. We further develop a lightweight global optimization module that directly refines non-uniform B-spline control points by incorporating loop-closure constraints derived from LiDAR-visual cues. We conduct extensive evaluations on public and experimental datasets across handheld, tracked, legged, and hybrid aerial-legged platforms, covering highly dynamic maneuvers with extreme accelerations. Compared with state-of-the-art multi-sensor odometry systems, RESPLE2 achieves competitive or superior estimation accuracy and robustness in the corresponding sensor configurations, particularly under aggressive motion, while maintaining real-time operation. We publicly release our code and experimental datasets at https://github.com/ASIG-X/RESPLE2.
introduction:
Recent advances in high-performance sensing and actuation technologies have enabled mobile robots to operate in increasingly diverse and challenging environments. Emerging platforms, including legged and hybrid locomotion systems equipped with multimodal sensors [26, 22], have been developed for demanding applications spanning search and rescue, logistics, healthcare, entertainment, household assistance, in situ forestry, and environmental monitoring [25, 18, 35, 3, 41].

Accurate and robust six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) egomotion estimation is essential for high-performance autonomy in these emerging scenarios. Odometry systems using cameras and inertial measurement units (IMUs) are well established [33]. Light detection and ranging (LiDAR) sensors complement cameras by providing accurate, illumination-invariant geometric observations over long ranges and across a wide field of view (FoV), motivating configurations such as LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO), LiDAR-visual-inertial odometry (LVIO), and LIO augmented with leg kinematics (LKIO) [45, 20, 2, 31]. Fusing these complementary measurements mitigates modality-specific degradation, improves estimation accuracy and robustness, and enables more informative scene maps. Nevertheless, aggressive platform dynamics, unstructured environments, and limited onboard computational resources continue to challenge reliable egomotion estimation [10, 30]. Beyond these operational challenges, most existing odometry systems remain sensor-specific and standalone, with limited extensibility to new modalities. Furthermore, they have been validated primarily on conventional aerial and wheeled platforms rather than on emerging embodiments deployed in demanding real-world mobile scenarios, such as highly dynamic (loco)motion and complex terrain interaction [22, 48].

Conventional multi-sensor estimation methods represent dynamic motion in discrete time and use recursive filtering or nonlinear sliding-window optimization, with motion states associated with specific timestamps at fixed frame rates. During online estimation, asynchronous sensor measurements are typically approximated, e.g., through temporal interpolation [33, 29]. This paradigm often scales poorly as sensor rates and the number of sensors vary, particularly when changing sensors without synchronized triggering. Moreover, measurements from many exteroceptive sensors, such as LiDARs and rolling-shutter cameras, exhibit motion distortion during agile maneuvers and require explicit modeling or compensation for undistortion in state estimation. These design choices can compromise the spatiotemporal fidelity of raw observations and alter underlying noise characteristics, potentially degrading estimation accuracy and robustness while increasing both methodological and engineering complexity [17, 45].

Continuous-time motion representations decouple the number and temporal placement of estimates from observations, facilitating the integration of asynchronous multi-sensor readings at their native timestamps without complicating system design. Piecewise-linear models show promise for LiDAR-only odometry, e.g., Traj-LO [53], due to simplicity and computational efficiency, but may inadequately capture nonlinear motion during rapid or aggressive maneuvers. A more advanced, well-studied approach uses exactly sparse temporal Gaussian processes (GPs), in which system dynamics are modeled as a Markovian LTV-SDE process, such as white-noise-on-acceleration (WNOA) or white-noise-on-jerk (WNOJ) [40, 27, 36, 14, 4]. B-splines, often cubic, represent 66-DoF motion as piecewise polynomial functions, with each segment defined by a local set of control points blended according to a sequence of chosen scalar times called knots of typically uniform intervals [28, 8, 16].

Most existing online continuous-time estimators solve maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) or maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation problems in a sliding-window fashion [13, 28, 16, 17]. Although these optimization-based methods generally achieve high accuracy and improve robustness to sensor degeneracy, their real-time deployment is challenging and often requires carefully designed solvers, which complicates the integration of additional sensor modalities.

Recursive Bayesian estimators, such as the extended Kalman filter (EKF), offer a methodologically lightweight alternative; however, they remain scarce and underexplored in continuous-time multi-sensor odometry systems and are restricted to a narrow, fixed set of sensor configurations. For example, CTE-MLO performs recursive estimation using a GP-based continuous-time representation for LiDAR-only odometry [36]. RESPLE is the first 66-DoF B-spline-based recursive motion estimator, supporting both LiDAR-only and LiDAR-inertial odometry [8]. But its uniform knot spacing imposes a globally fixed temporal knot interval, where accurate control-point estimation requires knot intervals to be short enough for the polynomial to capture aggressive motions, yet long enough to include sufficient sensor measurements to constrain all degrees of freedom at each update, increasing susceptibility to geometric degeneracy. It is therefore theorized that well-chosen, non-uniform knots can bring both accuracy and computational benefits [39, 16]. Despite preliminary efforts to develop non-uniform B-spline LVIO using sliding-window optimization [16], the broader methodological and practical potential of this motion-adaptive representation remains underexplored.

More fundamentally, despite its growing adoption in practical systems, the theoretical formulation of B-spline-based odometry systems remains incomplete. Regardless of whether estimation uses filtering or sliding-window optimization, or whether knot spacing is uniform or non-uniform, B-spline control points do not lie on the motion trajectory in general. Consequently, existing theory has not established exact kinematic models for the states (i.e., the control points) analogous to those used in discrete-time or GP-based continuous-time approaches. As a result, new control points have not been predicted or initialized along the trajectory by directly integrating kinematic information, such as IMU measurements. Furthermore, no existing non-uniform B-spline-based odometry system natively supports loop closure for global refinement.

To address these methodological and engineering limitations, we present RESPLE2, a novel recursive Bayesian estimation framework that represents continuous-time 6-DoF motion using non-uniform B-splines within an iterated extended Kalman filter (IEKF). Unlike existing B-spline-based estimators, our framework introduces a inertial-informed process model to guarantee exact prediction of control points located on the motion trajectory. Moreover, RESPLE2 enables a versatile estimation framework supporting a configurable fusion of LiDAR, camera, IMU, and leg joint measurements. Extensive real-world validation spans generic mobile platforms and, particularly, emerging robotic embodiments. More specifically, our key contributions are summarized below.

We propose the first recursive continuous-time estimator using non-uniform B-splines for multi-sensor odometry. Using the knot-clamping boundary property, the framework enables exact prediction of control points on the motion trajectory directly informed by inertial measurements and supports efficient and versatile multi-sensor fusion.

We propose the first recursive continuous-time estimator using non-uniform B-splines for multi-sensor odometry. Using the knot-clamping boundary property, the framework enables exact prediction of control points on the motion trajectory directly informed by inertial measurements and supports efficient and versatile multi-sensor fusion.

A lightweight optimization module is additionally developed for direct global refinement of non-uniform control points for correcting drifts at loop closures detected by LiDAR-visual cues, while preserving the local kinematic consistency of the continuous-time trajectory.

The framework enables diverse multi-sensor odometry systems, including LO, LIO, LVIO, LKIO, and LKVIO, within a unified design. We conduct extensive evaluations on legged, tracked vehicle, and hybrid legged-quadcopter platforms under challenging real-world conditions, including aggressive motion and exteroceptive degradation. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, RESPLE2 achieves comparable or superior odometry robustness and accuracy in real time and supports optional global refinement.

We publicly release the full system implementation and the experimental datasets.

title: EgoThumb: A Vision-Driven Supernumerary Robotic Thumb for Autonomous Grasp and Holding Assistance
authors: Jianyu Hou,Jiawei Fu,Weikang Wan,Minghui Jiang,Jiajun Li,Hao Su
comment: . Accepted to the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
abstract:
Supernumerary robotic fingers augment human dexterity by enabling a single hand to perform complex “hold-and-manipulate” tasks that typically require bimanual coordination.
However, existing devices are often hindered by bulky hardware that limits interaction to large objects and rely on explicit hand motion triggers that lack environmental context.
To address these challenges, we present EgoThumb, a fully open-source, vision-driven supernumerary robotic thumb.
EgoThumb features a compact, dual tendon-driven finger whose actuation is relocated to the forearm, reducing distal weight while enabling precise active joint control.
The system utilizes a visual imitation learning policy that maps egocentric images from a palm-facing camera directly to continuous joint positions.
By implicitly decoding human intent from visual cues capturing both the hand and the object of interest, EgoThumb achieves robust autonomous manipulation and strong generalization across diverse users and environments.
All hardware designs and software implementations are fully open-sourced at https://ego-thumb.github.io.
introduction:
The enhancement of human physical capabilities through robotic systems has long been a central goal of robotics research.
Existing literature in this domain typically falls into three branches: exoskeletons, prostheses, and supernumerary limbs.
Exoskeletons attach motors to human joints to improve existing capabilities, such as playing instruments [11] and walking [1].
Prosthetic devices replace missing limbs to restore lost functions, including hand manipulation [13] and locomotion [23].
In contrast, supernumerary robotic (SR) limbs attach additional robotic arms and grippers to the human body to augment functional capacity [26].
For instance, body-mounted robotic arms can support heavy loads during overhead assembly tasks [27].

While much of this prior work focuses on proximal limb augmentation, there is growing interest in mounting robotic fingers directly onto the hand or forearm to extend the degrees of freedom of the human hand [31].
These additional digits can actively collaborate with biological fingers, enabling a single hand to perform tasks that typically require bimanual coordination.
They have been explored across contexts ranging from assistive and therapeutic use for motor impairments [25] to able-bodied augmentation for skilled tasks [7].
Specifically, we focus on “hold-and-manipulate” tasks [32], where the SR finger must: 1) autonomously decide when to grasp and release an object, and 2) stably hold the object while the human hand interacts with it.

Despite their potential, existing SR fingers face two key limitations. First, their bulky hardware [34, 25, 10] suits large objects but hinders interaction with the smaller, everyday objects central to daily manipulation, such as the teacup in Fig. .2 (Stir Tea). Second, they are typically driven by teleoperation [20, 5] or low-dimensional hand-motion triggers [34, 32], which lack the autonomy and environmental awareness needed to infer intent from context, such as grasping the bottle in Fig. .2 (Unscrew Cap) as the hand approaches, without an explicit trigger motion.

To address these limitations, we present EgoThumb, a fully open-source, vision-driven supernumerary robotic thumb system.
EgoThumb actively perceives hand motion and the environment through vision to autonomously determine the optimal timing for grasping, holding, and releasing objects.
The key contributions of our work are as follows:

Hardware Design: Our system utilizes a dual-tendon actuation strategy for each joint, enabling active control of both flexion and extension to ensure precise position control.
Thus, the actuators are located on the forearm, resulting in a lightweight, wearable finger design.

Egocentric Perception: To achieve autonomous control with environmental awareness, we integrate a palm-facing camera that captures the egocentric visual context of both the hand motion and the surroundings.

Intelligent Autonomy: We formulate the control problem as a visual imitation learning task, training a policy to map egocentric images directly to joint positions.

Through these hardware and algorithmic advancements, EgoThumb achieves robust performance across four distinct real-world tasks without explicitly measuring hand motion.
It also demonstrates strong generalization capabilities across different users and varied environmental backgrounds.

1. Hardware Design: Our system utilizes a dual-tendon actuation strategy for each joint, enabling active control of both flexion and extension to ensure precise position control.
Thus, the actuators are located on the forearm, resulting in a lightweight, wearable finger design.

2. Egocentric Perception: To achieve autonomous control with environmental awareness, we integrate a palm-facing camera that captures the egocentric visual context of both the hand motion and the surroundings.

3. Intelligent Autonomy: We formulate the control problem as a visual imitation learning task, training a policy to map egocentric images directly to joint positions.

title: Learning Visuomotor Quadrotor Flight Through Dynamic Narrow Gaps via Differentiable Simulation
authors: Riccardo Bianco,Yunfan Ren,Jiaxu Xing,Davide Scaramuzza
abstract:
Threading a quadrotor through a moving narrow gap is a demanding test of agile flight, requiring centimeter-level spatial alignment and precise temporal execution.
We address this challenge using a control policy that operates directly on onboard visual and inertial measurements to output collective thrust and body-rate commands.
The task is difficult because success lies on a thin feasible manifold: small errors in timing, position, attitude, or visual observability cause collision.
Prior planning and learning methods rely on privileged state, teachers, planners, or distillation; learning dynamic narrow-gap traversal directly, from scratch, remains open.
We introduce a differentiable moving-gap formulation that gates centering, alignment, and smooth collision terms by signed distance to a time-varying gap plane, turning a sparse traversal event into a dense pathwise objective.
We integrate this formulation into a visual-feature-to-command policy trained in one stage from random initialization, without a teacher, planner, or distillation.
We validate our approach in both synthetic and real-world experiments.
In controlled benchmarks, we demonstrate that pathwise gradients significantly outperform score-function gradients for precision-critical tasks, yielding a 99.3%99.3\% success rate in simulation after only a few minutes of training on a single GPU.
Furthermore, the policy transfers directly to a real quadrotor, successfully crossing a dynamic narrow gap from varied initial conditions using onboard sensing and inertial measurements, achieving an 80%80\% success rate over 10 physical trials.



 Video: https://youtu.be/z-txORkhnrg


 Code: https://github.com/uzh-rpg/agile_narrow_gap_diffsim
introduction:
Agile quadrotors can move quickly through confined spaces, but useful motion is often constrained by windows, frames, shelves, machinery, debris, and other structures that leave only narrow passages.
Narrow-gap traversal is therefore a representative primitive for agile flight, requiring the vehicle to coordinate speed with whole-body geometric precision.
Dynamic gaps make the primitive harder: the quadrotor must fit through the aperture and arrive when it is traversable.
We study the onboard visual-inertial version of this problem, learning policies that use vision and inertial measurements to output collective-thrust-and-body-rate (CTBR) commands for static and moving gap traversal.

This setting combines thin spatio-temporal feasibility, partial onboard observations near crossing, and aggressive low-level control.
Prior work has made strong progress on agile quadrotor planning and narrow-gap traversal through model-based trajectory optimization [3, 11, 22, 4, 31, 17], learning-based control [10, 27, 26, 12, 6, 25], and differentiable simulation [23, 5, 34, 32].
Yet most of these methods rely on static apertures, privileged geometry, or teacher/planner pipelines.
This leaves open whether precision-critical moving-gap traversal can be learned end-to-end from random initialization, without a planner, teacher, or distillation.
A moving aperture changes the problem qualitatively: the policy must decide not only how to cross, but also when to commit to the crossing.

We argue that a central bottleneck is the quality of the learning signal.
Model-free RL methods such as PPO [19] estimate score-function (SF) gradients by treating the simulator as a black box, which can be too noisy on thin-manifold tasks.
Pathwise (PW) gradients differentiate through closed-loop rollouts [7, 14], but can become unreliable under stiffness, discontinuities, contacts, or chaotic dynamics [15, 21, 13].
Our key observation is that narrow-gap flight is unforgiving but still smooth: with differentiable quadrotor dynamics and smooth task costs, even failed rollouts indicate how to adjust centering, attitude, and timing.

We build on this observation with a differentiable moving-gap formulation that gates centering, alignment, and smooth collision terms by signed distance to a time-varying gap plane.
Integrated into a visual-feature-to-CTBR policy trained in one stage from random initialization, this formulation turns a sparse traversal event into a dense pathwise objective.
The framework supports privileged-state and onboard visual-inertial observations and requires no demonstrations, trajectory labels, privileged teacher, planner, or distillation.

We validate our approach in simulation and real-world flight.
In simulation, policies train in 0.40.4–5.65.6 minutes on a single GPU and reach ≥98.9%\geq\!98.9\% success with centimeter-level crossing accuracy.
In matched 1,000-environment, five-seed state-task runs, tuned PPO used 19×19\times more transitions and 45.5×45.5\times more training time than BPTT on moving gaps when averaging its four converged seeds.
Controlled benchmarks show that PW optimization succeeds with a single rollout per update, whereas SF optimization fails even with one thousand times more samples.
Deployed in the real world, a 10×\times38  cm quadrotor traverses a 25×\times80  cm moving gap using onboard sensing and inertial measurements, achieving an 80% success rate over 10 trials.

Contributions:
In summary, the contributions of this work are:

We demonstrate precision-critical vision-based static and moving traversal can be learned end-to-end through differentiable simulation without demonstrations, a teacher, a planner, or distillation.

We release an open-source differentiable-simulation framework for learning observation-to-CTBR policies under both privileged-state and onboard visual-inertial observations, converging in minutes on a single GPU.

We show that pathwise gradients provide useful learning signals on thin-manifold tasks where score-function gradients fail even with orders of magnitude more samples.

We deploy the visual-inertial moving-gap policy on a real quadrotor, closing the loop from differentiable training to physical agile flight.

1. We demonstrate precision-critical vision-based static and moving traversal can be learned end-to-end through differentiable simulation without demonstrations, a teacher, a planner, or distillation.

2. We release an open-source differentiable-simulation framework for learning observation-to-CTBR policies under both privileged-state and onboard visual-inertial observations, converging in minutes on a single GPU.

3. We show that pathwise gradients provide useful learning signals on thin-manifold tasks where score-function gradients fail even with orders of magnitude more samples.

4. We deploy the visual-inertial moving-gap policy on a real quadrotor, closing the loop from differentiable training to physical agile flight.

title: Kinematic Constraint-Referenced Evaluation for Articulated Object Manipulation
authors: Baptiste Bonin,Caro Strickland,Audrey Durand
abstract:
Manipulation policies are evaluated predominantly by binary task success, which cannot tell whether the commanded gesture is the one the object’s
kinematics admit. We introduce Constraint-Referenced Strategy (CRS), which projects the commanded end-effector twist onto the object’s joint axis,
separating progress along the joint from off-constraint waste. CRS requires a joint model and a joint-following scripted controller derived from it, but no recorded demonstration or learned judge. On 74 simulated articulated objects, success registers three transfer failures as lower rates but attributes none, while the two CRS channels give each a distinct signature.
A door-trained behavior-cloning policy opens drawers in 59 of 110 episodes, and in these passes it commands about 40×40\times the off-axis rotation of a
drawer-trained policy’s passes (1.271.27 vs. 0.0320.032 rad/s). Relative to a scripted controller scored with the same axis, CRS verdicts are unchanged
under joint-axis errors up to 30∘30^{\circ}; absolute thresholds tolerate about 8∘8^{\circ}.
introduction:
Manipulation policies are evaluated predominantly by binary task success [8, 6]. Success aggregates perception, grasping, execution, and strategy into a single bit, so two policies can fail for different reasons and obtain the same score (0). Success can also mislead, reporting a healthy-looking score (1) while the commanded gesture is wrong. For example, a behavior-cloning policy trained on doors opens held-out drawers in more than half of its episodes with the arcing gesture typical of doors, a rotation the drawer’s joint does not admit, and success scores each of these episodes as a pass. A good evaluation should measure the commanded gesture against the target’s kinematics.

Richer evaluation metrics exist, but most require additional information: demonstration-referenced distances need a recording on each object [5], subgoal scoring needs stages defined per task [2], and learned evaluators need a trained judge [1]. Across the dozens of tasks and objects a benchmark covers, this cost adds up. MetaFine [9], does evaluate the gesture, not only the outcome: it composes tasks from atomic skills whose checks reference the object’s geometry (a rotation passes only about the prescribed axis) and scores behavior by per-stage success and trajectory stability of the commanded actions. Two gaps remain, its geometry checks are pass/fail at a skill-specific tolerance, and its stability score, though task-independent and computed on the command, has no model of the object. Neither returns a graded, signed reading of how much of a command advances the joint and how much fights it. This reading must come from the command: on an articulated part, realized motion is admissible by construction, since a drawer can only slide along its rail, so off-constraint behavior leaves no trace in the part’s motion, only in the command and the constraint forces.

To provide this reading and complement [9], we introduce Constraint-Referenced Strategy (CRS), which uses the kinematics of the task as the reference. CRS is based on the idea that, under a rigid grasp, the articulated joint of an object defines exactly which end-effector motions advance it [7]. One screw axis encodes every valid opening mode. The reference is therefore mode invariant and needs no recorded
demonstration or learned action model. CRS scores a policy at reference states by projecting the commanded twist onto the joint’s axis, yielding a signature with two channels: commanded progress along the joint and
off-constraint waste (Figure 1).
Our experiments show clear benefits of CRS against a binary success evaluation (Figure 1 and Table 1).

title: When, Where, and What to Correct: Human-Guided Adaptive Residual Correction for Robot Policies
authors: Anukriti Singh,Maxime Caniot,Pratap Tokekar,Firas Abi-Farraj
abstract:
Imitation policies that reliably execute most of a manipulation trajectory can
still fail in localized regions requiring last-mile precision. Updating the full
policy or exploring residual actions everywhere treats this local failure as a
global learning problem. We introduce Adaptive Residual Correction
(ARC), a lightweight post-training module that uses reinforcement learning
(RL) to learn a residual correction on top of a frozen policy while using sparse
human corrections to structure autonomous exploration. Rather than treating
human corrections as imitation targets, ARC uses pre-intervention states to
determine when residual control should become active and correction
geometry to determine where in residual action space autonomous
refinement should explore; task reward determines what residual is
ultimately executed. Across three precision-manipulation tasks on a real robot,
ARC improves average task success from 33.3%33.3\% to 75.0%75.0\%. The human
corrections define task-dependent 2–3-dimensional subspaces of the seven-joint
residual space that retain 96.096.0–97.7%97.7\% of squared correction magnitude.
Together, these results show that sparse human corrections can localize and
constrain autonomous post-training without requiring the observed correction
itself to serve as the final action target
(link).
introduction:
Modern imitation-learning policies can acquire broad manipulation competence
from demonstrations, including complex closed-loop visuomotor behaviors
[14, 3].
Yet even a policy that reliably reaches the relevant interaction can remain
brittle to small execution errors and distribution shift, particularly when
success depends on a short precision-critical segment of the task
[14, 2]. In this
regime, collecting substantially more demonstrations or post-training the
entire policy treats a localized failure as a global learning problem. Residual
learning instead keeps the base policy fixed and learns only the additional
control required to correct its remaining failures
[2, 13, 1, 6].

Residual learning is most useful when the correction itself is similarly
targeted. Acting throughout the trajectory can degrade behavior the base policy
already performs well, while arbitrary action-space exploration wastes
interaction on unlikely motions. Sparse human corrections provide structure
for both problems. During an otherwise autonomous rollout, the human intervenes
only when needed by adding a residual adjustment to the base-policy action; we
refer to these intermittent adjustments as human corrections.
Human-in-the-loop methods show that sparse interventions can efficiently guide
policy improvement [8, 15], while intervention
timing itself carries information beyond the corrective trajectory
[12]. At autonomous deployment, no human is present:
the residual policy must recognize robot-controlled states in which a human
would soon have corrected, rather than states already altered by a
correction. Likewise, the coordinated multi-joint geometry of the correction
reveals which residual directions the human actually uses. Together, these
signals localize the temporal and action-space support in which residual
learning should operate.

The human correction itself, however, need not be the final action an
autonomous policy should reproduce. Recent methods use corrective actions
directly, or through latent representations, as supervision for learned
steering policies [9, 7], but a correction
is chosen to recover from the particular state encountered during intervention,
and directly imitating it does not encode whether its downstream consequence
leads to task success [15]. For example, a locally sensible
placement correction may still disturb another object and cause the task to
fail.

This distinction motivates Adaptive Residual Correction (ARC), a
lightweight plug-in module for improving a frozen base policy. During
otherwise autonomous rollouts, the human provides sparse residual corrections
only when needed. From approximately 8–10 such rollouts per task, ARC learns a
pre-intervention gate identifying WHEN residual control should become
active and a low-dimensional basis of the seven-joint residual action space
restricting WHERE autonomous refinement searches. These correction
rollouts are used only to learn the gate and corrective basis and are not added
to the RL replay buffer. ARC then collects separate autonomous experience
within this learned temporal and action-space support, and reinforcement
learning determines WHAT correction improves task outcome. The base
policy remains frozen and its original demonstrations are not revisited.

Relative to residual-RL methods
[2, 13, 1, 6], ARC restricts both
when the residual is active and where exploration occurs; relative to
correction-supervised methods [9, 7], it
uses human residuals to define the support of autonomous learning rather than
as targets for the final residual actor.

We evaluate ARC on three precision-manipulation tasks on a real robot:
aligning and stacking industrial trays, inserting a marker into a narrow groove,
and stacking cups into a fixed receiver. After two autonomous
collect–reward–update rounds, ARC improves average task success from 33.3%33.3\%
to 75.0%75.0\%. Experiments further show that pre-intervention states yield a gate
that transfers to autonomous execution, human residuals define stable
low-dimensional corrective supports, and directly predicting the human
correction produces residual behavior different from reward-driven ARC even
when supervision is restricted to the same corrective subspace.

title: Rendering-Free Event Frame Simulation for Fast Reinforcement Learning of Autonomous Robot Navigation
authors: Dequan Ou,Austin Lopez,Quentin Missinne,Christophe De Wagter,Guido C.H.E. de Croon
abstract: Event cameras offer low latency, high dynamic range, and milliwatt-level power consumption, making them ideal for agile robots such as tiny drones navigating through cluttered environments. However, existing simulators generally render photorealistic images before converting them into events, making large-scale reinforcement learning prohibitively slow. We propose an analytic event simulator that exploits what event cameras fundamentally measure—moving contrast edges—to synthesize event streams directly from scene geometry and ego-motion without visual rendering. Our simulator generates a 64×6464{\times}64 event observation in 17​μ17\,\mus on a single GPU—over 400×400\times faster than a state-of-the-art rendering pipeline—enabling end-to-end reinforcement learning for goal-directed obstacle avoidance to converge in under 30 minutes—three orders of magnitude faster than training on rendered events. Policies transfer zero-shot to physically based event simulations (ray-traced Isaac Sim). Our policy reaches 83% success in cluttered courses unseen during training (mid-difficulty traversability, Pτ≈0.57P_{\tau}\approx 0.57), at 2.4 m/s average goal velocity, and retains 70% in a simulated texture-dense indoor hall. Furthermore, we quantized the policy to a 1.2 MB int8 network running fully onboard a 56-gram Crazyflie equipped with a Prophesee GenX320 event camera and an OpenMV N6 microcontroller board. Without any fine-tuning, external processing, or positioning, the policy achieves an average success rate of 82% (5/5, 5/6, 4/6 flights) across three real-world obstacle courses of increasing difficulty. Code: https://github.com/tudelft/rendering-free-event-nav
introduction:
Flying robots such as tiny drones are attractive for search-and-rescue, inspection, and monitoring in confined, GPS-denied spaces, yet reliable autonomous navigation in such settings remains a fundamental challenge.
Conventional navigation stacks such as Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) [2] demand heavy sensing suites and power-hungry onboard computers that small platforms cannot carry.

Recently, an extremely lightweight approach to navigation, Bee-Nav, has been introduced that achieves long-range navigation with minimal sensing and compute [3]. But for obstacle avoidance, it still relies on depth sensing.
Stereo depth cameras such as the Intel RealSense D435i (72 g, ∼3.5{\sim}3.5 W) deliver dense, reliable range images and are routinely carried by drones in the 500–1000 g class—but the camera alone approaches a Crazyflie’s entire takeoff weight.
Multi-zone Time-of-Flight arrays, by contrast, are light enough for any nano-drone (sub-gram), yet resolve only 8×88{\times}8 zones—too coarse for thin wires, slender poles, or fine vegetative clutter.
On sub-100-gram nano-drones such as the Bitcraze Crazyflie, the Size, Weight, and Power envelope binds tighter still, bounding the entire sensing, processing, and carrier payload to a few dozen grams and roughly a watt.
This rules out not only dedicated depth cameras but also the embedded GPU computers on which conventional event-processing stacks rely (e.g., an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX module: ∼70{\sim}70–100 g, 10–25 W).
Clutter-resilient obstacle avoidance within this envelope requires rethinking the sensing paradigm.

Event cameras are biologically inspired sensors that have emerged as a compelling modality for autonomous robots [4].
Operating asynchronously at microsecond temporal resolution with high dynamic range (>120>120 dB) and milliwatt-level power consumption, these neuromorphic sensors capture logarithmic brightness changes with negligible motion blur.
These characteristics are particularly advantageous for agile drones, where aggressive rotational maneuvers and unpredictable lighting frequently defeat frame-based cameras.

Event-based obstacle avoidance has accordingly been explored through optical-flow pipelines [5] and direct end-to-end learning [6] (Sec. II).
Training robust visuomotor policies with reinforcement learning (RL), however, remains fundamentally bottlenecked by event simulation: standard simulators synthesize events by interpolating pixel intensities across high-frame-rate rendered image sequences [7, 8], and even recent GPU-accelerated renderers [1] throttle the millions of closed-loop environment transitions that end-to-end RL demands.

In this work, we propose an approach to sidestepping rendering entirely.
Observing that event cameras fundamentally respond to moving contrast edges, we propose an analytic event proxy that synthesizes event streams directly from scene geometry and ego-motion.
Event generation costs 17​μ17\,\mus per frame, and end-to-end RL for goal-directed obstacle avoidance converges in under 30 minutes.
The learned policy transfers zero-shot to a physically based event simulation (83% success in unseen cluttered rooms). Quantized to a 1.2 MB int8 network running fully onboard a 56-gram Crazyflie with a Prophesee GenX320 event camera, it further achieves 100%, 83%, and 67% success (5/5, 5/6, 4/6 flights) in three distinct, increasingly difficult real environments, with all sensing, processing, and state estimation onboard.

The main contributions of this work are:

an ultra-fast, rendering-free analytic event proxy for navigation tasks that trains avoidance policies three orders of magnitude faster than rendered-event pipelines;

a sim-to-sim-to-real transfer study showing that policies trained purely in the proxy transfer zero-shot to photorealistic Isaac Sim and to a real Prophesee GenX320;

the first fully onboard, event-driven goal-directed navigation on a 56-gram Crazyflie, with all perception and inference on a sub-watt microcontroller.

1. an ultra-fast, rendering-free analytic event proxy for navigation tasks that trains avoidance policies three orders of magnitude faster than rendered-event pipelines;

2. a sim-to-sim-to-real transfer study showing that policies trained purely in the proxy transfer zero-shot to photorealistic Isaac Sim and to a real Prophesee GenX320;

3. the first fully onboard, event-driven goal-directed navigation on a 56-gram Crazyflie, with all perception and inference on a sub-watt microcontroller.

title: Predict the Swing, Match the Speed: Robotic Pipe Stabbing With Learned Stereo Vision and Residual Reinforcement Learning
authors: Mohamed Ashraf Mostafa,Taher El-Fakharany,Samir Khaled
comment: . Submitted to Geoenergy Science and Engineering
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
A joint of pipe hanging from the elevator is a pendulum about 9.6 m long and up to 1.3 t heavy. Before it can be made up, its pin has to be brought to rest over a box held in the rotary, a target a few centimetres wide. On rigs without a stabbing robot this is done by a floorhand with a hand on the pipe, sometimes helped by a tagline or a passive stabbing guide. The moving pipe is a known hazard: in a U.S. Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement report, the bottom of a stand being stabbed whipped when the link tilt moved and fractured a floorhand’s fingertip [1]. It also wears equipment. A pin that strikes the box face can damage threads and seals, and a guide that the pipe hits at full swing speed takes a shock load.

Drill floor robots have been field-tested and are offered commercially [2, 3], and full robotic drill floors have been studied for land rigs and drillships [4]. Stabbing guides have been fitted to drill floor robots and robotic roughnecks [3, 5], and a remotely operated stabber has been used in completion operations [6]. In the systems we reviewed, the tool waits at well centre until the swinging pipe reaches it, so the first contact takes place at whatever speed the swing has at that instant. We are not aware of a published system that estimates the swing of the joint and plans the capture around it (Section 2).

StabBot instead watches the swing for 0.8 s, fits a pendulum model whose frequency comes from the pipe tally, shadows the predicted pipe and closes in along a minimum-jerk path [7] so that the guide head arrives moving with the pipe. The face rollers then sense contact, and the last millimetres are closed by touch. Once the pipe is held, the robot brings it to rest over the box. When the elevator hangs off centre, the hanging pipe is tilted, and the robot places the pin nose over the box instead of the pipe axis at head height. As the block slacks off, wrist admittance lets the taper finish the alignment.

The study addresses two questions. The first is whether a robot that knows where the pipe will be can stab it more reliably and more gently than one that waits. The second is how much each of the tools usually proposed for such a robot (a predictive controller, a learned perception model and a learned control correction) adds. Both are answered with one paired benchmark in which every method runs on the same 200 random jobs. The contributions of this work are as follows.

Swing-aware capture for hanging tubulars: a tally-tuned pendulum Kalman filter, velocity-matched capture, a force-confirmed final approach and tilt compensation for an off-centre elevator (Section 4).

One open guide head for nine sizes, 238\frac{3}{8}-in. tubing to 20-in. casing, on which the pipe touches only free rollers, with at least 20 mm clearance on every other part (Section 3).

A stereo keypoint network that locates the pipe, the pin nose and the box mouth in 3-D with sub-millimetre median error and runs in the control loop at 30 Hz.

A residual reinforcement-learning policy that lowers peak force by a further 22% relative to the model-based controller it corrects. A reward failure met during its development is reported with its fix.

A 200-job paired benchmark with robustness, unseen-condition and ablation tests. StabBot seats 100% of joints against 74% for a fixed guide, and its median contact speed and median peak force are both lower by a factor of 7.8 (Section 6).

title: Which Hand Was Late? Diagnosis for Robot Failure Recovery in Bimanual Tool Use
authors: Baptiste Bonin,Caro Strickland,Audrey Durand
abstract: Failure diagnosers for robot manipulation are increasingly vision–language models (VLMs), trained and evaluated on single-arm failures produced by perturbing a successful demonstration. Bimanual tool use adds failures of other kinds: a tool that slips out of its socket while still held, two correct gestures made at different times, and attempts that fail for two reasons at once. On a simulated bimanual tool-use task whose failure causes are read from the recorded trace, we measure what each sensing channel lets a diagnoser tell. The tool’s slip is read on the tool hand; which hand was late is read on both arms, while a sensor on one hand reads its own hand’s delay and at most part of the other’s; and whether a late attempt was also pushed too weakly is not identifiable from passive sensing when the tool hand is late. Within two attempts, a repair policy that escalates when the cause is not identifiable repairs as many failures as one told the true cause. A VLM’s internal state carries the late hand almost perfectly, along a direction no closer to the one its answer reads than a random one; whether the answer reports it depends on the wording of the question.
introduction:
Imitation learning and recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled impressive advances in robotic manipulation [5, 2] and with them the question of what a robot should do when an attempt fails. Deployed in an open world, a robot will encounter mechanisms it has never interacted with before [12], and it will inevitably fail on some of them. Some of what a mechanism requires can only be found out by trying: a robot that has never opened a stiff lock cannot know in advance how much force it requires. What matters is whether it can learn from the attempt. Failures can also occur on familiar tasks when the robot misestimates quantities that are not directly observable, such as the force required to push a locked door open or the timing of the other hand’s action. In either case, a failure is useful only if its cause can be identified: to recover from a failure and learn from it, a robot must detect it, attribute it to its cause, and act on that cause.

A growing body of work addresses this problem through visual failure reasoning by asking a vision–language model (VLM). AHA [3] takes an image sequence and returns a natural-language explanation of the failure; RoboFAC [8] evaluates detection, identification and localisation from video; ViFailback [14] turns the diagnosis into visual corrections for a policy; and ARMOR [9] jointly refines detection and open-ended reasoning. These systems address detection, did the attempt fail?, and diagnosis, why did it fail? Both are learned from failures of a particular kind: each involves one arm acting on one object, is produced by perturbing a successful demonstration, and has a cause that is visible in the scene.

Bimanual tool use breaks each of these assumptions. Consider unlocking a utility cabinet with a square key: one hand seats the key in the lock and turns it, while the other pushes the door. The attempt can fail because a gesture was wrong (the key was never seated), because the tool slipped out of its socket under torque while still firmly held, because the lock needed more force than was applied, or because both hands did the right thing at different times. The last case is not a mistake of either arm but a relation between them. For such a failure, “why did it fail?” becomes “which hand was late?”, a question no single-arm taxonomy can ask (Figure 1). In this paper, we ask:

What must a failure diagnoser observe to tell which hand caused a bimanual tool-use failure, and
do VLM diagnosers report it when they observe it?

To answer this, we need a task in which the cause of each failure is known without relying on an
annotator’s reading of the video. We build a bimanual, tool-mediated lock in simulation, inject one fault per attempt with a scripted controller, and read the class of every failure from the recorded trace of the mechanism. We then apply the same probe to one sensing channel at a time, and to the internal representation and the language output of the same VLM. We do not propose a new diagnoser, we instead measure what a diagnoser needs. Our contributions are the following:

A tool-use task with known failure causes (Sec. 3), where the cause of each failure can be recovered from the trace, including failures with multiple simultaneous causes.

What can be diagnosed, and from where (Sec. 4): the tool’s slip is read on the tool hand and which hand was late on both arms, while whether a late push was also too weak is on no passive sensor when the tool hand is late. Sensor placement determines which of these signals are available.

Diagnosis determines repair (Sec. 5): failures with two causes are repaired only when both causes are corrected. A policy that asks only whether the hands overlapped, applies the matching correction and, if it fails, both (escalation) repairs as many failures within two attempts as one told the true cause.

The model represents the late hand (Sec. 6): the VLM’s state encodes which hand was late, even though this information is not read out by its answer.

title: Leveraging Distributed Sensing and Hyperdimensional Computing for Non-Line-of-Sight Passive Object Sensing
authors: Placido Mursia,Marco Rossanese,Francesco Devoti,Adrian Lendinez Ibanez,Lanfranco Zanzi,Xi Li,Xavier Costa-Perez
comment: To appear in the Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC), 2026
abstract:
In smart factory environments, passive entities such as humans and movable obstacles may interfere with autonomous robot operations, posing significant safety risks. Detecting potential conflicts between robots and entities outside their field-of-view (FoV) is therefore of paramount importance. However, conventional passive object detection systems rely on sensors such as LiDAR, radar, or cameras, which operate under direct line-of-sight (LoS) and are limited by obstacles and occlusions.
To overcome these limitations, integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) enables environmental perception via the communication infrastructure thanks to cooperation among distributed wireless devices. In this paper, we propose a framework for passive entity sensing beyond the robot’s FoV that relies solely on distributed channel measurements from the communication infrastructure to perform risk-aware classification. These measurements are embedded into high-dimensional representations using hyperdimensional computing (HDC), enabling robust and scalable learning without explicit channel reconstruction. Numerical simulations based on a commercial ray tracer and ROS-based validation in realistic smart factory scenarios demonstrate improved safety and enhanced path planning with up to 89%\% accuracy under severe occlusions, while maintaining low computational complexity.
introduction:
Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) represents a paradigm shift in 6G wireless systems, inherently coupling communication and sensing [1]. It promises unprecedented gains in throughput and latency while integrating artificial intelligence (AI), 3D coverage, and turning the wireless infrastructure into a distributed environmental perception layer [2].

This is particularly relevant in dynamic industrial scenarios, where humans and autonomous robots move through shared spaces and risk collisions, injuries, and operational disruptions [3]. In such environments, detecting passive entities, such as humans, nomadic or stationary objects that are not connected to sensing or communication systems, is therefore crucial for safety and reliability. Traditional onboard sensing based solely on LiDAR or cameras on the robot is constrained by the direct line-of-sight (LoS) field-of-view (FoV) of the sensor, and further limited by occlusions, walls, sensing range, and computational capacity. In this context, ISAC allows robots to leverage the mobile network as an external perception layer [4], obtaining contextual information about their surroundings–including areas beyond their direct FoV–and enabling network-aided navigation and collision avoidance.

Despite recent advances enabled by 5G systems and higher carrier frequencies, sensing passive entities remains challenging. Radar-like methods process backscattered echoes for object detection and human motion tracking [5], but often require complex hardware and signal processing [6]. Lower-complexity alternatives exploit power measurements [7], received signal strength [8], or channel fluctuations [9] to infer environmental changes from communication signals.

Unlike existing ISAC approaches relying on static sensing nodes and operating mainly under LoS conditions, we propose cooperative passive sensing of regions outside the robot’s direct sensing visibility. Since passive objects located around corners or behind shelving structures may not generate observable signatures within the robot’s FoV, the proposed framework leverages spatially distributed channel measurements, thereby complementing conventional sensing modalities. We consider an indoor smart factory where humans and robots operate concurrently, and obstacles may be just behind or around corners, which are invisible to a robot’s onboard sensors, as depicted in Fig. 1. By leveraging the distributed wireless infrastructure as a collaborative perception layer, our approach infers environmental changes and provides preemptive information on unseen passive objects, which might impact its planned trajectory, enabling proactive route adaptation and enhanced safety.

To achieve this, we combine the spatial diversity obtained through coordinated distributed sensing with the hyperdimensional computing (HDC) paradigm, supporting efficient learning in complex environments through high-dimensional representations [10]. While HDC has shown promise in several domains (see, e.g., [11, 12]), its use in wireless sensing remains largely unexplored.
This work therefore provides four main contributions: c1) a cooperative infrastructure-assisted distributed ISAC framework for risk-aware sensing of passive entities beyond the robot sensing range, c2) a low-complexity non-line-of-sight (nLoS) sensing method based on channel measurements, c3) a robust and scalable HDC –based sensing scheme, and c4) validation through extensive ray-tracing and robot operating system (ROS)-based experiments, and running on typical robot microcontroller unit (MCU) hardware.

title: World Dreamer v5-lite: A Multi-Robot World Action Model with One Dreamer
authors: Guoning Wu,Zijian Cai,Yuhang Zhang,Ying Liu,Yongbin Zheng(World Agents)
comment: . Guoning Wu and Zijian Cai share first authorship. Yongbin Zheng is the corresponding author
abstract:
Multi-robot control requires integrating distributed camera views while predicting separate action sequences.
Most vision–language–action and world-action models target one robot.
Combining multiple views alone does not establish spatial correspondence between them.
World Dreamer v5-lite is a multi-robot world-action model built around a shared world state ϕ\boldsymbol{\phi} for robot-specific action prediction.
Calibrated features from a pretrained video encoder populate ϕ\boldsymbol{\phi} in workspace coordinates; its spatial size remains fixed as views are added.
A vision–language model provides scene context and one query per robot.
The queries read ϕ\boldsymbol{\phi} and exchange pose-aware information, while their action streams remain separate.
Masked-view cooperative training withholds selected camera views from both visual branches while retaining all action targets.
This encourages the use of observations shared by other robots.
Pretraining uses more than 10,00010{,}000 hours of trajectories from 20 simulated robot types, RoboFactory, and real robots.
On RoboFactory, World Dreamer v5-lite achieves 74.0%74.0\% mean success, 23.7 percentage points above the strongest evaluated baseline.
Across four real-robot tasks, it reaches 78.8%78.8\% mean success, a margin of 13.8 points.
It also reaches 58.08%58.08\% overall on RoboCasa365.
introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models adapt pretrained multimodal backbones to robot control [31, 11, 3, 2, 16], and world-action models further couple action prediction with predicted visual dynamics [7, 12, 30].
These models inherit semantic knowledge from vision–language pretraining and, in the case of world-action models, knowledge of how scenes evolve from video pretraining.
Most of these models predict actions for a single robot.

Many manipulation tasks instead require several robots to work in a shared workspace, for example, when one robot holds an object while another operates on it [18].
This setting differs from single-robot control in three respects.
First, observations are distributed: each robot typically carries its own cameras, which move with it and capture only part of the workspace, and image patches from different cameras do not correspond to the same physical locations.
Second, control is separate while decisions are coupled: the robots may differ in embodiment and action space, yet the action of each robot depends on where the other robots are and what they are doing.
Third, observations are often incomplete: the camera of one robot may be occluded by another robot or by the manipulated object, so a robot must sometimes act on what other cameras observe.

Extending single-robot models to this setting is not straightforward.
Concatenating camera tokens does not, by itself, establish correspondence between views in workspace coordinates.
Separate policies preserve robot-specific controls, but a policy restricted to its own cameras cannot use observations from teammates.
Existing multi-agent policies can share information across robots [23, 17].
Even with this capacity, training with complete observations gives a robot little incentive to use another view when its own cameras already suffice.

World Dreamer v5-lite addresses these requirements with a shared world state ϕ\boldsymbol{\phi} built from calibrated video features in workspace coordinates.
A vision–language model conditions one query per robot on the current images and instruction; the queries read ϕ\boldsymbol{\phi} and exchange pose-aware information while their action streams remain separate.
Only observed video features enter the state used for action prediction, while an auxiliary future-video latent objective trains the video encoder.
During training, selected camera views are withheld from both visual branches, but every robot retains its action target, exposing the model to incomplete visual coverage.

Evaluation spans the multi-robot benchmark RoboFactory [18]11
1
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          The camera configuration of RoboFactory is modified so that each agent receives observations from its own cameras. All methods are evaluated under this setting., the household benchmark RoboCasa365 [14, 15], and four real-robot tasks.
The real-robot tasks use homogeneous LeKiwi teams [20] and heterogeneous LeKiwi–OpenArm teams [8].

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

A multi-robot manipulation framework, World Dreamer v5-lite, is proposed. Calibrated multi-view features from a pretrained video encoder form a shared world state ϕ\boldsymbol{\phi} read by all robots. Pose-aware agent queries exchange information across robots.

A masked-view cooperative training strategy is introduced. It withholds robot views from both visual branches while retaining all action supervision. This encourages each robot to act on observations shared by the others.

World Dreamer v5-lite achieves leading performance among the evaluated methods on RoboFactory and four real-robot tasks. Its mean success rate exceeds the strongest baselines by 23.7 and 13.8 percentage points, respectively. On RoboCasa365, it achieves competitive performance.

1. A multi-robot manipulation framework, World Dreamer v5-lite, is proposed. Calibrated multi-view features from a pretrained video encoder form a shared world state ϕ\boldsymbol{\phi} read by all robots. Pose-aware agent queries exchange information across robots.

2. A masked-view cooperative training strategy is introduced. It withholds robot views from both visual branches while retaining all action supervision. This encourages each robot to act on observations shared by the others.

3. World Dreamer v5-lite achieves leading performance among the evaluated methods on RoboFactory and four real-robot tasks. Its mean success rate exceeds the strongest baselines by 23.7 and 13.8 percentage points, respectively. On RoboCasa365, it achieves competitive performance.
