title: Ego-CEVR: Learning Cross-Embodiment Visual Representations from Human Egocentric Videos
authors: Keru Zhou,Zhirui Fang,Xinrun Xu,Yaopeng Lou,Zeyuan He,Zihao Zhu,Xinze Niu,Chen Wang,Tianfu Li,Samith Va,Bin Qian,Junwei Li,Wenjia Ding,Yicheng Xu,Chang Zhou,Ziwei Wang,Li Liu,Xiu Li,Maoqing Yao
abstract:
As egocentric video becomes increasingly available for embodied learning, an important research question is how to turn this low-cost, scalable source of data into robot manipulation capabilities.
Egocentric videos naturally provide rich context for high-level task understanding, while real-robot demonstrations with wrist observations and action annotations provide supervision for fine-grained action alignment.
We present Ego-CEVR, a data-native framework for hierarchical visual representation learning that assigns distinct learning objectives to global and interaction representations. The global module learns object relations, task state, and temporal progress through future prediction on egocentric video. The interaction module interprets wrist observations in global context and learns local alignment and contact cues through robot action supervision. Separate residual paths expose both representations to the action policy, preserving direct access to task context alongside fine-grained execution information.
Ego-CEVR supports independent pretraining of its global video module on large-scale egocentric videos and videos from diverse robot embodiments, without requiring robot action labels or paired wrist observations.
introduction:
In recent years, a series of works [1, 2, 3, 4] and their applications have marked the rapid development of embodied manipulation. More and more embodied data from various sources such as egocentric video (Ego), Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) and cross embodiments data have been applied to the training of models.[5, 6, 7] As embodied data scale up, different types of data are expected to play distinct roles in robot learning.[8] An important challenge is to systematically use data from diverse sources with varying forms of supervision. [9, 10, 11]. However, how can we design data-native models that are specifically tailored to these various data sources in order to make better use of the data from these different sources? This issue has not yet been fully discussed.

VLA policies transfer visual and linguistic priors to robot control, yet semantic generalization does not always translate into faithful execution on unseen tasks [12, 13, 14].
Predictive world models learn how scenes evolve during manipulation, but using this knowledge for precise local control remains challenging [15, 16, 17].
Integrating semantic understanding, world modeling, and action generation is therefore a promising direction [18, 19].
To benefit from heterogeneous video and robot data, such integration must also specify which representations can be learned without actions and how robot supervision should ground them in local control.

Reusing manipulation experience from humans or other robots requires handling differences in morphology, action space, and local interaction geometry [20, 21].
Despite differences in embodiment, similar manipulation tasks often involve similar changes in the spatial and functional relationships between objects.
Egocentric videos and robot head-camera videos can therefore both provide supervision for learning task-level visual representations [5, 22].
Wrist observations provide a closer view of the end effector and its target, revealing local cues for action alignment and contact. Video prediction alone may not sufficiently ground these cues in robot actions. We therefore learn global task context through video prediction and local interaction representations through robot action supervision.

Following this principle, we introduce Ego-CEVR, a data-native framework for hierarchical visual representation learning (Figure 1).
It learns global task context from human egocentric and robot head-camera videos through future prediction, and learns local interaction representations from wrist observations under robot action supervision. Wrist features query the global representation, establishing a hierarchy in which local interaction draws on task context while the global representation is computed independently of the interaction module.

Experiments on LIBERO [23], LIBERO-Plus [24], RoboTwin 2.0 [25], and real robots show improvements in task success and robustness. Ablations further examine the contributions of hierarchical representation learning and multi-source video pretraining.

Our main contributions are:

We propose a data-native framework that incorporates multi-source egocentric videos and action-labeled robot demonstrations at different training stages to learn task-level and local execution knowledge.

We develop a few-shot cross-embodiment adaptation procedure that combines task knowledge learned from video with a few demonstrations from the target robot.

We design a hierarchical representation learning architecture that learns distinct yet complementary representations for high-level task understanding and fine-grained action alignment.

1. We propose a data-native framework that incorporates multi-source egocentric videos and action-labeled robot demonstrations at different training stages to learn task-level and local execution knowledge.

2. We develop a few-shot cross-embodiment adaptation procedure that combines task knowledge learned from video with a few demonstrations from the target robot.

3. We design a hierarchical representation learning architecture that learns distinct yet complementary representations for high-level task understanding and fine-grained action alignment.

title: Autonomous fixed-wing interception using reinforcement learning
authors: Daan van Hamersveld,Ewoud Smeur,Iurii Kriachko
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Neural and Evolutionary Computing (cs.NE); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
comment: MSc thesis, Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, Delft University of Technology, 2026.
abstract:
Medium altitude, long endurance unmanned aerial systems such as Shahed-type strike drones are an unanswered threat in modern conflicts. Conventional air defense systems are too expensive to provide a feasible large-scale solution. Quadcopter interceptors are a cheap, battle-proven alternative, but their extremely limited flight time restricts them to low altitude targets at short range, whereas fixed-wing platforms have the endurance to reach higher altitude targets from longer distances. However, such interceptors are still operated manually. Recent developments in learning-based controllers show potential for automation. In this work, a fixed-wing interceptor is presented that is controlled by a neural network that maps filtered monocular vision observations directly to actuator commands. The policy was trained in a custom Python environment using reinforcement learning and proximal policy optimization. The policy was then deployed on a fixed-wing platform and tested in real interception scenarios. As a baseline, two classical guidance controllers were also developed and tested in simulation.
The policy is able to intercept targets both in simulation and in real flight. In simulation, the policy outperforms the classical controllers under most conditions. The interceptor was ultimately successfully validated in real flight by intercepting maneuvering fixed-wing targets. This novel system shows the potential of artificial intelligence for autonomous control of fixed-wing interceptor drones.
introduction:
Medium Altitude Long Endurance (MALE) Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) pose a credible threat in modern warfare [1][2]. In both the Ukraine-Russia conflict as well as the recent Iran-Israel/US war, the systems used can be classified into two broad groups. Firstly, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance drones, which are generally fixed-wing UAS with varying imaging capabilities. They typically fly at 2-3 km altitude at speeds up to 150 km/h. Secondly, Shahed-type strike drones, which are delta-wing kamikaze drones that typically fly at 1-2 km altitude at speeds reaching above 250 km/h. They carry a large explosive payload and have high endurance, allowing for long-range (up to 2000 km) targeted ground strikes.

To answer these threats, low cost interceptor drones are emerging as an alternative to expensive conventional air defenses such as fighter jets and missiles. Interceptors carry an explosive payload which is detonated when close enough to neutralize the target. Hence, such systems are single-use, meaning a minimal onboard sensor suite is preferred for affordability. A ground-based radar system can typically provide a mid-course guidance target lock with a few hundred meters error. However, terminal guidance requires meter-level accuracy and hence is currently mainly vision-based, as monocular cameras are inexpensive and easy to source. Traditional guidance laws such as Proportional Navigation (PN) and Pure Pursuit (PP) [3][4][5] need a constant Line Of Sight (LOS) and struggle against maneuvering targets. Consequently, current interceptors are mostly manually controlled during terminal guidance.

Vision-based relative state estimation can be done in many ways for a variety of applications, including drone racing [6], target tracking [7], aerial refueling [8] and also interception [9][10][11]. For interception purposes, the bounding-box [12][13][11] is an effective and easy to implement proxy to a relative state. Turning visual observation into effective guidance for interception has been done using classical control approaches such as PP [9] and PN [14].

Recently, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has been successfully applied to UAS control tasks such as stabilization [15], attitude control [16], acrobatics [17], drone racing [18][6] and also interception [7][19][20], with controller authority varying from high level planning to direct actuator command. While promising, for interception the real challenge lies in transferring these results from simulation to a real, uncontrolled environment. Recent work suggests that end-to-end learning-based controllers can achieve high sim-to-real transfer robustness by implementing domain randomization [21].

In MALE interception scenarios, fixed-wing drones can be superior to quadrotors due to their better endurance, allowing them to intercept targets from longer ranges and at higher altitudes. Studies on RL controllers for fixed-wing platforms are sparse. However, obstacle avoidance [22], path following [23] evasion [24] and interception with perfect state knowledge [20] have been carried out in simulation. In real environments, studies have demonstrated successful attitude holding [25] and landing [26].

Fixed-wing, vision-based interception using a learning-based controller in a real environment is lacking in the literature. Most interception studies are done in simulation and using a quadrotor model, whilst realistic perception and sim-to-real transfer are usually not addressed.

In this work, a learning-and monocular vision-based fixed-wing interceptor is presented and demonstrated to successfully intercept MALE targets in a real environment. Shown in figure 1, the interceptor is built entirely with off-the-shelf components. An RL controller is trained in simulation which replaces the guidance and control of a conventional autopilot. A neural network directly maps filtered visual and flight controller information to actuator commands. The performance of the RL controller is validated against baseline PN and PP controllers in simulation. Finally, the RL controller is tested on real flight interceptions of fixed-wing, MALE UAS.

The main contributions of this work are therefore:

Development of an end-to-end neural network enabling autonomous fixed-wing interception of maneuvering targets with limited onboard sensing.

Development of a monocular vision- and learning-based, autonomous, fixed-wing interceptor able to intercept MALE targets in a real environment.

Development of a RL framework inspired by [19], incorporating fixed-wing dynamics and a real computer-vision algorithm.

1. Development of an end-to-end neural network enabling autonomous fixed-wing interception of maneuvering targets with limited onboard sensing.

2. Development of a monocular vision- and learning-based, autonomous, fixed-wing interceptor able to intercept MALE targets in a real environment.

3. Development of a RL framework inspired by [19], incorporating fixed-wing dynamics and a real computer-vision algorithm.

title: Electric-Field Induction Motor with Discrete Circuit Elements and Improved Rotor Dynamics
authors: Alex S. Miller,Jeffrey H. Lang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY); Applied Physics (physics.app-ph); Instrumentation and Detectors (physics.ins-det)
abstract: Electric-field-based actuators and machines lead the design space at the nanoscale and in biological systems, while having the potential to be used in favorable macroscale applications which prioritize minimal mass, performance in a vacuum, or performance in high temperatures. Electric-field induction motors consist of a set of stator electrodes which induce opposite charges onto a movable rotor surface. In earlier work, rotor surfaces for electric-field induction motors have been made of single continuum materials, which are limited in possible resistivity, permittivity and circuitry characteristics. To enhance design freedom, we develop a rotor for electric-field-based machines which may be constructed out of discrete circuit components between a finite number of conductive vanes. Magnetic-field induction motors, which are common in machinery, often utilize “deep bar” rotors, consisting of conducting bars which decrease the rotor time constant with increasing frequency using the skin depth effect. We propose, analyze, design and demonstrate a macro-scale electric-field induction motor which uses circuitry on the rotor surface to emulate the “deep bar” design, providing improved torque over a wide range of speeds.
introduction:
Electric-field-based motors and machines remain an underexplored area of motor-development, with potential applications from medical devices to space technology. The performance of electric-field machines scales with working gap surface area, whereas performance of magnetic-field machines scales with volume [25]; due to this tradeoff, electric-field machines provide leading performance on the micro and nano scale [3][30]. Indeed, motors and actuators in biological systems are all electric-field-based, employing nano-scale gaps. Researchers have been recently able to make electrostatic motors using folded DNA [33]. Electrostatic machines also excel in applications that prioritize minimal mass, such as small aerial vehicles [34] and applications that prioritize low material thickness, such origami foldable actuators [26]. Macro-scale electrostatic machines have also been explored for industrial equipment targeting high efficiency and long working life [22]. With multiplicative gains from dielectric gap fluids [9], increases in machine area-to-gap ratio, and optimizations in motor packaging systems, electric-field motors are beginning to approach the performance of magnetic machines in macro-scale industrial applications [8][22].

Electrostatic motors have been developed since the 1740s [17], with numerous topologies and configurations developed. Direct-current electrostatic motors have been implemented using corona discharge between the rotor and stator for charge transport [17]; these motors are simple and capable of very-high operating voltage, but limited in efficiency and are constrained to a relatively small range of physical scales due to reliance on corona discharge through the gap medium. Similar commutation techniques have also been implemented with brushes [34]. Variable-capacitance machines use synchronous alternating-current electric fields to drive the rotor from lower-capacitance positions to higher capacitance positions. These motors, analogous to magnetic variable-reluctance machines, have seen extensive development [32][4][16][10], but the requirement that the excitation be synchronized to the rotor position complicates controller design and the configuration of the excitation limits the potential across the gap to only half of the excitation. Permanent electret machines, analogous to permanent magnet machines, use a permanently charged electret in the rotor to maintain high electric fields [17] [13]. Like a permanent-magnet motor, these may be used with a commutator for simple operation, but are limited in their capability due to the limited strength of possible electret materials [13]. Separately-excited motors use an electrically-driven rotor and stator, with a synchronous field pattern, to achieve a optimal gap field configurations for a range of speeds [11][22]. Separately-excited designs are appropriate for low-speeds, and have seen successful development for industrial applications; however, this topology requires a slip-ring to transmit power to the rotor, adding significant mechanical complexity, especially at micro scales and high speeds, and requiring synchronous controller schemes [11][22].

Electric-field-based induction machines, analogous to magnetic-field induction machines, use a moving electric field excitation in the stator, along with charge-relaxation in the rotor to induce an asynchronously traveling electric field in the rotor [24][25], as shown in Fig. 1. Electric-field-based induction machines are often known in the literature as electro-quasistatic induction machines, while they are, in fact, electro-quasistatic, due to the charge relaxation on the rotor; this paper, these terms are used interchangeably. The asynchronous nature of induction machines negates the need for a shaft encoder for most operation, and they have high maximum efficiency. Additionally, since they are asynchronous, high-voltage drive electronics may be simplified, running at a fixed frequency for the course of motor operation.

However, previous electro-quasistatic induction machines relied on a precisely-selected material on the rotor to achieve a determined speed-torque behavior; selecting and depositing an appropriate rotor conductor in the ranges needed for good motor performance is challenging. In previous work, rotor conductor selection required navigating a design tradeoff between choosing either high starting torque and high efficiency at the operating point, a significant tradeoff not experienced by separately-excited machines.

Early electric-field induction motors, built in the 1860s, consisted of a cylindrical ebonite rotor surrounded by four copper electrodes, excited with a radial electric field [17]. These designs were elaborated on with tighter gaps between the rotor and stator, more stator poles, and new rotor insulator materials [4]. Subsequent macro-scale induction motors with glass rotors were made to test torque characteristics [6] and achieve position control [27]. With the emergence of micro electro-mechanical manufacturing techniques, many new electric-field-based actuation systems emerged. Induction micromotors were able to achieve speeds in excess of 50,000 rpm, with gaps on the order of 3 µ​m3\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} [29][21][36][35].

In this paper, we address two of the major challenges that have limited electric-field induction motor designs of the past. First, we implement a rotor conductor based on discrete off-the-shelf components instead of a hard-to-find continuous material coating, facilitating adjustability of design parameters, consistent manufacturing and replicability of results. Second, we design and implement circuits on the rotor of the electro-quasistatic induction motor, which bring new design options for attaining both high starting torque and high efficiency. We design and implement an induction motor testbed, and evaluate the speed-torque characteristics of these new circuit techniques.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning of Co-Adaptive Hip Exoskeleton Control (MARL-Exo) for Metabolic Energy Reduction
authors: Yifei Yuan,Jakob Wolf,Ghaith Androwis,Xianlian Zhou
abstract:
Objective: This study aims to determine whether a hip-exoskeleton policy trained in simulation, by co-adapting with a musculoskeletal human model under a metabolic-energy reward, reduces the metabolic cost of walking in new users without per-user tuning, and how mechanical-power shaping affects the learned assistance.
Methods: We developed MARL-Exo, a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework in which a full-body human model (304 muscle actuators; randomized anatomy, gait, and speed) and a bilateral hip-exoskeleton policy are trained concurrently in two stages. The exoskeleton observes only delayed hip kinematics and its past commands; its reward includes muscle metabolic power from a physiologically based energetics model, alone (Metabolic) or with mechanical-power shaping (Metabolic + Power). The Metabolic policy was deployed and tested without retraining in eight healthy adults walking at 1.25 m/s, using indirect calorimetry.
Results: In simulation, the Metabolic policy reduced modeled muscle metabolic power by 13.8% relative to no-device walking, versus 8.8% for Metabolic + Power. On hardware, MARL-Exo reduced net metabolic rate by 18.3±6.6%18.3\pm 6.6\% relative to Passive in all eight participants. Relative to No-Exo, the mean reduction was 7.4±10.0%7.4\pm 10.0\%; six participants more than offset the 13.1%13.1\% device-wearing penalty, walking up to 24.2%24.2\% below their No-Exo cost.
Conclusion: A metabolically informed policy co-adapted in simulation transferred to users without per-user tuning and consistently reduced the metabolic cost of walking with the device, while explicit power shaping reduced the simulated benefit.
Significance: Unlike per-user human-in-the-loop optimization, this approach yields a single population-level controller and allows assistance objectives to be screened in simulation before human testing.
introduction:
Powered lower-limb exoskeletons are being developed both for gait rehabilitation and for augmenting healthy walking [1, 2]. Among them, hip exoskeletons are especially attractive because the hip musculature performs a large fraction of the positive work of level locomotion, so assistance there can offload muscles that do much of the work of walking. Delivering that benefit efficiently is challenging because the wearer is not a passive plant. Once a device applies torque at a joint, the mechanics of gait change, and the neuromuscular system responds by recruiting muscles differently and re-coordinating the limbs [3]. Each side of the interaction thus changes the operating conditions of the other, and the controller is tuned against a wearer who is still adapting. The problem is compounded by the choice of objective: active devices can shape the assistance profile flexibly, but the benefit they deliver depends strongly on what the controller is optimized for, and on how well that objective reflects the wearer’s response. Human-in-the-loop optimization tunes the objective directly on the wearer, but it demands long per-user experiments that must be repeated for every user and condition [4, 5].

Learning the controller in musculoskeletal simulation offers a way around those experiments, since the wearer’s response can be simulated rather than measured. A neural network control policy for a full lower limb exoskeleton coupled to a musculoskeletal model was first used to learn robust assistance for walking [6], and a similar idea was used for joint human–exoskeleton training with sim-to-real transfer that produced a control policy for a hip exoskeleton that lowered metabolic cost without subject-specific tuning [7]. The paradigm has since been extended to speed- and slope-aware assistance through muscle-synergy priors [8], to reflex-based human models paired with end-to-end hip policies [9], to human-aligned simulation of assistance parameters [10], and to asymmetric gait [11], squatting [12], sit-to-stand [13], and running [14].

Two gaps remain in this literature. First, the mutual adaptation of human and device is mostly left implicit: when both policies are optimized at once, each shifts the data distribution seen by the other, and training can drift toward oscillatory torque, mistimed assistance, or divergence. Second, the effort terms used in training are typically proxies such as muscle activation or work. Luo et al. [7] explicitly chose activation over a metabolic-rate term because of calibration and reward-smoothness concerns, and other controllers use kinematic tracking or activation-based effort [8, 12]. What a wearer ultimately experiences is metabolic energy, which a musculoskeletal simulation can compute directly but which, to our knowledge, has not been used as a term of the exoskeleton policy reward. The closest examples are of two kinds. Exo-Plore rewards a simplified activation-weighted energy expression rather than a physiological muscle-energetics model [10]. Barati et al. [9] optimize their reflex-based human model with Umberger’s energetics as the objective; however, this objective was not incorporated into the exoskeleton policy reward, which instead used an activation-based effort term.

Curriculum learning is a natural remedy for the first gap, since decomposing a hard learning problem into ordered stages improves stability [15] and physiological plausibility [16, 17]. We previously proposed Staged Multi-Agent Training (SMAT), a four-stage curriculum trained on a compact 26-muscle model [18, 19]. Here we ask two further questions. Can co-adaptive training remain stable, and transfer to real users, when the human is a far richer full-body model with a population of body sizes and gaits? And how does physiological energetics, with and without explicit mechanical-power shaping, influence the assistance learned through human–exoskeleton co-adaptation, and can the resulting policy transfer to human users?

This study addresses both questions with MARL-Exo, a multi-agent framework built on a full-body model with 304 Hill-type muscle actuators. Its human policy outputs residual joint targets adapted to a reference gait trajectory, which a learned muscle-activation layer converts into muscle activations. Its exoskeleton policy sees only intentionally delayed hip kinematics and its own recent commands, so that it can run on inexpensive wearable sensing. Training uses a two-stage schedule (human-only gait, then joint co-adaptation), and the exoskeleton reward includes the metabolic power of the hip muscles, evaluated with a muscle-energetics model, either alone (Metabolic) or together with explicit mechanical-power shaping (Metabolic + Power). The Metabolic policy was deployed on the same hardware and eight-participant cohort of the SMAT evaluation [19]. The contributions are as follows:

title: AuRaSim: A Ray-Tracing Based Automotive FMCW Radar Simulator for Dynamic Scenarios
authors: Zhaoze Wang,Changxu Zhang,Tai Fei,Christopher Grimm,Yi Jin,Claas Tebruegge,Markus Gardill
abstract: Modern simulators can generate synthetic camera and LiDAR data with accurate annotations for downstream tasks. In contrast, automotive radar simulation remains less mature because it requires not only a 3D engine to model dynamic objects in the scenes but also electromagnetic material properties, antenna configurations, wave propagation mechanisms, and coherent signal synthesis. Existing frameworks are either proprietary or overly simplified, limiting the scalability of radar raw measurements. This paper presents AuRaSim, a ray-tracing-based automotive frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar simulation framework for dynamic scenarios. Rather than implementing all components from scratch, AuRaSim builds on Blender for efficient dynamic-scene construction and Sionna RT for graphics processing unit (GPU)-accelerated electromagnetic ray tracing, while introducing radar-specific adaptations for path-resolved propagation with complex coefficients, motion-aware Doppler modeling, and subsequently coherent multi-channel analog-to-digital converter (ADC) cube synthesis based on waveform configurations. Quantitative comparison between simulated and measured range–Doppler maps in digital-twin scenarios achieves a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 0.147 and a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 16.93 dB, demonstrating the accuracy and fidelity of the synthetic signal. AuRaSim therefore provides a complete and extensible platform for reproducible automotive radar simulation and research. Project homepage: https://wangzhaoze.github.io/aurasim.
introduction:
Automotive frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar is a crucial sensing modality for autonomous driving because it provides direct velocity measurements and remains robust under adverse environmental conditions, where camera- and
LiDAR-based perception may degrade [1]. However, radar measurements are typically sparse, noisy, affected by the multipath effect, and have limited angular resolution, which challenges conventional signal processing algorithms in complex traffic situations.

Recent deep learning based methods have shown promising performance in overcoming some of these limitations, but their development is still constrained by the lack of large-scale and accurately annotated radar datasets. Compared with camera and LiDAR data, radar raw signals are more challenging to interpret and annotate directly because they require specialized domain knowledge, making high-quality ground-truth acquisition much more expensive. Although several automotive radar datasets have been released in recent years (e.g., [2, 3]), their scale and annotation variety remain more limited than widely used camera- and LiDAR-based benchmarks such as KITTI [4] and nuScenes [5].

Existing approaches to radar data synthesis can broadly be summarized as data-driven and physics-based methods. Data-driven approaches learn the distribution of recorded data and synthesize radar representations using conditional generative models [6, 7]. Such methods can efficiently reproduce measurement statistics and sensor effects that are difficult to formulate analytically. Their applicability is nevertheless often hardware-specific, because the learned distribution is inherently conditioned on the waveform and antenna layout represented during training, such that deviations from these settings can induce domain shifts and degrade generalization to unseen radar hardware. Physics-based simulation instead derives radar measurements from explicit scene, hardware, and propagation models [8]. This enables controlled configuration variation while providing exact scene state as ground truth, making it attractive for radar dataset generation.

However, building a complete automotive radar simulator remains challenging for several reasons. First, realistic driving scenarios require a dynamic 3D scene representation, including environmental geometry, vehicle movements, and articulated or deformable road users. Second, geometrically accurate 3D assets must be assigned electromagnetic material properties for roads, vehicles, buildings, and other traffic participants. Third, relevant electromagnetic propagation mechanisms, including specular and diffuse reflection, diffraction, and multipath propagation, must be modeled to reproduce realistic radar returns, including distributed environmental echoes and multipath-induced ghost targets. Fourth, noise, calibration errors, interference, and other sensor effects remain difficult to reproduce accurately. Finally, resolving these interactions over multiple antenna channels and successive radar frames is computationally expensive. Consequently, automotive radar simulation requires careful trade-offs among physical fidelity, computational efficiency, and practical scenario construction.

Current simulation tools address these challenges to different degrees, with many approaches relying on simplifying assumptions. General-purpose autonomous-driving simulators such as CARLA
[9] provide dynamic traffic environments and radar
detections but use simplified ray-casting models. Similarly, MATLAB employs a
measurement-level probabilistic radar model to generate detections
[10]. Commercial radar simulation tools such as
Remcom WaveFarer [11], Altair Feko [12] and dSPACE AURELION
[13] provide higher-fidelity radar simulation. These platforms demonstrate that physically detailed automotive radar simulation is feasible, but their proprietary and closed-source nature limits wide application within the academic community. This motivates an accessible and extensible framework for flexible research and efficient synthetic-data generation.

In this work, we present AuRaSim, an end-to-end automotive radar simulation framework that addresses this gap by building upon and substantially extending the capabilities of two complementary open-source technologies rather than implementing a complete rendering and propagation stack from scratch. Blender [14] provides a mature solution for constructing complex polygonal scenes, managing reusable 3D assets, i.e., object models and materials, and representing time-varying animations. Sionna RT is an open-source ray tracer originally developed for radio-propagation modeling in communication systems and provides electromagnetic material models and path solvers supporting specular and diffuse reflection, diffraction, and transmission [15]. AuRaSim integrates the complementary capabilities of Blender [14] and Sionna RT [15] and substantially extends them to form an end-to-end automotive FMCW radar simulation framework.

Our main contributions are threefold: (1) We develop a unified scenario-to-signal simulation pipeline that produces path-resolved propagation data, multi-channel analog-to-digital converter (ADC) samples, and derived radar products while preserving a consistent representation of scene state, sensor geometry, and waveform timing. (2) We integrate radar-specific adaptations to the underlying propagation pipeline, including field-of-view-aware ray sampling, propagation-path filtering, and a vertex velocity field that enables Hit-Point Doppler (HPD) modeling for complex dynamic objects. The effectiveness of these components is evaluated through dedicated ablation studies. (3) We establish a digital-twin-based validation workflow by reconstructing representative real-world measurement scenarios with matched 77-GHz radar configurations and quantitatively comparing simulated and measured radar data, including range–Doppler representations, to evaluate the signal fidelity of the proposed simulator.

title: Learning Quality-Controllable Robot Policies with Iterative Hindsight Relabeling
authors: Sinjae Kang,Dong Kyu Shin,Jaehong Kim,Kamin Lee,Hyoeun Kim,Kaixin Wang,Li Zhao,Seonghyeon Ye,Kimin Lee
abstract: Robot policy evaluation often relies on a binary success signal for task completion. In real-world deployment, however, desired execution behaviors are also defined by quality attributes such as execution speed and motion smoothness, which need to be dynamically controlled according to task requirements. To address this, we introduce Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), a robot policy that enables inference-time control over both individual quality attributes and their combinations. To extend the controllable quality range beyond initial demonstrations, we further propose an iterative hindsight relabeling loop: QCP collects online rollouts under target quality labels, adds successful trajectories to the dataset, relabels the accumulated trajectories in hindsight according to their measured quality, and fine-tunes the policy. Experiments on Robomimic and RoboEval demonstrate that QCP consistently improves both task execution quality and success rates across iterations, producing successful rollouts that exceed the quality of the initial demonstrations. Finally, we validate QCP on real-world manipulation tasks, where controlling speed increases throughput in conveyor operations and controlling transport stability improves success when carrying wine glasses, demonstrating that quality-controllable policies yield practical gains in physical deployment.
introduction:
Robot foundation models have shown strong generalization across tasks, environments, and objects (Black et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026).
These policies are usually trained with behavior cloning (BC) on successful demonstrations, which treats every successful trajectory as equally desirable regardless of how the task was executed.
As a result, the learned policy reproduces the mixture of execution behaviors in the data, whether fast or slow, smooth or jerky, and offers no way to steer toward the behavior a deployment actually requires.
In practice, however, the desired behavior of a robot is not defined by task success alone (Wang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Mao et al., 2026) and different tasks call for different quality attributes.
For example, a robot deployed on a conveyor line should prioritize execution speed, whereas a robot carrying wine glasses on a tray must prioritize transport stability.

To address this, prior work has proposed quality-controllable policies whose execution behavior can be adjusted along a chosen quality axis at inference time (Zhan et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2025; Petitbois et al., 2026).
However, such policies are trained on static demonstration datasets, which typically cover only a bounded quality range and lack the high-performance regimes needed in deployment (e.g., maximum speed or ideal smoothness).
Our goal is therefore not only to learn a quality-controllable policy, but also to continuously expand its controllable range beyond the initial demonstrations through online data collection and policy updates.

In this paper, we introduce Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), which addresses this limitation of BC by making execution quality an explicit conditioning input (Figure 1).
For each demonstration, we measure the target quality attributes with rule-based score functions and quantize the scores into discrete quality labels.
The policy is then trained to generate actions conditioned on both the observation history and these labels.
Rather than averaging over execution behaviors, QCP learns task completion from all successful trajectories while distinguishing how each one was executed.
At inference time, the user specifies a target label to steer execution behavior, for example, requesting the highest speed label for conveyor operations.

To extend the controllable quality range beyond the demonstrations, we pair QCP with iterative hindsight relabeling.
At each iteration, we collect rollouts conditioned on the highest quality label, keep the successful ones, relabel them by the quality they actually achieved, and add them to the dataset.
We then recompute the quality labels of all trajectories and retrain the policy.
As higher-quality rollouts accumulate, the highest label comes to represent progressively higher quality, allowing the policy to reach operating regimes absent from the initial demonstrations.
Because quality is measured by rule-based score functions, this loop requires no manual quality annotation.

Experiments on Robomimic (Mandlekar et al., 2022) and RoboEval (Wang et al., 2025) show that QCP with iterative hindsight relabeling improves both target quality and task success across iterations, outperforming quality-filtered BC and RL baselines (Mao et al., 2024; Petitbois et al., 2026; Wagenmaker et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2026).
Iterative relabeling pushes the quality distribution well beyond the range of the initial demonstrations, reaching an IQR-normalized Wasserstein distance above 1.5.
Beyond single-attribute control, QCP controls multiple attributes jointly, improving six quality attributes simultaneously in RoboEval.
Finally, in real-world experiments, controlling execution speed substantially increases throughput in conveyor operations, and controlling transport stability improves success when carrying wine glasses on a tray.

title: PDRVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Physical Dynamics Representations
authors: Hanqing Wang,Zhaotian Cai,Ruichuan An,Bohan Zeng,Tao Zhang,Yilin Chen,Xu Jiang,Kaiquan Chen,Chongyang Wu,Haoran Li,Fan Yang,Mingan Lin,Wentao Zhang,Zenan Zhou,Youzheng Wu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but their understanding of physical dynamics remains limited. Video world models can capture scene dynamics, yet generating future videos introduces high latency into the control loop. We introduce PDRVLA, whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts physical tokens from vision–language features to condition action generation without online video generation. The module learns through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision through a frozen pretrained video world model. Training relies entirely on publicly available data, expanded through human-to-robot synthesis, subtask annotation, and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotation. Across four simulation benchmarks, PDRVLA achieves success rates of 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv. Ablations show improved future prediction with world-model supervision and evaluate how subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT training affect action success.
introduction:
Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models connect visual observations and language instructions to robot control, drawing on pretrained vision–language models (VLMs) and demonstrations from heterogeneous robots (Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence, 2025). Their understanding of the physical world, however, remains limited. For example, a recent analysis reports weak encoding of object physical properties across several VLA policies and unreliable adaptation of their motions to changes in object mass (Xu, 2026). For manipulation, recognizing the current scene is only part of the problem: grasping, moving, and placing objects also change their configurations and spatial relationships. Anticipating how a scene evolves during interaction can provide useful context for action selection, motivating representations that connect current observations with future appearance, geometry, and motion.

Pretrained video world models offer a complementary way to learn physical dynamics by predicting how scenes change over time (Team Wan et al., 2025). Incorporating these models into robot policies can connect future prediction with action generation (Kim et al., 2026). However, generating future videos within the control loop adds latency to action generation. Recent approaches instead use video prediction during training to shape compact representations that can condition a policy without online video generation (InternRobotics, 2026; Tang et al., 2026).

Following this direction, we introduce PDRVLA, a VLA model with a lightweight Physical Dynamics Module (Figure 1). The module extracts a fixed set of physical tokens from intermediate VLM features. The action expert uses these tokens alongside the final-layer VLM features to generate actions. We train the module with two complementary objectives. Direct supervision uses future RGB, depth, and optical-flow latent features as targets, encouraging the tokens to encode future appearance, geometry, and motion. A frozen pretrained video world model conditioned on the physical tokens provides auxiliary supervision for temporal prediction. Joint policy training then combines action and vision–language (VL) objectives with continued direct future prediction. The resulting policy uses physical tokens for action generation without running the video model during control.

Our training corpus is built entirely from publicly available datasets. It combines real-robot, handheld UMI, and simulated trajectories with general and robotics-oriented VL data, and is expanded through egocentric human-to-robot synthesis. Subtask and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotations provide additional supervision for task stages, scene understanding, progress assessment, and next motion. Together, these sources support training across heterogeneous embodiments and complementary forms of action and language supervision.

We evaluate PDRVLA on LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023), LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025), RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025a), and SimplerEnv (Li et al., 2024), achieving success rates of 99.3%, 89.9%, 93.6%, and 81.5%, respectively. Ablation studies show that world-model-assisted supervision improves future prediction. Additional experiments examine the effects of subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT annotations on policy performance.

The report makes three contributions:

We introduce PDRVLA, whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts compact physical tokens from intermediate VLM features to complement the final-layer features used for action generation. We train these representations through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision from a frozen video world model. Direct future prediction continues during joint policy training, while deployment uses the learned physical tokens without running the video generator.

We assemble a cross-embodiment training corpus entirely from publicly available datasets, integrating real-robot, handheld UMI, and simulated demonstrations with general and robotics-oriented VL data. Our data pipeline standardizes heterogeneous trajectories, expands embodiment coverage through egocentric human-to-robot synthesis, and adds subtask and ECoT annotations, supporting joint learning of robot actions and language responses about task stages, scene context, progress, and next motion.

We evaluate PDRVLA on four simulation benchmarks and conduct targeted analyses of physical-representation learning and policy performance. The results show improved future prediction with world-model assistance and characterize the effects of subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT annotations on action success across tasks and inference settings.

title: VLA-Stem: A Lightweight Safety Mechanism for Vision-Language-Action Models via Reinforcement Learning
authors: Bojun Zou,Wenhao Yu,Jiaohao Li,Jiaxuan Lin,Guanting Ye,Haohan Geng,Weihao Yu,Yanyong Zhang,Jianmin Ji
abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for end-to-end robotic control, integrating high-level reasoning with low-level action execution. However, most existing VLA models are primarily designed for static manipulation tasks in unconstrained environments, failing to account for safety-critical scenarios that involve spatial constraints or dynamic obstacles.
Fine-tuning VLAs on obstacle-avoidance data is a straightforward solution, but collecting such data is costly, especially for dynamic scenarios, and may degrade their original task capabilities.
To address these limitations, we propose VLA-Stem, a lightweight, reinforcement-learning-based safety mechanism for VLA systems.
Without fine-tuning the underlying VLA policy, VLA-Stem converts its action chunks into motion references and uses trajectory-level guidance to preserve their spatial intent while allowing flexible motion and timing adjustments.
Conditioned on these references, robot proprioception, and local obstacle information, the Stem policy adaptively modifies execution at inference time, preserving the original task intent while enabling responsive adaptation to spatial constraints and dynamic obstacles.
To achieve robust and sample-efficient policy learning in complex environments, we adopt a teacher–student distillation framework combined with curriculum learning. We evaluate VLA-Stem on reference following, static spatial constraints, and dynamic obstacle avoidance. Across six constrained simulation settings, VLA-Stem achieves 52.8% average collision-free task success versus 23.7% for the strongest safety baseline, while preserving base-policy performance in obstacle-free settings; real-world experiments further show consistent collision reductions under static and dynamic obstacles.
These results demonstrate that VLA-Stem couples high-level VLA task intent with rapid, reflex-like responses to immediate physical risks, providing a brainstem-inspired mechanism for robust robot execution.
introduction:
Embodied intelligence aims to integrate robotics with artificial intelligence for general real-world interaction, with Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models emerging as a prominent direction. State-of-the-art VLA models [1] adopt end-to-end architectures that combine high-level capabilities with low-level action execution. This resembles human behavior, where deliberate reasoning guides bodily actions to accomplish diverse real-world tasks.
However, we argue that this paradigm overlooks another fundamental aspect of biological intelligence: basic physiological and sensorimotor functions, such as postural regulation and rapid reflexive responses, which operate through lower-level neural circuits including the brainstem.
In contrast, most existing VLA policies lack an explicit counterpart to such lower-level responsive regulation.
Therefore, VLA policies should not only learn what to do and how to do it, but also remain responsive to the safety demands of physical interaction.

Building on this perspective, we aim to endow VLA systems with the ability to react to immediate physical risks while remaining coordinated with their task-directed behavior (Fig. 1). Existing approaches mainly follow two directions. One is to learn collision-aware manipulation behaviors from large-scale avoidance data [2]; however, collecting such data is labor-intensive and costly, especially in dynamic environments, and adapting a pretrained VLA requires additional training of the task policy itself. Another direction is to augment a frozen VLA with a conventional safety module. For example, VLSA [3] introduces control-theoretic constraints to modify unsafe VLA actions during execution. While this modular design provides an explicit mechanism for satisfying local geometric constraints, it primarily focuses on action-space safety and ignores the coordination between safety responses and the task-directed behavior of the VLA, leading to restricted corrective behaviors, reduced task success, and limited adaptability in complex dynamic environments. This motivates a mechanism that does not treat safety adaptation independently of VLA task intent, but instead tightly integrates safety responses with VLA task execution.

To address these limitations, we propose VLA-Stem, a lightweight, brainstem-inspired RL-based safety mechanism that couples VLA task intent with rapid responses to physical risks. Specifically, VLA-Stem uses the short-horizon trajectory generated by the base VLA as a reference for its intended motion, and jointly conditions on this reference trajectory, robot proprioception, and local obstacle information to generate executable actions. To support such flexible execution, we introduce a trajectory-level guidance objective that preserves the spatial intent of the motion reference while relaxing strict temporal alignment. We further adopt teacher–student distillation with curriculum learning to facilitate structured exploration and improve the learned policy’s recovery capability under safety-induced deviations. As a result, VLA-Stem improves execution safety and robustness without sacrificing task performance or incurring additional training cost for the base policy.

We evaluate VLA-Stem across multiple manipulation tasks and scenarios, including obstacle-free execution, static spatial constraints, and dynamic obstacle avoidance. Results show that VLA-Stem reduces safety violations while maintaining base-policy task performance, demonstrating its potential as an inference-time safety mechanism for VLA policies.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose VLA-Stem, a lightweight, reinforcement-learning-based safety mechanism for VLA models that directly integrates VLA task intent with runtime safety adaptation to physical constraints, without fine-tuning the underlying policy.

We design a trajectory-level guidance objective that uses the base VLA trajectory as a reference motion, allowing flexible local motion and timing adjustments while preserving task behavior. We further introduce a teacher–student distillation framework with curriculum learning to improve recovery from obstacle-avoidance-induced deviations.

We conduct extensive experiments across multiple manipulation scenarios in both simulation and the real world, demonstrating improved collision-free task success and direct sim-to-real transfer of the Stem policy without real-world training or fine-tuning.

1. We propose VLA-Stem, a lightweight, reinforcement-learning-based safety mechanism for VLA models that directly integrates VLA task intent with runtime safety adaptation to physical constraints, without fine-tuning the underlying policy.

2. We design a trajectory-level guidance objective that uses the base VLA trajectory as a reference motion, allowing flexible local motion and timing adjustments while preserving task behavior. We further introduce a teacher–student distillation framework with curriculum learning to improve recovery from obstacle-avoidance-induced deviations.

3. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple manipulation scenarios in both simulation and the real world, demonstrating improved collision-free task success and direct sim-to-real transfer of the Stem policy without real-world training or fine-tuning.

title: Generalizable Target-Less Joint Intrinsic-Extrinsic Camera-LiDAR Calibration using Deep Pixel-Point Correspondences
authors: Simon Bultmann,Daniele Cattaneo,Abhinav Valada
abstract:
Accurate camera-LiDAR calibration is an essential prerequisite for robust multi-modal perception in robotics.
Recent target-less methods based on learned pixel-point correspondences achieve high extrinsic calibration accuracy and generalize across environments.
However, they operate on rectified images with known camera intrinsics, restricting their applicability to systems whose cameras have already been individually calibrated.
We present a fully automatic, target-less framework that jointly estimates camera intrinsics, radial-tangential distortion, and camera-LiDAR extrinsics from raw images and LiDAR scans.
Our method generalizes deep correspondence-based calibration from rectified images to raw cameras through intrinsic- and distortion-aware correspondence learning via synthetic augmentations.
During calibration, we iteratively couple correspondence prediction and nonlinear optimization to jointly refine the camera parameters and relative sensor transformation.
We evaluate our approach on an unseen camera-LiDAR configuration from the KITTI dataset and on three real robotic platforms in a zero-shot manner.
The results demonstrate that joint calibration with our generalized pixel-point correspondence network improves extrinsic accuracy over correspondence-based methods using pre-calibrated cameras, while additionally recovering accurate intrinsics.
introduction:
Accurate camera-LiDAR calibration is a fundamental requirement for robotic systems that fuse complementary visual and geometric information for robust perception in real-world environments [1, 2, 3, 4].
To this end, measurements from both modalities must be related, e.g., by projecting LiDAR points into the camera image, requiring accurate camera parameters and a rigid six degree-of-freedom (6 DoF) relative sensor transformation. Calibration errors lead to spatially inconsistent measurements and can directly degrade downstream perception performance.

Camera-LiDAR calibration has traditionally been performed using specially designed targets and controlled acquisition procedures.
These include checkerboards or fiducial markers for camera intrinsic calibration [5], hybrid visual-geometric targets that can be detected by both cameras and LiDARs [6, 7], and larger structured calibration environments [8].
Although target-based approaches achieve high accuracy, they are labor-intensive and require dedicated equipment and expert supervision. The need to repeat the procedure after sensor replacement, vibration, mechanical stress, or thermal effects makes them difficult to scale across large robotic systems or fleets.

To overcome these limitations, recent research has focused on target-less calibration using naturally occurring scene structure.
Existing approaches derive calibration constraints from semantic objects or keypoints [9], geometric primitives such as edges and planes [10], sensor motion [11], or learned multi-modal correspondences [12, 13, 14].
For camera-LiDAR matching, optical-flow-based methods such as I2DLoc [15] and CMRNext [13] currently set the state of the art.
These methods formulate pixel-point matching as dense displacement estimation between projected LiDAR scans and RGB images. Building on this paradigm, MDPCalib [11] combines motion-based initialization with learned correspondences to obtain a fully automatic target-less extrinsic calibration pipeline. However, existing deep correspondence-based methods operate on rectified images with known camera intrinsics and therefore require calibrating each camera beforehand.

We bridge this gap with a fully automatic, target-less framework that jointly estimates camera intrinsics, radial-tangential distortion, and camera-LiDAR extrinsics from raw images and LiDAR scans across diverse robotic platforms, as illustrated in Fig. 1.
Our method generalizes deep correspondence-based calibration from rectified images to raw, distorted cameras through intrinsic- and distortion-aware correspondence learning with physically plausible camera-parameter augmentation.
During calibration, we use the current intrinsic and extrinsic estimates to project the LiDAR scan into the image and provide the network input for pixel-point correspondence prediction. The predicted correspondences then jointly update the calibration parameters via nonlinear optimization, providing the estimates for the next projection. This iterative feedback loop progressively recovers both the camera parameters and the relative sensor transformation.

Generalization across sensor configurations is particularly important for practical learning-based calibration. Common evaluation on an unseen sequence from the same rigidly mounted camera-LiDAR pair does not establish generalization to an unseen sensor configuration, since the camera intrinsics and sensor transformation remain unchanged and can lead to overfitting to sensor-specific projection patterns [16]. We mitigate this problem by training across multiple datasets and sensor setups, separating learned correspondence estimation from geometric optimization, and augmenting camera parameters, while focusing our evaluation on camera-LiDAR configurations not represented during training.

In summary, our main contributions are:

A fully automatic, target-less framework for jointly estimating camera intrinsics, radial-tangential distortion, and camera-LiDAR extrinsics from raw sensor observations.

Intrinsic- and distortion-aware pixel-point correspondence learning with physically plausible camera-parameter augmentation, enabling a single network to operate across diverse raw camera configurations.

An iterative calibration procedure that couples correspondence prediction with joint nonlinear optimization.

Extensive evaluations comprising an unseen camera-LiDAR configuration from the KITTI dataset and zero-shot transfer to three real robotic platforms without sensor-specific retraining.

We will release the code and pre-trained models upon acceptance.

title: Tokens of Motion: Primitive Motion Learning for Human-Humanoid Skill Transfer
authors: Hanwen Ren,Meng Zheng,Wenzhe Cui,Benjamin Planche,Zhongpai Gao,Anwesa Choudhuri,Terrence Chen,Ziyan Wu
abstract:
Human videos provide a scalable source of manipulation experience, yet transferring them to robots remains challenging because human demonstrations lack robot-compatible actions and differ substantially from robots in embodiment and kinematics. We propose Motion Primitives for Action Composition and Transfer (M-PACT), a framework that addresses this challenge by factorizing primitive motion learning from embodiment-specific motion realization. This separation allows us to learn generalizable and reusable motion primitives from large-scale 3D human hand-pose trajectories, while requiring only limited embodiment-specific robot data to ground these primitives into executable motions. Specifically, we first discover local motion segments from human hand trajectories and learn a compact primitive-motion representation that captures recurring manipulation patterns independently of robot embodiment. Given task and observation context, these primitives are then selected and composed, while a lightweight embodiment-specific decoder maps them to robot motions. Crucially, transferring to a new embodiment preserves the learned primitive representation and requires adapting only the realization model, substantially reducing the dependence on costly robot demonstrations.
Experiments across EgoDex, HoloAssist, and HumanoidEveryday demonstrate cross-dataset and cross-embodiment transferability of proposed M-PACT, with lightweight decoder adaptation achieving strong humanoid motion reconstruction using as few as ∼\sim100 robot demonstrations. These results establish factorized primitive learning as a scalable bridge from large-scale human motion data to humanoid manipulation.
introduction:
Developing robots capable of diverse manipulation in unstructured environments remains a central goal in robotics and artificial intelligence. Most manipulation policies are learned from robot-centric experience, including demonstrations collected through teleoperation or kinesthetic teaching and interactions acquired through reinforcement learning or autonomous exploration. Although such data provide directly executable actions, collecting them at sufficient scale and diversity remains costly and difficult across tasks, environments, and embodiments Brohan et al. (2022); O’Neill et al. (2024). Human videos offer a compelling alternative: they are abundant and capture diverse object interactions, behavioral strategies, and long-horizon activities in natural settings Grauman et al. (2022). They can therefore complement limited robot demonstrations and broaden the task and behavioral coverage of robot learning systems Kareer et al. (2025). However, human demonstrations lack robot-compatible action supervision, while human and robot effectors differ substantially in morphology, kinematics, appearance, and feasible action spaces Kareer et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025). Directly imitating human trajectories can consequently produce ambiguous or kinematically infeasible robot actions. Bridging this embodiment gap requires representations that abstract away embodiment-specific execution while preserving transferable motion structure,
for effective and generalizable robot control.

Vision-language-action (VLA) models (Pertsch et al., 2025; Black et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Brohan et al., 2023) offer a promising framework for general-purpose manipulation by mapping visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions. Recent models such as Ψ0\Psi_{0} Wei et al. (2026), H-RDT Bi et al. (2026), and Being-H0 Luo et al. (2025) further pretrain on large-scale egocentric human videos before adapting to specific robot embodiments, demonstrating the potential of human data to broaden behavioral coverage. However, two limitations remain. First, human videos lack robot-executable actions, so converting them into control supervision still requires costly robot demonstrations or computationally intensive human-motion estimation. Second, existing pretraining paradigms often couple human motion with scene appearance and context rather than explicitly isolating transferable motion structure, limiting generalization across scenes, tasks, and embodiments.

Existing human-to-robot skill transfer approaches primarily bridge the embodiment gap by geometric alignment of human hand and robot trajectories Kareer et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025); Shi et al. (2025); Haldar and Pinto (2025); Zhou et al. (2026); Li et al. (2024), visual transformation of human demonstrations into robot-centric observations Li et al. (2025); Lepert et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2026a), or reconstructing hand-object interactions and retargeting to dexterous robot hands Wang et al. (2024); Mu et al. (2026); Singh et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2026b); Paliwal et al. (2026); Lai et al. (2026).
However, hand-object manipulation is inherently compositional and behaviorally multimodal: a single task may comprise heterogeneous motions such as grasping, lifting, placing, etc., each admitting multiple valid executions. Representing such a skill as a monolithic, full-trajectory supervision signal requires an imitation-learning policy to model long and highly variable motion sequences while simultaneously resolving human-robot embodiment differences, making learning difficult and limiting the reuse of shared behaviors across tasks.
Recent approaches have begun to introduce temporal hierarchy,
however, these methods generally transfer human behavior through complete trajectories Singh et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025), coarse semantic subtasks Mu et al. (2026); Shi et al. (2025), fixed-horizon trajectory and action predictions Haldar and Pinto (2025); Zhou et al. (2026). Consequently, recurring local motion patterns can remain coupled to task-level ordering and global scene context, limiting their systematic recomposition and transfer across novel tasks and environments.

To this end, we propose to learn Motion Primitives for Action Composition and Transfer (M-PACT), a framework that learns localized primitive motions from human videos by factorizing transferable interaction structure from scene- and embodiment-specific realizations. This factorization allows individual primitives to be transferred across embodiments and compositionally reused across tasks and environments. At its core, a self-supervised motion segmentation module, SkillSeg, partitions 3D human hand trajectories using frame-level kinematic cues,
and maps the resulting segments into an embodiment-agnostic vocabulary of primitive-motion tokens, by Embodied Primitive Motion Tokenization (EPMT) module. Learned from web-scale egocentric video corpora, EPMT transforms abundant, behaviorally diverse, and cost-effective human pose trajectories into reusable manipulation primitives.
We then condition these primitive representations on contextual features from visual foundation models and perform lightweight fine-tuning using labeled video-motion-action data, enabling M-PACT to select, compose, and realize primitives for diverse manipulation tasks. By separating reusable motion structure from task-specific context and robot-specific control, our approach substantially reduces the need for costly robot demonstrations while improving generalization across tasks and scenes. In summary, our contributions are threefold:

We propose to learn a motion tokenizer, EPMT that discovers localized, embodiment-agnostic primitive motions from human hand trajectories. Trained on low-cost, web-scale hand-pose data extracted from egocentric videos, EPMT learns primitive tokens that can be reused for skill transfer across embodiments.

We introduce M-PACT, a multi-stage transfer framework that integrates EPMT with context-aware visual representations to select and compose primitive tokens and ground them into embodiment-specific, robot-executable actions. This design supports manipulation tasks of varying horizons with lightweight fine-tuning on labeled video-motion-action data.

We evaluate motion reconstruction, cross-dataset representation reuse, humanoid decoder adaptation, and contextual primitive prediction across three datasets, complemented by qualitative real-world humanoid demonstrations.

1. We propose to learn a motion tokenizer, EPMT that discovers localized, embodiment-agnostic primitive motions from human hand trajectories. Trained on low-cost, web-scale hand-pose data extracted from egocentric videos, EPMT learns primitive tokens that can be reused for skill transfer across embodiments.

2. We introduce M-PACT, a multi-stage transfer framework that integrates EPMT with context-aware visual representations to select and compose primitive tokens and ground them into embodiment-specific, robot-executable actions. This design supports manipulation tasks of varying horizons with lightweight fine-tuning on labeled video-motion-action data.

3. We evaluate motion reconstruction, cross-dataset representation reuse, humanoid decoder adaptation, and contextual primitive prediction across three datasets, complemented by qualitative real-world humanoid demonstrations.

title: Spiking Neuromorphic Control for Periodic Orbits Stabilization in Underactuated Robots: A Greedy Lyapunov-Based Approach
authors: Maksim Surov,Oleg Sumenkov
abstract: This work investigates the use of event-based spiking controllers, implemented as spiking neural networks, for trajectory tracking in underactuated robots. Specifically, we address the problem of stabilizing a prescribed periodic orbit. It is well known that, by applying the method of transverse linearization to the robot dynamics in a neighborhood of a periodic trajectory, the dynamics can be approximately described by a linear time-varying system with periodic coefficients (a periodic LTV system). The problem of orbital stabilization can therefore be reduced to stabilizing the trivial solution of this LTV system. We show that a previously proposed Lyapunov-based greedy design, originally developed for LTI systems, can also be extended to the corresponding linearized transverse dynamics, which take the form of a periodic LTV system. This enables the construction of a feedback controller for orbital stabilization of the robot. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated on the trajectory stabilization problem for the butterfly robot.
introduction:
Neuromorphic control is an emerging paradigm in control systems engineering, inspired by the event-driven information processing of the human brain. Although the underlying principles of spike-based computation and neuromorphic engineering date back to the 1990s [1, 2], their application to control systems has gained renewed attention in recent years, with successful experimental demonstrations reported, for example, in [3, 4]. Thus, spike-based control shows potential for energy-efficient, robust, and computationally simple control, motivating further investigation of its use in control systems.

Despite this progress, a significant gap remains between practical implementations and the theoretical justification of neuromorphic control systems. Several studies in neuromorphic control [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12], among others, have addressed this gap by developing stability analysis tools for event-driven systems.

In particular, for LTI systems, several approaches have recently been proposed. The emulation-based approach [8, 13, 11] uses integrate-and-fire neurons with fixed-amplitude spikes and provides practical stability guarantees for the resulting closed-loop system. An alternative, referred to as the greedy Lyapunov-based approach [10, 12], generates neuron spikes according to a local minimization principle, enabling Lyapunov-based stability analysis of the resulting hybrid closed-loop dynamics.

Building on recent results for LTI systems [12], we extend spiking neuromorphic control, in which the control input is represented as a sum of constant-amplitude spikes, to the stabilization of periodic orbits in underactuated robots. This control problem arises in many robotic and engineering applications, including walking bipeds [14], pendulum-like systems [15], spacecraft [16], and others. Several approaches have been developed to address this problem, including transverse linearization [17], energy shaping [18], eigenmanifold stabilization [19], and many others. The underactuated nature of these systems, with fewer control signals than degrees of freedom, makes the stabilization problem challenging. Moreover, when the control signals are restricted to sums of constant-amplitude spikes, it is not immediately clear whether the tracking problem admits a solution or what stabilization properties can be achieved with this type of controller in principle.

This paper demonstrates that a spiking neuromorphic controller emitting fixed-amplitude pulses can achieve practical stabilization of a reference periodic orbit. We show that the dynamics of a robot with spiking inputs can be approximated by a hybrid system expressed in local transverse coordinates near the target orbit, reducing the original problem to the stabilization of an auxiliary hybrid LTV system. To stabilize this auxiliary system, we employ the greedy Lyapunov-based approach originally developed for LTI systems [12]. Building on this framework, we provide a constructive design procedure for spiking neuromorphic controllers and establish practical stability of the reference orbit. The approach is experimentally validated on a butterfly robot testbed.

The paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the problem statement and preliminaries on orbital stability and transverse linearization. Section III presents the main result on greedy Lyapunov-based spiking neuromorphic control design. Section IV presents experimental results on the stabilization of a periodic motion of a butterfly robot using a spiking neuromorphic controller. Finally, Section V concludes the paper.

title: KEPT: Conformal Keepouts Kept in Planning for Enclosed-Space Navigation in Degraded Sensing
authors: Eric Minwoo Kim,Jong-Kook Kim
abstract:
Autonomous vehicles in enclosed spaces such as tunnels and mines rely on range maps that smoke, dust and fog make inaccurate.
Conformal prediction calibrates a keepout around the mapped walls that covers the true unsafe set at a chosen probability.
Typically an unmodified planner treats the keepout as an inflated obstacle, and nothing ensures that the vehicle can stop before the keepout as it moves when sensing degrades.
In narrow passages this margin and the planner’s buffer close the route, and existing remedies recover reach by relaxing the coverage level.
This paper conditions the conformal margin on a label-free severity estimate to hold coverage near its target as degradation varies.
A planning and control layer enforces one braking-distance condition on the keepout at plan time and at every command, takes the measured tracking residual as its only margin and never alters the keepout.
The keepout is validated on ground-robot smoke recordings and the closed loop in simulated quadrotor flights in a foggy tunnel against the standard deployment.
In closed-loop simulation the proposed system substantially reduces entries into the calibrated keepout and reaches numerically more goals than the deployment pattern in both calibration regimes, an observed gain of 3.2 percentage points pooled whose per-regime confidence intervals include zero. The per-class keepout holds its coverage near the target on held-out recordings.
introduction:
Autonomous vehicles in tunnels, mines and collapsed structures navigate narrow passages on range maps that smoke, dust and fog make inaccurate [1, 2, 3].
Conformal prediction calibrates a keepout around the mapped walls that covers each point of the true unsafe set at a chosen probability without a noise model [4, 5].
This coverage concerns the map, whereas staying out of the keepout and reaching the goal depend on planning and control.

In the usual deployment the planner treats the conformal set as an obstacle [6, 7, 8] and keeps its own clearance buffer and collision check [9, 10].
In a narrow passage the buffer can close routes the keepout leaves open, and neither safeguard budgets the braking distance to a keepout that grows as degradation reveals walls late.
Remedies lower the confidence level until a plan exists [8, 11] or soften the constraint into a cost [12, 13], giving up coverage or compliance.
Conformal barrier filters act only at the command [14, 15], and plan-and-command checks target the motion of other agents [13, 16].

Unlike these approaches, the proposed framework, KEPT (keepout enforcement in planning and tracking), leaves the keepout and its confidence level unchanged and enforces one braking-distance condition on it at plan time and at every command.
Its components, conformal calibration, barrier functions and the planner, are established [4, 17, 9], and the contributions lie in how the margin is conditioned, where the condition acts and what is measured.
KEPT calibrates a one-sided bound on the LiDAR distance error and uses the resulting keepout in planning and in command filtering.
By the robust-constraint argument of Lindemann et al. [6], adapted to perception error, an executed cell outside the keepout lies outside the true unsafe set whenever its perception error satisfies the calibrated bound.
Statistical coverage at executed queries and the compliance of the vehicle set the scope of this implication and are treated separately.

A keepout whose conformal margin is calibrated offline per severity class, and run-time margin selection, which picks the margin for each viewing direction and sweep from a label-free severity estimate. Coverage stays near target as fog varies around the vehicle and along the route, unlike a pooled margin [7] or adaptive conformal inference [18, 19], which needs online error feedback. Per-class validity is tested on ground-robot smoke recordings.

The planning layer of KEPT, the planning and execution component that lets the framework use its calibrated keepout during navigation. It coordinates trajectory planning and command-level safety filtering by holding both to consistent constraints on the same certified keepout, which is never relaxed. The vehicle thereby enters the keepout in markedly fewer flights and reaches numerically more goals, a joint outcome obtained inside the certificate rather than by weakening it.

A closed-loop evaluation of simulated quadrotor flights in which a keepout calibrated on real or simulated data is replayed identically for every stack, measuring executed keepout entries, reach and coverage on the same cells against the conformal deployment pattern and each enforcement point alone. Compliance improves substantially and observed pooled reach is numerically higher.
