title: Retrieve to Act: Motion Primitive Graph Retrieval for Robust VLA Execution
authors: Pham Tri Quang,Bao-Ngoc Dao,Minh Duc Nguyen,Duc-Duy Nguyen,Hung T. Ho,Linh Dang Le,Trong-Bao Ho,Thien-Loc Ha,Tan Q. Nguyen,Tuan Dam,Vu N. Duong,Daniel Sonntag,Ngan Le,Khoa D. Doan,Jan Peters,An Thai Le,Duy M. H. Nguyen,Vien Anh Ngo
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies demonstrate remarkable semantic generalization, yet remain highly vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) visual shifts during execution. While existing test-time methods attempt to suppress spurious visual cues, they fundamentally overlook the rich, uncorrupted kinematic priors embedded in the policy’s own training experience. We introduce Retrieve to Act (R2A), a test-time scaling framework that formulates OOD robustness purely as a geometric motion primitive retrieval problem. R2A bypasses fragile visual features by structuring successful training demonstrations into an offline spatiotemporal motion primitive graph. During inference, a query-dependent Graph Neural Network dynamically localizes the robot’s ongoing execution within this graph, retrieving structurally compatible future motion primitives. These retrieved geometric priors are then seamlessly harmonized with the frozen VLA’s predicted actions via a learned, dimension-wise gating mechanism, adaptively rectifying erroneous spatial trajectories while preserving the policy’s local reactivity. Extensive experiments across three state-of-the-art VLA architectures, GR00T N1.7, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and StableVLA, demonstrate that R2A consistently and significantly enhances robustness against diverse contextual perturbations. R2A achieves absolute success rate improvements of up to +12% in simulation benchmarks (LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin2.0-Plus) and +40% in real-world deployments, without requiring any finetuning of the base policies.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models pretrained on large-scale datasets demonstrate remarkable semantic generalization, seamlessly interpreting novel instructions and adapting to diverse tasks (Black et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025). However, this semantic capability often masks a severe kinematic fragility: even minor out-of-distribution (OOD) visual shifts, such as an altered camera angle, a novel background texture, or changed lighting, can cause catastrophic execution failures (Fei et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025). Under these conditions, the underlying task semantics remain identical, yet the policy’s action generation diverges wildly from safe trajectories. This reveals a critical bottleneck for real-world deployment: while pretrained VLAs know what to achieve, their over-reliance on perturbation-sensitive visual features causes them to easily lose track of how to physically execute the task.

A natural approach to improving robustness is to finetune pretrained policies with augmented datasets that explicitly expose the models to perturbed conditions (Xu et al., 2026a; Guo et al., 2026). However, exhaustively curating data and finetuning across the infinite long-tail of real-world environmental variations is both costly and practically impossible. Meanwhile, recent test-time scaling methods attempt to improve robustness without modifying model parameters by emphasizing task-relevant visual cues (Hancock et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a), adapting via in-context information (Jang et al., 2026; Sridhar et al., 2025), or steering action generation away from undesirable behaviors (Liu et al., 2026b; Nguyen et al., 2026a). While these approaches help mitigate the influence of visual noise or steer policies away from failure states, they fundamentally ignore a powerful asset: the policy’s own successful training experience. The precise motion patterns, spatial relationships, and temporal transitions required to solve the task are already embedded in the training demonstrations. The challenge is that contextual perturbations obscure the correspondence between the current OOD observation and these learned motion primitives, preventing the policy from reusing its own prior successes.

Retrieval offers a natural mechanism to recall this prior experience, but applying flat retrieval to robotic trajectories is notoriously difficult. Prior robot-learning methods often retrieve demonstrations based on affordance similarity (Kuang et al., 2024), motion correspondence (Lin et al., 2024a), or trajectory conditioning (Park et al., 2026). However, demonstrations are not isolated visual snapshots; they are highly structured spatiotemporal executions (Xu et al., 2026b). Standard retrieval methods that match visual embeddings fail to capture this sequential geometry, conflating two distinct problems: where does the current execution lie within the trajectory space, and what specific motion primitive should follow? To recover from an OOD-induced error, a retrieval mechanism must dynamically align the robot’s ongoing geometric context with the underlying structure of prior demonstrations, entirely independent of visual noise.

To bridge this gap, we introduce R2A (Retrieve to Act), a test-time scaling framework that formulates OOD robustness purely as a geometric experience retrieval problem. R2A bypasses fragile visual features by organizing successful training demonstrations into an offline motion primitive graph. Nodes encode the pure kinematic geometry of past executions (poses, states, and frame-wise changes), while edges capture the spatiotemporal transitions across and within tasks. At the onset of an episode, a diffusion-based rectification module first projects any out-of-distribution initial robot states back into the established training manifold. During continuous execution, R2A then utilizes a query-dependent Graph Neural Network (GNN) to dynamically propagate the VLA’s current kinematic trajectory through the graph. This explicitly localizes the robot’s current progress and retrieves the most structurally compatible future motion primitives. A learned harmonization module then adaptively weight-fuses this retrieved geometric prior with the VLA’s predicted actions. By doing so, R2A seamlessly rectifies erroneous trajectories caused by visual OOD shifts, restoring successful motion patterns without altering the frozen VLA parameters.

We evaluate R2A across three diverse VLA architectures, including GR00T N1.7 (Bjorck et al., 2025), π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025), and StableVLA (Fu et al., 2026), under seven types of systematic perturbations in LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025). R2A consistently improves the robustness of all three policies, achieving gains of up to +12%+12\% in success rate. We further evaluate π0.5\pi_{0.5} on the challenging RoboTwin2.0-Plus benchmark (Zhang et al., 2026c) where R2A improves the success rate from 56.8%56.8\% to 66.2%66.2\%. On a real-world task with Aloha embodiment, R2A similarly achieves up to a 40%40\% improvement in success rate over the corresponding base policies, demonstrating substantial gains in physical deployment.

title: Remember Where You Walk: Learning Spatial Memory for End-to-End Legged Robot Exploration
authors: Leon Magnus,Nico Bohlinger,Jan Peters,Oleg Arenz
abstract:
Humanoids and other legged robots operating in complex environments must remember information that leaves their field of view and only becomes relevant much later. Reinforcement learning policies address this using memory networks such as LSTMs that are trained end-to-end with the policy to memorize such task-relevant aspects. Yet, such architectures often fail to preserve sufficient information over long horizons. In this work, we propose a network architecture based on Hadamard memory that specifically targets robot navigation. Our Local Spatial Matrix Memory (LSMM) enables RL agents to store generic task-relevant information at specific, position-based memory cells, enabling flexible and spatially grounded memorization. We evaluate LSMM on the task of autonomous maze exploration, where it matches the maze coverage of strong recurrent and
finite-history baselines while being the only architecture that
remembers the maze layout, reducing the reconstruction error threefold. We provide videos and code for our experiments at: https://leonmgns.github.io/RememberWhereYouWalkWebiste/
introduction:
Thanks to breakthroughs in Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), legged robots can now traverse rough terrain, jump over obstacles, and navigate toward goal positions using policies trained in highly-parallelized simulations or directly in the real world [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].
These policies usually follow velocity commands or short-horizon waypoints [6, 7], leaving the higher level planning to a human operator and making the system not fully autonomous.
Autonomous exploration of an unknown environment is a fundamentally different problem.
Now, the robot must not only reason and control its body in a local frame, but also decide where to go and remember where it has already been, to navigate and explore efficiently [8].
This turns locomotion into a long-horizon partially observable navigation problem in which the current local observation is not enough [9].

Memory-augmented policies address this problem by leveraging an observation-action history with architectures such as Long Short-Term Memorys (LSTMs) [10], Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) [11], Transformers [12], or simply concatenating history for an Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) [13].
However, unstructured recurrent states, through LSTMs or GRUs, easily mix or overwrite spatially distinct information, as credit-assignment is tricky, and finite-context approaches, like Transformers or concatenation, discard old observations in less than a second with the typical history lengths [13, 14].
Classical navigation systems avoid this problem by explicitly registering and using observations in spatial maps, but typically separate mapping, planning, and locomotion into individual components, losing out on potential end-to-end efficiency [15, 16, 17].

In this work, we introduce LSMM and evaluate it for end-to-end maze exploration.
The layout of our matrix memory is aligned with the environment’s frame and indexed using a position estimate.
At every step, the policy modifies only a small window in the memory around the robot’s position through learned calibration and update matrices, while the rest of the memory is not updated.
A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) [18] encoder transforms the spatial memory into features used by both the policy and an auxiliary maze-reconstruction head.
This combines the information persistence of index-based updates and the locality of map-based navigation with learned latent representations and end-to-end locomotion control, without any explicit path planning or waypoint commands.

We formulate long-horizon, goal-free maze exploration as an end-to-end locomotion problem.
We train our method for the Unitree Go2 quadruped in procedurally generated mazes and compare LSMM against unstructured recurrent and finite-history architectures.
Our experiments provide comprehensive empirical evaluations in simulation and deployment in the real-world, demonstrating LSMM’s capabilities on maze reconstruction, exploration efficiency, robustness to localization noise, and generalization to unseen mazes.

title: A Bi-level Co-design Framework for Lunar Monoped with 2D Jump and Landing Control
authors: Sanjay Ramkumar,Suraj Kumar
abstract: Legged robots for lunar exploration must be designed for low gravity where reduced contact forces and long flight phases make the leg morphology and controller choice interdependent. We study this for a planar monoped in lunar gravity (1.625 m/s21.625\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{/}\mathrm{s}^{2}) with a bi-level co-design framework: a differential evolution outer loop searches over link lengths, and each candidate is evaluated on a vertical jump by either a Quadratic program based task-space controller (QP-TSC) or a direct-collocation based trajectory optimization. The two controllers differ on the optimal link lengths : trajectory optimization outperforms the QP-TSC across most of the design space (by 17% in Cost of Transport (COT) at their respective optimums). We then extend to a 2D jump, where trajectory optimization with centroidal angular momentum regulation produces stable in-place and forward jumps, and an LQR controller absorbs impact and stabilizes the robot after touchdown, demonstrated on a baseline morphology (both links 0.3 m).
introduction:
Legged robots are a candidate for exploring lunar terrain where wheeled rovers cannot reach, and in low gravity the most efficient gaits are those with long flight phases, as in hopping and pronking [1, 2]. This same property makes control harder. When flight phases are long relative to stance, attitude cannot be regulated through ground reaction forces alone, so angular momentum acquired at take-off must be handled during flight to avoid a crash landing [3].

The central question we try to answer is whether the optimal leg morphology of a lunar hopper depends on the controller used to evaluate it. We study it in a vertical (1D) jump of a planar monoped in lunar gravity. A bi-level framework searches over link lengths with differential evolution, and each candidate is evaluated by one of two inner controllers: a QP-TSC or a direct-collocation trajectory optimizer.

A vertical jump hides the problems that dominate in practice: pitch, horizontal motion, and landing. We therefore also develop a planar (2D) jump and landing controller. A trajectory optimization that regulates centroidal angular momentum produces in-place and forward jumps, and an LQR controller absorbs the impact and stabilizes the robot after touchdown in simulation. We characterize the landing’s region of attraction empirically over touchdown conditions, since formal estimation for hybrid legged systems is difficult because of contact resets [4].

title: How Much Can Best-of-N Help a World Action Model? Measuring Selectable Headroom and Realizing It in Closed Loop
authors: Haojia Gao,Yue Cao,Yumin Liu,Haohua Que,Mingkai Liu,Guanqiu Guo,Zhuo Zou,Bokui Chen,Xueqian Wang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict the visual consequences of the actions they generate, which makes test-time selection a natural way to improve a fixed policy: imagine the futures of candidate actions and execute the best one. The benefit of selection is bounded by the selectable headroom, how much better the best candidate truly is, but the standard estimate, which executes each candidate once and keeps the best outcome, conflates candidate quality with the randomness of everything that follows. We introduce a denoised counterfactual protocol, based on bitwise-reproducible branching, repeated continuations, held-out oracles, and common random numbers, that measures the headroom a selector can realize, and use its measurements to build a fail-gated selector. Across four WAMs, two benchmarks, over 100,000 branched rollouts, and pre-registered tests, we find that (i) the standard estimate overstates the selectable headroom of native samples: bounds from 17 continuations per candidate place its selectable share between 24% and 66% for three WAMs; (ii) structured action perturbations create up to 16 points of selectable headroom; and (iii) in both WAMs with action-conditioned imagination, imagined futures carry candidate-outcome information with no detectable loss relative to real futures, information that the value head of Cosmos Policy leaves unused. Deviating from the policy chunk only when a readout of the WAM predicts failure, the selector raises closed-loop task success from 76.9% to 81.6% on held-out episodes of training tasks, with the largest gain where the policy fails most often, and from 62.6% to 69.8% on unseen tasks.
introduction:
World action models, which extend video-prediction policies and joint video-action models [11, 50, 21, 29, 58], jointly produce an action chunk, a prediction of the scene after the chunk is executed, and an estimate of its value [25]. This structure makes a simple form of test-time compute available to any WAM: sample several candidate chunks, imagine where each of them leads, and execute the chunk whose imagined future looks best. Sampling-and-verification schemes of this kind, established for reasoning with language models [9, 33, 45], have improved vision-language-action (VLA [24, 5]) policies [27, 36, 23, 28], and verifiers specific to WAMs have been proposed [56, 55].

How much can such selection gain? The answer is fixed before any scorer is chosen: the gain is bounded by how much better the best candidate in the pool truly is. We call this quantity the selectable headroom. Yuan et al. [53] measure it directly with counterfactual branching. They restore the same simulator state, execute each of 16 sampled candidates, continue each candidate with the policy until the episode ends, and find that choosing the candidate with the best outcome would raise success from 68.9% to 79.2%, whereas learned values, image similarity, and VLM judgments recover little of this gain.

This estimate executes each candidate once. Everything that happens after the candidate, including every later policy query, is random, so the candidate with the best realized outcome is partly the candidate whose continuation happened to go well. Selecting and scoring on the same random draw is the optimizer’s curse [44], the same bias that double estimators remove in reinforcement learning [48]. The question that matters for selection is therefore how much of the oracle gain a selector could ever realize.

We answer this question with a denoised counterfactual protocol (Fig. 2a). Every candidate is executed from a bitwise-reproducible simulator snapshot and continued several times. The realizable part of the headroom is measured by a held-out oracle that selects on some continuations and is scored on others; a variance decomposition separates the effect of the candidate from its interaction with the continuation; and every evaluator is run with common random numbers, so that all candidates are compared under the same evaluation randomness. Using more than 100,000 branched rollouts of four WAMs, namely Cosmos Policy [25], Flex-π\pi [51], Fast-WAM [54], and Streaming-WAM [22], on RoboCasa [37] and LIBERO-Plus [14], we establish the following results, each supported by pre-registered tests.

The single-continuation oracle is dominated by continuation randomness (Sec. 5.1). Under the protocol of Yuan et al. [53], we reproduce a 12.3-point oracle gain, yet a selector that observes three independent outcomes per candidate realizes only 9% of it on a fresh continuation, and 98% of the candidate-specific outcome variation is re-drawn when the continuation seeds change. The same holds for all four WAMs on LIBERO-Plus. With 17 continuations per candidate, the selectable share lies between 24% and 52% of the single-continuation oracle for Cosmos Policy and between a third and two thirds for Flex-π\pi and Fast-WAM (Fig. 1).

The single-continuation oracle is dominated by continuation randomness (Sec. 5.1). Under the protocol of Yuan et al. [53], we reproduce a 12.3-point oracle gain, yet a selector that observes three independent outcomes per candidate realizes only 9% of it on a fresh continuation, and 98% of the candidate-specific outcome variation is re-drawn when the continuation seeds change. The same holds for all four WAMs on LIBERO-Plus. With 17 continuations per candidate, the selectable share lies between 24% and 52% of the single-continuation oracle for Cosmos Policy and between a third and two thirds for Flex-π\pi and Fast-WAM (Fig. 1).

Structured proposals create selectable headroom (Sec. 5.2). Native samples are nearly identical and offer almost no selectable headroom over the policy chunk, whereas displacing the policy chunk along the robot axes creates headroom of which 67–95% survives held-out evaluation for all four WAMs. This headroom lies where the policy chunk fails, and it exceeds the chunk by 4.5–16 points on both benchmarks and for all four WAMs.

The imagination carries the signal that the value head misses (Sec. 5.3). On both WAMs with action-conditioned imagination, a linear readout of the imagined future ranks candidates with no detectable loss relative to the same readout of the real future; for Cosmos Policy, the signal resides in the predicted consequence rather than in the encoding of the action. The value head, although accurate at the state level (AUROC 0.90), recovers almost none of this signal.

A selector built on the findings improves on the policy (Sec. 5.4). A learned failure gate decides whether to deviate from the policy chunk, and a learned ranker decides where to go, so the selector deviates only where the policy is likely to fail, which is where the headroom lies, and executes the policy chunk unchanged everywhere else. Frozen and pre-registered, it raises closed-loop task success from 76.9% to 81.6% on reserved episodes of the training tasks, by 10.7 points where the policy fails most often, and, when re-trained without the test tasks, from 62.6% to 69.8% on unseen tasks.

These results show when test-time selection can help a WAM: the headroom worth pursuing is created by proposals that displace the policy chunk rather than by native samples, the imagined futures of the model already carry information that ranks these proposals, and what is missing is a readout trained to compare sibling actions rather than to value states. Together, the results give a concrete recipe for test-time compute in a WAM: spend it on consequential proposals at states where the policy is likely to fail, score them with readouts trained on branch outcomes, and use the held-out oracle, at the cost of one extra continuation per candidate, to know in advance how much a selector can gain. We package the protocol and the branching data as HeadroomBench (Sec. 6), which will be publicly released.

The same holds for all four WAMs on LIBERO-Plus. With 17 continuations per candidate, the selectable share lies between 24% and 52% of the single-continuation oracle for Cosmos Policy and between a third and two thirds for Flex-π\pi and Fast-WAM (Fig. 1).

2. Structured proposals create selectable headroom (Sec. 5.2). Native samples are nearly identical and offer almost no selectable headroom over the policy chunk, whereas displacing the policy chunk along the robot axes creates headroom of which 67–95% survives held-out evaluation for all four WAMs. This headroom lies where the policy chunk fails, and it exceeds the chunk by 4.5–16 points on both benchmarks and for all four WAMs.

3. The imagination carries the signal that the value head misses (Sec. 5.3). On both WAMs with action-conditioned imagination, a linear readout of the imagined future ranks candidates with no detectable loss relative to the same readout of the real future; for Cosmos Policy, the signal resides in the predicted consequence rather than in the encoding of the action. The value head, although accurate at the state level (AUROC 0.90), recovers almost none of this signal.

4. A selector built on the findings improves on the policy (Sec. 5.4). A learned failure gate decides whether to deviate from the policy chunk, and a learned ranker decides where to go, so the selector deviates only where the policy is likely to fail, which is where the headroom lies, and executes the policy chunk unchanged everywhere else. Frozen and pre-registered, it raises closed-loop task success from 76.9% to 81.6% on reserved episodes of the training tasks, by 10.7 points where the policy fails most often, and, when re-trained without the test tasks, from 62.6% to 69.8% on unseen tasks.

title: Acoustic Signature Optimisation for Bioinspired Flapping-Wing Micro Aerial Vehicles
authors: Yi Lun Duh,Krispin C. V. Broers,Sophie F. Armanini
abstract:
Flapping-wing micro air vehicles are prized for quiet flight, yet the few existing measurements show engineered wings to be 15–30 dB louder than the animals they imitate.
This paper investigates two passive geometric approaches to reduce the acoustic signature of a flapping membrane wing, and applies these to an exemplary wing.
A significant sound source in flapping wings is the impulsive click radiated at stroke reversal, when a slack membrane snaps between two curvatures. Our first noise-reduction approach optimises the wing’s venation layout, based on an analytical model of the reversal click as a dynamic snap-through of the membrane.
The optimised venation pattern was manufactured and resulted in a reduction of up to 8 dB during the reversal snap in experiments.
During testing, the venation was found to be sensitive to orientation rather than thickness.
Secondly, an additive trailing-edge fringe inspired by hummingbird feathers was shown to further reduce the broadband swoosh by 3–4 dB at no lift cost, matching a cut serration wing without removing lifting area.
introduction:
Micro aerial vehicles are increasingly deployed in confined, cluttered spaces shared with people and wildlife, where safety and unobtrusiveness matter as much as endurance. Flapping-wing micro aerial vehicles (FWMAVs) suit such settings well, because their wings are light and compliant and the wingtips slow to a stop at each stroke reversal, so a collision carries far less energy than the fast, stiff rotor of a comparable multirotor [1]. This ability to operate safely in tight spaces makes FWMAVs attractive for tasks such as infrastructure inspection, wildlife observation and indoor monitoring. Tasks that operate close to animals or people, in particular, benefit directly from quiet flight and an unobtrusive vehicle. Low acoustic emission is repeatedly cited as a key advantage of flapping over rotary-wing flight, yet the claim is rarely tested. Across the FWMAV literature, only a handful of studies measure noise at all [2, 3, 4, 5], and two recent comprehensive FWMAV reviews compare flight time, mass, mechatronics, control and autonomy, but neither reports the acoustic signature of a single platform [1, 6].

The few available measurements contradict the assumption of quietness [1, 2, 3]. E.g., a Mylar-membrane wing on carbon rods was found to emit 68.8 dBA at 10 Hz in Ref. [3], and the Nano Hummingbird produced 79.7 dBA at 42.5 Hz, compared to the 40–50 dB produced by a live hummingbird [2]. Engineered flapping wings are therefore 15–30 dB louder than the animals they imitate. Keennon et al. also found, that most of the noise is produced at stroke reversal, when the large angular acceleration makes the membrane “pop through from the fore-stroke configuration to the aft-stroke configuration in an unstructured and violent manner,” likened to a sail snapping as a yacht tacks [2]. This impulsive event, which we call the reversal snap, occurs twice per cycle and was reaffirmed by Wu et al. [5], yet no subsequent design has set out to suppress it.

How a wing turns its motion into sound explains why this event is so loud and how it might be quietened. During flapping, an unsteady surface force pushes on the surrounding air. The time derivative of that force radiates to the far field [7]. A wing is quiet when its push on the air is smooth and loud when that push changes abruptly, as it does when the membrane snaps through. Clark [8] catalogues several mechanisms by which a flapping wing emits sound, and two of these dominate for a membrane FWMAV.

The first is the broadband swoosh radiated by the vortical flow shed near the trailing edge, which is controlled by the shape of that edge, or its serration.
The second is the bistable snap, whose radiated sound is the atonal reversal click, produced when a slack membrane cannot carry the reversal inertia in tension and instead inverts its curvature. The strength of the click is set by the bending stiffness of the membrane and by how that stiffness is distributed, which a layout of bonded carbon stiffeners, known as the wing venation, can reshape.

Existing work suggests that the membrane and the edge both influence the noise, but existing work has not attempted to use either the venation layout or the edge geometry to reduce noise.
Lu et al. [3] cut perceived noise by 12 dBA by replacing the Mylar membrane with a dielectric elastomer, and Debiasi et al. [4] reduced membrane rustling by tensioning it with bonded stiffeners, a structural effect since a tensioned sheet cannot snap through. Wu et al. [5] provide the most detailed measurement to date, finding the wings rather than the transmission to dominate and to radiate as a stroke-plane dipole. They assign low-, mid- and high-frequency content to aerodynamic loading, transmission resonance and membrane flutter with vortex shedding, with the pitching phase near reversal identified as the primary noise generator.

These two design variables are themselves well studied, but for performance rather than for sound. Insect wings are stiffened membranes whose venation sets how a wing of a given size distributes its stiffness [9], and flapping freshly cut insect wings in helium show that fluid forces barely affect wing bending, which supports a damped structural model with no fluid loading [10]. Building on this, venation and graded rigidity have been optimised for lift, thrust and efficiency [11, 12, 13, 14], but never as an acoustic variable. Edge serrations are equally well characterised on rigid geometries, where the fixed-wing airfoil literature shows sawtooth cuts reducing broadband scattering noise by a few decibels, improving with tooth height until they saturate [15, 16], and Ji et al. [17] report up to 6.8 dB reduction on a rigid flapping-wing in hover. Serrations on a flexible membrane wing under flapping loads have, to our knowledge, not been studied. The reversal click and the trailing-edge swoosh are therefore identified noise sources, and the venation layout and the edge serration are geometric variables that could be set to reduce the noise sources without active actuation.

In this paper, we propose a wing design framework (see Fig. 1) for acoustically optimising flapping wings utilising an integrated wing layout manufacturing process.
This process enables the implementation of a venation layout optimisation loop, which is combined with an experimentally optimised trailing-edge fringe design, addressing both main sources of noise in the flapping wing.
Our main contributions to lowering the acoustic signature of flapping-wing robots are the following:

Venation layout optimisation model for improved acoustic signature during stroke reversal.

Venation layout optimisation model for improved acoustic signature during stroke reversal.

Bioinspired trailing-edge fringes as an additive membrane pattern reducing the wing’s aerodynamic swoosh noise.

Integrated manufacturing approach allowing design freedom in wing shape and venation layout.

Experimental investigation of the proposed wing design framework using a microphone and load cell test setup.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows: In Sec. II, the proposed wing design framework and its strategies for noise reduction are described. Sec. III explains the architecture of the acoustic optimisation model. The experimental evaluation of the mitigation strategies is then presented in Sec. IV, followed by the conclusions in Sec. V.

1. Venation layout optimisation model for improved acoustic signature during stroke reversal.

2. Bioinspired trailing-edge fringes as an additive membrane pattern reducing the wing’s aerodynamic swoosh noise.

3. Integrated manufacturing approach allowing design freedom in wing shape and venation layout.

4. Experimental investigation of the proposed wing design framework using a microphone and load cell test setup.

title: From 12 to 200 Demonstrations: How ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA and $π_{0.5}$ Scale on a Low-Cost Arm
authors: Simon Cowling
abstract: We trained four widely used imitation-learning policies, ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA and π0.5\pi_{0.5}, on nested subsets of 12, 25, 50, 100 and 200 teleoperated demonstrations of one pick-and-place task with distractor objects, using one fixed training recipe per policy. Every trained model was then run on a physical SO-101 arm on a fixed set of object placements: 1,340 scored episodes in 126 blocks.
introduction:
Low-cost arms and open-source software have made real-robot imitation learning accessible to small laboratories and individuals. A SO-101 arm costs a few hundred dollars in parts (Knight et al., 2024), and the LeRobot library (Cadene et al., 2024; Cadene et al., 2026) provides recording, training and evaluation for a range of policies behind one interface. Someone starting a new task therefore faces two practical questions at once: which policy to train, and how many demonstrations to record.

The literature does not answer either question well for this setting. Each policy was introduced on different robots, tasks and data volumes. ACT was shown with 50 demonstrations per task on a bimanual rig (Zhao et al., 2023), Diffusion Policy on a different set of simulated and real tasks (Chi et al., 2023), and the vision-language-action models SmolVLA (Shukor et al., 2025) and π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Black et al., 2025a) after pretraining on large multi-robot datasets. Pretrained models are expected to need fewer task demonstrations; models trained from scratch are cheaper to train and run. Recent benchmarks on low-cost arms compare several of these policies at one data size, or at a few sizes with twenty trials per model (Section 2), which is too few to say which differences are real.

This paper reports a controlled study of that question on one physical task. We recorded 225 teleoperated demonstrations of a pick-and-place task with two distractor objects, fixed nested subsets of 12, 25, 50, 100 and 200 demonstrations, and trained ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA and π0.5\pi_{0.5} on each subset with several training seeds. Every trained model was run on the arm on ten fixed object placements under a 30-second limit. In total we scored 1,340 episodes in 126 blocks over 17 days, and recorded joint states, commanded actions and both camera streams for every episode.

The contributions are:

Scaling curves for four policies on one physical task. Success against number of demonstrations from 12 to 200, with confidence intervals and a trend estimate for each policy, including a reversal of order between ACT trained from scratch and fine-tuned π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Section 4.1).

Scaling curves for four policies on one physical task. Success against number of demonstrations from 12 to 200, with confidence intervals and a trend estimate for each policy, including a reversal of order between ACT trained from scratch and fine-tuned π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Section 4.1).

A stage-by-stage account of failure taken from the recordings. Each episode is placed on a four-stage ladder using joint and wrist-camera data, which shows where each policy loses episodes and how that shifts with data (Section 4.2).

Initiation failure. Two of the four policies often never start moving. For Diffusion Policy we show by intervention on the training data that removing an idle lead-in from the start of the demonstrations removes the failure (Section 4.3).

Recipe sensitivity of π0.5\pi_{0.5}. Two fine-tuning recipes that differ in which weights are trained give 4% and 65% success across the same data budgets, a larger effect than the amount of data had for any policy except ACT (Section 4.4).

How much a block of ten episodes can tell you. Re-tests of the same checkpoint, a separation of seed-to-seed variation from measurement noise, and an audit of the operator’s scoring against the recordings (Sections 3.6 and 4.5).

The study has a narrow base and one structural confound, and both shape how the results should be read. We state them here; Section 7 gives the full list of limitations.

One task, one arm, one operator. The rankings are for this task and setup. We make no claim that they transfer to other tasks.

One task, one arm, one operator. The rankings are for this task and setup. We make no claim that they transfer to other tasks.

Recipes, not architectures. Each policy was trained with one fixed recipe, close to the library’s documented defaults. The comparison is between policies as a practitioner would typically run them, not between architectures at their best.

Fixed training length. The number of training steps was the same at every data budget, so a model trained on 200 demonstrations saw each frame about 17 times less often than one trained on 12. Where a curve flattens or falls at 100 and 200 demonstrations, this study cannot tell a ceiling from under-training (Section 5).

Testing was dimmer than training. Main-comparison blocks ran at roughly half the illuminance of the demonstrations. All policies faced this shift, though not to an identical degree.

title: RAVEN: A Unified Active SLAM System for Rapid Autonomous Visual Exploration with Aerial Robots under Localization Uncertainty
authors: Xinyi Chen,Yichen Zhang,Chenxing Jiang,Shaojie Shen
comment: Conditionally accepted to the IEEE Transactions on Robotics
abstract:
Active simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) addresses the problem of planning robot motion to build complete and accurate maps of unknown environments through efficient exploration while maintaining high localization accuracy.
This raises a dilemma between exploring unknown spaces to expand coverage and exploiting visited regions to perform active loop closures.
Despite numerous prior works on ground robots, aerial robots with high agility and constrained sensor suites face more significant localization drift and thereby demand dedicated active SLAM planning.
Moreover, a unified strategy that adapts performance based on task-specific priorities remains an open question.
In this article, we introduce RAVEN, a unified active SLAM framework for Rapid Autonomous Visual ExploratioN using quadrotors, which systematically accounts for localization uncertainty.
The framework starts with identifying frontiers and active loop closure candidates, from which global tour candidates are generated.
These candidates are evaluated using a utility vector that separately quantifies exploration efficiency and localization accuracy, and the final tour is selected according to a prioritization parameter ranging from [0,1][0,1].
Finally, a perception-aware navigation planner generates smooth execution trajectories that minimize visual state estimation error based on the online Fisher information field that provides visual localization information in real-time.
Benchmark evaluations demonstrate that RAVEN outperforms state-of-the-art active SLAM methods, highlighting its advantages in producing a spectrum of performance across prioritizations.
Fully onboard field experiments with a customized stereo-inertial quadrotor further validate its practical applicability in challenging environments.
The source code will be released to benefit the community.
introduction:
Aerial robots are increasingly deployed in a wide range of real-world applications, such as search and rescue [1], structural inspection [2], and 3D reconstruction [3], capitalizing on their superior maneuverability and versatility.
To achieve full autonomy in these applications, aerial robots must be capable of performing localization of themselves within the environment, mapping the traversed space, and planning subsequent navigation motions.

While the fundamental problem of simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) [4] often relies on passive operations, active perception [5, 6] introduces the paradigm of incorporating decision-making strategies to optimize sensor data acquisition for specific perceptual objectives.
As conceptually illustrated in Fig. 1, active localization [7] focuses on navigation strategies with the perceptual objective of enhancing the robot’s state estimation accuracy, typically assuming prior environmental knowledge.
Active mapping [8], often referred to as classic exploration, addresses the problem of complete environment coverage and map construction for unknown environments under ideal localization assumptions.
Unifying both perspectives, active SLAM [9] aims for the ultimate goal of constructing the most accurate and complete environmental map, through efficient exploration of the unknown environments while maintaining high localization accuracy.

Since the pioneering studies [5, 6], the increasing attention toward active SLAM has been producing research advances from diverse perspectives and methodologies.
One of the core challenges of active SLAM is the exploration-exploitation dilemma [12, 13], where the robot must balance two conflicting objectives: exploring unknown spaces to expand mapping coverage and exploiting previously visited regions to reduce localization uncertainty through loop closures.
Various metrics have been proposed to quantify these exploration and exploitation utilities based on information theory [14] or the theory of optimal experiment design [15].
However, the incompatible magnitudes of these fundamentally different quantities require careful manual tuning of weighting parameters for different environments, which is later circumvented by automatic balancing utility functions [16, 17].
Nevertheless, this implicit mechanism disregards user preferences on prioritizing either exploration efficiency or localization accuracy to meet specific task requirements.
Another challenge is that active SLAM frameworks for aerial robots remain relatively rare [18], despite extensive research on ground robots.
The high agility of aerial robots exacerbates localization drift, which can severely degrade map quality and increase the risk of loop closure failures.
Consequently, minimizing state estimation error during navigation execution is also crucial yet often neglected by existing active SLAM methods [19] that primarily focus on active loop closure.
Furthermore, aerial robots typically operate with constrained sensor suites and limited computational resources, necessitating active SLAM algorithms to balance performance with computational efficiency for real-time operation.
These aspects underscore the critical need for a systematic active SLAM framework for aerial exploration under localization uncertainty.

To bridge these gaps, this work introduces RAVEN, a unified active SLAM framework for Rapid Autonomous Visual ExploratioN in unknown environments using a stereo-inertial quadrotor.
This framework is designed to ensure exploration efficiency while accounting for localization uncertainty throughout the standard active SLAM planning workflow[18]: goal identification, utility evaluation, and action execution.
In the first phase, vantage points are identified, including frontiers [20] and active loop closure (ALC) candidates.
ALC candidates are carefully selected historical poses with high potential to establish valid loop closures that improve localization accuracy.
To extend the planning horizon beyond the next immediate goal, we generate global tour candidates that cover unexplored regions and integrate active loop closures.
In the second phase, these global tour candidates are evaluated using utility vectors that separately quantify the expected exploration duration and expected pose graph information.
Instead of combining these two objectives into a single utility function, this framework treats them as separate components and allows for user-defined prioritization ranging from [0,1][0,1].
This enables system flexibility in task-specific planning behavior and unifies the classical exploration problem into the active SLAM framework.
Finally, action execution toward the target goal from the selected global tour is performed with a perception-aware planner, which generates trajectories minimizing visual state estimation error.
To support real-time replanning, an online Fisher information field (OFIF) is incrementally constructed, allowing constant-time queries of the amount of information from observations at specific camera poses for visual odometry.
In summary, the proposed framework optimizes exploration motions that balance exploration efficiency and vehicle localization accuracy according to a user-defined prioritization, producing complete volumetric maps with task-specific accuracy in unknown environments.

We conduct extensive benchmark comparisons with state-of-the-art exploration planners [21, 16, 19, 22] using a lightweight simulator, demonstrating that RAVEN achieves a more effective balance between exploration efficiency and localization accuracy.
Real-world experiments conducted with a fully autonomous aerial robot further validate RAVEN’s practical applicability in challenging environments.
The source code will be released to benefit the community.
The contributions of the present work are as follows:

A systematic active SLAM framework designed for autonomous aerial exploration that comprehensively accounts for localization uncertainty throughout goal identification, utility evaluation, and action execution;

A systematic active SLAM framework designed for autonomous aerial exploration that comprehensively accounts for localization uncertainty throughout goal identification, utility evaluation, and action execution;

A trading-off mechanism to the exploration-exploitation dilemma, which eliminates the need for manual parameter tuning while allowing user-defined prioritization between exploration efficiency and localization accuracy;

An incrementally constructed online Fisher information field (OFIF) for constant-time queries of visual localization information at specific poses, which facilitates real-time replanning of the active SLAM pipeline;

Extensive validation through a lightweight simulator and fully onboard real-world experiments in challenging environments. The implementation will be released for reproducible benchmarking and further research.

title: GAWM: A Compact Latent World-Action Model for Multi-Task Robot Manipulation
authors: Yang Liu,Xiaoli Liu,Liuzhao Li,Yuduo Song,Muyuan Liu,Xiang Gao
abstract: World-action models (WAMs) incorporate the prediction of future observations into robot policy learning. However, most WAMs build on billion-parameter vision-language or video-generation backbones, which incur high training cost and inference latency. In this letter, we present GAWM (Geometry-Aware World Model), a compact multi-task WAM that predicts future observations in the latent space of a frozen DINOv3 encoder. GAWM compresses the features of each camera view into a small set of tokens. A lightweight predictor, conditioned on the task rather than on actions, forecasts these tokens at two future horizons. The forecast is supervised with the dense patch features of future frames, which requires it to encode the spatial layout of the future scene. An action decoder directly regresses a chunk of future actions from the current and predicted tokens. With fewer than 100M parameters and no robot or video pretraining, GAWM outperforms billion-parameter WAMs on RoboTwin 2.0 and performs comparably to billion-parameter VLAs on LIBERO. On a dual-arm robot, it achieves lower action-prediction error on held-out demonstrations than a fine-tuned billion-parameter VLA, with substantially lower inference latency. Ablation studies show that the latent world model substantially improves performance when training data or training time is limited. Code is available at https://github.com/gaoxiang12/ga-wm.
introduction:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have become a dominant paradigm for robot manipulation, transferring web-scale vision-language pretraining to action generation [1, 2, 3, 4]. Most VLAs, however, map the current observation directly to actions, without explicit supervision on how the scene will evolve. World-action models (WAMs) address this limitation by additionally predicting future observations [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11]. Some WAMs employ the prediction only as an auxiliary training target, whereas others condition the action generator on it at test time. Such foresight can provide the policy with an explicit representation of task progress, which is most beneficial when test scenes differ from the training data, e.g., under visual perturbations [12, 13, 14].

Most existing WAMs derive this foresight from large backbones. LingBot-VA, Motus and Fast-WAM build on the 5B-parameter video generator Wan 2.2 [30, 8, 31, 9], and LaWAM on a 2.1B-parameter VLA backbone [10]. The WAMs built on video generators predict future video frames and thus devote much of their capacity to appearance details irrelevant to control. Generating these frames also requires iterative denoising, which takes 4.5 s per query for LingBot-VA [10]. Such models are costly to train and difficult to deploy on onboard computers.

Many deployed robots lack the onboard computational resources to run such models. They typically perform a fixed set of tasks repeatedly, for which reliable, low-latency execution matters more than understanding open-ended instructions. Compact policies are well suited to this setting. They operate at high control rates on onboard computers and can be trained at low cost for a new task set. On closed task sets, their success rates are comparable to those of billion-parameter VLAs [29]. This motivates a hierarchical design [32, 33], in which a language model interprets instructions and selects the task, and a compact policy executes it. This letter focuses on the compact policy and asks whether it can benefit from foresight without a large backbone.

Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) offer a lightweight route to foresight, as they predict representations instead of pixels [34, 35]. Compact JEPA world models such as LeWM [36] and that of Liu et al. [37] rely on a small predictor. Their predictors, however, are conditioned on actions and support a planner that searches over candidate action sequences toward a goal image. Such planning not only limits the control rate, as the predictor must evaluate many candidates at every control step, but also requires a goal image to specify each task. A reactive policy, in contrast, avoids both costs by computing actions without search, which in turn requires a predictor that forecasts the future implied by the task rather than by candidate actions.

We present GAWM (Geometry-Aware World Model), a compact multi-task WAM that extends JEPA-style latent prediction to reactive control (Fig. 2). GAWM encodes each camera view into 64 tokens from multi-layer features of a frozen DINOv3 ViT-S encoder [38], as in LiLa-WAM [11]. A lightweight predictor, conditioned on a task code rather than on actions, forecasts these tokens at two future horizons in parallel. An action decoder in the style of Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) [39, 29] regresses an action chunk from the current tokens, the forecast, the robot state and the task code. As in LiLa-WAM, the forecast is supervised with the frozen encoder’s patch features of future frames. This dense target requires the forecast to encode the future positions of the gripper and objects. The target comes from a frozen encoder and therefore cannot collapse, removing the need for a regularizer such as SIGReg [40]. GAWM employs neither a vision-language model (VLM) nor a video generator, which dominate the size of existing WAMs.

With 77M parameters and no robot or video pretraining, GAWM-S, the ViT-S variant, achieves success rates of 93.9% and 93.1% in the clean and randomized settings of RoboTwin 2.0 [41] (Fig. 1), outperforming billion-parameter WAMs (Table I). On LIBERO [42], it attains 95.6% with 38M parameters, above the 3.2B-parameter π0\pi_{0}. On a dual-arm robot, GAWM-S achieves lower action-prediction error on held-out demonstrations than a fine-tuned billion-parameter VLA, with substantially lower inference latency. These results show that, on a fixed task set, a policy can achieve high success without language input. Ablations show that the world model yields large gains when training data or training time is limited.

The main contributions of this letter are summarized as follows:

We propose GAWM, a compact JEPA-style WAM for reactive control, in which a task-conditioned predictor forecasts the latent tokens of a frozen encoder and an action decoder regresses actions from this forecast.

We show that, without a VLM or a video generator, a multi-task policy with fewer than 100M parameters exceeds billion-parameter WAMs on RoboTwin 2.0, and predicts real-robot actions more accurately than a fine-tuned billion-parameter VLA.

Through ablations, we show that the world model yields large gains, especially when training data or training time is limited. Further analyses show that the forecast encodes the future spatial layout of the scene and that the action decoder attends to it in temporal order.

1. We propose GAWM, a compact JEPA-style WAM for reactive control, in which a task-conditioned predictor forecasts the latent tokens of a frozen encoder and an action decoder regresses actions from this forecast.

2. We show that, without a VLM or a video generator, a multi-task policy with fewer than 100M parameters exceeds billion-parameter WAMs on RoboTwin 2.0, and predicts real-robot actions more accurately than a fine-tuned billion-parameter VLA.

3. Through ablations, we show that the world model yields large gains, especially when training data or training time is limited. Further analyses show that the forecast encodes the future spatial layout of the scene and that the action decoder attends to it in temporal order.

title: State estimation for a hybrid rigid-continuum space manipulator system
authors: Lorenzo Ticozzi,Patricio A. Vela,Panagiotis Tsiotras
abstract:
Spacecraft-mounted robotic manipulators can support long-term operability of orbiting assets by conducting tasks such as on-orbit assembly, repair, upgrade, and refueling.
In this context, the integration of continuum/soft robotic mechanisms into space manipulator designs promises to reduce stowage volume and mass, as well as to improve
operational safety through the inherent mechanical compliance of soft structures.
This work presents a novel state reconstruction pipeline for a hybrid soft-rigid space manipulator, in which the distal link is a tendon-driven continuum robot.
The estimation problem is formulated as a maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference problem over the hybrid manipulator’s configuration, conditioned on discrete, noisy measurements from joint encoders and a vision-based sensing pipeline.
The resulting soft-constrained optimization problem is transcribed as a factor graph, providing a compact representation for fusing heterogeneous measurements with the rigid-soft kinematic model.
Furthermore, the adoption of the Geometric Variable Strain (GVS) approach yields a minimum-order parameterization of the configuration, a property expected to facilitate model-based feedback control design in future work.
The proposed implementation is validated in simulation on a closed-loop trajectory where, for better realism, position measurements for the continuum link are obtained by means of a simulated visual pipeline leveraging synthetic photorealistic images.
The state reconstruction accuracy and computational performance confirm the potential of the proposed framework for hybrid soft-rigid robotic applications in orbit.
introduction:
Technological advances, together with the standardization of satellite subsystems, have democratized access to space and enabled large-scale satellite production and operation.
This trend drives sustained growth of the space economy, projected at an average annual rate of 9%. [1]
At the same time, the rapid expansion of the Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite population and the associated growth of space debris are challenging the current space exploitation model, motivating the search for a more sustainable paradigm.

Significant effort has therefore been devoted to developing robotic on-orbit servicing (OOS) capabilities, aimed at enabling value-added tasks such as on-orbit assembly, refueling, and maintenance.
Autonomous spacecraft-mounted manipulators are a key enabling technology for this vision, owing to their versatility across a wide range of OOS missions. [2]
Designing and operating such systems, however, remains challenging, as it must reconcile stringent accuracy and safety requirements with uncertain and dynamic operating conditions.

Historically, the majority of the literature on the subject has focused on modeling [3, 4] and control design [5, 6, 7] for rigid or rigid-flexible space manipulators.
More recently, however, soft and continuum robotics elements have been introduced into the field, motivated by the reduced mass and inertia afforded by tendon-driven architectures and by the inherent compliance of continuum manipulators.
Specifically, cable actuation for space manipulators was first investigated through the Tendon-Actuated Lightweight In-Space MANipulator (TALISMAN) prototype, [8, 9] followed by several studies addressing modeling and control design for tendon-actuated rigid arms. [10, 11]
In parallel, the dynamical model was derived for the so-called Continuum-Manipulator Space Robot (CMSR), [12] consisting of two tendon-driven continuum manipulators, modeled as Euler-Bernoulli beams, mounted on a satellite base; follow-up studies addressed control design for the CMSR. [13, 14]
While these works pioneered spacecraft-mounted continuum manipulators, the CMSR dynamical model was formulated as a non-minimal set of differential-algebraic equations (DAEs), thereby complicating simulation, analysis, and control design.
Building upon the Geometric Variable Strain (GVS) formulation, [15] a later work addressed these limitations and introduced a minimal-order dynamical model for a hybrid soft-rigid space manipulator system. [16]

While the current state-of-the-art reflects a growing interest in leveraging soft robotics principles for OOS missions, several aspects of the problem remain underexplored.
In particular, existing state estimation methods for continuum robots are largely developed and validated under the assumption of a fixed base, with sensing relying on an external motion capture system or using fiber-embedded strain sensors. [17]
These assumptions are incompatible with platforms operating in space, where the base is a free-floating satellite bus whose own pose is uncertain, and where onboard sensing may be constrained to only vision and encoder measurements.
Conversely, conventional state estimation methodologies for rigid-body space manipulators have yet to be adapted to the case of continuum robotic links.
In particular, a probabilistic state reconstruction framework for the combined satellite-bus and continuum manipulator platform, jointly accounting for base and appendage uncertainty within a consistent kinematic and sensing model, has yet to be investigated.

Motivated by the previous knowledge gap, this article presents a framework for the complete state estimation of a hybrid soft-rigid space manipulator system (HSMS).
The proposed contribution bridges the geometric HSMS model and recent factor graph-based problem formulations for continuum-robot state estimation, [16, 18] with the following advantages.
First, the proposed approach is general and can be readily specialized to any soft-rigid kinematic chain and sensor configuration.
Second, it achieves sensor fusion at the system level: information is propagated across the entire kinematic chain, improving estimation accuracy and robustness under partial sensing.
Third, it is scalable and computationally efficient, a critical requirement for space-grade hardware.
The proposed framework is evaluated in simulation, with continuum-link position measurements generated via stereo triangulation using photorealistic synthetic images.

title: Structure-Actuation Co-Design of All-Electric Heavy-Duty Robotic Manipulators
authors: Mohammad Bahari,Amir Hossein Barjini,Jouni Mattila
abstract:
This paper presents a mixed discrete–continuous multiobjective
bilevel framework for the structure–actuation co-design of
all-electric heavy-duty robotic manipulators. The upper level
optimizes manipulator geometry and actuation topology, while
joint-specific lower-level searches construct feasible archives
of discrete motor, gearbox, and screw configurations. A
system-level coordinator selects actuator packages according to
hardware mass, co-design cost, and loss-aware supply energy, and
the resulting actuator masses are fed back to the robot model
until a mass-consistent fixed point is obtained. Evaluation on a
full-pose S​E​(3)SE(3) benchmark with a 100-kg tool payload yields
eight feasible nondominated designs, all satisfying the 12
prescribed poses. Actuator-mass coupling converges in three iterations
for every reported design. A fixed-design ablation shows that
one-pass sequential sizing changes hardware mass by up to
2.13%, co-design cost by 10.20%, and supply energy by 9.40%
in magnitude. Payload screening further reveals increasing
mass–cost–energy demand and changes in competitive mechanism
topology with carried load.
introduction:
Heavy-duty robotic manipulators require high payload capacity,
extended reach, and reliable operation under demanding loads,
for which hydraulic actuation has traditionally been attractive
[1]. Advances in electromechanical
actuators (EMAs), together with the efficiency limitations of
hydraulic systems, are motivating all-electric alternatives
[2, 3, 4]. Electrification,
however, is not simply an actuator-replacement problem.
Manipulator geometry and mechanism topology determine
workspace, mechanical advantage, structural loading, and
actuator demand [5, 6, 7], whereas the
selected motor–transmission packages determine actuator mass,
reflected inertia, torque–speed capability, and efficiency
[8, 9]. Since these package masses
subsequently modify the robot dynamics and structural loading,
mechanical design and actuator selection form a coupled
structure–actuation problem rather than sequential sizing
stages [10].

Integrated robot design has consequently received increasing
attention. Simulation-aided and cascaded formulations have
jointly optimized hardware and motion variables
[11, 12, 13], while bilevel
optimization has been applied to morphology–behavior
coordination [14]. System-level electrical-drive
optimization has likewise demonstrated the value of coordinating
interacting component designs [15]. Discrete
component selection [16], joint
motor–motion optimization [17],
linkage-energy optimization [18], and bilevel
coordination of manipulator operation and EMLA efficiency
[19] have further extended this direction.

This paper develops a mixed discrete–continuous multiobjective
bilevel framework for structure–actuation co-design. The upper
level optimizes an 11-variable mechanical design comprising
link dimensions, mechanism topology, and linkage geometry,
while joint-specific lower-level searches construct bounded
archives of feasible EMA/EMLA packages. Their Cartesian product
is coordinated at the system level according to hardware mass,
co-design cost, and loss-aware supply energy. The selected
actuator masses are then fed back into the rigid-body and
structural models until an actuator-mass fixed point is reached.
Evaluation uses a full-pose S​E​(3)SE(3) benchmark, a nominal
co-design study, payload-sensitivity, and a
fixed-design ablation of the mass-feedback loop.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the system model and benchmark, Section III describes the proposed bilevel co-design framework, Section IV discusses the results, and Section V concludes the paper.

title: Omni-IGN: Onboard Image-Goal Navigation for Drones with Omnidirectional Vision
authors: Zichen Yan,Rui Huang,Shenao Wang,Yucong Wang,Nuthasith Gerdpratoom,Lin Zhao
abstract: Image-goal navigation (ImageNav) requires an agent to reach a location specified by a goal image in an unknown environment. For drones, this task demands exploration, goal-directed navigation, and collision avoidance under limited onboard computing resources. Existing aerial ImageNav methods are built on single-view observations, requiring additional rotation and exploration to search for goal-relevant cues outside the field of view. In this paper, we present Omni-IGN, a fully onboard ImageNav system that integrates quad-fisheye perception, an attention-based reinforcement learning (RL) policy, and a collision-aware safety layer. The policy adaptively fuses goal-relevant features across multiple views to provide directional guidance for continuous navigation. The quad-fisheye RGB images support both ImageNav and obstacle avoidance without a dedicated depth sensor. On Habitat benchmarks, Omni-IGN achieves the best performance among continuous-action baselines. Moreover, flight tests in IsaacSim validate the effectiveness of integrating learning-based depth estimation with the action safety layer for collision avoidance. Finally, real-world experiments demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer without any fine-tuning or external localization. The code and model checkpoints will be released upon acceptance.
introduction:
Aerial ImageNav requires a drone to search an unknown 3D environment and reach the location where a goal image was captured. Specifying destinations through images enhances drone autonomy and provides greater flexibility in mission execution, as the drone can discover a route without requiring an operator to map the environment or prescribe a trajectory in advance. This capability can reduce manual preparation in unknown or unstructured environments, enabling rapid deployment for time-critical tasks such as disaster rescue.

In this work, we investigate fully onboard omnidirectional ImageNav for drones, aiming to exploit broad visual coverage for more efficient goal search. Observations from all directions help capture goal-relevant cues beyond the forward field of view (FoV), reducing unnecessary rotations and repeated exploration [1, 2]. Yet the central challenge is to turn this panoramic view into timely, goal-directed flight commands. Goal-relevant cues may occupy only one view, remain visually ambiguous, or be absent during exploration. Processing all views indiscriminately increases both computational cost and visual distraction. An effective policy must therefore extract useful goal-relevant cues while retaining the spatial context needed for exploration, all within limited onboard computational resources.

Existing studies address only parts of this problem under more limited task settings. Prior aerial ImageNav methods rely on single-view observations [3, 4, 5]. For drones equipped with omnidirectional vision, most studies instead target individual capabilities, including mapping and localization [6], exploration [7], and obstacle avoidance [8]. OMNI-DRL [9] combines omnidirectional perception with point-goal navigation and obstacle avoidance. However, ImageNav provides no compass guidance toward the target. The drone must actively explore the environment to discover the goal while avoiding collisions. Exploration, goal seeking, and collision avoidance are therefore tightly coupled. Real-world deployment further requires this coordination to remain robust to sim-to-real visual discrepancies that may affect both goal recognition and obstacle perception.

To enable efficient inference and smooth control, an end-to-end pipeline that directly maps visual observations to continuous velocity commands is necessary. Compared with the discrete action space used in TSGM [10], continuous control enables smoother motion and more responsive maneuvering, making it more compatible with drone dynamics. SIGN [4] demonstrates velocity control for aerial ImageNav and highlights the increased training difficulty introduced by continuous actions, but considers only a single camera view and runs in an offboard mode. Our setting involves both high-dimensional panoramic observations and continuous control, increasing the difficulty of extracting goal-relevant visual representations while simultaneously learning effective exploration behaviors.

Collision avoidance presents an additional challenge for real-world deployment. Existing ImageNav benchmarks prioritize goal-reaching performance but neglect collisions. Although minor collisions may be tolerable for ground robots, even brief contact with obstacles can destabilize a drone and lead to crashes. Depth provides a direct measurement for assessing collision risk, but obtaining it through a dedicated depth sensor adds weight, cost, and hardware complexity. We therefore seek to integrate depth-based collision avoidance into aerial ImageNav while keeping the sensing configuration compact and lightweight. Achieving the aforementioned capabilities within limited onboard resources presents a further system-level challenge.

To address the above challenges, we present Omni-IGN (Omnidirectional Image-Goal Navigation), a fully onboard aerial ImageNav system for which we design a shared quad-fisheye RGB sensing rig and integrate an end-to-end RL policy with a collision-aware safety layer supported by stereo depth estimation (see Fig. 1). We jointly encode each of the four camera views with the goal image and introduce a self-attention module (see Fig. 2) to adaptively fuse the resulting features for continuous velocity prediction. In parallel, we estimate stereo depth from overlapping views of our camera rig and use a collision-aware safety layer to correct unsafe actions before sending them to the flight controller. This design couples goal-conditioned navigation with geometric action correction while keeping both functions within a fully onboard pipeline.

Our main contributions are as follows:

To the best of our knowledge, Omni-IGN is the first fully onboard implementation of omnidirectional ImageNav on drones. We introduce a self-attention module that adaptively weights goal-conditioned visual features across four views, providing directional guidance for the RL policy and significantly reducing repeated exploration.

We employ a quad-fisheye RGB rig shared by ImageNav and collision avoidance, and integrate stereo depth estimation from overlapping views with a safety layer that corrects unsafe actions. This safety mechanism integrates seamlessly with the continuous-action ImageNav policy without requiring a dedicated depth sensor.

We evaluate Omni-IGN through simulation benchmarks and real-world flight experiments. Omni-IGN achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance among continuous-action baselines on Habitat benchmarks [11, 12, 13]. IsaacSim validates the reliability of depth estimation and safety layer for collision avoidance, while real-world flights demonstrate successful zero-shot sim-to-real transfer without fine-tuning.

We introduce a self-attention module that adaptively weights goal-conditioned visual features across four views, providing directional guidance for the RL policy and significantly reducing repeated exploration.

2. We employ a quad-fisheye RGB rig shared by ImageNav and collision avoidance, and integrate stereo depth estimation from overlapping views with a safety layer that corrects unsafe actions. This safety mechanism integrates seamlessly with the continuous-action ImageNav policy without requiring a dedicated depth sensor.

3. We evaluate Omni-IGN through simulation benchmarks and real-world flight experiments. title: Keeping Contact: Task-Adaptive Friction Margins for Bimanual Non-Prehensile Manipulation
authors: Qian Ying Lee,Lin Yang,Domenico Campolo
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
abstract: Maintaining contact in non-prehensile manipulation requires more than nominal friction cone feasibility: a force barely inside the cone and one well inside it are both feasible, but they provide different margins against slip and contact loss. This paper uses signed friction distance to measure friction margin in force space and derives a task-adaptive margin from the force correction needed to balance pivot moment deviations in bimanual tilting. The resulting contact margins are embedded in a sequence of second-order cone programs (SOCPs), each giving a globally optimal contact force solution at a tilt angle. The optimizer balances the object about an environmental pivot while keeping robot and pivot contact forces away from the nominal friction boundary. Optimizer-level results show interpretable force redistribution and adaptation to object property changes. Real-world experiments demonstrate successful execution under object property variations and model mismatch, while fixed margin and no-margin comparisons illustrate the importance of adapting the margin to task demand. These results support signed friction distance margins as a force planning mechanism for maintaining contact in bimanual non-prehensile manipulation. Project page: https://keeping-contact.github.io/
introduction:
Non-prehensile manipulation extends robotic manipulation beyond rigid grasping by exploiting contact interactions as part of the task mechanics. This enables behaviors such as pushing [11], rolling [25], and pivoting [26]. Since the resulting motion is governed by frictional contacts, planning must reason about both contact motion and forces. Recent optimization-based formulations incorporate trajectory optimization with frictional contact constraints and simultaneous contact selection [21, 27]. In these formulations, friction constraints primarily specify admissible contact forces or contact modes along the motion. Yet admissibility does not specify where a maintained contact force lies within the friction cone: a nominally feasible force profile may still operate near a friction boundary and remain sensitive to modeling error or tracking deviation.

A useful clue comes from everyday manipulation. When lifting an unfamiliar object, a person rarely knows its inertial parameters exactly, yet contact is often maintained stably. Rather than regulating contact force at the minimum value that barely avoids slip, people maintain a margin above the slip threshold and adjust it as perceived task demand changes [23, 10]. This contrasts with friction cones used only as feasibility tests: a force that barely clears the boundary and one well inside the cone are accepted alike, although only the latter carries a meaningful margin. The question is thus not merely whether a planned force is feasible, but what margin it should maintain and how that margin should vary with the task.

Motivated by this view, we plan contact forces by lower bounding their signed distance from the nominal friction boundary. This lower bound gives each maintained contact a force space margin against deviations from the planned force. The remaining question is how to choose this margin along the motion: a fixed value treats margin as uniform, while a task-adaptive value can vary with the force demand imposed by the manipulation task. We study this construction on the planar bimanual tilting task in Fig. 1. This task has a structured but nonuniform force requirement: the gravitational moment varies with tilt angle and object properties, changing the forces required from the two robot contacts. The motion is especially sensitive to slip at the initial and final configurations, making sufficient tangential support and friction margin important throughout the tilt. Unlike prior pivoting studies that often rely on symmetric robot–object contact arrangements [9, 26], our setup uses non-opposing contacts and exploits an environmental pivot to accomplish the task. Maintaining both robot contacts is therefore central to the task, since slip or contact loss at either contact can lead to task failure.

In summary, the main contributions of this work are:

We use signed friction distance to the nominal friction boundary as an explicit force space measure of margin for contact force planning.

We introduce a task-adaptive margin construction that lower bounds this signed distance based on the force demand required by the task.

We embed this margin in a convex force planner with globally optimal contact force solutions and evaluate it in real-world experiments.
