title: ActiveAlign: Aligning Egocentric Manipulation via Active Perception
authors: Ri-Zhao Qiu,Bowen Wen,Yifeng Jiang,Chen Tessler,Eric Heiden,Xue Bin Peng,Xiaolong Wang,Stan Birchfield,Erwin Coumans
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Real2Sim2Real) enables structured world representations for planning, interpretability, and safe execution. Most existing approaches rely on passive perception, which creates real2sim gaps due to imperfect observation. Inspired by how humans perceive actively through actions, we propose ActiveAlign, a framework that leverages active perception to align the Real2Sim2Real gap from interactions. ActiveAlign introduces two complementary modules: (i) ActiveAlign-Waving, which performs hand-eye calibration by exploiting active hand motions and differentiable rendering, and (ii) ActiveAlign-Touching, which refines object alignment through tactile feedback to achieve millimeter-level precision. Together, these capabilities enable strong real2sim alignment. We demonstrate that ActiveAlign-Waving can be used to curate simulation environments for open-sourced uncalibrated robot manipulation datasets, and demonstrate on a real Unitree G1 robot that ActiveAlign enables fine manipulation of millimeter-scale objects such as pressing buttons and moving sliders.
introduction:
Robots operating in real-world environments must perceive, reason, and manipulate with high reliability. Successful manipulation depends on accurate object discovery, tracking, and alignment, as even millimeter-scale errors can cause failures in tasks such as pressing a button or adjusting a slider. Just as visual feedback in autonomous driving allows humans to verify safety and correctness, Robot manipulation benefits from interpretable visual and physical feedback to ensure safe execution.

Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Real2Sim2Real) methods  [34, 52, 39, 19, 13, 46, 32, 7, 26] address these challenges by constructing structured simulation assets that enable planning, policy training, and interpretability. While prior art has advanced simulation fidelity and asset generation, many papers focus on learning from passive perception only, which does not consider how the robot itself can actively close the sim-to-real loop. Most closely to our work, Moran et al. [34] proposed to perform real2sim from robot trajectories, but the solution is tailor-made for static ALOHA setting.

On the other hand, humans rely on active perception: we move our heads to resolve occlusions, wave our hands to perceive depth cues, and use tactile sensing to refine object alignment. Inspired by human manipulation, our insight is that performing perception on static images is not sufficient for aligning real2sim2real. We propose ActiveAlign, a framework that leverages active perception to close the loop for Real2Sim2Real pipelines in a fully end-to-end manner. ActiveAlign uses egocentric perception from robots, and actively executes human-like motions —including camera movements, hand waving, and tactile exploration— to improve simulation-to-reality alignment.

Specifically, ActiveAlign-Waving formulates camera parameter calibrations as an online optimization problems with multiple observations, which can be solved by active actuation and differentiable rendering. We further demonstrate that tactile alignment mitigates cumulative errors in perception, calibration, and actuation, enabling fine manipulation tasks such as pressing a small button or moving a slider with millimeter-level accuracy.

title: When Black-Box Robot Policies Fail: Online Sensor Diagnosis and Repair with a Transparent Surrogate
authors: Marc Ziegler,Batu Özen,Sami Mentes,Thomas Waschulzik,Alois Knoll
comment: Accepted at the Conference on Robot Learning 2026 Workshop on the Science of Physical AI Safety (SPAIS)
abstract: Robot foundation models may generalize across tasks and embodiments, but their actions still depend on sensors that can fail. When the policy is frozen or inaccessible, can an external monitor diagnose and repair corrupted inputs without access to its internals? We test a structured surrogate that separates periodic gait from sensor-dependent corrections to guide input repair around a frozen locomotion policy. On simulated Go2, offline diagnosis raises walking success from 259/640 to 429/640 episodes; online repair reaches 382/640, with no triggers in 64 held-out fault-free episodes. A matched boosted-tree surrogate predicts clean actions similarly well but yields no detected repair improvement over no repair. Separate fits improve walking on Go1 and ANYmal C, although phase-aware gradients perform better. Evidence remains limited to one policy and a partly screened simulated fault suite; robot foundation model and hardware validation remain open.
introduction:
Robot foundation models promise transfer across tasks and
embodiments [9, 7], yet their actions depend on
reliable sensor observations. When internals are inaccessible,
monitors see only inputs and actions. We study the frozen multi-embodiment
URMA locomotion policy [2]. On Go2 at 0.5​m/s0.5\,\mathrm{m/s}, a 0.3​rad/s0.3\,\mathrm{rad/s} yaw-gyroscope
bias prevents walking in 16/16 episodes. Classical diagnosis uses plant or
sensor models [6], whereas gradient attribution and VLA
steering require policy access [13, 16, 5, 3]. Runtime guardrails constrain
plans [11], while masked training builds sensor
robustness into the policy [10]. Unusual sensor readings may nevertheless result from legitimate disturbances.

Prior work distills locomotion into boosted trees or symbolic
expressions [1]. Structured controllers and sparse
mixtures also expose control structure [14, 17]. Our surrogate separates
periodic gait from sensor-dependent corrections, ranks abnormal input
contributions, and guides repair. The frozen policy produces every action,
so the surrogate never replaces the controller.

We contribute diagnosis and repair without policy gradients, paired offline
and online evaluations, and tests on three quadrupeds. This controlled setting motivates external supervision for robot foundation
models [15]. Direct validation on those models
remains open.

title: Trace-WAM: Learning to Act via 3D Motion Prediction for World Action Models
authors: Xu Hu,Changjie Wu,Linzhe Shi,Hang Zhang,Chen Yang,Lingjun Zhang,Guowen Zhang,Mu Xu,Junran Peng,Qing Li,Zhaoxiang Zhang
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) learn representations for robot control by coupling future visual prediction with action generation. Successful manipulation depends primarily on how the robot and task-relevant objects evolve, whereas future-video prediction must also reconstruct the appearance and background of the entire scene. We therefore propose Trace-WAM, which augments video-action learning with future 3D motion prediction as an auxiliary objective. This objective supervises temporal point correspondence together with image-plane displacement and depth change, directly describing the interaction dynamics and spatial changes involved in manipulation. To this end, we adopt a three-branch Mixture-of-Transformer (Tri-MoT) architecture to jointly learn video prediction, motion prediction, and action generation. The motion expert predicts future trajectories from current visual features, allowing motion supervision to shape the representations used for action generation. Because the action expert does not consume predicted trajectories, inference retains the current-observation policy path: a single visual forward pass followed by action denoising. Experiments on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus demonstrate strong in-distribution performance and out-of-distribution generalization, with particularly clear gains over Fast-WAM under limited demonstrations and distribution shifts.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [18, 33, 14] adapt pretrained vision-language representations to robot control, learning to generate actions from visual observations and language instructions. Despite their strong policy-learning capabilities, most VLAs focus on action prediction without explicitly modeling how the scene evolves during execution. World Action Models (WAMs) incorporate this future evolution into policy learning by combining future visual prediction with action generation [12, 48]. Built on pretrained video models, WAMs transfer rich spatiotemporal priors to robot manipulation by learning from future observations together with action sequences.
Yet successful manipulation depends primarily on how the robot and task-relevant objects change over time, whereas future RGB prediction must also model texture, illumination, and background appearance across the entire scene.
This difference motivates a complementary target that emphasizes interaction dynamics while retaining the rich visual context learned from future RGB.
Recent approaches enrich policy representations by augmenting visual prediction with auxiliary supervision for geometry, semantics, and interaction structure. These objectives include depth and geometric prediction, semantic feature learning, and supervision of affordances and goal regions [12, 30, 47, 49, 53, 24], encouraging representations to capture spatial layout and task-relevant interaction constraints. A per-frame or region-level target, however, does not by itself identify how the same physical locations evolve throughout an interaction, a distinction also emphasized by 4D-WAM [42]. This temporal correspondence connects the current scene to the sequence of changes required to complete a manipulation task.

We therefore focus on 3D motion as an auxiliary prediction target for WAM representation learning, motivated by two complementary properties. First, each trajectory connects a point in the current observation to its positions at successive future steps, revealing the coordinated motion of the robot and task-relevant objects (Fig. 1(a)). Second, depth change complements image-plane displacement by describing motion toward or away from the camera.
In our annotation census, among point tracks moving by at least 2% of the image diagonal over 32 steps, 79.3% in LIBERO and 32.9% in Piper exhibit depth changes of at least 5% of their initial depth (Fig. 2(a)). Depth variation therefore accompanies a substantial fraction of visible motion in both simulation and real-world annotations. Its value for policy learning is supported by our depth ablation: retaining the depth component improves LIBERO-Plus success from 82.4% to 84.5% (Fig. 2(b)).
These properties describe the temporal and spatial changes involved in manipulation.

Based on this formulation, we propose Trace-WAM, which jointly learns future video prediction, future 3D motion prediction, and action generation. We represent motion using trajectories anchored to a fixed grid in the current image, combining image-plane displacement with depth change relative to each point’s initial position. Whereas 4D-WAM [42] transfers trajectory knowledge by aligning temporal feature changes and source-to-destination relations with those of a pretrained 4D tracking model, Trace-WAM directly predicts motion trajectories under an auxiliary objective. This objective adds explicit supervision for subsequent robot and object motion to video-action representation learning.
Concretely, Trace-WAM uses video, motion, and action experts with a structured attention mask (Fig. 3). During training, the video, motion, and action objectives jointly optimize the model, using future 3D motion as an additional learning signal for the representations used in action generation. At inference, we retain the Fast-WAM [48] policy path: the video backbone processes current RGB observations once, and the action expert denoises an action chunk using cached visual features, language, and proprioception. As summarized in Fig. 1(a), Trace-WAM requires no future-video or motion prediction at inference.

We evaluate Trace-WAM on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus, covering both in-distribution control and out-of-distribution generalization. Trace-WAM achieves strong performance across these settings, with particularly clear gains over Fast-WAM when demonstrations are limited and under distribution shifts (Fig. 1(b)). Experiments on a real robot further show higher success rates across three physical manipulation tasks. These results support 3D motion prediction as an effective auxiliary objective for WAM policy learning. Our contributions are:

We introduce Trace-WAM, which jointly learns future video prediction, future 3D motion prediction, and action generation within a three-branch architecture.

Future 3D motion provides auxiliary supervision for video-action representation learning without requiring future video or motion prediction at inference.

Experiments on three manipulation benchmarks demonstrate strong in-distribution performance and out-of-distribution generalization, while real-world evaluations show consistent gains across three physical tasks.

1. We introduce Trace-WAM, which jointly learns future video prediction, future 3D motion prediction, and action generation within a three-branch architecture.

2. Future 3D motion provides auxiliary supervision for video-action representation learning without requiring future video or motion prediction at inference.

3. Experiments on three manipulation benchmarks demonstrate strong in-distribution performance and out-of-distribution generalization, while real-world evaluations show consistent gains across three physical tasks.

title: ExecDiffuser: Closing the Sample-to-Execution Gap in Diffusion Planning
authors: Shuo Pei,Bosun Liang,Saihui Zha,Chen Sun,Huachun Tan,Yong Wang
abstract:
Generative planners are often evaluated by the trajectories they can generate, although closed-loop driving ultimately depends on the single candidate committed to control. We identify this mismatch as the sample-to-execution gap and show that improving proposal quality alone
can worsen the executed decision. Here, we introduce ExecDiffuser, a recurrent proposal-to-execution framework that couples candidate generation, trajectory selection, and subsequent replanning through shared execution semantics. Intent-Guided Diffusion Proposal (IGD) assigns hypothesis responsibility and shapes trajectories with execution-conditioned supervision. Execution-Grounded Selection (EGS) learns a candidate-conditioned publication utility, commits one trajectory to control, and returns it as context for the next planning cycle. Across nuPlan, InterPlan, and NAVSIM, ExecDiffuser achieves leading closed-loop performance against strong state-of-the-art baselines. Under a unified
five-seed protocol, it obtains an average score of 85.62, improving over Diffusion Planner and FlowDrive by 4.02 and 1.31 points, respectively. On NAVSIM, it achieves 92.6 PDMS under the official evaluation pipeline. Matched counterfactual analysis further shows that ExecDiffuser more
reliably converts strong candidates into committed decisions, while prefix interventions confirm that this advantage persists after physical execution
and subsequent replanning.
introduction:
Autonomous driving planners repeatedly use sensory observations, map
and route context, and recent vehicle motion to produce a future ego
trajectory for downstream control [1, 2, 3, 4]. In closed-loop operation, however, the
environment responds only to the trajectory committed at the current
planning cycle. This commitment determines the vehicle’s immediate
motion and changes the interaction state from which the planner must
subsequently replan.

Generative planners are attractive because uncertain and interactive
scenes often admit multiple plausible maneuvers. Diffusion- and
flow-based planners therefore produce candidate sets rather than a
single deterministic trajectory. Recent work improves proposal quality
through flexible guidance, multimodal anchors, latent or bridge
representations, reinforcement fine-tuning, and flow matching
 [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12].
Recent variants also reduce sampling redundancy, introduce
spatiotemporal or scene-adaptive guidance, and explicitly improve
trajectory feasibility [13, 14, 15, 16]. These advances raise the quality and
coverage of the candidate set, but only one trajectory is ultimately
committed to control. A better proposal set therefore need not produce
a better executed decision.

This distinction exposes a gap between proposal generation and
trajectory commitment. A planner may already contain a strong maneuver
in its candidate set, yet commit a weaker alternative because the
selector was not trained to compare realized candidates under the
current execution context. We refer to this mismatch as the
sample-to-execution gap. A controlled diagnosis reveals a
counterintuitive failure. With the imitation-based selector fixed,
stronger proposal learning raises counterfactual oracle-best quality
from 90.33 to 91.36, but lowers committed quality from 89.82 to 89.64.
As a result, candidate-publication regret increases from 0.51 to
1.72. Thus, improving the proposal ceiling alone can make the final
closed-loop decision worse.

The underlying cause is a mismatch between how proposals are organized
and how decisions are executed. Proposal learning typically assigns
responsibility to latent hypotheses according to imitation proximity
or geometric matching. Commitment, in contrast, must rank the realized
trajectories using evidence available at the current planning cycle,
including driveability, route adherence, predicted interactions,
progress, comfort, and recent execution history. When these stages are
optimized independently, the hypotheses that receive proposal
supervision are not necessarily aligned with the evidence required for
controller-facing selection. The problem is inherently recurrent: each
committed trajectory changes the vehicle and interaction state, which
in turn affects subsequent planning. Candidate generation, trajectory
commitment, and replanning should therefore be connected through a
common execution interface.

We introduce ExecDiffuser, a recurrent framework that connects proposal
learning and controller-facing publication through shared execution
semantics. IGD improves candidate availability through
execution-conditioned responsibility and trajectory shaping, while
EGS learns a candidate-conditioned publication utility and returns
the selected trajectory as recurrent context. We separate these effects
through matched counterfactual evaluation and prefix interventions that
test whether the initial publication alters subsequent closed-loop
replanning. Under a unified five-seed protocol, ExecDiffuser outperforms the
reproduced Diffusion Planner and FlowDrive baselines in all six nuPlan
settings, with consistent gains on interaction-intensive InterPlan and strong
performance on NAVSIM. Our contributions are
threefold:

We formulate the sample-to-execution gap and introduce

title: HC2Robot: Hyper-Connection Transformers with Predicted Foresight for Multi-Terrain Humanoid Parkour
authors: Wenhao Xu,Yanheng Mai,Yifei Fu,Nan Zheng,Yanbo Zhou,Zirui Huang,Mingsheng Ling,Xinjue Wang,Renjing Xu
abstract: Humanoid parkour requires robots to reason about future footholds and whole-body motions over highly discontinuous terrain. We revisit the information asymmetry in asymmetric actor-critic learning for perceptive humanoid locomotion: the critic exploits privileged simulator signals during training, whereas the deployable actor operates solely from onboard perception. We argue that the key is not exposing privileged information to the actor, but learning a deployable approximation of it to narrow the information gap between training and deployment. We present HC2Robot, a deployable perceptive humanoid parkour framework consisting of a Predicted Foresight Module (PFM) and a Hyper-Connection (HC) Transformer. PFM predicts from deployable observations the policy-conditioned timing, location, and support quality of each foot’s next touchdown event, converting privileged supervision into a deployable latent representation that provides the actor with predicted touchdown information without privileged runtime sensing. The HC Transformer further enhances temporal reasoning through learnable multi-stream routing, while a future motion prediction head provides short-horizon motion priors for regularization. Across stairs, gaps, high platforms, and slopes, HC2Robot achieves a mean simulated traversal success rate of 97.60% and consistently higher safe foothold rates than strong perceptive locomotion baselines, supporting improved traversal performance and geometric foothold support under deployable sensing.
introduction:
Humanoid parkour demands traversal of stairs, gaps, platforms, and slopes while maintaining dynamically feasible whole-body motion [1, 2]. Success requires the controller to coordinate perception, contact timing, and body motion well before each foothold is realized. While massively parallel reinforcement learning has enabled robust locomotion [3, 4], proprioception-only policies lack foresight of upcoming terrain discontinuities [5, 6]. Depth-conditioned perception extends this horizon with geometric priors [7, 8], enabling scalable perceptive parkour over challenging terrain [9, 2].

Two challenges remain for deployable perceptive parkour. First, temporal representations must effectively integrate proprioceptive and depth-conditioned information. Conventional residual Transformers use a single residual stream [10, 11]; multi-stream routing offers additional paths for cross-layer feature mixing, complementing recent advances in cross-modal fusion, mixture-of-experts, and reference-gait priors [12, 13, 14]. Second, simulator-derived contact and support signals enhance learning but are unavailable at deployment [15, 16, 5]. We train an auxiliary estimator with simulator-derived labels to make task-relevant predictions available to the actor.

HC2Robot addresses these challenges through two complementary mechanisms. A Hyper-Connection (HC) Transformer [17] replaces the conventional single residual pathway with learnable multi-stream aggregation and mixing, enabling richer cross-layer information exchange while evaluating each attention and feed-forward sublayer only once. A Predicted Foresight Module (PFM), trained with asymmetric actor–critic learning [15, 18], forecasts each foot’s next touchdown event—its time-to-contact, touchdown location, and support quality—from deployable actor features and fuses the forecast into the policy. Additionally, an auxiliary motion predictor adopted from ParkourFormer [19] provides two-step future AMP states for motion regularization [20]. All prediction pathways remain deployment-compatible, using simulator information solely as training supervision.

We evaluate HC2Robot on stairs, gaps, high platforms, and slopes; the results demonstrate that combining HC feature reuse with PFM foothold foresight consistently improves traversal success and safe foothold rate over strong baselines.
Fig. 1 summarizes the framework.

Our contributions are as follows:

A Hyper-Connection Transformer that replaces standard residual connections with learnable multi-stream aggregation and mixing, enabling richer temporal feature reuse while evaluating each attention and feed-forward sublayer only once.

A Predicted Foresight Module (PFM) that forecasts the timing, location, and support quality of each foot’s next touchdown event through a continuous time-to-event formulation, providing supervised foothold foresight without a fixed prediction offset or privileged signals in the deployment interface.

Simulation results across four challenging terrain classes demonstrating that HC2Robot consistently improves traversal success and safe foothold rate over strong perceptive parkour baselines.

2. A Predicted Foresight Module (PFM) that forecasts the timing, location, and support quality of each foot’s next touchdown event through a continuous time-to-event formulation, providing supervised foothold foresight without a fixed prediction offset or privileged signals in the deployment interface.

3. Simulation results across four challenging terrain classes demonstrating that HC2Robot consistently improves traversal success and safe foothold rate over strong perceptive parkour baselines.

title: TAPESTRY: A Single Backbone for Video Generation and Robot Control
authors: Jeremy A. Collins,Seungjae Lee,Rachanon Wachakorn,Krishnan Srinivasan,Animesh Garg,Vitor Campagnolo Guizilini,Paarth Shah
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
comment: Accepted to Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026
abstract:
Pretrained video generation models encode rich priors about physical interactions, but leveraging them for robot control typically requires either resource-intensive video generation at test time or action heads trained from scratch that do not fully utilize the pretrained backbone. We introduce Tokenizing Actions as Video Patches in a Shared Transformer Policy (TAPESTRY), a world action model that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion transformer into a robotic policy without requiring video generation at inference. Our key idea is to treat robot actions as single-patch tokens in the video model’s latent space. A lightweight linear projection maps each action timestep to the patch dimensions of the pretrained VAE, and the resulting tokens are processed by the same patchifying layers and transformer backbone used for video. The shared backbone is optimized through three diffusion objectives sampled per minibatch element:
Video diffusion uses VAE latents from robot and human videos to establish dynamics priors. Joint video+action diffusion trains on robot demonstrations using a coupled diffusion timestep and an asymmetric attention mask. Action-only diffusion denoises actions conditioned on clean image latents. At test time, the model generates a compact action token sequence in a single DDIM step from pure noise, producing smooth action chunks at 8484 ms per action chunk on consumer hardware and avoiding the cost of full video generation. Across simulation benchmarks and real-robot experiments, TAPESTRY achieves strong performance with substantially lower inference cost than comparable joint video–action policies. More information can be found at tapestry-wam.github.io.
introduction:
Video generation models have emerged as an effective method of distilling internet-scale knowledge about physical interactions into robotic policies.
Trained on up to millions of hours of human and real-world video, these models learn rich priors over how the visual world evolves in response to actions, priors difficult to acquire from the limited robot demonstration datasets available today.
The central question for robot learning is: how can we best transfer these priors to learn policies that generalize across tasks, environments, and embodiments?

Existing approaches span a spectrum of coupling between the video model and the robotic policy, each with characteristic tradeoffs.
At one end, methods such as UniPi [9] and DreamGen [15] use a video generation model to synthesize visual rollouts and then extract actions via a separately trained inverse dynamics model.
This pipeline leaves the video model architecturally unmodified but compounds errors across two generative stages and requires expensive frame generation at test time, limiting real-time deployment.
A lighter-weight alternative, exemplified by Video Prediction Policy [14] and mimic-video [34], extracts intermediate latent representations from a pretrained video backbone and conditions a downstream action head on these features.
This avoids full video generation but limits knowledge transfer, since the action head is trained from scratch and cannot directly access the backbone’s pretrained weights.
The most tightly coupled approaches share a single backbone across video and action diffusion. These include prior work UWM [36], UVA [19], and concurrent works Cosmos Policy [17], DreamZero [31], Fast-WAM [33], and GigaWorld-Policy [23].
These methods achieve the deepest integration, but each either trains from scratch without a pretrained video prior, pays a heavy inference-time token cost, or predicts actions with a separate module trained from scratch.

Our insight stems from a simple observation: the dynamics priors useful for action prediction reside in the weights of the video backbone, not in the generated pixels.
Although generating full video sequences is one way to access these priors, we identify that it is unnecessary if the end goal is fast, closed-loop action prediction.
Specifically, by representing action tokens as patchified video tokens aligned with video pretraining, robot actions inherit the backbone’s dynamics priors without the overhead of pixel-space generation, reducing online inference cost.

We apply this idea in Tapestry, a method that re-purposes a pretrained video diffusion transformer into an action-generating policy.
The key mechanism is treating each action timestep as a single patch in the video VAE latent space: a lightweight linear projection maps the raw action vector to the VAE’s patch dimensions, an affine-free layer normalization matches the per-token mean and variance of the VAE latents, and the resulting pseudo-patch is fed through the same patchifying convolution that the backbone uses for video tokenization.
The backbone is then jointly fine-tuned on three diffusion objectives sampled per minibatch element: standard video diffusion on VAE latents from a large mixture of robot and human videos, joint video++action diffusion on paired robot demonstrations, and action-only diffusion that denoises actions conditioned on clean image latents.
At test time, only the action pathway is used: the model denoises a compact sequence of action tokens conditioned on the current observation and a language instruction, in a single DDIM step from pure noise.
This produces smooth action chunks at 8484 ms per chunk on a single RTX 5090, ∼44×{\sim}44\times faster than an optimized DreamZero [31] on the same GPU (§4.3). We validate the approach on a challenging action-free variant of the LIBERO benchmark and on a real-world bimanual manipulator, demonstrating generalization to novel objects, novel motion primitives, and composed multi-step behaviors.

Our key contributions are as follows:

Action-as-VAE-patch tokenization.
We design an action tokenizer that reuses the video VAE patchifying convolution and matches the per-token mean and variance of its latents, adding only 12801280 parameters so the same DiT weights act on robot actions and video natively.

Three-objective joint training with a shared backbone.
A single pretrained video diffusion backbone is co-trained on video diffusion, joint video+action diffusion, and action-only diffusion. The joint branch uses an asymmetric attention mask and a coupled diffusion timestep across modalities.

Single-step inference.
Under our diffusion schedule, a single DDIM step from pure noise
reduces inference to one forward pass on a short action token sequence, producing smooth, jerk-free action chunks. We analyze why this eliminates the high-frequency noise in world action models.

Real-world bimanual deployment.
We evaluate Tapestry on a real bimanual manipulator, showing generalization to novel objects, novel motion primitives, and composed multi-step tasks.

title: Gradient flow of magnetic inclination and intensity as a GPS-free guidance mechanism
authors: Zayed Herma,Philippe Cardin,Andréa Vassilev
abstract: It is well established that some animals, such as sea turtles, sense the Earth’s magnetic field and use it as a primary cue for long-distance navigation across the vast and featureless ocean. This remarkable ability has inspired the development of bio-inspired magnetic navigation (BIMN), which seeks to mimic these animals to develop robust and frugal navigation methods. BIMN exploits the Earth’s magnetic field, sometimes described as “Nature’s GPS”, as a natural navigation infrastructure, providing a potential alternative to vulnerable satellite navigation systems. However, unlike geographic coordinates, magnetic coordinates extracted from the Earth’s magnetic field do not provide a one-to-one mapping to geographic locations. Different locations can exhibit similar magnetic signatures, creating ambiguity and making BIMN inherently more challenging. Despite this fundamental challenge, we demonstrate that, within predefined regions of the Earth, magnetic inclination and intensity provide sufficient information to navigate to any destination. By formulating BIMN as a gradient flow control and guidance problem, we show that the resulting gradient flow act as current that carries the system and can be controlled to guide it through intermediate waypoints toward the desired destination. The resulting framework provides a GPS-free navigation mechanism with potential applications in both engineering and biology. In engineering, it can be used to establish a geomagnetic navigation infrastructure through which prescribed routes can be defined and followed, while in biology, it can be used to analyse the migration routes of animals known to rely on magnetoreception.
introduction:
The Earth’s magnetic field is one of the few consistently available sources of spatial information across the vast, featureless ocean. Sea turtles undertake remarkable long-distance migrations, suggesting that they may rely heavily on geomagnetic cues for navigation (Walker et al., 2002; Lohmann & Lohmann, 2019). It is well established that these animals sense the Earth’s magnetic field through magnetoreception (Johnsen & Lohmann, 2005), a sensory ability that humans are not believed to possess (Chae et al., 2022). However, despite lacking this natural ability, humans have long exploited the Earth’s magnetic field for navigation. Since the Middle Ages, magnetic needles used as compasses have enabled sailors to navigate across the oceans (Jackson et al., 2000). More recently, technologies such as magnetometers have enabled artificial sensing of the Earth’s magnetic field, allowing autonomous systems to implement navigation strategies inspired by these species. Such geomagnetic navigation provides a robust alternative to satellite-based navigation in GPS-denied environments, particularly because it is inherently resilient to jamming and spoofing. These characteristics have motivated the development of bio-inspired magnetic navigation (BIMN), which aims to provide robust and frugal navigation techniques using the Earth’s naturally available magnetic field (Zhongwei Zhao et al., 2014; Qi et al., 2018; Taylor, 2018; Zhang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021a; Gill & Taylor, 2024; Herma et al., 2026).

The main challenge in developing BIMN methods lies in the fact that the mechanisms by which these animals use the Earth’s magnetic field for navigation remain incompletely understood. Nevertheless, two complementary mechanisms have been proposed to explain their navigation, known in the literature as the magnetic map sense and the magnetic compass sense, in which the Earth’s magnetic field provides directional (compass sense) and positional (map sense) information, much like a global positioning system (GPS) (Johnsen & Lohmann, 2005; Lohmann et al., 2007; Goforth et al., 2025). This is supported by growing evidence that animals likely use magnetic parameters such as intensity, inclination, and occasionally declination, which characterize the Earth’s magnetic field (see figure 1(a)) and exhibit spatial variations that can be used for navigation (Dennis et al., 2007; Brothers & Lohmann, 2015). Although no clear consensus has emerged in research on animal navigation regarding the precise interpretation of these two mechanisms (Lohmann et al., 2023), their translation into engineering applications generally follows a common practical framework, which can be implemented as follows. First, the magnetic parameters associated with a given destination are memorized, providing a practical representation of the magnetic map sense. These parameters form a set of magnetic coordinates that identifies the destination, analogous to the GPS coordinates used to identify a location on Earth. During navigation, the local magnetic parameters are continuously measured, providing the magnetic coordinates of the current location. A BIMN method can then compare these local magnetic coordinates with those of the destination to infer the direction toward it, as illustrated schematically in figure 1(b). In this way, the method used to infer this direction provides a representation of the magnetic compass sense. The process can be understood through a simple analogy with GPS. In GPS navigation, the current coordinates are continuously compared with the destination coordinates to determine the direction in which to move. Similarly, a lost person may recognize a familiar landmark from far away and move toward it, progressively reducing the visual distance until reaching it. BIMN follows a similar principle. However, unlike GPS coordinates, magnetic parameters do not uniquely identify a location on Earth. Different locations can exhibit similar magnetic signatures, creating ambiguity and making BIMN more challenging. Beyond this non-uniqueness, two additional difficulties arise. First, even when navigation toward the destination is possible, the resulting trajectory may be far from optimal in terms of path length. Second, some regions of the Earth’s magnetic field exhibit gradient degeneracy, where the spatial gradients of two magnetic parameters become nearly aligned or nearly vanish. For example, nearly parallel spatial gradients provide limited independent directional information, while weak spatial gradients insufficiently constrain the direction of motion (Boström et al., 2012). In both cases, the navigation method may fail to identify a suitable direction toward the destination. These challenges are shown in figure 1(c) using intensity and inclination as magnetic coordinates. These magnetic parameters are obtained from the International Geomagnetic Reference Field (IGRF) (Beggan et al., 2026), a standard model of the Earth’s main magnetic field that is updated every five years using measurements collected worldwide.

The three main difficulties (non-uniqueness of magnetic coordinates, unnecessarily long trajectories, and gradient degeneracy of magnetic parameters) raise a fundamental question about the reliability of BIMN. Most proposed methods do not discuss the validity of their approach across different areas. In other words, they do not characterize magnetic regions in which a given BIMN method is suitable for navigation. Moreover, its ability to generalize even within a specific area is not guaranteed. These methods differ mainly in how they infer the local direction of motion, as if correctly identifying this direction were sufficient, without taking the complexity of the magnetic environment into consideration. Simulations are typically limited to a single trajectory between one starting point and one destination. This serves only to illustrate the feasibility of the proposed approach rather than to demonstrate its general applicability, since successful navigation between one pair of locations does not guarantee successful navigation between other locations in the same region. This leads to the central question addressed in this work: How can we characterize the regions and conditions under which BIMN is reliable? In other words, are there regions and navigation strategies for which navigation from any starting point to any destination is possible without encountering the three difficulties described above?

This study is based on the method proposed in (Herma et al., 2026), which estimates the gradients of magnetic parameters to capture their local spatial variations. It then uses gradient descent to determine the local direction of motion that minimizes the difference between the measured magnetic coordinates and the corresponding target coordinates. This is analogous to navigating toward a familiar landmark by progressively reducing the visual distance to it. While the original method uses gradient descent for navigation, it does not directly address the three main challenges. For example, the method can become trapped in a local minimum due to gradient degeneracy or converge to another global minimum that does not correspond to the actual destination due to the non-uniqueness of magnetic coordinates. We therefore study the more general structure of the resulting gradient flow, which is the set of trajectories generated by the gradient descent dynamics, to enable reliable navigation throughout predefined regions. We show that, within certain regions separated by well-defined frontiers, it is possible to perform BIMN from any initial location to any desired destination. A similar problem has been considered in (Gill & Taylor, 2024), where navigable regions are characterized using local stability analysis around the destination. However, the size and shape of these regions depend on the choice of specific navigation parameters, and local stability does not guarantee navigation between arbitrary locations within these regions. In our case, stability near the destination is naturally guaranteed because, under the gradient descent mechanism, the destination acts as an attractor (a stable equilibrium corresponding to a global minimum). We therefore go beyond this local property and characterize regions in which navigation between arbitrary initial and destination locations can be guaranteed. We formulate navigation as a guidance and control problem, where the gradient flow can be seen as a current carrying the system toward the destination, which can be controlled and guided by selecting appropriate intermediate destinations. In particular, we prove that a suitable sequence of intermediate destinations always exists, enabling reliable navigation to the final destination (see section 2). A simulation example illustrates this result and shows how intermediate destinations can be used to guide the system toward the final desired destination. Finally, we compare our results with four iconic sea turtle migration trajectories reported in (Putman, 2018; 1) to assess whether the regions identified in our work are consistent with observed migration paths known to rely on the Earth’s magnetic field for navigation (Lohmann & Lohmann, 1993; Lohmann et al., 2007) (see section 3).

As an important practical consequence, the proposed BIMN framework enables the creation of “invisible” magnetic routes, defined by sequences of magnetic waypoints that guide the system along prescribed paths, analogous to conventional air routes in which aircraft navigate through sequences of predefined geographic waypoints. In this way, we provide a basis for further developing an alternative navigation infrastructure that does not depend on satellite positioning. Such an approach may become increasingly important as growing space debris and cascading collisions associated with Kessler syndrome threaten satellite infrastructure and the services that rely on it, including navigation (Kessler & Cour‐Palais, 1978; Mariappan & Crassidis, 2023; Thiele et al., 2026).

title: RynnWorld-Latent: A Cross-Embodiment World Model Conditioned on Universal Latent Actions
authors: Haoyu Zhao,Yinzhou Tang,Zixuan Wang,Minghao Zhu,Dongchi Huang,Xingyue Zhao,Qin Zhao,Kehan Li,Siteng Huang,Xin Li,Zhenyu Zeng,Mingxiu Chen,Deli Zhao,Zhongyu Li

abstract:
Learning controllable world dynamics from heterogeneous interaction videos is challenging because robot embodiments use incompatible action spaces, while human videos lack native control labels. We present RynnWorld-Latent, a cross-embodiment video world model that uses the 3D-grounded latent actions introduced by RynnLAM as a shared conditioning interface.
This representation enables joint pretraining on human interaction videos, robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts without requiring a common native action space. Built on a pretrained video transformer, RynnWorld-Latent combines global action tokens with an identity-initialized local pathway that aligns actions with future video latents. We pretrain on 23 datasets comprising approximately 553.5M frames and adapt the model to target robots through post-training. The framework supports two data-generation routes: digital teleoperation uses target robot commands to generate action-video demonstrations, while latent-action synthesis transfers source motion to an edited initial frame and pairs the resulting rollout with retargeted pseudo robot actions. Experiments show improved video prediction metrics on public benchmarks and two real-robot platforms, alongside qualitative action following when different action sequences share the same initial observation. Synthetic mid-training improves policy success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and both generation routes improve real-world policy success rates over real-demonstration-only training in the evaluated settings.
These results support universal latent actions as a scalable interface for learning controllable visual dynamics across heterogeneous embodiments.
introduction:
World models, which predict future states conditioned on actions, have long been theorized as a cornerstone of generalist robot intelligence (Sutton, 1991; LeCun et al., 2022; Richens et al., 2025). The recent progress of large-scale video generation has catalyzed a new class of video world models, in which future dynamics are represented directly in visual space (Zhao et al., 2026b; Zhao et al., 2026c; Agarwal et al., 2025; Ali et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026e; Zhao et al., 2026a; Zhao et al., 2025). These models achieve impressive visual fidelity and provide a promising substrate for learning physical dynamics from large-scale video corpora. However, when applied to robotic manipulation, language-conditioned video generators face an interface mismatch: their primary control signal is a task-level description, while physical interaction is governed by continuous, frame-level causal interventions.

Language describes semantic intentions at a coarse temporal granularity. An instruction such as “pick up the cup” specifies a task outcome, but does not determine the precise trajectory by which the outcome is achieved. In contact-rich manipulation, small differences in timing, contact order, gripper state, or camera motion can lead to substantially different futures.
Without fine-grained motion or action conditioning, a text-conditioned model must represent multiple plausible trajectories for the same instruction, making precise control over manipulation dynamics challenging.
Moreover, natural language alone is not a convenient interface for specifying temporally precise interventions, such as closing the gripper earlier while maintaining the same preceding motion.
These limitations motivate an explicit action-conditioning interface for controllable video world modeling.

A natural solution is to condition world models on robot actions (Gao et al., 2026). However, directly using raw robot actions introduces a severe alignment bottleneck. Different embodiments operate in heterogeneous kinematic spaces, with different joint counts, coordinate conventions, control frequencies, and hardware limits. As a result, a world model conditioned on raw actions is difficult to scale across platforms. At the same time, large-scale human videos contain abundant interaction dynamics without robot-specific control labels, while simulation actions need not match a target robot’s control space. What is needed is not a stronger action encoder for a particular robot, but a shared action interface that represents interaction-related visual change while abstracting away platform-specific control conventions.

We argue that latent actions provide such an interface. Instead of representing actions as robot commands, latent actions describe what changed between observations. Distilled from video in a self-supervised manner, continuous latent actions provide a shared description of visual transitions without requiring identical hardware control interfaces. Human hands, robot grippers, and simulated agents may differ drastically in their low-level control signals, yet their visual transitions can share motion and interaction patterns.
By encoding heterogeneous videos into a shared latent-action representation, a single world model can be pretrained on human interactions, robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts under a unified action-conditioning objective, without requiring their native control spaces to be aligned.

In this work, we introduce RynnWorld-Latent, a cross-embodiment video world model built upon RynnLAM (Zhao et al., 2026d), the 3D-grounded latent-action representation introduced in RynnVLA-Latent (Zhao et al., 2026d). While RynnVLA-Latent (Zhao et al., 2026d) uses these descriptors as supervision targets for policy pretraining, our work investigates their complementary role as conditioning signals for learning controllable visual dynamics. RynnWorld-Latent predicts future video from an initial observation and a sequence of continuous latent actions, without requiring text conditioning or a common native robot action space. Technically, we combine global action tokens with an identity-initialized, frame-aligned local conditioning pathway within a pretrained video diffusion transformer. The local pathway exploits the temporal correspondence between latent-action extraction and video-latent compression, allowing each action descriptor to condition its corresponding future video latent.

A central idea of this work is that RynnWorld-Latent should not be viewed only as a future predictor, but as a data-generation engine for scalable robot learning. This leads to two complementary generation modes. First, after target-robot post-training, RynnWorld-Latent can be conditioned on target robot actions and support interactive digital teleoperation (Zhao et al., 2026c): operator control signals are mapped to target actions and drive video generation, producing paired action-video data without requiring additional physical robot execution. Second, the latent-action-conditioned model enables data synthesis from existing videos. Given a source video, we extract its latent-action sequence, edit the first frame to replace the embodiment or environment, and generate a new rollout conditioned on the edited first frame and the original latent actions. First-frame editing specifies the new visual embodiment or environment, while the latent-action sequence guides the interaction dynamics. The resulting rollout has motion close to the source video, but appears under a new embodiment or environment. These generated rollouts can be paired with retargeted pseudo robot actions for downstream VLA training.

We evaluate RynnWorld-Latent from three complementary perspectives. First, we assess action-conditioned video prediction on public world-model benchmarks and held-out demonstrations from two real-robot platforms, measuring prediction fidelity after target-robot adaptation. Second, we investigate latent-action controllability through qualitative comparisons that vary the supplied latent-action sequences while holding the initial observation fixed, and illustrate cross-embodiment motion transfer through first-frame editing. Third, we examine the utility of world-model-generated data for downstream policy learning. Synthetic mid-training improves success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, while both latent-action-driven synthesis and digital teleoperation improve observed closed-loop policy success on the evaluated real-world manipulation tasks. These evaluations jointly characterize prediction fidelity, qualitative action following, and downstream training utility.

Our main contributions are as follows:

We present RynnWorld-Latent, a text-free, latent-action-conditioned video world model,
which uses frozen RynnLAM descriptors as a shared conditioning interface for learning visual dynamics from human interaction videos, heterogeneous robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts without aligning their native control spaces.

We design an action-conditioning mechanism that combines global action tokens with locally identity-initialized, frame-aligned injection, associating transition descriptors with the corresponding future video latents.

We enable latent-action-guided generation under edited robot embodiments and environments, and adapt the world model to native robot-action conditioning. The resulting latent-action synthesis and digital-teleoperation pipelines generate data that improves downstream policy learning in the evaluated settings.

1. We present RynnWorld-Latent, a text-free, latent-action-conditioned video world model,
which uses frozen RynnLAM descriptors as a shared conditioning interface for learning visual dynamics from human interaction videos, heterogeneous robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts without aligning their native control spaces.

2. We design an action-conditioning mechanism that combines global action tokens with locally identity-initialized, frame-aligned injection, associating transition descriptors with the corresponding future video latents.

3. We enable latent-action-guided generation under edited robot embodiments and environments, and adapt the world model to native robot-action conditioning. The resulting latent-action synthesis and digital-teleoperation pipelines generate data that improves downstream policy learning in the evaluated settings.

title: Making Self-Driving Laboratories Auditable:A Unified Framework for Hybrid Actions,Measurements, and Safe Execution
authors: Zihan Zhang,Zeyu Wu,Xin Zhang,Mingyu Luo,Haohui Que,Tong Zhu
abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are laboratory systems that couple experimental planning, automated execution, and measurement feedback in a closed loop. Integrating flexible robot control with the typed application programming interfaces (APIs) and continuous measurements exposed by laboratory instruments remains an execution-interface challenge. To address this challenge, we propose a traceable framework comprising four components: LAM (Lab Action Model), OpenSDL, Safe-SDL, and L3-Bench. LAM is a proposed measurement-conditioned policy architecture that extends vision-language-action paradigms to generate both continuous robot trajectories and typed instrument API calls. OpenSDL is an execution substrate with an initial control implementation, designed to map role-level operations to heterogeneous devices, coordinate execution, and record timestamped causal events. The proposed Safe-SDL runtime gate combines pre-dispatch schema and resource checks with signal temporal logic monitoring during execution, including extended waiting periods. L3-Bench (Level-3 Laboratory Benchmark) specifies an episode-level evaluation protocol covering physical outcomes, timing, reproducibility, safety violations, and fault recovery. Together, these components provide an end-to-end design for linking hybrid action generation, monitored device execution, measurement feedback, and experimental evaluation, addressing coordination and traceability challenges in SDL workflows.
introduction:
Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are laboratory systems that couple experimental intent and planning to automated execution and measurement feedback in a closed loop [1]. This approach can accelerate materials discovery and reaction optimization while reducing the need for repeated manual intervention [1, 2, 3]. Their defining operation is a repeated decision cycle: (i) a machine-readable objective is translated into experimental operations; (ii) those operations are executed by instruments and robots; (iii) measurements and device states are collected; and (iv) the resulting evidence is used to inform the next decision. Through this cycle, experimental throughput can be increased and condition search or hypothesis testing conducted systematically across many trials [4, 5, 2, 3]. To implement this cycle, practical SDLs combine planning tools for step (i), device control for step (ii), sensing and data acquisition for step (iii), and data analysis and decision-making for step (iv). Data and provenance management link these stages, while human supervision supports oversight and intervention throughout the cycle [1].

Representative developments have showcased how experimental procedures and robot actions can be represented, executed, and recorded. In 2019, Steiner et al. described Chemputer, which encoded chemical procedures as executable programs, separating hardware-independent procedures from platform-specific connectivity and device drivers [5]. In 2023, Boiko et al. introduced Coscientist, which combined language-model reasoning with documentation search, code execution, and laboratory APIs to plan and perform chemical experiments [6]. In 2024, Kim et al. introduced OpenVLA, a vision-language-action (VLA) model connecting visual observations and language instructions to learned robot control [7]. In the same year, Bai et al. developed a dynamic knowledge graph framework for distributed SDLs that supports shared ontologies and cycle-level provenance, with limited granularity for exact operation timing under hardware constraints [8]. In 2026, Ren et al. introduced LabVLA, which applied VLA policies to laboratory protocols while acknowledging that measurement-driven protocol revision had not yet been demonstrated [9]. IvoryOS provides an interoperable web interface for orchestrating Python-based SDLs [10]. Established standards address device connectivity and provenance. SiLA 2 (Standardization in Lab Automation) describes instrument capabilities through typed Features, Commands, and Properties, supporting discovery, command execution, and property subscriptions [11]. Provenance standards provide a formal basis for representing auditable records. The World Wide Web Consortium’s PROV Ontology (W3C PROV-O) represents entities, activities, and agents through generation, usage, attribution, and qualified relations carrying roles and time information [12]. PROV-CONSTRAINTS defines validity, equivalence, and event-ordering constraints for provenance records [13]; the companion PROV-SEM Working Group Note provides first-order semantics for the PROV data model [14]. ProvONE extends PROV with scientific workflow structure and execution provenance [15], while Research Object Crate (RO-Crate) packages research artefacts with Schema.org-based structured metadata [16].

These approaches establish provenance representation and consistency rules. Our execution-interface contribution concerns their coupling to measurement-conditioned hybrid actions, pre-dispatch gating, clock-domain-aware timestamping, and timed safety monitoring. We position SDL-Traj as a proposed PROV-O-aligned laboratory profile, reusing core provenance relations and adding application-specific terms for device capabilities, monotonic-clock metadata, and signal temporal logic (STL) robustness. Explicit vocabulary mappings, PROV-O export, SiLA 2 adapters, and conformance tests remain implementation targets. For example, reaction and cooling waits require monitoring to remain active and link fresh or stale measurements, pending calls, verified completion events, and gate decisions. Such execution records must preserve both scientific context and the conditions under which physical actions were admitted. These requirements motivate a shared interface linking measurement-conditioned action generation with execution, monitoring, and evaluation. We therefore propose a traceable framework comprising LAM (Lab Action Model), OpenSDL, Safe-SDL, and L3-Bench.

LAM is designed to generate a hybrid output consisting of continuous robot trajectories and typed instrument API calls from task instructions, visual observations, robot states, and instrument measurements. Its proposed architecture extends the VLA framework with typed telemetry and shares multimodal context between a continuous motion expert and a discrete function-calling head. OpenSDL, with an initial control implementation, is designed to map role-level operations to heterogeneous devices and coordinate operations according to their dependencies, waiting requirements, and completion conditions. Its event model links measurements, device states, and execution outcomes to dispatched commands and runtime decisions in timestamped causal records. In the proposed loop, updated observations and confirmed events provide context for subsequent LAM action proposals. Safe-SDL is the proposed runtime gate for schema and resource checks before dispatch and monitoring of formalized temporal constraints throughout execution, including extended waiting periods. Timeouts, degraded measurement quality, or insufficient safety margins are intended to trigger action blocking and predefined degradation or safe-abort procedures. L3-Bench (Level-3 Laboratory Benchmark) specifies an episode-level evaluation protocol covering protocol-specific physical outcomes, timing, reproducibility, safety violations, and fault recovery. Here, L3 denotes measurement-conditioned adaptation within an experiment, as defined in the task-specific classification of Section 2.1. End-to-end LAM training, cross-device transfer experiments, and systematic hardware and safety validation remain to be completed; improvements in throughput, adaptability, and fault recovery are hypotheses to be tested through the proposed evaluation.

title: Learning Side-by-Side Navigation for Personal Mobility Vehicles from Human Drivers
authors: Luis Yoichi Morales,Florent Ferreri
abstract:
This paper presents an approach to achieve side-by-side autonomous motion
with a pair of personal mobility vehicles (PMVs). Given a global path, two
PMVs plan cooperatively so as to hold a social formation that lets the
passengers hold a conversation, while keeping the ride safe and smooth.
Each vehicle runs its own sampling-based model-predictive planner; the
planners exchange
nothing but the odometry each vehicle could observe of the other, and the
joint decision is expressed as a pair of utility matrices over pairs of
candidate trajectories, resolved by a common rule.
The behavioural parameters are fitted by inverse reinforcement learning from
409409 minutes of driving by ten pairs of people in human-driven PMVs in an
indoor environment, and the lanes the pair can use are derived offline from
the corridor itself rather than fixed by hand. A safety layer the cost cannot
override executes a move only if the vehicle can still brake clear, measured
from its whole body, and a vehicle that is stuck reverses along its own path
and continues. In closed-loop simulation over
2424 runs in the conditions the drivers were recorded in and
2424 in four generated obstacle layouts, no vehicle entered a
wall or a cone. The pair holds conversational formation for
60.5%60.5\% and 68.9%68.9\% of the time among obstacles
(anticlockwise and clockwise) and 81.2%81.2\% and
91.5%91.5\% in a clear aisle, against the drivers’
34.0%34.0\% and 36.0%36.0\%, and
52.9%52.9\% and 56.0%56.0\%, and it matches
their speed. It keeps
one lateral formation where the drivers alternated between a close diagonal
and a wide abreast one, and it varies far less.
Experimental results are based on a differential drive kinematic simulator running on ROS 211

introduction:
Current robot systems can achieve reliable long-term navigation in dynamic environments with pedestrians around [1, 2]. Recent works have placed attention to the pedestrian flow to be able to pass-by walking people in a social manner [3, 4, 5]. These robot navigation approaches consider the humans passing by and the overall safety but do not consider their own motion smoothness.

Differently from standard mobile robots, autonomous PMV’s carry human passengers, so the navigation must be safe and comfortable for the passenger.
PMV’s can provide transportation services in a smaller scale than car-like vehicles in locations such as hospitals, retirement homes, houses, attraction parks. Moreover, in some remote rural areas, there is the need to provide mobility assistance to isolated aged people where PMV’s have the potential to provide personal last mile services such as autonomus ride shares [6] and autonomous personal vehicles on demand [7].

While PMV’s could provide mobility services in remote areas and independence for aged people [8], it is important to allow the passengers to move together in groups with partners allowing them to engage in conversations with other pedestrians or PMV passengers.
Mobility independence and the ability of socializing are relevant factors that impact well-being and health [8],
impacting the quality of life of aged persons as leaving home allows people to keep social and physical activities preventing mental capacity decline on aged people [9, 10].
Moreover, it has been reported that poor or limited social interactions increases the risk of dementia [11].

Regarding people interacting in groups, it has been found that the majority of people tend to move in groups [12].
At low densities people tend to walk in small social groups of two to five people where they tend to walk in side-by-side formation in order to keep direct line of sight to engage in interaction [13].
Within large groups subgroups composed of two or three people emerge [14].
People act cooperatively with their partners, keep social formation and anticipate their movement to keep pace.
Despite being previous works and proposed approaches to develop models to keep pace with their side by side partners [15, 16, 17, 18],
currently there are no autonomous navigation systems which can reliably move alongside partners in a cooperative way or be integrated into a social group.

Humans achieve side-by-side motion by performing shared planning. In a shared planning activity humans share goals and intentions and hold the partner accountable for his role [19]. While moving together as a shared activity we shared the common intention of moving towards a destination which is different from the case of moving alongside a stranger by chance where we just happen to collaborate or negotiate traffic for a short period of time [19].

Figure 1 shows an image of a pair of partners moving alongside as a social mobile group. An agent is composed of a passenger and a PMV. The PMV
transports the passengers while he/she has a conversation with another partner.
The vehicles share their pose and velocities, anticipate the partner’s future location and jointly plan their next control action to be able to keep side-by-side formation. A motion planner computes the linear and angular velocities of each vehicle so that the navigation results in smooth and comfortable for each passenger.

In our knowledge, this is the first work which treats autonomous navigation of PMV’s as a social group where anticipation of the partner for side-by-side formation is crucial to keep a social interaction between passengers.

title: On Shaky Ground: Characterising Non-Rigid Base Effects in Mobile Manipulation
authors: Zongyuan Zhang,Christopher Lehnert,Will N. Browne,Jonathan M. Roberts
comment: . Accepted at the Australasian Conference on Robotics and Automation (ACRA 2026)
abstract: Mobile robot manipulators extend contact-task capability beyond the workspace of fixed robot installations, but their bases must also sustain the forces generated by the task. On lightweight platforms, base motion and support compliance can change the force and motion realised at the workpiece. How these non-rigid base effects manifest during sustained contact remains insufficiently characterised. This paper investigates non-rigid base effects in mobile robot manipulators through a sanding case study combining exploratory simulation with experiments on two lightweight, unactuated wheeled testbeds. Joint measurements of contact force, tool motion, and base vibration show that sustained contact coexisted with substantial task error: under low base–ground resistance, only 54–70% of a 100 N command was realised, with tool-centre-point errors reaching 100 mm. Increasing base–ground resistance during contact improved force realisation and arrested further tool displacement, while base vibration did not vary consistently with force-tracking error in the tested conditions. These observations illustrate how non-rigid base behaviour can affect contact-task execution and highlight the value of examining force, motion, and vibration together when characterising lightweight mobile manipulation.
introduction:
Fixed-base industrial manipulators are widely used for contact-rich processes such as sanding, polishing, and assembly. Their rigid bases enable accurate motion and force control, but limit operation to a fixed workspace. Mounting the manipulator on a mobile robot extends the operating workspace and allows the tool to be carried between work areas, making mobile manipulators attractive for tasks involving large or distributed structures such as aircraft, ships, and building surfaces [11].

This mobility, however, introduces additional challenges in contact tasks. Contact forces are transmitted through the manipulator and the mobile base to the ground. Existing mobile machining systems often use deliberately heavy automated guided vehicles or track-mounted platforms [8, 19, 18, 15] to increase stiffness and stability during contact. Lightweight mobile platforms are easier to move and deploy, but their lower mass, limited wheel traction, and compliance at the wheel–ground interface can lead to base motion and vibration under contact load.

Figure 1 illustrates these effects. Normal and tangential forces at the sanding tool are transmitted through the manipulator to the base. If the horizontal reaction exceeds the available traction, the base can slip. If the resultant wrench moves the zero-moment point outside the support polygon, the system can lose static stability. Compliance in the tyres, suspension, or ground surface can also introduce oscillation of the base and manipulator. These behaviours are collectively referred to as non-rigid base effects. They affect contact-task performance because base motion contributes to tool centre point (TCP) error [20], while base vibration and deformation can disturb the contact force. Under force control, the arm commands tool advance relative to its base, whereas the contact force depends on the tool–workpiece compression. Base motion away from the workpiece under the contact reaction can therefore absorb part of the commanded advance and contribute to a sustained force shortfall and to undesired tool motion relative to the workpiece, even while contact is maintained.

Existing work has examined mobile-manipulator stability, wheel slip, machining accuracy, compliance, and contact-force control, but there is limited experimental characterisation of how base motion manifests simultaneously in realised contact force and tool motion relative to the workpiece during sustained contact on lightweight mobile manipulators. This paper addresses this gap through a sanding case study combining exploratory simulation with experiments on two instrumented lightweight wheeled testbeds. Their unactuated bases serve as mechanical surrogates for mobile robot bases (Section 4.1). The study addresses three questions: (i) What non-rigid base effects arise under contact forces? (ii) How do base–environment coupling, arm posture, tool excitation, and support compliance affect force realisation, tool motion, and base vibration? (iii) Do the principal response patterns persist across different lightweight platforms?

The contributions are:

An experimental characterisation of non-rigid base effects in force-controlled sanding, showing that sustained contact coexisted with force shortfall and TCP error, and that increasing base–ground resistance during contact improved force realisation and arrested further tool displacement;

An assessment of how these effects vary with commanded force, arm posture, tool excitation, and support compliance on two lightweight mobile platforms, with base-vibration measurements providing a complementary view of the dynamic response.

1. An experimental characterisation of non-rigid base effects in force-controlled sanding, showing that sustained contact coexisted with force shortfall and TCP error, and that increasing base–ground resistance during contact improved force realisation and arrested further tool displacement;

2. An assessment of how these effects vary with commanded force, arm posture, tool excitation, and support compliance on two lightweight mobile platforms, with base-vibration measurements providing a complementary view of the dynamic response.
