title: TOPS: Reshaping Flow Source and Transport for Multi-Task Robot Manipulation
authors: Tuo An,Chuhao Zhou,Jiahua Dong,Jingliang Li,Jiaqi Bai,Jindou Jia,Jianfei Yang
abstract:
Flow-based policies for language-conditioned multi-task manipulation commonly share a single Gaussian source prior and a common linear transport path across tasks.
However, reliably executing multiple tasks with distinct motion requirements
remains challenging for a shared policy.
We introduce TOPS (Task-Oriented Priors and Schedules), which adapts the flow source prior and interpolation schedule to each task without modifying the network architecture.
TOPS first constructs multimodal task sources from reverse-mapped expert action sequences, allowing language instructions to select where generation begins. Guided by source-target covariance mismatch, it then slows the transition toward expert actions early in denoising and accelerates it later along directions requiring expansion. Under a Gaussian endpoint model, our analysis shows that this schedule adjustment can lower an upper bound on velocity-prediction risk. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN demonstrate improved performance across in-distribution, perturbation and cross-environment settings, alongside better data efficiency. Using one integration step, TOPS raises LIBERO-10 success from 53.44% to 69.67% compared with ten-step Standard Flow Matching (FM), while reducing inference time to approximately one-sixth of the baseline. TOPS also yields consistent gains when transferred to the large-scale
flow-based π0.5\pi_{0.5} policy across all four evaluated settings. Real-world experiments further demonstrate improved task success, including an increase from 20% with standard FM to 80% with TOPS on the upper-drawer opening task.
introduction:
Real-world manipulation exhibits substantial behavioral diversity.
Different tasks require distinct motion patterns, and even a given
goal can be achieved through different contact strategies, motion
trajectories, and temporal execution patterns.
Diffusion and flow-matching
models (Funk et al., 2024; Chi et al., 2025; Braun et al., 2024)
capture such multimodal action distributions directly and have
become widely used in imitation learning.
This expressive power has also carried the generative paradigm
from task-specific visuomotor control to language-conditioned
multi-task and generalist robot policies (Yan et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025b; Black et al., 2025a).
In this setting, a shared policy must accommodate the motion
requirements of different tasks and execute each task reliably.

However, a shared policy can perform well on some tasks yet struggle
to execute others reliably (Haldar et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2023a; Ren et al., 2026).
A shared policy must capture multiple action
modes within a task and substantially different action distributions across
tasks (Wu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026).
Existing approaches introduce or redesign policy components to
improve multi-task performance, using feature
modulation (Haldar et al., 2024), visual selection (Huang et al., 2025),
instruction-generated parameters (Ren et al., 2026), and expert
routing (Deng et al., 2026).
In flow policies (Lipman et al., 2022), the network must recover distinct
task-specific action distributions from a shared Gaussian source
under a common linear transport path.
Before changing the policy architecture as in prior work, we step back to the generative process itself and ask: could adapting
the source prior and transport to each task improve multi-task
performance without changing the policy
architecture?
To investigate, we reverse a trained multi-task flow policy and trace
expert actions back to their source samples (Tang et al., 2026).

As shown in Figs. 1(a,b), reverse-mapped expert actions exhibit task-dependent organization under the warm-up policy, with further subclusters within individual tasks. These patterns motivate us to investigate whether fitting task-specific sources to the reverse images and directly denoising from the corresponding region can improve policy learning.
To further understand what changes are needed to reach expert actions, we analyze the covariance mismatch between these sources and the corresponding expert-action distributions using a Gaussian optimal-transport map. Its eigenvectors define orthogonal axes, each representing a weighted combination of action components across timesteps. We find expert actions have substantially greater standard deviation than source samples only along a few axes. We refer to this source-to-target increase as expansion. Yet conventional flow matching (Lipman et al., 2022; Black et al., 2025a) starts every task from a single task-independent Gaussian and applies the same linear interpolation schedule along every axis. This leaves the network to recover task-specific action structure from shared noise, while interpolation timing remains unchanged despite the unequal source-to-target changes revealed by our analysis.

Motivated by these findings, we introduce TOPS
(Task-Oriented Priors and Schedules)
for multi-task flow policies.
It fits a Gaussian mixture with low-rank covariance
structure (Tipping and Bishop, 1999) to each task’s reverse-mapped samples,
allowing language instructions to select the source.
Along expansion axes, TOPS slows interpolation toward expert
actions early and accelerates it later, retaining linear
interpolation elsewhere.
Under a Gaussian endpoint model (Albergo et al., 2025),
we show that adapting interpolation can lower an upper bound
on velocity-prediction risk.
This risk captures the irreducible error that arises when the
same interpolated action sequence corresponds to different
velocity targets.
On LIBERO-10, our schedule reduces estimated time-integrated
directional risk on expansion axes by 18.5%18.5\% relative to
linear interpolation (Fig. 10).
In controlled 2D experiments with few integration steps,
it also places more samples in target regions than linear
or fast-then-slow schedules (Fig. 7).
Together, these choices support efficient few-step action generation.

We evaluate TOPS on LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023a),
LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025), CALVIN (Mees et al., 2022),
and three real-world multi-task suites.
With the same backbone as the baselines, TOPS achieves the highest
mean performance across two in-distribution and two out-of-distribution
settings, covering perturbations and unseen environments,
using one schedule-aware step.
Compared with ten-step Standard FM (Lipman et al., 2022),
it raises LIBERO-10 success from 53.44% to 69.67%
while reducing inference latency to approximately one-sixth.
Limited-data evaluations also show gains across all simulation
benchmarks: on CALVIN ABC→\toD, TOPS trained on 30% of
demonstrations outperforms all evaluated baselines trained on 50%.
These gains also extend to the large-scale flow-based π0.5\pi_{0.5} policy
in all four settings, raising LIBERO-Plus success from 64.4%
to 69.0% and CALVIN ABC→\toD average chain length
from 3.033 to 3.744.
Real-world gains include 80% success on upper-drawer
opening, compared with 20% for Standard FM.

To recap, our contributions are threefold:

• We construct
task-specific sources by fitting Gaussian mixtures with
low-rank covariance structure to reverse-mapped expert action
chunks, enabling language-guided source selection.

• We introduce
slow-then-fast scheduling along expansion directions identified
by Gaussian optimal transport, motivated by an upper
bound on velocity-prediction risk under independent
Gaussian endpoints.

• Experiments
show that TOPS achieves the highest mean performance across the
main in- and out-of-distribution simulation settings with one
schedule-aware step, while reducing latency and improving data
efficiency. Gains also extend to the large-scale π0.5\pi_{0.5}
policy and real-world tasks.

title: RoboSTD: Zero-Shot Single-to-Dual Transfer via Sagittal Mirroring for Bimanual Learning
authors: Hongyu Wu,Chong Liu,Shaoxuan Xie,Shaqi Luo,Hanyu Feng,Shihan Wu,Guocai Yao
abstract:
Bimanual robot manipulation plays an important role in real-world robotic applications, but the high cost of collecting bimanual demonstrations limits the scalable development of bimanual policy learning. Meanwhile, existing single-arm manipulation data are difficult to directly transfer to bimanual systems due to the Single-to-Dual gap in
action spaces, coordination requirements, and arm-side spatial preference.
To address this issue, we propose RoboSTD, a zero-shot Single-to-Dual data construction method for bimanual robot learning. RoboSTD first applies sagittal-plane mirroring to observations,
proprioception, and actions to construct executable contralateral
pseudo-demonstrations. It then uses an LLM to generate structured
spatio-temporal coordination constraints that guide the reconstruction
of pseudo-bimanual supervision across workspace regions and task stages.
We evaluate RoboSTD on the AgileX ALOHA platform in both RoboTwin simulation and real-world settings. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of RoboSTD for bimanual policy learning. Without requiring additional bimanual demonstrations, RoboSTD increases the average number of collected cups to 2.11×\mathbf{2.11\times} that of the single-arm baseline in the cup collection task. Project page:
https://huahungy.github.io/RoboSTD/
introduction:
Bimanual robot manipulation enables complex tasks that are difficult to efficiently perform with single-arm systems through coordinated use of two arms, making it important for real-world robotic applications [1, 2]. However, compared with single-arm learning, bimanual policy learning faces a more severe data bottleneck. Collecting high-quality bimanual demonstrations requires not only recording the trajectories of both arms, but also maintaining spatial relationships, execution timing, and task-role coordination, making data acquisition substantially more complex and expensive. Previous studies have identified demonstration collection cost and
teleoperation burden as major bottlenecks for scalable robot learning
 [3, 4, 5]. Therefore, reducing the dependence on real bimanual demonstrations is critical for scalable bimanual robot learning.

Meanwhile, the amount of single-arm manipulation data accumulated by the robot learning community represents a valuable resource for robot learning. However, how to reuse such single-arm data for bimanual learning remains underexplored. This gives rise to a Single-to-Dual gap, involving differences in action spaces, coordination requirements, and spatial preferences across arm sides. An overview of this challenge and our approach is shown in
Fig. 1. To investigate this phenomenon, we randomly sample 10,000 trajectories
from Open X-Embodiment [6] and compute the spatial
locations of end-effector events. As shown in
Fig. 2(a), only 35.7% of these events
occur in the left workspace, whereas 64.3% occur in the right
workspace, corresponding to a 28.6 percentage-point spatial
imbalance. We further evaluate the pretrained
π0\pi_{0} [7] and the non-pretrained
ACT [1] on 10 tasks in
RoboTwin 2.0 [8]. As shown in
Fig. 2(b), π0\pi_{0} achieves average success rates
of 66.3% and 75.9% on left- and right-arm tasks,
respectively, corresponding to a Bias Gap of 9.6 percentage points.
In contrast, ACT achieves 50.0% and 50.4%,
with a Bias Gap of only 0.4 percentage points.
The right-side preference observed in both the data distribution and
the pretrained policy suggests that upstream spatial imbalance may be
reflected in arm-side performance, potentially hindering
balanced Single-to-Dual transfer.

To address this gap, we propose RoboSTD, a zero-shot
Single-to-Dual data construction method for bimanual robot learning.
Here, zero-shot denotes requiring no additional task-specific
bimanual demonstrations, rather than zero-shot policy inference.
RoboSTD consists of two stages. First, sagittal-plane mirroring
transforms observations, proprioception, and actions
 [9, 10] to construct
executable contralateral pseudo-demonstrations. Second, LLM-guided spatio-temporal reconstruction infers arm assignment,
precedence, and conflict constraints from context to compose
original and mirrored skills into pseudo-bimanual supervision.

We evaluate RoboSTD using the AgileX ALOHA platform in both the RoboTwin 2.0
simulation environment [8] and real-world settings.
In the simulation effectiveness experiments over 10 RoboTwin tasks, policies
trained with 100 native bimanual demonstrations per task achieve an
average success rate of 67.6%, while those trained with
RoboSTD-generated supervision from only 50 single-arm demonstrations
per task achieve 66.5%. The small 1.1 percentage-point
gap shows that RoboSTD can construct effective bimanual supervision from fewer single-arm demonstrations. In the spatial generalization task, RoboSTD extends skills originally limited to a unilateral workspace to the full bimanual workspace, achieving a 2.11×\mathbf{2.11\times} increase in the average number of collected cups over the single-arm baseline. In the long-horizon sandwich-making task, RoboSTD further improves the
task success rate and average completion, demonstrating stronger temporal coordination. These results demonstrate that sagittal-plane mirroring and
LLM-guided spatio-temporal reconstruction can effectively extend
single-arm demonstrations into useful bimanual supervision.

The main contributions are summarized as follows:

We identify and analyze arm-side spatial preferences in robot data and pretrained policies, and reveal their potential impact on balanced bimanual learning.

We propose RoboSTD, a zero-shot Single-to-Dual data construction method that converts existing single-arm demonstrations into bimanual supervision.

We demonstrate RoboSTD’s effectiveness for Single-to-Dual transfer, improving workspace coverage and long-horizon coordination in real-world bimanual tasks.

1. We identify and analyze arm-side spatial preferences in robot data and pretrained policies, and reveal their potential impact on balanced bimanual learning.

2. We propose RoboSTD, a zero-shot Single-to-Dual data construction method that converts existing single-arm demonstrations into bimanual supervision.

3. We demonstrate RoboSTD’s effectiveness for Single-to-Dual transfer, improving workspace coverage and long-horizon coordination in real-world bimanual tasks.

title: From Biological Curves to Soft Modular Robots: Learning-Based Inverse Design with Uncertainty-Guided Refinement
authors: Dixiang Wang,Minghao Zha,Arifur Rahman,Yinhong Qin,Yitao Jiang,Shiyang Lu,Zebing Mao,Muhao Chen,Luyang Zhao
abstract: Animals exhibit diverse shape-changing behaviors, from the undulatory swimming of eels to the arching movements of inchworms. Reproducing these biological shapes with modular soft robots offers a promising approach to developing versatile bioinspired robotic systems. However, translating a desired shape into a feasible robotic configuration remains challenging. Existing cable-driven modular soft robots rely on computationally expensive physics-based modeling and combinatorial search for inverse design, making it difficult to efficiently reproduce diverse target shapes. To address this challenge, we present a learning-based real-to-sim-to-real framework that translates biological curves into robotic configurations through surrogate-assisted inverse design and uncertainty-guided refinement. The proposed method combines learned inverse prediction with targeted candidate exploration, using a fast forward surrogate to evaluate and select suitable designs. The learned forward surrogate reduces deformation prediction time from 1.53 ×\times 105 ms to 0.0008 ms, achieving approximately a 1.9 ×\times 108-fold speedup. At the same time, the proposed inverse design method reduces design time from 1.99 ×\times 106 ms to 4.18 ms. On 5,000 test samples generated from previously unseen threading patterns, the method achieves a 93% shape reconstruction success rate under surrogate-based evaluation. Physical demonstrations with four bioinspired robots further illustrate the translation of biological curves into realizable robotic shapes.
introduction:
Nature exhibits a rich diversity of shape-changing behaviors, from the swimming motions of eels [1] to the slithering of snakes [2] and the arching movement of inchworms [3].
Despite their distinct biological mechanisms, many of these deformations can be represented as geometric curves, providing a common description of diverse biological shapes [4, 5].
This observation motivates a real-to-sim-to-real approach to bio-inspired robot design, in which shapes observed in nature are abstracted into target curves, translated into feasible robotic configurations through simulation, and reproduced by physical robots, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Soft robots are particularly suitable for this purpose, as their compliant structures enable flexible and adaptable deformations [6, 7, 8, 9]. However, translating a desired geometric curve into a physically realizable robotic shape requires identifying appropriate structural configurations and actuation parameters [10, 11, 12].

SoftSnap, a previously developed cable-driven modular soft robotic platform, provides one possible approach to realizing such target curves [13]. Each untethered module integrates onboard actuation, control, and power, enabling different bending curves through variations in cable-threading patterns and cable lengths. Multiple modules can be assembled using customized snap-together connectors to construct more complex robotic shapes. To predict the resulting deformation, SoftSnap employs a physics-based quasi-static forward model that uses iterative numerical optimization to minimize bending energy under a cable-length constraint. Although this model captures the deformation behavior, repeated forward evaluations can be computationally expensive (152.75 s in average). The original platform also supports inverse design through a search-based approach that enumerates possible threading configurations, filters geometrically infeasible candidates, and evaluates the remaining configurations using the physics-based forward model. However, the number of possible threading configurations grows combinatorially with the number of ribs and available holes. Consequently, the inverse design process becomes computationally expensive due to both the large number of candidate configurations and the repeated numerical optimization required for forward evaluation. Restricting the number of evaluated candidates can reduce computational cost but may overlook configurations that better reproduce the target shape.

Learning-based methods offer a promising approach to reducing the computational cost of repeated physics-based evaluations. Previous studies have used neural networks to predict soft robot deformation [14, 15, 16], estimate cable tensions for desired tip positions in soft manipulators [17], and perform inverse design using learned forward surrogates [18, 19, 20, 21].
However, inverse design for the SoftSnap platform presents additional challenges due to its mixed discrete-continuous design space and non-unique inverse mapping [22]. Specifically, different combinations of cable-threading patterns and cable lengths can produce identical or nearly identical shapes, represented by their bending-angle vectors. This one-to-many relationship makes direct inverse prediction challenging [23, 24]. Conventional regression methods, such as those using mean squared error, may average cable lengths associated with different valid solutions, while selecting the most probable hole at each rib may combine threading choices from different feasible configurations. As a result, the predicted threading pattern and cable length may fail to reproduce the target shape accurately. Exhaustively evaluating alternative configurations, however, would reintroduce substantial computational costs. These challenges motivate an approach that combines fast inverse prediction with targeted candidate exploration and efficient surrogate-based evaluation.

To enable efficient inverse design within this real-to-sim-to-real workflow, we propose a surrogate-assisted approach that combines learning-based prediction with uncertainty-guided candidate refinement. First, a large-scale dataset is generated using the physics-based quasi-static model and curated to remove invalid and unstable samples. A forward surrogate is then trained to efficiently predict robot deformation given a cable-threading pattern and target cable length. Next, an inverse neural network is trained to jointly predict the cable-threading pattern and cable length from a target curve represented by a bending-angle vector. The inverse model is initially trained using supervised classification and regression losses, followed by end-to-end fine-tuning through a pretrained, frozen forward surrogate to minimize angular reconstruction error. Once trained, the inverse model generates an initial design, which is further improved through uncertainty-guided candidate refinement. Specifically, uncertain threading positions are identified using classification-logit margins, and alternative configurations are explored with adaptive search budgets. For more uncertain cases, local cable-length adjustments are also introduced. The forward surrogate then evaluates the resulting candidates and selects the configuration with the lowest predicted reconstruction error. Finally, physical demonstrations of biologically inspired soft robots illustrate the framework’s potential for translating target geometric curves into realizable robotic shapes.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: (a) A data-driven forward modeling framework that integrates physics-based data generation, data curation, and a learned forward surrogate to efficiently predict robot deformation without repeated numerical optimization during inference.
(b) A surrogate-assisted inverse design approach that combines learning-based inverse prediction with uncertainty-guided candidate refinement to selectively explore alternative cable-threading patterns and cable lengths, improving target-shape reconstruction without exhaustive search.

title: SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models
authors: Jiaming Hu,Shi Bo,Yan Zheng,Tian Wang,Florian Dubost,Alejandro Mottini,Junze Liu,Arvind Srinivasan,Kai Zhong,Kun Qian,Sharon Gao,Vianne Gao,Houyu Zhang,Qingjun Cui
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) enable world models to plan from images
by predicting future embeddings. However, their visual prediction objectives do not explicitly
incorporate task-relevant state information, so the physical state that determines task progress
may not be reliably captured in the latent space. Supervising world models with simulator state can make planning
more informative, but it requires deciding which state features matter. Features are typically selected by hand or weighted uniformly, and a uniform weighting gives every standardized state feature equal influence, so
redundant coordinates can overcount the same variation, while irrelevant ones can obscure
task-relevant differences. To address this limitation, we propose SWIM (State Weighting with Inverse-Dynamics Model), which learns state weights from offline trajectories by predicting recorded actions from current states and observed future displacements. The learned weights quantify each feature’s contribution to action prediction and define a weighted state metric for state-supervised training, which we demonstrate by aligning latent and state distances. The inverse-dynamics model is used only during training, so the
resulting world model plans from images with no additional planning-time computation. Across
five simulated robotic manipulation tasks, SWIM consistently improves planning success over
uniform state weighting.
introduction:
World models support planning by predicting the consequences of candidate actions before execution (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2019; Chua et al., 2018). Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) perform this prediction in latent space without reconstructing future observations (LeCun, 2022; Assran et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2025). For example, LeWorldModel (LeWM) jointly learns an image encoder and action-conditioned latent dynamics through a next-embedding prediction objective and anti-collapse regularization (Maes et al., 2026). At planning time, candidate action sequences are evaluated using the Euclidean distance between predicted terminal and goal embeddings. However, the prediction objective does not explicitly require the latent space to represent the physical state that determines task progress. Although probing shows that JEPA latents encode physical quantities (Maes et al., 2026), forward prediction alone does not ensure that task-relevant physical state is reliably identifiable or well separated in latent space, which can limit downstream planning (Yan and others, 2026; Zeng et al., 2026).

This has motivated supervising world models with the simulator states recorded alongside offline data, which provide a direct signal of task progress: TC-WM aligns compact visual representations with proprioceptive state (Fu et al., 2026), PhyLatent and PSG-JEPA ground latent representations in physical state (Zeng et al., 2026; Yan and others, 2026), and SCALE aligns latent distances with task-state distances during world-model training (Hu et al., 2026). These methods take the supervising state as given, so their effectiveness depends on how the state is selected and weighted. Although state variables contain information relevant to planning, different coordinates may encode overlapping information, while others may be irrelevant to the task. Assigning equal weights to all coordinates can therefore overemphasize redundant information and introduce irrelevant variation into the state supervision, while selecting coordinates by hand requires task-specific expertise. This motivates learning the relative contributions of state features rather than treating all coordinates equally.

A key question is how to determine these weights. Prior action-based objectives, including inverse-dynamics models (which infer the action that produced an observed state change) and PLDM (Agrawal et al., 2016; Pathak et al., 2017; Sobal et al., 2025), shape latent representations directly but do not address how individual state coordinates should be weighted. Since actions directly influence future state transitions and task outcomes, we leverage recorded actions to identify state changes that are informative about behavior: a coordinate whose change helps infer the action reflects the agent’s behavior, whereas a redundant or unaffected coordinate adds little information. This provides a behavior-grounded surrogate for state relevance.

Building on this idea, we propose SWIM (State Weighting with Inverse-Dynamics Model), a two-stage framework for learning behavior-informed state supervision. First, a gated inverse-dynamics model learns continuous state weights by predicting recorded actions from current states and observed future displacements. Its training combines the log-likelihood of recorded actions, discrimination between matching and mismatched state changes, and regularization. The learned weights define a weighted state metric that can replace the hand-specified state in state-supervised training; we then demonstrate it by calibrating JEPA latent geometry through SCALE (Hu et al., 2026). This approach requires neither reward nor success labels. Because the inverse-dynamics model and simulator states are used only during training, the world model still plans from images without additional inference-time computation.

Our contributions are as follows: (i) We introduce an inverse-dynamics approach to automatically learn the relative importance of state features from offline trajectories. (ii) We demonstrate the learned state metric in SCALE, aligning JEPA latent distances with weighted state distances to better support downstream planning. (iii) We evaluate SWIM on five OGBench manipulation tasks (Park et al., 2025) with the cross-entropy method (CEM) and iCEM planners over five training seeds, where it consistently improves over uniform state weighting , and we analyze how the learned weights respond to structured distractors.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work, and Section 3 introduces latent-space planning and state-distance supervision. Section 4 presents SWIM, followed by the experiments in Section 5. Section 6 discusses limitations and concludes. The appendices provide implementation and evaluation details, an analysis of the state transformation and learned weights, and additional experimental results.

title: Mimetic Embodiment Transfer of Human-Humanoid Interaction from In-the-Wild Videos
authors: Nghia Le,Khang Nguyen,Ba Long Tran,Thi Quynh Nhu Pham,Binh Nguyen,Tuong Do,Erman Tjiputra,Hoan Nguyen,Tung D. Ta,Baoru Huang,Hai-Nguyen(Hann)Nguyen,Anh Nguyen
abstract: Enabling a humanoid to interact naturally with human partners requires preserving not only individual motions but also the spatial, semantic, and contact relationships underlying the interaction (i.e., hugging, dancing, hand-shaking, etc.). Furthermore, a practical solution should generalize across various humanoid embodiments with distinct morphologies and kinematic constraints. To tackle this challenge, we propose HumiTransfer, a mimetic embodiment transfer framework that converts in-the-wild human-human interaction videos into physically plausible human-humanoid interactions. HumiTransfer first reconstructs 3D human motion with consistent foot-ground contact, then transfers one participant to a target humanoid embodiment via interaction modeling, using weighted joint-relative directions and anatomical offsets to prioritize interaction-critical inter-body relationships, while post-retargeting optimization enforces balance, contact, and collision avoidance. Subsequently, we apply HumiTransfer to 1,2001,200 in-the-wild videos, producing approximately 500,000500,000 frames of diverse interactions for the 2626-DoF Unitree R1 Edu and the 2323-DoF HighTorque Mini-hi humanoid robot, resulting in our HumiMimic dataset. Across both robots, HumiTransfer achieves superior motion fidelity, preserves inter-body relationships, and maintains contact accuracy compared with existing baselines. Moreover, we demonstrate that HumiMimic supports motion generation methods for synthesizing interactive humanoid motions following a human partner. Finally, our real robot deployments confirm the physical executability of the transferred motions in real-world settings.
introduction:
Humans are adept at participating in the social world not only through explicit instruction but also by observing and responding to others’ behaviors [1]. Such a capacity is commonly referred to as mimesis: the representation and communication of experience through interaction in both semantic and dynamic manners [2, 3]. Indeed, interaction cannot be acquired by imitating isolated motions alone. Meaningful human-to-human interactions fundamentally arise from the evolving relationship between participants. For example, making a humanoid dance with another human requires not merely reproducing the learned whole-body motions, but also being aware of interpersonal spacing and orientation, synchronizing their rhythm and movement phase, coordinating contact, and continually adapting to the partner’s motion despite variations in embodiment. Herein, mimesis offers a natural account of how observed human behavior can translate into actions for humanoid robots, connecting motion recognition, motion generation, and embodied communication, thus opening up a vast range of applications in human-humanoid interactions.

In practice, existing humanoid motion datasets [10, 13, 14] are predominantly collected through high-fidelity teleoperation or motion-capture systems in controlled environments. Although these pipelines provide accurate, robot-compatible motions, they are often tied to specific embodiments and capture only a subset of interaction behaviors within limited environments. Advances in scene-aware and occlusion-robust human pose estimation [15, 16], mesh-based body fitting [17], and learning-based monocular reconstruction [18] have made it possible to recover whole-body human motion from videos. Despite promising results, they often overlook human-human interactions due to the scarcity of suitable datasets. Publicly available videos, by contrast, contain abundant and diverse human-human interactions captured in real-world settings, offering a scalable source for deriving human-humanoid interaction motions.

Recent advances in whole-body motion learning [19, 20, 21] have expanded the range of human-like behaviors that humanoids can synthesize. Still, learning behaviors such as human-to-human interactions remain fundamentally constrained by the availability and diversity of training data: a humanoid must not only reproduce an individual motion but also coordinate with its human partner [22]. Meanwhile, retargeting methods offer a means of converting observed human behavior into embodiment-specific compatibility, yet existing approaches [23, 24, 25] primarily optimize single-agent motion, neither preserving the inter-body relationships underlying the interaction nor identifying which semantic cues to optimize across embodiments. Therefore, the central challenge of mimetic embodiment transfer is to translate one participant’s motion into a humanoid embodiment while preserving the interaction semantics with its human partner.

To tackle this challenge, we propose HumiTransfer, a new mimetic embodiment transfer framework that translates in-the-wild human-human interactions into human-humanoid interactions, as shown in Fig. . HumiTransfer takes various interaction sequences as video frames to extract human motion, then transfers one human participant’s poses to two distinct humanoid embodiments: the 2323-DoF HighTorque Mini-hi and the 2626-DoF Unitree R1 Edu, resulting in our HumiMimic dataset. We also benchmark existing retargeting methods to showcase the diversity and complexity of interactions in HumiMimic. In summary, our main contributions are twofold as follows:

We propose HumiTransfer, a mimetic embodiment transfer framework that translates one human into a humanoid while preserving the semantics and distances underlying the interaction and satisfying embodiment-specific kinematic and physical constraints.

We introduce HumiMimic, a scalable embodied dataset that contains 1,2001,200 human-humanoid interaction sequences (∼500,000{\sim}500,000 frames) by extracting body frames from in-the-wild human-human interaction videos. Our code and dataset will be made publicly available.

1. We propose HumiTransfer, a mimetic embodiment transfer framework that translates one human into a humanoid while preserving the semantics and distances underlying the interaction and satisfying embodiment-specific kinematic and physical constraints.

2. We introduce HumiMimic, a scalable embodied dataset that contains 1,2001,200 human-humanoid interaction sequences (∼500,000{\sim}500,000 frames) by extracting body frames from in-the-wild human-human interaction videos. Our code and dataset will be made publicly available.

title: Camera-to-Quadruped Robot Pose Estimation from Sequential Images
authors: Seobin Hwang,Ji-Seong Beom,Yeong-Jun Cho
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Quadruped robots are increasingly deployed in hazardous environments such as disaster response and facility inspection, where external-camera monitoring is essential for safe operation.
This setting is challenging because quadrupeds are articulated systems with time-varying leg joints, leg symmetry, and frequent self-occlusions, which make keypoint correspondence ambiguous.
Moreover, no public benchmark exists, making quantitative comparison difficult.
To address these challenges, we propose QuadPose, which estimates the full-body 18-DoF pose (6-DoF base pose + 12-DoF joint angles) from monocular video sequences, and introduce QuadSyn, the first camera-to-quadruped robot pose benchmark.
On QuadSyn, QuadPose achieves 92.18% PCK@2.52.5 px, 95.54% PCK-AUC, 85.94% ADD@20 cm, 66.98% ADD-AUC, and 3.65∘ mean joint-angle error at approximately 33 FPS.
Code and dataset will be publicly available.
introduction:
Quadruped robots are increasingly deployed for patrol, inspection, and monitoring in hazardous environments [4], where real-time external-camera monitoring is essential for safe operation.
However, 2D tracking only provides the robot’s location in the image plane, which is insufficient to assess whether it is stable, moving as intended, or approaching dangerous states.
Effective monitoring therefore requires estimating the robot’s full-body 3D pose, including the 6-DoF base pose (position and orientation) and the articulated joint configuration.

In practice, such monitoring often relies on fixed external cameras due to cost, maintenance, and reliability constraints.
As a result, only monocular video is available, without robot-side sensors (e.g., an IMU) or robot–camera extrinsic calibration.
Under these conditions, depth and 3D orientation remain inherently ambiguous from 2D boxes or keypoints, making it difficult to consistently relate image observations to the robot’s kinematic state over time.
Estimating the robot’s full-body 3D pose from a monocular camera remains a key challenge.

This problem can be formulated as camera-to-robot pose estimation from external videos.
Existing approaches broadly fall into two categories: mesh-based and keypoint-based.
Mesh-based methods estimate pose by aligning the input image with rendered views of a CAD/mesh model [12].
Keypoint-based methods detect 2D keypoints and recover the 6-DoF base pose by solving a Perspective-n-Point (PnP) problem with known 3D keypoints [5], or by learning a direct mapping from images to pose [13, 16, 22, 6].
Most existing approaches target manipulators or drones, benefiting from fixed-base setups or rigid-body assumptions that simplify pose estimation.

In contrast, as shown in Fig. 1(a), a quadruped has a 6-DoF base pose and time-varying leg joints, so a single 6-DoF pose is insufficient.
We estimate an 18-DoF state (6-DoF base + four 3-DoF legs), requiring 12 keypoints per frame (Fig. 1(a)–\raisebox{-.9pt}{\scriptsize1}⃝).
Second, left–right and front–rear symmetry introduces ambiguity in keypoint correspondence, and self-occlusion during gait reduces the visual cues (Fig. 1(a)–\raisebox{-.9pt}{\scriptsize2}⃝).
In addition, no public benchmark exists for camera-to-quadruped pose estimation, making fair comparison difficult.
Much of the prior work focuses on the robot’s onboard sensing, while external-camera 3D pose estimation remains less explored.

To address this challenge, we propose QuadPose, which estimates the 18-DoF full-body pose of a quadruped robot from monocular video sequences (Fig. 1(b)).
Our key idea is to improve 2D keypoint quality, as accurate keypoints are critical for reliable 3D pose recovery.
Specifically, a keypoint-focused token selector mitigates leg appearance ambiguity caused by symmetric limbs.
In addition, skeleton-aware masked attention exploits kinematic connectivity to improve robustness under self-occlusion during gait (Fig. 1(a)–\raisebox{-.9pt}{\scriptsize2}⃝).
Given stable 2D keypoints, QuadPose first predicts the 12-DoF joint angles and estimates the 6-DoF base pose, reconstructs 3D keypoints via forward kinematics, and then corrects residual errors using a refinement head.
Additionally, we introduce a new dataset QuadSyn to enable reproducible evaluation.

We evaluate QuadPose on the proposed QuadSyn benchmark and demonstrate consistent improvements over existing baselines.
Experimental results show that our keypoint-focused modeling improves 3D pose accuracy under symmetry and self-occlusion, while the refinement stage further reduces reconstruction errors.
QuadPose achieves 95.54% PCK-AUC and 66.98% ADD-AUC while running at about 33 FPS.
In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

Full-Body Pose Estimation for Quadruped Robots.
To our knowledge, we present the first camera-to-quadruped full-body pose estimation framework that recovers an 18-DoF state, including the 6-DoF base pose and 12 joints.

Robust 2D-to-3D Pose Recovery.
We propose selector tokens and skeleton-aware masked attention to mitigate 2D keypoint ambiguity, while a refinement head further reduces 3D reconstruction errors.

New Quadruped Pose Dataset.
To our knowledge, we build and release the first public camera-to-quadruped pose benchmark dataset.

1. Full-Body Pose Estimation for Quadruped Robots.
To our knowledge, we present the first camera-to-quadruped full-body pose estimation framework that recovers an 18-DoF state, including the 6-DoF base pose and 12 joints.

2. Robust 2D-to-3D Pose Recovery.
We propose selector tokens and skeleton-aware masked attention to mitigate 2D keypoint ambiguity, while a refinement head further reduces 3D reconstruction errors.

3. New Quadruped Pose Dataset.
To our knowledge, we build and release the first public camera-to-quadruped pose benchmark dataset.

title: OpenJaws: An Open Hardware UMI Framework with Stereo Localization for Generalist Manipulation
authors: Adithyavairavan Murali,Yash Oza,Karanbir Chahal,Neel Jawale,Silas De Vries,Hesam Rabeti,Erwin Coumans,Balakumar Sundaralingam,Stan Birchfield
abstract: Handheld data-collection interfaces such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) allow manipulation demonstrations to be gathered in the wild without a robot in the loop, but the quality of the resulting action labels is bounded by the accuracy of vision-based localization. Existing systems recover end-effector pose from monocular visual-inertial odometry, which is subject to scale ambiguity and drift, or delegate tracking to closed-source modules and external infrastructure that reintroduce cost and setup burden. We present OpenJaws, a fully open hardware and software framework for sensorized UMI that improves localization and simplifies deployment across robot platforms. OpenJaws pairs a modular, 3D-printed gripper exposing a standardized ISO adapter with a low-cost stereo camera to recover metric camera trajectories. We further introduce UMI-Loc-Bench-v1, a benchmark quantifying real-world localization accuracy for handheld data-collection devices, and show that stereo localization substantially outperforms monocular alternatives. Finally, we demonstrate that policies trained on data collected with OpenJaws can be deployed on a real robot across multiple tasks. Hardware, software, and data are released under a commercially permissive license. Code, data, and videos can be found at the website: https://open-jaws.github.io/
introduction:
We have witnessed a cambrian explosion in robot foundation models in recent years  [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. These models rely on large training datasets, causing leader-follower teleoperation systems, such as ALOHA [7] and GELLO [8] to become workhorses of the industry. However, teleoperation is difficult to scale because it requires a kinematically identical copy of the robot, severely limiting in-the-wild data collection. Furthermore, predicting policy actions in joint space does not, by construction, easily generalize across different robot embodiments.

To address this scaling bottleneck, the breakthrough work of the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) [9] proposed a portable, handheld gripper for collecting data independent of the robot arm, where robot action labels are extracted offline using visual-inertial localization. A crucial (and typical) design choice is to define the policy action space in relative end-effector task space, which enables robot-arm-agnostic deployment.

Despite UMI’s significant potential, however, a large UMI-to-real gap exists, manifesting as several engineering pain points when deploying a UMI policy. First, the quality of the policy action labels is affected by Simultaenous Localization and Mapping (SLAM), such that localization errors introduce noise into the labels, affecting policy training. Second, the original UMI required a separate, actuated parallel-jaw electric gripper at deployment time. A mount must be designed for the finger holder, and great care must be taken to ensure that the kinematics (e.g. stroke length) of the handheld device match those of the deployment gripper. One must also ensure that the relative coordinate transformation between the wrist camera and the Tool Center Point (TCP) remains consistent during both data collection and deployment. Given this UMI-to-real gap and the associated system integration challenges, the most proficient UMI-based manipulation stacks are private and closed-source [10, 11]. Other recent and concurrent works [12, 13, 14] co-design the handheld UMI data collection device with the deployment gripper.

Inspired by the above work, we propose a fully open framework with open-source software (OSS) and hardware under a commercially permissive license. In OpenJaws, we simplify cross-embodiment deployment by adopting the ISO 9409-1-50-4-M6 flange mounting standard, allowing the gripper to be mounted directly on common collaborative robots without a new adapter. Our design is modular, built using open electronics modules (e.g., Dynamixel and Arduino). For localization, the original UMI work [9] used monocular-inertial Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) with a single GoPro camera. However, a monocular camera, by design, cannot capture metric information. Other recent UMI approaches have proposed using VR tracking devices or native industrial visual-odometry frameworks on smartphones (Apple ARKit) [16], both of which are closed-source and expensive; VR headsets may also require the user to wear a separate device for triangulation. We propose a simpler alternative: using a low-cost stereo camera and running open-source localization frameworks from the SLAM and Structure from Motion (SfM) literature. With multi-view stereo, we obtain metric information for free, as triangulating corresponding pixels across two views (as shown in Fig. 2) separated by a known physical baseline resolves absolute scale. Despite the presence of popular SLAM benchmarks for autonomous driving [17] and indoor scene reconstruction [18, 19], no localization benchmarks exist in the context of policy-based robotic manipulation and UMI. As such, we present a large-scale, stereo-based localization dataset, UMI-Loc-Bench-v1, which allows us to systematically evaluate visual localization in a data distribution representative of UMI-based manipulation policies.

Overall, we make the following contributions with OpenJaws. First, we present a modular, stereo-based open software and hardware framework for sensorized UMI. Second, with this stereo-based UMI gripper, we build a localization benchmark, UMI-Loc-Bench-v1, to evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art, in-the-wild stereo-based localization techniques relative to existing monocular approaches. Third, we release simulation assets for OpenJaws and demonstrate compelling agentic real-to-sim performance on UMI-Loc-Bench-v1, potentially opening paths for future research in sim-to-real and sim-real co-training [20]. Finally, we demonstrate that this system can be used to train action-chunking policies and deploy them on a real robot system.

title: REACH: An RL-based Hierarchical Humanoid Crawling Framework for Adaptable Confined Space Traversal
authors: Shengzhang Xu,Yuning Guo,Weiyi Hu,Yifeng Xu,Zhongyu Li,He Kong
comment: To appear at IEEE Humanoids 2026; Project pagethis https URL
abstract: Humanoid locomotion in confined spaces requires continuous height adaptation across multiple locomotion modes, yet most existing approaches remain limited to height-adjustable bipedal walking. We present REACH, an RL-based hierarchical framework that enables a Unitree G1 humanoid to traverse height-constrained environments through variable-height bipedal walking and crawling. The learned policies regulate body height over complementary command ranges of 1.271.27–0.500.50 m in bipedal locomotion and 0.500.50–0.200.20 m in crawling, extending traversal beyond the clearance limits of crouched walking. To address contact-rich crawling dynamics, we employ a history-conditioned latent representation that captures terrain and interaction context from proprioceptive observations. A bidirectional transition policy further connects crouched bipedal locomotion and crawling across large kinematic and contact discontinuities. These skills are integrated with a LiDAR-based planner that converts point clouds into collision-free three-dimensional paths and locomotion commands, including proactive height targets. Real-world experiments demonstrate accurate height and velocity tracking, robust terrain traversal, reliable mode transitions and confined-space traversal with the proposed pipeline. Code and videos are available at https://aislab-sustech.github.io/REACH/.
introduction:
Confined-space traversal is essential to extending humanoid robots from structured settings to environments with
narrow passages [1, 2]. However, the existing literature remains dominated by bipedal gaits [3], with torso height either fixed or adjusted only for crouched walking. This restriction prevents existing systems from accessing severely constrained spaces. In recent years, reinforcement learning (RL) has substantially enhanced humanoid mobility and robustness [4, 5, 6] or posture adaptation under complex terrain and overhead constraints [7, 8, 9, 10].
Nevertheless, most approaches remain bipedal and are limited by leg workspace:
aggressive crouching reduces maneuverability and balance margins.

However, extending a conventional humanoid from bipedal walking to another motion modality, e.g., crawling, introduces a few challenges. First, the two modes differ substantially in configuration–directly switching between two independently trained policies requires the robot to pass through dynamically sensitive intermediate states and can produce discontinuous actions, imbalance, or falls. Second, crawling is intrinsically contact-rich: body segments such as the palms, wrists, knees, feet interact with the environment, generating impacts and disturbances that are difficult to model, leading to severe sim-to-real gaps.

Towards a practical solution for large-range height adaptation, robust multi-contact control, smooth transitions between locomotion modes,
we present REACH (see Fig. REACH: An RL-based Hierarchical Humanoid Crawling Framework for Adaptable Confined Space Traversal), an RL-based hierarchical framework for adaptable confined-space traversal using an unmodified Unitree G1 humanoid. Inspired by latent terrain-inference approaches such as DreamWaQ [11], we design a history-conditioned latent adaptation module tailored to contact-rich humanoid crawling. The module extracts terrain and interaction context from proprioceptive histories, improving robustness to multi-contact disturbances and real-world deployment conditions. A bidirectional motion-tracking policy connects crouched walking and crawling, enabling stable transitions across large kinematic and contact discontinuities. At the upper level, an adapted EGO-Planner [12] converts onboard LiDAR observations into collision-free 3D paths and proactive height commands. This hierarchical decomposition separates perception and planning from locomotion, allowing integration with other navigation methods. Our main contributions are:

An adaptable locomotion framework that extends locomotion beyond the clearance limits of crouched walking. More specifically, the proposed framework enables variable-height bipedal walking (from 1.27 to 0.50 m) and crawling with height commands from 0.50 to 0.20 m (in experiments, traversal of clearances as low as 0.400.40 m).

A history-conditioned latent adaptation mechanism and a bidirectional
transition policy for contact-rich crawling and bipedal–crawling switching.

A practical planner–controller hierarchy that interfaces learned
skills with LiDAR-based planning, validated successful real-world confined-space experiments.

transition policy for contact-rich crawling and bipedal–crawling switching.

title: CARD: Contact-Anchored Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Cunxi Dai,Botao He,Francois R Hogan,Wei Pan,Rao Fu,Wen-Han Hsieh,Ruoshi Liu,Jitendra Malik,Guanya Shi,Akash Sharma
abstract: Humans are dexterous, but traditional data collection paradigms such as teleoperation, kinesthetic teaching, and wearable exoskeletons force humans to act through the robot embodiment, bottlenecking their dexterity. Retargeting can avoid this. However, existing methods purely translate kinematics and ignore the real-world contact dynamics essential for task success. We present CARD: Contact-Anchored Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation, a simulator and object-free framework that retargets human demonstrations to robot actions by explicitly preserving contact force targets. CARD unifies human data sources including video, motion capture, and tactile gloves via a shared hand–contact representation and generates explicit contact force targets in addition to kinematics. To maintain these contact targets during hardware open-loop replay, CARD also introduces a tactile tracking controller. For video which does not contain an explicit tactile source, we present Vid-HACO, our video-to-contact model that sets a new state of the art. Across our video, glove, motion-capture data and the GRAB dataset, CARD maintains contact on 4343–78%78\% of contact frames, while kinematic and object-aware retargeting methods maintain contact on <10%<10\% and 22.5%22.5\% of the frames respectively. Further, integrating our formulation into physics-based retargeting improves strict task success from 12% to 32% on GRAB [70]. Finally, we show that our tactile tracker is critical to reproduce demonstrated forces during hardware replay. These results establish that contact preservation via CARD is a scalable interface for transferring human dexterity to robots.
introduction:
Human demonstrations are the most scalable source of data for dexterous manipulation, yet nearly every way we collect them today, whether teleoperation [89, 77, 10], wearable exoskeletons [11, 87, 79], or kinesthetic teaching [63, 8], forces humans to act through a robot embodiment, limiting dexterity to what the interface allows. Retargeting natural human motion removes this bottleneck. However, existing methods [22, 56] treat retargeting as a kinematic problem of mapping fingertip positions or joint angles. Further, retargeting often requires scene reconstruction followed by heavy optimization in simulation, and even recent contact-centric formulations [33, 84, 66] still presuppose an object model or a simulator. For manipulation with contact, reconstructing kinematics alone is not enough: millimeters of embodiment mismatch decide whether a replayed trajectory hovers, slips over, or crushes the object.

We present CARD, a retargeting framework that treats contact force targets as a first-class citizen. Instead of relying on object geometry, CARD uses per-link contact force targets extracted from a human demonstration, comprising a center of pressure, a push direction, and a force, to solve for robot configurations that place semantically matched robot links on every contact force target inside the demonstrated friction cone. CARD produces contact force targets alongside the joint trajectory without relying on object information, therefore it needs no simulator, object mesh, or object pose estimate. Consequently, rigid, articulated, and deformable objects need no special handling.

CARD is agnostic to the demonstration source: any modality containing hand pose and contact can be used. To make heterogeneous sources interchangeable, we introduce a unified hand–contact representation that turns monocular video (through Vid-HACO, our video contact model), tactile gloves, and marker-based motion capture into a common interface: a MANO mesh sequence with one contact force target per hand region. Because every contact force target is bound to the human hand surface, retargeting to a new robot requires only a semantic map from hand regions to robot bodies.

On hardware, CARD pairs retargeting with a tactile tracking controller, an integral admittance loop over joint impedance that maintains the demonstrated contact forces during replay. Together they enable open-loop replay of dexterous human demonstrations on multiple robot embodiments mounted on a 7-DoF arm. Here open-loop means no object pose estimate and no learned policy. The only feedback is the fingertip force loop that maintains the demonstrated contact forces. We prioritize open-loop replay to demonstrate the retargeting quality of CARD over policy learning, since a closed-loop policy confounds retargeting fidelity with other issues such as learning error, partial observability and the like.

Concretely, our contributions are:

Contact-Anchored Retargeting: A simulator and object-free formulation that optimizes contact reach, friction-cone alignment, force weighting, and contact stability per frame with a fast GPU sampling optimizer.

Unified Hand–Contact Representation: A shared interface that maps video (through Vid-HACO, our video hand-contact model), tactile gloves, and motion capture into contact force targets with whole-clip force synthesis for sources that measure no force.

Tactile Tracking Controller: A real-world force tracking controller with feedforward force that replays contact-rich tasks open-loop faithfully on physical hardware.

Cross-Embodiment Generalization: Cross-embodiment retargeting through a semantic map, shown on four robot hands from a 22-DoF dexterous hand down to a parallel-jaw gripper.

Across video, glove, and motion-capture sources, CARD achieves state-of-the-art contact fidelity, matching demonstrated contact on 43–78% of contact frames where kinematic retargeting reaches under 10%, while retargeting methods needing object information [18] only reach 22.5%. Further, our trajectories transfer to the real world through open-loop replay, where the tactile tracker raises success from 4 to 25 of 30 trials over position-only replay.

1. Contact-Anchored Retargeting: A simulator and object-free formulation that optimizes contact reach, friction-cone alignment, force weighting, and contact stability per frame with a fast GPU sampling optimizer.

2. Unified Hand–Contact Representation: A shared interface that maps video (through Vid-HACO, our video hand-contact model), tactile gloves, and motion capture into contact force targets with whole-clip force synthesis for sources that measure no force.

3. Tactile Tracking Controller: A real-world force tracking controller with feedforward force that replays contact-rich tasks open-loop faithfully on physical hardware.

4. Cross-Embodiment Generalization: Cross-embodiment retargeting through a semantic map, shown on four robot hands from a 22-DoF dexterous hand down to a parallel-jaw gripper.

title: A Trainable CPG Framework for Quadruped Locomotion
authors: Xiyan Liu,Yide Liu,Guoyong Mao,Shaoxing Qu
abstract:
We present CPG–ENN, a trainable quadruped locomotion framework that
combines explicit neural coordination with learned motion realization.
A symmetry-based eight-neuron central pattern generator (CPG) supplies gait
rhythms, while a pretrained, leg-shared execution neural network (ENN) maps
rhythmic signals and trajectory parameters to joint-angle references without
online inverse kinematics. A single feedback policy modulates six
physically interpretable trajectory variables. The controller
tracks planar velocity and yaw-rate commands across walk, trot, pace,
bound, and pronk without gait-specific learned controllers or
transition-specific rewards. Simulation yields 99.39%99.39\% transition success
across all 20 directed gait pairs and all source–target speed combinations
from {0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0}​m/s\{0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0\}~\mathrm{m/s}. Ablations show high
cross-gait transition feasibility without transition exposure; exposure
mainly refines gait acquisition and velocity transients. Comparisons with
AllGaits and Walk These Ways demonstrate accurate gait–speed
regulation, and Unitree Go2 experiments validate five gaits and their transitions.
introduction:
Locomotion is a fundamental animal capability supporting foraging,
reproduction, migration, and predator avoidance. Precocial foals move
independently shortly after birth, showing that locomotor capability can
emerge without systematic training [1]. Yet experience
refines interlimb coordination and movement patterns 
[2]. Trained dressage horses, for example, perform
passage and piaffe with spatiotemporal patterns distinct from trot 
[3]. Locomotion is therefore innately organized
yet trainable: neural mechanisms generate rhythmic coordination 
[4], while learning refines its expression.
This motivates a robotic architecture
preserving explicit rhythm generation while enabling learned modulation.

Learning-based controllers already produce multiple gaits and transitions
with one policy, using learned motion patterns or explicit rhythm generators 
[5, 6, 7].
Central pattern generators (CPGs) produce coordinated rhythmic
signals [8]. Some methods explicitly map these
signals to foot trajectories, then apply inverse
kinematics (IK) [7, 9].
We explore a different approach: retaining CPG coordination while learning
a mapping from its signals to motion with independently defined trajectory shapes.

Generating gait rhythms alone does not ensure accurate speed tracking. An existing eight-neuron CPG supported five quadrupedal
gaits and their transitions [10], but relied on
predefined gait-specific motion parameters. Step-length scaling changed
speed without tracking a target velocity, and some transitions showed
lower success rates and large speed transients.
These limitations motivate a single feedback controller that retains the
CPG’s multi-gait coordination while improving speed tracking and gait transitions.

We therefore develop a trainable CPG–ENN framework. The CPG provides
rhythmic coordination, while a leg-shared execution neural network (ENN)
learns to map CPG signals and motion parameters to joint targets.
Offline IK converts independently defined foot trajectories
into joint-angle supervision. During control, the ENN generates joint
targets, and one feedback policy adjusts six motion parameters using
target velocities and proprioception. We examine whether this architecture
supports reliable transitions without transition training and what such
training improves.

The main contributions are as follows:

(1) Trainable CPG–ENN Architecture:
We separate explicit neural rhythm generation from learned motion
realization through a leg-shared joint-space mapping and a single
six-dimensional feedback-modulation interface.

(2) Unified Multi-Gait Control:
A single policy realizes walk, trot, pace, bound, and pronk on the
Unitree Go2 (Fig. 1), using the same modulation space
and reward formulation, without gait-specific
learned controllers or gait-style rewards. The CPG specifies gait
rhythm, while the policy adapts motion to locomotion commands and
proprioception.

(3) Reliable Gait Transitions:
The controller achieves an overall success rate close to 100%
across all 20 directed gait pairs. Ablations show that reliable
transitions persist without transition training; transition training
mainly shortens gait-acquisition time and reduces post-switch
velocity error.

title: A generalist policy for muscle-driven control across individual musculoskeletal models
authors: Bozhao Wang,Yinglei Zhu,Zhengqing Li,Zhiyuan Zhang,Weiming Kang,Yiheng He,XinJun Liu,Senhao Hou,Huichan Zhao,Xiaoqiang Tang
comment: . Project website:this https URLBozhao Wang and Yinglei Zhu contributed equally to this work
abstract:
Differences in musculoskeletal morphology challenge policy reuse across
individual models. Here we present MyoAcross, a framework that combines
individual musculoskeletal model construction, morphology-conditioned policy
learning and virtual model augmentation to enable muscle-driven reference-
motion tracking without individual fine-tuning. Across 31 held-out individual
models, MyoAcross achieves 99.24% completion and reduces tracking error by
22.60% relative to an unconditioned multilayer perceptron. Policy reuse
extends to models of 22 held-out individuals constructed from single-image
shape estimates, measured height and body mass, and, with asymmetry
augmentation, to models with unilateral lower-limb shortening. Comparisons
with measurements from 120 additional individuals show agreement in vertical
ground reaction force waveforms and channel-dependent agreement between
simulated muscle activations and electromyography. These results establish a
common control framework for comparative simulations of movement across
individual musculoskeletal models.

title: RoboAuto: Autonomous Robot Program Search through Multi-Level Physical Understanding
authors: Buzhao Liu,Jianing Ye,Xiu Yuan,Yangtong Feng,Chengsong Huang,Tyler Dinh,Yevgeniy Vorobeychik,Ning Zhang,Chongjie Zhang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract:
Recently, LLM-based autonomous agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in iteratively generating, evaluating, and refining executable solutions.
In robotic manipulation, Code-as-Policy enables these agents to search over modular and editable robot programs.
However, effective program search requires physical understanding: agents must understand how objects can be manipulated, how scene geometry constrains actions, and why interactions succeed or fail.
Existing methods rely mainly on execution feedback for program refinement, often leaving these physical questions unresolved.
To address this limitation, we introduce RoboAuto, a framework for robot program search that explicitly organizes the physical understanding at the object, scene, and interaction levels through three complementary components.
First, the hierarchical knowledge base combines executable skills with object-centric knowledge of affordances, spatial relations, and action effects, which can be learned from embodied data and online task solving.
Second, scene grounding connects this knowledge to the current environment by identifying relevant objects and resolving action-critical quantities.
Third, multi-stage planning with self-designed experiments checks whether each stage produces its expected physical effects and actively tests competing hypotheses to resolve physical uncertainties.
RoboAuto achieves superior performance across five benchmark families, attaining an 89.1% success rate on short-horizon LIBERO-PRO tasks and more than twice the mean success rate of ASPIRE on LIBERO-PRO Long and LIBERO-Plus. It also outperforms ASPIRE and π0.5\pi_{0.5} on three challenging long-horizon real-robot tasks requiring precise manipulation.
We further demonstrate that the hierarchical knowledge base transfers across simulators and embodiments, and that program search performance scales with the size of the knowledge base. Project page: https://roboauto-ai.github.io/.
introduction:
Recent advances in autonomous research and coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) [39, 26, 47] highlight the promise of a self-evolving problem-solving paradigm in which an agent generates an executable solution, evaluates its outcome, and uses the resulting evidence to improve subsequent attempts. Code-as-Policy [23] naturally extends this paradigm to robot manipulation by representing robot behaviors as executable programs. Given an instruction such as “put the mug on the plate,” a coding agent can generate a program over perception and control primitives, execute it in the environment, and revise it based on the resulting rollout.

Recent autonomous Code-as-Policy methods instantiate this generate, execute, and revise loop. CaP-Agent0 supports multi-turn program revision with structured feedback [13]; ASPIRE exposes multimodal execution traces and accumulates validated repair knowledge in a skill library [25]; and RHO searches over policy repositories using reward and execution feedback [11]. These methods demonstrate the value of execution feedback and retained experience for robot program search.

However, Figure 3 reveals persistent gaps in physical understanding in our baseline runs. In Figure 3(a), CaP-Agent0 repeatedly attempts a physically unsuitable top-down grasp on a book, indicating that repeated code-level search cannot always compensate for missing knowledge of object affordances. This type of failure motivates a hierarchical knowledge base that complements object-centric physical knowledge acquired from embodied data with executable skills accumulated through online task solving. In Figure 3(b), ASPIRE attempts to grasp a mug by descending to a hardcoded height transferred from another mug, causing the gripper to close on air. This failure shows that even a valid strategy must be instantiated using the geometry of the current scene, motivating a dedicated grounding stage that identifies task-relevant objects and physical quantities with visual tools. In Figure 3(c), CaP-Agent0 proceeds to place a pan despite failing to activate the burner, motivating multi-stage planning and grounded verification of intermediate effects. Moreover, observing a failed knob rotation does not establish how far the knob must turn. Resolving this uncertainty requires active physical exploration through autonomously designed experiments that test specific hypotheses.

Motivated by these observations, we introduce RoboAuto (Fig. 2), a framework for autonomous robot program search through multi-level physical understanding. Its hierarchical knowledge base combines object-centric physical knowledge about affordances, spatial relations, and action effects with executable skills. Physical knowledge is acquired from embodied data and refined through online experience, while the skill library expands as verified programs are discovered through task solving. For each task, RoboAuto retrieves relevant knowledge and skills and grounds them in the current scene, using visual tools, including Molmo2 [10] and SAM 3 [4], to identify task-relevant objects and measure action-critical quantities. Through multi-stage planning with grounded verification, it plans over stage dependencies and verifies each stage’s physical outcome before proceeding. When available evidence leaves a physical uncertainty unresolved, RoboAuto formulates competing hypotheses and conducts self-designed experiments to distinguish them. The resulting evidence refines the physical knowledge, while verified programs expand the skill library, improving both the current solution and future program search.

We evaluate RoboAuto on tasks from five benchmark families. On LIBERO-PRO Long [52], RoboAuto achieves a mean success rate of 73.4%, compared with 30.8% for ASPIRE [25], the strongest coding-agent baseline on average. On LIBERO-Plus [12], it reaches 90.3%, compared with ASPIRE’s 44.7%, while achieving 89.1% on the short-horizon LIBERO-PRO [52] tasks. On contact-rich Robosuite [54] tasks, RoboAuto obtains 90.6% mean success, compared with ASPIRE’s 81.0%. To evaluate knowledge transfer, we apply the hierarchical knowledge base acquired in LIBERO [24] to RoboTwin 2.0 [6], which features a different simulator and a bimanual robot embodiment. RoboAuto achieves a 91.5% success rate, compared with 24.5% without a knowledge base. Knowledge-base scaling experiments further show that larger knowledge bases consistently improve program-search performance. RoboAuto also outperforms ASPIRE and π0.5\pi_{0.5} on three challenging long-horizon real-robot tasks requiring precise manipulation.

Our contributions are:

We identify key limitations of existing autonomous Code-as-Policy methods in physical knowledge, scene grounding, intermediate verification, and active exploration.

We introduce RoboAuto, which addresses these limitations through a hierarchical knowledge base, scene grounding, multi-stage planning with grounded verification, and autonomously designed experiments.

Across five benchmark families, RoboAuto substantially improves program-search performance and demonstrates knowledge scaling and transfer across simulators and embodiments.

1. We identify key limitations of existing autonomous Code-as-Policy methods in physical knowledge, scene grounding, intermediate verification, and active exploration.

2. We introduce RoboAuto, which addresses these limitations through a hierarchical knowledge base, scene grounding, multi-stage planning with grounded verification, and autonomously designed experiments.

3. Across five benchmark families, RoboAuto substantially improves program-search performance and demonstrates knowledge scaling and transfer across simulators and embodiments.

title: GRAFT: Geometry-Aware Residual Adaptation for Foundation Trackers
authors: Liang Li,Guoyao Zhang,Xingyu Chen,Sikai Wu,Qianyang Wu,Yuhang Lin,Renjing Xu,Mingliang Zhou,Diyun Xiang
abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) provide reusable whole-body motion priors: given a kinematic reference, they generate coordinated joint commands for motion replay, teleoperation, and VLA control. However, trained primarily on flat-ground motion, BFMs lack an explicit mechanism to adapt foot placement, swing clearance, and contact timing to local terrain. Many terrain-aware BFM approaches address this limitation by retraining or fine-tuning the tracker together with perception, incurring substantial data and computation costs while coupling ordinary tracking to the perception pathway. To bridge this gap, we propose GRAFT, a geometry-aware residual adaptation framework for frozen behavior trackers. GRAFT preserves the BFM parameters and motion-reference interface, while a lightweight adapter adds terrain-conditioned corrections only to lower-body execution targets. The adapter is trained with task and foot-geometry rewards, regularized to suppress unnecessary corrections on flat ground, and distilled from privileged terrain observations to onboard depth. Because the frozen BFM already provides whole-body reference tracking and nominal locomotion, GRAFT reduces terrain learning to a focused execution-adaptation problem. We instantiate the framework on four frozen trackers and evaluate stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation. We further validate it through real-world deployment on a Unitree G1, where the adapted SONIC tracker traverses terrain with onboard depth and unmodified references.
introduction:
A behavior foundation model (BFM) learns a single whole-body tracking policy from a large corpus of human motion: given a kinematic reference, it outputs joint commands [1, 2, 3]. Motion references form its sole upstream command interface. The same BFM can therefore be driven by a recorded clip, an online teleoperator, or a high-level policy such as a vision-language-action (VLA) model, without retraining for each source. This shared reference interface is what lets one released tracker serve several upstream command sources.

These corpora, however, are recorded almost entirely on flat, empty ground, and the environment enters neither the policy’s observation nor its reward. A BFM therefore learns how to approximate a reference kinematically, not how to place its feet on the surface it is actually crossing. Changing the reference does not supply what is missing. Given a clip of a person climbing stairs, the policy reproduces the motion in the air but does not actually climb the stairs, because the foot placement, swing clearance and contact timing the steps require were never part of what it was trained to produce.

Current approaches give BFMs scene-interaction ability by pairing motion with reconstructed scene geometry and retraining [4], or by fine-tuning a pretrained model together with a terrain encoder [5, 6]. These approaches are effective, but they change the deployed tracker and couple ordinary tracking to the terrain-perception pathway. Constructing terrain-paired motion data requires annotation and processing at scale, together with the compute to retrain on it. Fine-tuning a behavior prior on a narrow new task can also degrade the reusable prior, which motivates residual adaptation on a frozen backbone elsewhere [7].

To address this problem, we propose GRAFT. The frozen BFM processes the unmodified reference, while a separately trained adapter adds geometry-conditioned corrections to the lower-body execution targets; the upper-body targets remain those of the frozen tracker, since they are what a teleoperator or a VLA is commanding. A deployment gate controls whether the correction is applied at all.

The key idea is to separate reusable whole-body motion generation from terrain execution adaptation. The BFM retains responsibility for reference tracking, nominal locomotion, and whole-body coordination; the adapter learns only the terrain-dependent deviation from this nominal execution. We train it with foot-clearance and placement penalties and suppress its output on flat ground, then distill a teacher trained under privileged terrain observations into a student that reads onboard depth. This decomposition turns terrain adaptation into a focused execution problem without rewriting the upstream reference or modifying the released tracker.

Our contributions are:

We introduce GRAFT, a terrain-adaptation framework that adds geometry-conditioned lower-body corrections to a frozen behavior tracker while preserving its parameters and its motion-reference interface, with a gate that can be switched off at deployment; mid-run disabling and re-enabling are verified in simulation.

We introduce GRAFT, a terrain-adaptation framework that adds geometry-conditioned lower-body corrections to a frozen behavior tracker while preserving its parameters and its motion-reference interface, with a gate that can be switched off at deployment; mid-run disabling and re-enabling are verified in simulation.

We propose GRAFT as a general framework for adapting frozen behavior foundation trackers to terrain interaction. We instantiate the framework on four distinct trackers, training a separate adapter for each, and show that the same residual structure and reward family acquire terrain traversal while keeping flat-ground corrections small.

We validate GRAFT through real-world deployment on a Unitree G1. The SONIC adapter is distilled from privileged terrain observations to onboard depth, and the resulting tracker traverses terrain with unmodified references; a separate composite-course simulation verifies mid-run residual disabling and re-enabling.
