title: SVIn+: Multi-Modal Framework for Robust Underwater State Estimation using 3D Sonar, Visual-Inertial, Water-Pressure, and DVL
authors: Chinmay Burgul,Xiaoming Zhao,Yewei Huang,Michalis Chatzispyrou,Marios Xanthidis,Ioannis Rekleitis,Alberto Quattrini Li
abstract:
As expansion and scalability in underwater operations becomes more important and challenging, autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) become more relevant and the necessity for reliable autonomy more critical.
A fundamental challenge in any autonomous underwater operation, from control to safe navigation and mapping, is state estimation; a notorious hard problem to address, especially in low visibility conditions.
In this paper, we tackle this problem, by presenting SVIn+, a multi-sensor framework for robust state estimation of AUVs equipped with an IMU, cameras, a water-pressure sensor, a Doppler Velocity Log (DVL), and a compact 3D sonar.
This framework extends an established open-source state-of-the-art visual-inertial SLAM, SVIn, by integrating water-pressure and DVL measurements into a tightly-coupled nonlinear optimization formulation resulting in improved estimates.
To leverage the structural information of recently available 3D acoustic sonars while maintaining computational efficiency, we introduce a hierarchical architecture that incorporates estimates from a decoupled front-end via KISS-ICP, treated as relative pose factors within the factor graph.
The proposed framework is validated through field deployments in a shipwreck and coral reef, demonstrating drift mitigation and global consistency.
To support further research in underwater multi-modal fusion, the code and the datasets can be found on project website https://cmburgul.github.io/projects/svin+/ https://dartmouthrobotics.github.io/svin-plus
introduction:
Reliable autonomy in underwater robotics needs robust Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) in perceptually degraded GNSS-denied environments [1], ranging from confined shipwrecks to dynamic coral reefs.
These underwater environments are characterized by many perceptual challenges, including light attenuation and limited visibility.

Despite the plethora of SLAM approaches in the literature, robust state estimation in underwater domains remains an open problem.
Traditional Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) is prone to catastrophic failure due to feature tracking loss in turbid waters or motion-blur artifacts during high-dynamic maneuvers [2].
Integrating water-pressure sensors (e.g., [3]) and Doppler Velocity Logs (DVLs) (e.g.,  [4, 5, 6]) can mitigate water-column depth and velocity drift; however, these sensors provide no environmental context, leaving the system unable to perform the loop closures for global consistency.
Furthermore, although 2D multibeam sonars can offer some situational awareness, they suffer from geometric ambiguity in complex 3D structures [1].

While a 3D acoustic sonar capable of generating volumetric point clouds has recently become available, and initial studies have begun to explore its potential, its integration into standard multi-sensor SLAM pipelines remains underexplored. Although compact 3D sonars conceptually resemble terrestrial LiDARs, their point clouds are significantly sparser, have a lower update rate (5 Hz), and are heavily corrupted by acoustic multipath noise.
The few existing works have primarily addressed sonar-inertial configurations [7] or visual-inertial-acoustic fusion [8, 9], without considering the full suite of sensors commonly used in Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUV).

In this paper, we introduce a tightly-coupled multi-modal state estimation framework that achieves robust state estimation in challenging underwater environments. Our framework fuses inertial, camera vision, DVL, and water column depth from water-pressure sensor measurements into the factor graph. To provide structural consistency and mitigate trajectory drift, we integrate relative pose factors derived from a KISS-ICP front-end, which processes the point cloud from a recently released 3D acoustic sonar.
This decoupled approach abstracts 3D sonar data into relative 6D pose factors, preserving factor graph sparsity and enabling real-time operation on embedded hardware.

In summary, our main contributions are the following:

Multi-modal state estimation framework, where vision, IMU, DVL, and water-pressure measurements are integrated in a tightly-coupled non-linear optimization for robust state estimation.

Hierarchical 3D sonar integration, with a decoupled front-end via KISS-ICP for computational efficiency.

Real-world validation in complex environments including shipwrecks and coral reefs, with the release of the associated code and datasets to the community.

title: Whole-Body Humanoid Control via Stochastic Motion Tokenization
authors: Michael Drolet,Oleg Arenz,Jan Peters
comment: Accepted to the 2026 IEEE-RAS International Conference on Humanoid Robots (Humanoids 2026). (c) 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses
abstract:
While velocity-commanded RL policies are effective for controlling quadrupeds, they are a limited interface for humanoids that need to perform complex whole-body motions.
Furthermore, RL tracking policies for whole-body motions typically have limited information about the desired future motion, preventing them from performing controlled deviations to achieve long-term task success; such information is particularly relevant when a controller must prepare for transitions between behaviors.
We address these challenges using concise motion representations that can be generated by a high-level controller, given a behavior label or text command.
These representations can be fed directly into a tracking policy to provide a detailed motion reference.
Our method exhibits a high degree of flexibility in performing real-world robot motions such as dancing, fighting, or walking based on conditional information.
At matched capacity, our adopted stochastic motion tokenizer reconstructs motions from the Unitree G1 at a level that exceeds state-of-the-art approaches such as finite scalar quantization (FSQ) and the vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-VAE).
The resulting discrete interface conditions whole-body tracking policies that execute generated dance, fight, and walk motions lasting 16.816.8 s each and a 3535 s fight-to-dance sequence on a physical Unitree G1.
introduction:
Whole-body humanoid motion is high-dimensional and, at any instant, admits many plausible continuations: from mid-stride, a human may keep walking, turn, gesture, or transition into an entirely different behavior.
Classical humanoid control builds on dynamic models and optimization [1, 2, 3] or motion primitives [4], while RL-based approaches [5, 6] can exhibit emergent behaviors but require reward specification, which is challenging to define explicitly for tasks such as human-like locomotion.
Controllers built around fixed gait generators or single-clip tracking fail to capture this multiplicity, ultimately reproducing only one trajectory or motion style well.
At the same time, methods based on maximum likelihood, such as behavioral cloning, require action labels via methods such as teleoperation or kinesthetic teaching, which is difficult to scale and infeasible for dynamic locomotion behaviors.
Furthermore, maximum likelihood is mode averaging, leading to muddied behaviors on unimodal policies.

A natural question is how to resolve the dilemma of choosing between a specialist policy that can perform one task very well and a generalist policy that can perform many tasks less effectively.
We address this problem by grouping motion into larger chunks and providing them as concise motion representations to a reinforcement learning policy, enabling it to focus on a particular motion that can be decided at a higher abstraction level.
This separation is inspired by motor learning theory [7], which argues that, through practice, motor skills become grouped to abstract away nuances exhibited at each timestep.
This principle also appears in robot learning: Diffusion Policy and ACT both predict chunks of future actions rather than isolated commands [8, 9], leading to better performance than traditional imitation-learning methods [10].
We therefore view it as a necessity to understand how to group motions in an unsupervised and efficient way, similar to the problem of tokenizing sentences in natural language processing.
Ideally, the abstracted representations should be i) compact for computational efficiency and generative utility, ii) seamlessly composable for long-horizon tasks, and iii) expressive enough to capture a wide range of sequences.
Our proposed framework is tailored to humanoid whole-body motion; however, the same key principles can be extended to other embodiments and problem settings.

To achieve these desirable characteristics, we use a motion tokenizer in the form of a discrete variational autoencoder (VAE).
Discrete VAEs offer high bit-efficiency compared to their continuous counterparts, and their categorical representations make them amenable to downstream generative tasks through the cross-entropy loss, which naturally leads to multimodal posterior sampling.
However, popular discrete tokenizers, such as FSQ and VQ-VAE, are either deterministic or limited to simplified distributions based on the mean-field assumption, which prevents them from correlating different tokens.
Furthermore, unlike their continuous counterparts, which aim at generative modeling, they are motivated from a compression perspective and are unable to control their entropy for optimizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO).
Instead, we adopt DAPS [11] for the first stage of our pipeline, which is a stochastic discrete autoencoder whose encoder admits a categorical distribution that is factorized autoregressively and has controlled entropy.
When using DAPS to encode (or tokenize) motions to discrete latents (or tokens), we find that reconstruction is consistently better at matched bottleneck capacity.
Building upon this stage, we propose a second-stage model, TrajectoryGPT, to generate a motion sequence autoregressively, and train it using the frozen VAE to encode prediction targets for autoregressive next-token prediction, as is common in related work [12].
TrajectoryGPT enables us to schedule and sequence units of motion, all of which would be plausible under the distribution of trajectories in the training dataset.
Because TrajectoryGPT is additionally conditioned on a context that describes the motion, it serves as an interface between the human and the robot.
This general interface can be extended beyond labels or text to include goal-conditioned information or vision input.
Finally, we realize these units of motion using a low-level tracking policy, as part of our third stage.
The tracking policy receives a buffer of latent codes—where tokens in the buffer can be set to special wildcard tokens for transitions—to help inform the policy of the upcoming intended behavior.
In this regard, the policy can be seen as a decoder responsible for realizing the physical motion (under domain randomization for sim-to-real transfer).
In short, our contributions are:

A novel application of a stochastic motion tokenizer for the 29-DoF Unitree G1 with a matched comparison against existing state-of-the-art methods [13, 14], across two motion datasets with multiple seeds.

A context-conditioned TrajectoryGPT that generates whole-body humanoid motion autoregressively, including from scratch, i.e., with no prior motion context.

Deployment on a physical Unitree G1 (Fig. 1) of tracking policies trained entirely in simulation on a repertoire of behaviors sampled from our expressive model.

title: Ground Sample Distance Constrained k-Coverage Viewpoint Planning via Set Multi-Cover Formulation
authors: Waleed Bin Khalid,Chul Min Yeum
abstract: Drone-based 3D reconstruction and inspection require viewpoints that satisfy image-quality constraints while observing each surface region multiple times, which overlap-based planning heuristics do not guarantee. We study ground sample distance (GSD)-constrained kk-coverage viewpoint selection for structures represented by surface voxels. Candidate viewpoints are generated along outward surface directions, screened with distance, viewing-angle, field-of-view, and occlusion tests, and augmented for voxels with insufficient visibility. Selection is then posed as set multi-cover with per-voxel coverage demands. We propose a dynamically weighted greedy heuristic that prioritizes remaining coverage deficits and scarce viewing alternatives, and compare it with sequential overlap-based pruning and an integer linear programming (ILP) formulation on the same candidate pools. Across two structures, four voxel resolutions, and three coverage requirements, the proposed approach achieves full or near-full kk-coverage with compact viewpoint sets, using only 3.00–16.39% more viewpoints than ILP while offering an interpretable selection process based on coverage deficits and viewpoint availability.
introduction:
Autonomous aerial inspection and 3D reconstruction require a set of camera viewpoints that observe all surface regions and satisfy image-quality constraints governing reconstruction fidelity. In such applications, image resolution is commonly expressed through ground sampling distance (GSD), which directly determines the recoverable surface detail in the reconstructed model [1, 2, 3].

Photogrammetric flight planning commonly recommends 6060–80%80\% image overlap to support reliable reconstruction [1, 4]. Under idealized strip-imaging assumptions, a forward overlap ρ\rho implies that a surface point appears in approximately 1/(1−ρ)1/(1-\rho) consecutive images, motivating multi-view redundancy. However, overlap is a global acquisition heuristic and does not directly enforce that each surface region is observed a prescribed number of times under sensing constraints, particularly in the presence of self-occlusions and complex geometry.

In this study, we address the viewpoint generation and selection problem for aerial inspection of structures with known geometry (in a world coordinate frame). Specifically, we aim to generate a compact set of camera viewpoints, each defined by a waypoint and a camera orientation, that satisfies prescribed GSD and kk-coverage requirements. The GSD constraint enforces a spatial-resolution bound under the adopted sensing model, while the kk-coverage requirement seeks observations of each surface region from at least kk distinct viewpoints to support multi-view observation.

We formulate inspection viewpoint planning as a GSD-constrained kk-coverage problem over a voxelized surface representation. Surface voxels represent discrete observable regions, and candidate viewpoints are generated to satisfy geometric constraints derived from a prescribed GSD bound and maximum oblique viewing angle. Each candidate viewpoint observes a subset of surface voxels, yielding a set multi-cover formulation that seeks at least kk observations per voxel, subject to the visibility available in the candidate set.

We construct a sensing-compliant candidate set and select a smaller subset of viewpoints using a globally informed greedy kk-coverage heuristic, evaluated against an integer linear programming (ILP) reference formulation over the same candidate set. Viewpoint selection is explicitly decoupled from downstream tour generation, allowing discrete coverage requirements to be evaluated independently of trajectory optimization. The resulting framework enables explicit evaluation of sensing-constrained multi-view coverage under the adopted geometric sensing model.

title: A Singularity Avoiding Track Model for Race Car Optimization
authors: Adwait Verulkar,Behzad Danaei,Srikanth Sivaramakrishnan,Ryan Trinter
abstract:
A track fitting pipeline is presented that converts a measured racetrack point
cloud into a closed, C4C^{4} differentiable, three-dimensional
surface model suitable for high-fidelity Modelica race-car optimization.
The surface is a Monge patch,
parametrised by a curvilinear arc-length coordinate measured along the
minimum-curvature line (MCL) and a signed lateral offset, with a height
polynomial of user-selectable degree capturing the
cross-sectional elevation profile.
The choice of MCL as the reference line is deliberate since anchoring the
same surface on the geometric centre-line can cause adjacent normals to
cross inside the drivable region on tight corners. The resulting
non-injective parametrisation assigns multiple curvilinear addresses to the
same three-dimensional point and returns invalid road geometry.
The MCL is obtained from a quadratic program that minimises integrated curvature subject to track-boundary, periodicity,
and jerk-regularisation constraints. By reducing total curvature while
remaining within the track bounds, the MCL moves the region of parametrisation
breakdown outside the drivable strip on all circuits studied, keeps the normal
map injective across the full track width, and yields a more linear
time-to-arc-length transformation for minimum lap-time problems.
The fitted surface and the associated track widths are exported as periodic
piecewise-quintic C4C^{4} B-splines, solved as a nonlinear program. The exported
splines are consumed directly by TrackJoint, a Modelica MultiBody
component that enforces the two degree-of-freedom kinematic road constraint via
d’Alembert’s principle. We also describe the parts of that Modelica
implementation that set the export format: how the splines are stored on a
shared knot vector as tunable parameters, how a segment is found in constant
time and evaluated in Horner form, why index reduction forces C4C^{4}
continuity, how the chassis is stacked relative to the track frame, and how the
FMI 3.0 export is used by the CasADi/IPOPT toolchain. A companion paper
Sivaramakrishnan et al. (2026) derives the joint in full.
introduction:
The track model is a crucial component of minimum lap-time simulations of high-performance vehicles. The contact-patch normal load, the gravitational
projections in the body-fixed frame and the kinematic constraints that
keep all four wheels on the road are all expressed in terms of the road
surface and its first two derivatives Limebeer and van de Merwe (2025); Limebeer et al. (2023). Inaccuracies in the track model therefore propagate directly into the
predicted lap time, tyre forces, suspension loads and aerodynamic
behaviour, degrading the fidelity of the entire simulation.

The community has converged on a curvilinear (s,n)(s,n) description for
roads since the work of Cossalter et al. (1999); the recent survey by
Limebeer and van de Merwe (2025) summarises the line of development.
Three-dimensional refinements followed: the Frenet–Serret ribbon of
Perantoni and Limebeer (2015) parametrises the road by an
arc-length spine plus an orthonormal moving frame and works well on
typical racing layouts but assumes lateral flatness;
Lovato et al. (2021) and Limebeer et al. (2023) remove that
assumption by superimposing a Monge-patch elevation correction on top
of a Frenet ribbon; and most recently
Limebeer and van de Merwe (2025) dispense with the ribbon altogether
and obtain the surface as a free Monge-patch parametrisation

A secondary effect compounds the singularity in the same corners:

The primary contribution of this paper is a pipeline that fits a
singularity-avoiding parameterisation of any track surface
discretised by a point cloud, the only requirement being that the
point cloud has unique and sorted indices along the longitudinal and
lateral directions. The key component is the minimum-curvature

Heilmeier et al. (2020). Once the reference line is obtained, the
pipeline fits the Monge patch in lateral polynomials of degree NN

optimisation problems.

Racing-line generation has its own large literature that the proposed
pipeline draws on. Direct minimum-time optimal control
Perantoni and Limebeer (2015) provides the true optimum but is
expensive and requires a vehicle model. Sequential or geometric
approaches such as the minimum-curvature quadratic program of
Braghin et al. (2008) and the iterated, constraint-aware
formulation of Heilmeier et al. (2020) are within a fraction of a
percent of the time-optimal solution while being orders of magnitude
faster and vehicle-agnostic; the two-step decomposition of
Kapania et al. (2016) alternates path and velocity profile. The novel contribution of this paper is to repurpose the
minimum-curvature line of Heilmeier et al. (2020) and
Braghin et al. (2008) not as a driving target but as the
curvilinear reference that anchors the Monge-patch surface
parametrisation of Limebeer and van de Merwe (2025), thereby
certifying injectivity of the Frenet map on the full track strip.

The rest of the paper is organised as follows.
Section 2 develops the fitting pipeline, from the
minimum-curvature quadratic program to the C4C^{4} piecewise-quintic
export. Section 3 shows how the Modelica
TrackJoint component uses those splines, and why the
differential-algebraic equation it forms needs each property of the
export format. Section 4 reports the effect on the
conditioning of a full-circuit minimum lap-time problem.

title: A 2-DOF MultiBody Track Joint for Race Car Optimization
authors: Srikanth Sivaramakrishnan,Behzad Danaei,Adwait Verulkar,Ryan Trinter
abstract:
TrackJoint is a Modelica MultiBody component that turns a
three-dimensional road surface into a joint with two degrees of freedom.
The two joint coordinates are the distance travelled along a reference
line and the sideways offset from that line. Together they give the
position, orientation and angular velocity of a single frame_b
connector. All road geometry reaches the joint as a small set of periodic
piecewise-quintic splines, so one component can represent any circuit whose
splines have been fitted beforehand. The road constraint is closed with
d’Alembert’s principle. The two generalized forces that
belong to the joint coordinates are set to zero, so no Lagrange multipliers are needed.
The joint is connected to a multibody race car in Dymola and the pair is
exported as one FMI 3.0 FMU. The same FMU is then used for time-domain
simulation and for CasADi/IPOPT minimum lap-time optimization, with no
change to the model in between. This works because the joint keeps the
arc-length coordinate as a real state and publishes its time derivative,
which is the quantity that lets the problem be rewritten with distance
We report results for minimum lap time simulations on
the Singapore Formula 1 circuit.
introduction:
Race-car simulation in Modelica relies on a road model
that generates accurate surface geometry in terms of position,
orientation and angular velocity for each tire contact patch.
Inside a generic MultiBody vehicle simulation this is naturally expressed by
a Modelica joint that constrains the chassis of the vehicle
to lie on the road surface while leaving the in-plane road
coordinates free. For ideal flat surfaces this role is filled by
Modelica.Mechanics.MultiBody.Joints.Planar. Although analytically defined ribbons have been used in earlier
race-car work Perantoni and Limebeer (2015); Lovato et al. (2021), they are
typically hand-coded inside a surrogate optimization model rather
than packaged as a reusable MultiBody component. The idea of a
reusable path-following joint that constrains motion to a
spline-parametrized curve has been formulated symbolically in a
graph-theoretic multibody setting by Hall et al. (2014).
This method is used to reduce complex automotive suspension linkages into a single degree-of-freedom joint for computational efficiency.
A more closely related precedent is the
Claytex.Mechanics.MultiBody.Joints.Rail
joint of the commercial Claytex library Briant (2021), which constrains a
frame_b to follow a one-dimensional B-spline rail
parametrized by arc length ss and resolves the wrench through
the spline-derivative projection that we also adopt below. The
Claytex component is, however, restricted to a curve: it leaves a
single translational degree of freedom and exposes the orientation
either as a heading frame slaved to the rail tangent or as three
independent angle splines.

This paper presents TrackJoint, a Modelica MultiBody joint
that takes the Claytex Rail idea as its starting point
and extends it from a 1-DOF rail to a 2-DOF Monge-patch racetrack
surface. The body is now free to move both along a planar
reference line (ss) and laterally across it (ww); the
orientation triad is constructed analytically from the surface
partials rather than from a separate angle table; and the wrench
is closed by two d’Alembert relations rather than one. The
underlying surface model is the Monge patch
Limebeer and van de Merwe (2025); do Carmo (1976)

The contribution of this paper is a Modelica implementation of a
track joint that exposes the road surface as a single reusable
MultiBody component suitable for both time-domain simulation and
optimization. For efficiency the per-step evaluation is
implemented with Horner expansion of the Monge cubic, constant-time
segment lookup on the uniform break vector and a shared spline
evaluator, so that the same component is cheap to evaluate at every collocation point of a CasADi/IPOPT
Andersson et al. (2019); Wächter and Biegler (2006) minimum lap-time
problem. The model also ensures sufficient accuracy to the LiDAR measurements of the track and can be used in time-domain simulation of a
multibody race car driven around a closed circuit.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows.
Section 2 recalls the Monge-patch surface
formulation and fixes the notation used by the joint.
Section 3 derives the joint equations from
(1)–(2).
Section 4 discusses the Modelica
implementation and the FMI export. Section 5
reports the two downstream use cases.

title: HIDRA: Hierarchical Dual-Routing Attention for Replay-Free Lifelong Imitation Learning
authors: Fanqi Yu,Matteo Tiezzi,Cigdem Beyan,Tommaso Apicella,Vittorio Murino
comment: This is the authors' preprint, accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Conference. The final version is available in the NeurIPS 2026 proceedings
abstract:
Robotic agents operating in real-world environments must adapt continuously from a stream of multimodal demonstrations, often under constraints that preclude storing or revisiting past data. In this replay-free, single-pass lifelong imitation learning setting, sequential updates can progressively distort the representation space, making expert-based approaches particularly sensitive to routing interference, causing expert selection to degrade over time.
We propose HIDRA, a structured routing framework that mitigates this issue through a hierarchical dual-attention mechanism, which decouples instruction-level expert retrieval from context-dependent refinement. To further stabilize routing under representation drift, HIDRA introduces a key-level geometric regularization that enforces both alignment within tasks and separation across tasks. The resulting approach enables reliable expert selection while supporting an expandable set of experts for continual adaptation.
We evaluate HIDRA on several LIBERO benchmark suites, including more challenging variants with heterogeneous task sequences and paraphrased language instructions. Our approach consistently outperforms both replay-free and replay-based baselines, improving AUC and forward transfer while maintaining low forgetting, with stronger gains under high interference and language variation. The code is available at: https://github.com/yfqi/HIDRA.
introduction:
Robotic agents deployed in the real world must adapt continuously as they interact with dynamic, non-stationary environments. Unlike offline imitation learning pipelines that rely on curated datasets and multi-epoch optimization, real robots receive an unbounded stream of demonstrations and observations, often under constraints that prevent storing or revisiting past data Lesort et al. (2020). Enabling robots to learn online, in a replay-free, single-pass manner, is therefore central to the long-standing goal of lifelong robot learning Silver et al. (2013); Liu (2017).

This continuous streaming perspective differs fundamentally from standard lifelong imitation learning (LIL) formulations, which typically assume discrete task boundaries and repeated access to past trajectories Liu et al. (2023a); Wan et al. (2024); Lee et al. (2024); Yu et al. (2026). Instead, a robot operating in the wild encounters a temporally correlated flow of multimodal data, including visual observations, language instructions, and proprioceptive feedback that rarely can be revisited  Thrun and Mitchell (1995); Jang et al. (2022). Recent vision language action (VLA) models, spanning early systems such as RT-2 Zitkovich et al. (2023) and Octo Team et al. (2024) to more recent large-scale policies (e.g., GR00T 1.5 Bjorck et al. (2025), π0​.5\pi_{0}.5 Intelligence et al. (2025), π0.7\pi_{0.7}  Intelligence et al. (2026), SmolVLA Shukor et al. (2025)), illustrate the promise of pretrained backbones for general-purpose robotic control. Multi-task benchmarks like LIBERO Liu et al. (2023a) further highlight their capacity for compositionality and transfer Liu et al. (2023b); Yu et al. (2026); Hu et al. (2022).
Yet these high-capacity representations tend to entangle instruction semantics and fine-grained context, making them fragile under sequential updates. In a single-pass setting where revisiting data is impossible, such entanglement leads to irreversible errors, a phenomenon also observed in continual learning with pretrained feature extractors Tiezzi et al. (2024a); Zhou et al. (2024). More critically, single-pass learning demands rapid adaptation, yet such entanglement hinders the effective utilization of distinct knowledge, slowing router convergence and making it difficult to establish reliable routing decisions from a single exposure to incoming data.

The impact of representation entanglement is particularly pronounced in LIL, where the agent must integrate heterogeneous demonstrations while preserving previously acquired behaviors. This challenge becomes more severe when adaptation is performed on top of pretrained backbones, a common paradigm in modern visuomotor and vision-language-action (VLA) systems, where large models provide broad perceptual and linguistic priors before deployment. In such settings, sequential updates in a streaming regime can induce representation drift and catastrophic forgetting, progressively distorting the general-purpose features learned during pretraining Wan et al. (2024); Yu et al. (2026).

Capturing both task semantics and context-dependent variations within a shared embedding further intensifies the plasticity–stability trade-off Kirkpatrick et al. (2017); Kemker et al. (2018); Wang et al. (2024). In modular or expert-based architectures, this manifests as routing interference, where learning new tasks shifts the representation space and disrupts previously established expert assignments, causing routing errors to accumulate over time in the absence of replay. Existing approaches based on parameter-efficient fine-tuning Hu et al. (2022); Houlsby et al. (2019); Ding et al. (2023); Xin et al. (2024) or dynamic expert libraries Lei et al. (2025) often rely on multi-epoch optimization or access to stored demonstrations to stabilize training, limiting their applicability in strict streaming regimes. In practice, these restrictive conditions are the norm. Human demonstrations are expensive and often cannot be stored due to privacy, memory, or deployment constraints Ravichandar et al. (2020); Celemin et al. (2022); Zare et al. (2024). A robot learning from a live stream of demonstrations must instead rely on online, replay-free, single-pass updates, where each trajectory provides a single opportunity for adaptation. Under these constraints, routing mechanisms must reliably disentangle instruction-level intent from rapidly shifting context, even as internal representations drift.

To operate effectively in this setting, we introduce a Hierarchical Dual-Routing Attention mechanism (hidra) that decouples instruction-driven expert retrieval from context-driven refinement, reducing interference and enabling stable expert selection without replay. We additionally introduce a key-level geometric regularization strategy that structures the routing space and improves separability among experts under representational drift. Together, these components define a streaming LIL framework with an expandable expert set that learns from multimodal data streams without storing past demonstrations (see Fig. 1). We assume known task boundaries during lifelong adaptation, following the standard LIL protocol Liu et al. (2023a); Wan et al. (2024); here, “streaming” refers to single-pass, non-revisitable task-wise data arrival rather than boundary-free task discovery.

Our contributions are: (i) a dual-routing attention mechanism that separates instruction semantics from contextual adaptation, enabling reliable expert selection under replay-free, single-pass learning; (ii) a key-level geometric regularization strategy that stabilizes routing by enforcing structure in the expert-selection space;
(iii) a unified streaming LIL framework with expandable expert libraries that achieves robust performance and forward transfer while maintaining low forgetting on diverse, long-horizon manipulation tasks with varied language instructions and object interactions, particularly under heterogeneous task sequences and language variation.

title: SG^2SLAM: Spatial Geometry-Informed 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM for Monocular Outdoor Navigation
authors: Ziang Guo,Didar Seyidov,Yixiao Zhou,Xuefeng Zhang,Ali Alridha Abdulkarim,Chen Min,Zufeng Zhang,Dzmitry Tsetserukou
abstract: Monocular outdoor navigation requires robust camera motion estimation and a dense, navigable map, where 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM serves this task through an explicit differentiable parameterization and closed-form projection. However, typically, the geometry is recovered by associating 2D pixels with 3D points, so a modular SLAM system absorbs tracking error into the map, leading to cascading degradation. To address these gaps, we present SG2\text{SG}^{2}SLAM, which couples streaming spatial geometry with a ray-conditioned 3DGS kernel. Streaming spatial geometry replaces the per-frame cross-dimensional correspondence with a chunk-level metric prior that supervises tracking and mapping from one source. A ray-conditioned kernel extends each primitive with a viewing-direction subspace that senses the monocular camera viewpoints. The joint optimization over spatial geometry and poses ensures a globally consistent map and trajectory outcome. Experiments on the KITTI and Waymo Open datasets show that our SG2\text{SG}^{2}SLAM surpasses the per-frame association baselines in the monocular outdoor navigation task. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
introduction:
Recovering camera motion and creating a dense, navigable map of the environment from a monocular RGB stream remain core capabilities for autonomous navigation. Coupling 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) has rapidly become a mainstream research direction, as its explicit, differentiable parameterization is naturally compatible with online tracking and mapping [1]. However, in monocular outdoor navigation, which is the deployment scenario of practical interest, the 3DGS SLAM suffers from an undetermined global scale and further exposes two concrete gaps that we identify below.

Existing SLAM systems recover geometry through the 2D–3D matching paradigm, in which 2D pixel observations are associated with 3D points [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. The 2D–3D association is, however, intrinsically cross-dimensional. The 3D to 2D projection irreversibly discards depth, and the inverse recovery is a non-convex problem that is sensitive to outliers, reprojection noise, and mismatched feature scales. Under the conditions of outdoor monocular navigation, these sensitivities compound. Within a modular SLAM architecture, tracking errors from 2D–3D correspondences are absorbed into the 3D map, which then provides a degraded reference for the next round of matching, producing a slow but unbounded drift that is particularly hard to localize and correct.

The 3DGS map becomes geometrically ambiguous while absorbing tracking errors. 3DGS is mainly optimized against a photometric loss for novel view synthesis, which admits multiple geometrically distinct Gaussian configurations that produce indistinguishable renderings. In outdoor sequences, this manifests as floating Gaussians, broken thin structures, and inconsistent surface normals [7]. These artifacts are tolerable for view synthesis but are directly harmful for navigation due to the pollution of depth information, where downstream tasks such as collision checking and traversability estimation consume the map.

To mitigate these gaps in outdoor monocular conditions, we propose SG2\text{SG}^{2}SLAM, a 3DGS SLAM built on streaming spatial geometry and a monocular-depth-aware ray-conditioned 3DGS kernel, where the frontend streams poses, point maps, and per-pixel confidence from windows of frames to form chunking, with a metric depth network supervising the metric scale. Then, the backend refines the 3DGS map, conditioning each primitive on the viewing ray with spatial geometric supervision and keeping the mapping consistent and aware under monocular camera conditions. Chunks are then fused by a joint global graph optimization over spatial geometry and poses. Our contribution is as follows:

We present a 3DGS SLAM built on streaming spatial geometry. Compared to the baselines based on pairwise 2D pixel matching and cross-dimensional correspondences, our SG2\text{SG}^{2}SLAM improves both frontend tracking and backend mapping.

We render 3DGS through a ray-conditioned kernel in closed form, where the mean and covariance span a spatial block and a viewing-direction subspace, thus removing the blending at grazing angles that may produce floating primitives.

We fuse chunks through joint global graph optimization over the spatial geometry and poses, which keeps the map and trajectory globally consistent and settles the fusion of all chunks in a single solve.

1. We present a 3DGS SLAM built on streaming spatial geometry. Compared to the baselines based on pairwise 2D pixel matching and cross-dimensional correspondences, our SG2\text{SG}^{2}SLAM improves both frontend tracking and backend mapping.

2. We render 3DGS through a ray-conditioned kernel in closed form, where the mean and covariance span a spatial block and a viewing-direction subspace, thus removing the blending at grazing angles that may produce floating primitives.

3. We fuse chunks through joint global graph optimization over the spatial geometry and poses, which keeps the map and trajectory globally consistent and settles the fusion of all chunks in a single solve.

title: ASPEN: Adaptive Semantic Reasoning via Command Persistence Prediction for Efficient Navigation VLAs
authors: Vieri N. Akustia,Bin Hu
abstract: Navigation vision-language-action (VLA) policies repeatedly invoke costly semantic reasoning even when the next command remains unchanged. Command reuse can reduce computation but risks missing instruction-dependent turns or stops. We introduce ASPEN, an event-triggered scheduler based on command persistence prediction: estimating whether the frozen base policy would reissue its previous command. A lightweight multimodal predictor combines temporal observations, language instructions, execution history, and cached VLA confidence. At eligible command boundaries, sufficient predicted persistence permits command reuse. Otherwise, ASPEN triggers fresh semantic reasoning from the VLA. Evaluated with frozen NaVILA on cross-dataset RxR-CE val-unseen, ASPEN reduces VLA calls by 9.5% and estimated inference time by 8.1%, including scheduling overhead. It maintains comparable navigation performance and preserves identical baseline action sequences on 92.1% of episodes.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies connect visual observations and language instructions to robot behavior Driess et al. (2023); Zitkovich et al. (2023); Kim et al. (2025). In navigation, these policies can generate high-level commands that are executed through a downstream action interface Krantz et al. (2021); An et al. (2025); Zheng et al. (2024); Zhang et al. (2024); Cheng et al. (2025). However, repeated invocation of a large VLA incurs substantial cost when successive decisions produce the same command. We study when this semantic reasoning can be omitted while retaining the behavior of a frozen navigation policy.

Existing efficiency methods use action-sequence prediction Zhao et al. (2023); Chi et al. (2025); Ghosh et al. (2024), selective computation and compression Zhang et al. (2026); Yang et al. (2025), temporal caching Xu et al. (2025); Wu et al. (2026), and adaptive execution Tan et al. (2025); Li et al. (2026); Wang et al. (2026). FlashVLA Tan et al. (2025) combines action-history consistency and visual-token overlap to trigger reuse, whereas SP-VLA Li et al. (2026) schedules between a VLA and a lightweight action generator using motion history. In navigation, substantial visual change can accompany continued forward motion, while the current view alone may not establish whether an instructed landmark has already been passed. The relevant scheduling question is therefore not simply whether the scene or motion has changed, but whether the base policy’s next command would change given the instruction and execution history.

We introduce ASPEN, which predicts this command persistence from temporal observations, language, execution history, and cached VLA confidence. Following the event-triggered principle Tabuada (2007); Heemels et al. (2012), the scheduler chooses between repeating the previous command and refreshing NaVILA. Unlike a lightweight replacement controller, its predicted command distribution is used to schedule the base policy, not to select a different executable command. Our contributions are (i) command-persistence-based scheduling for a frozen navigation policy, (ii) a context-conditioned predictor with explicit eligibility check, and (iii) cross-dataset evaluation from R2R-CE to RxR-CE Krantz et al. (2020); Ku et al. (2020), demonstrating reduced estimated inference cost with similar observed success and high action-sequence agreement.

title: Learning Multi-Phase Robot Loco-Manipulation via Phase-Conditioned Policy Optimization
authors: Simone Manni,Annika Wollschläger,Dario Bellicoso,Abel Gawel,Marco Hutter,Simon Le Cleac'h,Jan Brüdigam
abstract:
Complex whole-body loco-manipulation requires executing diverse maneuvers, such as crouching, grasping, and locomotion, within a single long-horizon task. While performing simple pick-and-place behaviors is well-established, scaling to complex, long-horizon tasks remains difficult. Currently, this challenge is addressed by relying on human motion data and correspondingly humanoid platforms, which limits platform independence and introduces substantial data processing overhead.
Instead, we extend proximal policy optimization (PPO) to train a single policy for multi-phase tasks across diverse robotic hardware, leveraging prior task structure to shape behavior. Our method adapts PPO using a phase-conditioned critic, phase-gated reward functions, and a multi-phase reset curriculum to guide exploration. To support varied hardware, we employ a decoupled hierarchical control architecture that separates lower-level balancing dynamics from high-level phase execution.
We demonstrate multi-stage loco-manipulation skills on hardware on both the Unitree G1 and a Boston Dynamics Spot equipped with a manipulator arm, and validate our design choices through ablations. Our approach enables the acquisition of complex loco-manipulation behaviors purely through environment interaction while directly incorporating high-level task structure into policy learning.
introduction:
Loco-manipulation is an essential capability for deploying mobile robots in real-world environments, where they must navigate, interact with, and reconfigure their surroundings. Although reinforcement learning (RL) methods have been increasingly employed with success in short-horizon pick-and-place tasks [1, 2], they usually struggle in long-horizon settings due to the large exploration space and complex contact mechanics [3, 4].

Additionally, complex loco-manipulation tasks, such as lifting and carrying a box, mandate coordinating distinct physical modes (walking, crouching, rising) within a unified policy. This poses a major challenge for standard reward tuning, which might cause training to collapse into unwanted local minima, such as learning to kick or drag a box instead of lifting and carrying it. To bridge this gap, recent work increasingly relies on human motion datasets [5] and demonstrations, driving the widespread adoption of humanoid platforms in research. While effective, this paradigm requires substantial data processing overhead and results in platform-specific methods that fail to generalize to diverse robotic hardware. More recent approaches have successfully solved humanoid loco-manipulation tasks by learning through autonomous environment interaction, without human guidance [6, 7, 8]. However, they only focus on simple table-to-table object transportation, ignoring the distinct physical transitions, such as low crouching and rising, required to pick up or deposit an object directly from the ground.

Crucially, long-horizon tasks are inherently compositional and naturally break down into a sequence of distinct behavioral stages, each demanding specialized local control. For example, a box-lifting policy can be split into approaching, crouching and lifting phases. Exploiting this inherent multi-phase structure provides a promising route to tackle the exploration challenge without demonstration data. While traditional methods often rely on finite state machines to chain independently trained sub-policies sequentially—a strategy previously applied also to humanoid box-lifting [9]—managing transitions across highly dynamic regimes can be problematic. In contrast, consolidating these stages into a single policy natively manages inter-phase transitions and eliminates external orchestration. This strong multi-phase structure and the advantage of having a single policy to handle the entire task highlight the need for an RL framework that can explicitly leverage phase transitions to guide exploration and training.

To this end, we introduce a variant of the popular PPO [10] algorithm that incorporates the sequential nature of the task. A state machine segments the task into manageable behavior windows and masks MDP terms. The actor is forced to internalize task progression by predicting the current phase, and the critic is conditioned on the active phase to better capture local value changes. We evaluate our framework across two distinct platforms and multiple tasks, including a Spot quadruped maneuvering a tire and a Unitree G1 humanoid carrying a box. For the latter, we also resolve several sim-to-real issues to enable stable, prolonged grasping. Finally, through targeted ablations, we validate the impact of our core algorithmic choices.

Our contributions are as follows.

Unified Control Interface: To ensure compatibility, we first establish a common control interface across both platforms, extending the hierarchical RL framework originally developed for the quadruped to the humanoid.

Multi-Phase RL Framework: We design a multi-phase RL training framework built on top of PPO that conditions value estimation and the MDP on task phases, allowing a single unified policy to coordinate complex multi-stage tasks.

1. Unified Control Interface: To ensure compatibility, we first establish a common control interface across both platforms, extending the hierarchical RL framework originally developed for the quadruped to the humanoid.

2. Multi-Phase RL Framework: We design a multi-phase RL training framework built on top of PPO that conditions value estimation and the MDP on task phases, allowing a single unified policy to coordinate complex multi-stage tasks.

title: cuArms: GPU-Accelerated Conflict-Based Planning for Multi-Arm Manipulation
authors: Philip Huang,Fabio Ramos,Jiaoyang Li,Caelan Garrett,Lars Johannsmeier
abstract:
Multi-arm manipulation has the potential to dramatically improve the throughput, efficiency, and dexterity of many manipulation tasks.
Recent work coordinates multiple robot arms in a shared workcell by allocating and scheduling tasks for greater parallelism, jointly planning multi-arm motions, or directly learning multi-arm policies.
So far, these approaches are either too slow, rely on domain-specific assumptions, or scale poorly with the number of robots and task horizon.
Thus, we introduce cuArms, a conflict-based planner co-designed with GPU parallelism that efficiently decomposes the search space using reusable multi-modal roadmaps for individual robots and resolves conflicts and deadlocks through a lazy search.
To jointly optimize task assignment, schedules, motions, and manipulation skills, we integrate a high-level scheduler that proposes candidate skeletons for cuArms to ground into coordinated manipulation plans.
Experimental results show that our method establishes a new state of the art, with real-time initial solutions and anytime improvements in both motion quality and scheduling, without days of domain-specific training required by learning approaches.
Videos of both simulated and real-world industrial tasks are available on https://cuarms.github.io/.
introduction:
As robotic manipulator hardware becomes more widely available and less expensive, multi-arm robotic manipulation—using multiple arms to complete tasks in a shared work cell—becomes much more affordable and accessible. A multi-arm system improves task throughput with greater parallelization, increases space utilization on factory floors, and becomes necessary for tasks that require more dexterous solutions and bimanual coordination, or the handling of bulky parts.

Realizing this promise requires tightly coordinating the motions and manipulation skills of multiple robots that share the same workspace to avoid collisions.
Specifically, there are several technical challenges: task allocation (which robot is assigned to each task), scheduling (the order and duration of each robot’s actions), safety (robots must not collide), and reasoning over hybrid action spaces (e.g., contacts, grasps, kinematic modality changes, reachability).
Current research in this area is often domain-specific [1, 2], time-consuming [3, 4],
and cannot plan bimanual manipulation skills [3, 5].

To make these increasingly difficult problems tractable, we introduce cuArms, a new planner that tightly couples GPU acceleration
with a conflict-based multi-agent planner [6] to find long-horizon, multi-modal, and multi-arm manipulation plans.
This combination attacks the computational bottleneck from both sides: algorithmic decompositions reduce the search complexity, while GPU parallelism accelerates expensive geometric validations.
cuArms constructs a multi-modal roadmap [7] for each robot, searches the joint configuration space to resolve conflicts among robot motions and manipulation skills, and iteratively improves the resulting trajectory through shortcutting [8, 9].
A GPU-native implementation accelerates every stage using large batches of parallel geometric validity checks.
At the same time, our algorithm reuses computation and avoids excessive CPU-GPU communication by decomposing the geometry of different robots, movable objects, and environments.
Simulation and real-robot experiments show that cuArms finds initial plans in about 1 second across a variety of domains (e.g., Fig. 1), including an 8-arm, 40-task welding task, and improves solution quality up to 57%57\% with additional computations.
Furthermore, this efficiency makes full multi-arm task and motion planning (TAMP) tractable.
As shown in Fig. 2, we use a hierarchical schedule-then-coordinate approach that sequentially generates many candidate schedule skeletons and plans the full multi-arm trajectory with cuArms.
Our contributions are:

cuArms, a multi-arm manipulation planner that combines per-arm roadmaps, lazy conflict-driven joint search, and anytime trajectory refinement in a disaggregated architecture co-designed for GPU-batched computation.

Domain-agnostic, multi-arm task and motion planning by integrating cuArms with a high-level scheduler with support for collaborative bimanual manipulation skills, such as handover and carry.

Simulation and real-robot experiments for multi-arm manipulation, welding, and assembly tasks demonstrating the algorithm’s efficiency, quality, and scalability.

1. cuArms, a multi-arm manipulation planner that combines per-arm roadmaps, lazy conflict-driven joint search, and anytime trajectory refinement in a disaggregated architecture co-designed for GPU-batched computation.

2. Domain-agnostic, multi-arm task and motion planning by integrating cuArms with a high-level scheduler with support for collaborative bimanual manipulation skills, such as handover and carry.

3. Simulation and real-robot experiments for multi-arm manipulation, welding, and assembly tasks demonstrating the algorithm’s efficiency, quality, and scalability.

title: Program-Level Adversarial Co-Adaptive Self-Play for Robotic Security
authors: Leo Benaharon,Chi Zhang,Wei Zheng,Weifan Zhang,Yifan Wei
abstract:
Coding agents can adapt robotic software by revising executable programs, but successful responses to an evolving opponent may not remain effective. We present a framework for program-level adversarial co-adaptive self-play in which coding agents generate attacks and defenses from tested opponent code and mission feedback, without model fine-tuning. Environment-specific interfaces support external programs for autonomous driving and SDK-level defenses for humanoid locomotion.
Two eight-generation case studies reveal concrete software responses: a driving defender introduces direct-actuation recovery, while a humanoid defender revises incoming-state validation. These responses provide local task recovery but do not establish sustained robustness.
The framework makes such adaptation and limitations observable through executable artifacts and task-level evidence.
introduction:
Robotic cybersecurity must protect physical behavior as well as software access. A disclosed Unitree Go2 vulnerability exposed a DDS programming interface without authentication or authorization, permitting a network-adjacent attacker to install code later executed through a controller binding [12]. Such risks motivate proactive testing: develop attacks and candidate defenses before malicious exploitation, then evaluate their consequences for an ongoing robotic task.

Coding agents provide a way to study this interaction through executable programs. Prior work connects generated code to embodied control [6], develops executable skills through environmental feedback [13], and investigates code-mediated improvement and autonomous cyber co-evolution [9, 7]. In this work, we study a system-level
question: can agents attack an existing robotic stack and revise defenses effectively as
the opponent adapts?

Our framework implements program-level adversarial co-adaptive self-play. Attack-generating agents and a shared defense-generating agent are placed around a running robotic system. Programs submitted by agents are checked and frozen, executed on the robotic system, and returned with independently observed outcomes to inform subsequent revisions. Adaptation occurs in software and retained context rather than through arena-driven model fine-tuning. Environment-specific tasks and permissions determine what those programs may change.

We study this process in Autoware-CARLA and Unitree G1-MuJoCo. The driving configuration uses fixed attacker roles; the humanoid configuration additionally uses an orchestrator, development-time tests against frozen opponents, and separate clean, attack-only, defense-only, and joint episode executions. The studies reveal concrete program revisions alongside recurrent failures, motivating evaluation beyond a favorable individual match.

Our contributions are:

A robotic-security self-play framework with directly competing programs. Independent coding agents revise programs that execute together around an operating autonomy stack through robotic middleware and permitted software modifications.

A robotic-security self-play framework with directly competing programs. Independent coding agents revise programs that execute together around an operating autonomy stack through robotic middleware and permitted software modifications.

A mission-grounded evaluation protocol. The humanoid evaluation combines clean, attack-only, defense-only, and repeated joint trials to distinguish attack effectiveness, defense viability, and normalized task recovery.

Two eight-generation case studies of adversarial adaptation. Driving and humanoid experiments trace how agents develop countermeasures and counterattacks in response to each other, revealing targeted recovery alongside persistent failures.

1. A robotic-security self-play framework with directly competing programs. Independent coding agents revise programs that execute together around an operating autonomy stack through robotic middleware and permitted software modifications.

2. A mission-grounded evaluation protocol. The humanoid evaluation combines clean, attack-only, defense-only, and repeated joint trials to distinguish attack effectiveness, defense viability, and normalized task recovery.

3. Two eight-generation case studies of adversarial adaptation. Driving and humanoid experiments trace how agents develop countermeasures and counterattacks in response to each other, revealing targeted recovery alongside persistent failures.

title: Closed-Loop Aware Planning via Imitation-Free Speed Scoring for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
authors: Emad Aghajanzadeh,Thomas Schwarzfischer,Marc Kaufeld,Moritz Thoma,Ryan Pégoud,Manoj Rohit Vemparala,Pierpaolo Mori,Nael Fasfous,Johannes Betz,Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder,Ulf Schlichtmann
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. (8-page main paper, references, and supplementary material), 5 figures, 7 tables. Project page:this https URL. \c{opyright} 2027 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media
abstract:
End-to-end autonomous driving has predominantly relied on open-loop imitation learning for training, which presents two limitations. First, expert demonstrations show only one behavior per scenario, so the model cannot learn alternative valid behaviors and, in turn, cannot adapt to user-specified preferences at test time. Second, noise or ambiguity in these demonstrations can produce inconsistent, unreliable supervision for the end-to-end models.
Driving is inherently multi-modal: multiple different behaviors can be valid responses to the same scene, and this diversity arises largely from speed rather than path. We introduce a planning paradigm that learns the path through imitation while scoring a set of candidate speeds across multiple criteria with a learned function supervised by physically grounded safety constraints. We realize this paradigm as Closed-Loop Aware Planning for Autonomous Driving (CLAP-AD), a plug-in planning head that integrates with existing end-to-end driving models and, to our knowledge, is the first to enable explicit test-time control over their speed selection without speed-conditioned training. On Bench2Drive-Speed, CLAP-AD sets a new state of the art Speed-Adherence Score of 82.53, topping TFv6, the strongest baseline on this metric, by 12.9 points while retaining strong closed-loop driving performance. On Bench2Drive, it improves driving score by +28.5 and +32.7 over UniAD and VAD, and on NAVSIM v2, built on real-world driving data, EPDMS by +6.1 over its backbone. Project page: clap-ad.github.io.
introduction:
Recently, end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving has gained attention for transforming raw sensor inputs directly into driving decisions within a fully differentiable framework, with approaches such as UniAD [11], VAD [18], and TransFuser [7]. Imitation learning [21] is often the preferred paradigm for training such models, favored over reinforcement learning [42] for enabling stable, efficient open-loop training from expert demonstrations while avoiding complex reward design [6, 32, 20]. However, driving is inherently a multi-modal task, with multiple valid behaviors possible in the same scenario, and strictly imitating a single expert demonstration prevents the model from learning that alternative behaviors are also valid, contributing to a fundamental mismatch with closed-loop deployment [49, 13].

To improve closed-loop performance, one line of work disentangles path from speed, observing that a shared temporal-waypoint representation entangles a largely deterministic, lane-constrained path with a genuinely multi-modal speed [12]. Follow-up methods retain this separation but still imitate a single speed value or profile per class [33, 43, 47], leaving the multi-modality of driving speed unresolved. A separate line of work scores a fixed trajectory vocabulary against several driving criteria alongside an imitation score [26, 27, 40], yet the evidence for a benefit from these criteria over imitation alone in fully reactive closed-loop settings is mixed at best (Sec. 2). Across both lines, path and speed remain optimized under the same objective and architecture, overlooking their fundamentally different nature, and neither offers any support for user test-time controllability over the model’s decisions.

Motivated by this, we argue that path and speed should be learned under different objectives, retaining imitation learning for path prediction while replacing expert speed imitation with a multi-criteria scoring mechanism over a set of diverse speed classes. This formulation brings two key advantages. First, evaluating multiple candidate speeds along the predicted path yields a range of safe speed profiles, enabling explicit deployment-time customization of driving speed, a capability largely unexplored in existing E2E driving models. Second, since each criterion is supervised directly from physically grounded constraints rather than a single noisy expert trace, the model learns genuinely safe behavior per criterion, and the resulting scores are directly interpretable, letting us attribute driving failures to particular failures in speed score prediction. To realize this framework, we propose CLAP-AD, a plug-in planning head that integrates into existing E2E driving models: given upstream perception features, it first predicts a driving path, then scores candidate speed classes along it via dedicated, criterion-specific heads. As shown in Fig. 1, this design lets CLAP-AD substantially improve how faithfully each backbone follows a user-specified speed while retaining strong closed-loop driving performance.

We introduce a multi-criteria, imitation-free speed learning objective that explicitly models the suitability of multiple speed behaviors under physically grounded, safety-critical driving criteria, rather than directly imitating a single expert speed. This enables interpretable speed evaluation while better capturing the multi-modal nature of driving speed.

We introduce a multi-criteria, imitation-free speed learning objective that explicitly models the suitability of multiple speed behaviors under physically grounded, safety-critical driving criteria, rather than directly imitating a single expert speed. This enables interpretable speed evaluation while better capturing the multi-modal nature of driving speed.

We propose CLAP-AD, an extensible plug-in planning head that hierarchically predicts a driving path and uses a path-conditioned scoring function to evaluate candidate speed classes. We integrate CLAP-AD into three backbones: the well-established UniAD and VAD, as well as the recent, strong TFv6. To our knowledge, this is the first approach to bring explicit test-time speed control to existing E2E driving models without speed-conditioned training, allowing users to customize driving speed at deployment while the model continues to respect safety constraints (Fig. 1(b)).

We conduct extensive closed-loop evaluations on Bench2Drive, the recent Bench2Drive-Speed benchmark and NAVSIM v2, which is built on real-world driving data. CLAP-AD improves Speed-Adherence on every backbone, by up to +25.2+25.2 points. Our variants are the only ones in the comparison to reach the highly controllable regime above an adherence of 70 (Fig. 1(a)). This controllability comes at little to no cost in driving quality: CLAP-AD improves UniAD by +28.5 DS and VAD by +32.7 DS on Bench2Drive and LTFv6 by +6.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, while on TFv6 it retains driving performance within a few points of the baseline.

title: Rollback: Experience Backtracking in World Models for Policy Improvement
authors: Jiayi Luo,Yang Zhang,Liliang Chen,Nan Wang,Chen Gao,Boxiang Qiu,Zhuoxuan Li,Baorui Peng,Chuankang Li,Yuxiang Yan,Si Liu,Qingyun Sun,Shuicheng Yan,Maoqing Yao,Jianxin Li,Guanghui Ren
abstract:
Action-conditioned world models offer a scalable alternative to costly real-world interaction for improving robot policies.
However, existing world-model-based methods largely treat world models as forward-only surrogates of the physical environment, leaving untapped a capability no physical environment affords: rewinding to past decision points to explore counterfactual futures.
In this work, we introduce Rollback, a policy improvement paradigm that turns world models from passive simulators into counterfactual engines: it rolls back to critical decision points, branches into alternative actions, and contrasts their outcomes to attribute success to individual decisions.
This concentrates imagination where it matters most and distills counterfactual outcomes into fine-grained, action-level supervision without a separately learned value model.
Furthermore, we build a scalable training system that unifies distributed world-model search with asynchronous real-robot execution, forming a self-reinforcing cycle: real-world experience continually sharpens the world model, and a sharper world model in turn drives further policy improvement.
We term the world-model side of this cycle test-time physics grounding, a capability that hand-built physics simulators lack: while the world model serves as the training environment, real transitions from the policy it trains correct its dynamics through a lightweight LoRA pipeline.
Experiments on three challenging real-world tasks show that Rollback improves success rates over the strongest baseline by an absolute 10.67%, 11.11%, and 11.85% on block extraction, ball tossing, and tabletop curling, respectively, while achieving more stable improvement throughout training.
Although initialized from teleoperated demonstrations far below human level, Rollback surpasses the average success rate of human players on both ball tossing and tabletop curling within 8 hours of training.
introduction:
Action-conditioned world models have provided simulated environments for robot
policy training, offering a scalable complement to real-world
interaction [17, 18, 19].
By predicting the consequences of policy-generated actions, they allow policies
to collect experience and learn from imagined outcomes without physical
deployment [51, 56, 26].
Recent video world models extend this paradigm to diverse robotic tasks,
supporting policy evaluation [32, 14] and improvement through
synthetic experience [24, 50, 48].
These advances further extend to general-purpose robot policies, which can be
refined using imagined interactions and task feedback [49, 57].
Moving exploration and optimization into learned environments makes policy
learning less bound to physical trials.

Despite this progress, existing world-model-based policy learning
largely retains the trajectory-centric interaction protocol of real-world training,
using the world model primarily to generate forward rollouts whose
intermediate contexts are discarded afterward.
This overlooks a capability unavailable in physical RL: the ability to
“rewind and reconsider.”
While a physical environment cannot generally return to an identical
intermediate state after execution, a world model can restore a cached temporal
context, rewind to an earlier decision point, and explore alternative action
continuations from the same history.
This enables the policy to reconsider what it could have done differently at a
particular decision rather than restarting exploration from scratch.

Fully exploiting this capability, however, requires addressing three key
challenges as shown in Figure 1.
(i) Limited informative exploration.
Not all decisions are equally worth revisiting: along a trajectory, a few critical decisions determine the outcome, while alternatives to most others lead to similar results.
Independent rollouts cannot identify these consequential decisions or adaptively allocate exploration among them [11, 8].
(ii) Sparse decision-level supervision.
Trajectory-level feedback does not reveal which intermediate actions determine the outcome [2, 47].
Treating continuations independently preserves this credit-assignment problem, whereas learning an additional value model introduces extra modeling assumptions and potential estimation bias [35, 43, 12].
(iii) Biased world-model predictions.
Branching from policy-selected contexts may shift interactions beyond the world model’s training distribution, causing prediction errors to accumulate or be exploited during optimization [25, 53, 54, 9].
Without real-world grounding, imagined gains may not transfer to real robots.

To operationalize training-time experience backtracking and address these challenges, we present Rollback, a policy improvement paradigm that turns world models from passive simulators into counterfactual engines.
Rollback comprises three key components:
(i) Experience-backtracking tree search.
Starting from successful and failed real-world trajectories, Rollback rolls back to intermediate decision points and branches into alternative action chunks.
Monte Carlo tree search adaptively allocates simulation budget toward decisions whose alternatives lead to divergent outcomes, avoiding exhaustive branching [8, 46, 23].
(ii) Tree-structured value estimation.
Since sibling branches share a decision context, contrasting their downstream outcomes isolates the effect of individual actions.
Subtree-level outcome aggregation yields fine-grained, action-level advantage supervision without an additional learned value model.
(iii) World model–policy co-evolution.
A scalable training system unifies distributed world-model search with asynchronous real-robot execution.
Real-world experience continually refines the world model, which in turn provides more faithful imagination for search and policy improvement.
We call this test-time physics grounding: after pretraining, while the world model serves as the training environment for a policy, real transitions collected by that policy correct its predicted dynamics in the states the policy actually visits.
Most existing action-conditioned world models are trained offline and then used as fixed simulators [51, 56, 26, 15], which suffices for evaluation but not for policy learning, because an improving policy moves into exactly the states the simulator has seen least.

We evaluate Rollback on three challenging real-world robotics tasks: block extraction, ball tossing, and tabletop curling.
Across these tasks, Rollback improves success rates over the strongest baseline by an absolute 10.67%, 11.11%, and 11.85%, respectively.
Under matched interaction budgets, Rollback achieves faster and more consistent improvements in task success rates.
Within 8 hours of training with one physical robot, Rollback surpasses the average success rate of human players on both ball tossing and tabletop curling, although it is initialized from teleoperated demonstrations far below human level.
Our project website is available at rollback-wm.github.io.

In summary, our contributions in this work can be summarized as follows:

We propose Rollback, a policy improvement paradigm that exploits experience backtracking to turn world models from passive simulators into counterfactual engines, supported by a training system unifying distributed world-model search with asynchronous real-robot execution.

We design an experience-backtracking search that concentrates imagination on critical decision points, and a tree-structured value estimation that distills counterfactual outcomes into fine-grained, action-level supervision without a separately learned value model.

Extensive experiments on three challenging real-world robotics tasks demonstrate that Rollback achieves higher success rates and more stable improvement.

1. We propose Rollback, a policy improvement paradigm that exploits experience backtracking to turn world models from passive simulators into counterfactual engines, supported by a training system unifying distributed world-model search with asynchronous real-robot execution.

2. We design an experience-backtracking search that concentrates imagination on critical decision points, and a tree-structured value estimation that distills counterfactual outcomes into fine-grained, action-level supervision without a separately learned value model.

3. Extensive experiments on three challenging real-world robotics tasks demonstrate that Rollback achieves higher success rates and more stable improvement.
