title: E0.5: From Reconstructive to Future-Predictive 3D Foundations for Robotic World-Action Modeling
authors: X-Era AI Lab Team:Jianhao Lai,Zhihao Zhan,Zhiquan Liao,Qichang Li,Shubin Chen,Zhiyuan Liu,Hongsen Lei,Jianman Lin,Xiaoxin Lin,Ke Gong,Baiyue Gu,Shiming Chen,Junlin He,Longqi Yang,Junrong Xiao,Haolin Luo,Xiaojuan Su,Jianfeng Li,Yu Luo,Xu Sun,Likui Zhang,Jusheng Zhang,Qinhan Lyu,Tianshui Chen,Liang Lin,Guangrun Wang
abstract: World-action models (WAMs) offer a promising framework for embodied intelligence, yet mainstream approaches remain centered on video foundation models or vision-language models. Even when geometric features extracted by 3D models such as VGGT are incorporated, they are typically passed into a video model or VLM that serves as the primary backbone, leaving 3D geometry as an auxiliary input or prediction target rather than the native foundation for world modeling. We present E0.5, a geometry-native world-action model built directly on 3D foundation models. E0.5 introduces two key innovations. First, it adopts a 3D foundation model as the primary backbone, making 3D geometry the native representation for both world modeling and action prediction. Second, it explicitly predicts future 3D states together with actions, enabling the model to capture geometric world dynamics beyond action-only modeling or future video prediction. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 first demonstrate the effectiveness of E0.5 without embodied-data pretraining, achieving success rates of 89.90% and 50.09% under clean and randomized settings, respectively. Building on these results, we further pretrain E0.5 on more than 160k robot trajectories from AgiBotWorld-Beta, jointly learning robot actions and future geometry within the pretrained 3D foundation. This embodied pretraining improves mean real-world manipulation success rates by approximately 15 and 7 percentage points on AgileX Piper and Zerith H1, respectively. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of geometry-native foundations to acquire robot interaction knowledge and transfer it to physical manipulation. E0.5 embodies this geometry-native approach as a member of the VWA family of world-action models.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation requires understanding not only the current spatial structure of a scene, but also how that structure may change as the robot acts. World-action models (WAMs) provide a framework for learning this relationship by jointly modeling robot actions and future world states (Song et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026). A central design question is therefore what kind of representation should underpin this joint modeling of actions and their physical consequences. Mainstream WAMs build on video foundation models or vision-language models, leveraging their capabilities in visual generation and semantic understanding. Although these models can incorporate geometric information, their primary computation remains organized around a video or vision-language backbone, rather than a native geometric foundation. This distinction motivates us to investigate an alternative: building WAMs directly on 3D foundation models, so that action generation and future-state prediction are learned within a shared geometric backbone.

Introducing 3D information into an existing model only partially addresses this requirement. Recent methods incorporate features extracted by geometric models into a vision-language or video backbone, or use these features as auxiliary supervision for the backbone’s representations (Yang et al., 2026d; Guo et al., 2025). Such approaches enrich spatial understanding, but retain a vision-language or video foundation model as the primary backbone, rather than building directly on a 3D foundation model. More generally, geometry can serve as an additional input or prediction target without becoming the representational foundation for world modeling and action generation. We investigate a complementary approach: making a 3D foundation model the core backbone, training it to predict geometric futures together with actions, and expanding its capacity within this geometric modeling framework.

We present E0.5, a geometry-native world-action model built directly on 3D foundation models. Following this principle, E0.5 brings together two key innovations: 3D foundation backbones that provide native geometric representations, explicit future 3D state prediction coupled with action generation. These components jointly define the model’s representational basis and predictive objective. Figure 1 summarizes these distinctions, contrasting E0.5 with video and VLM-centered models.

First, E0.5 adopts a 3D foundation model as its primary backbone, placing geometric representations at the center of both world modeling and action prediction. The geometric backbone serves as the core model on which these capabilities are learned, extending the role of 3D models beyond front-end feature extraction or auxiliary supervision. Our implementation uses VGGT-Omega (Wang et al., 2026a) as an example of a pretrained 3D foundation model. While such models recover the geometry of observed scenes, E0.5 develops this foundation into a predictive geometric backbone that learns future world states jointly with robot actions.

Second, E0.5 explicitly predicts future 3D states together with actions. Reconstructing current geometry provides information about the scene at the time of observation; predicting future geometry additionally requires modeling how its spatial configuration evolves during interaction. This distinction aligns the geometric objective with the predictive role of a WAM. It also offers an alternative to future video prediction, whose targets encompass both geometric changes and variations in visual appearance. Our hypothesis is that directly supervising future 3D states encourages the backbone to learn spatial structure and dynamics that remain useful across environments, supporting generalization when observations differ from those encountered during training.

This design also advances the use of 3D backbones beyond current-state reconstruction and restricted adaptation. VGA (Song et al., 2026b) uses a native 3D backbone with current-scene geometric supervision and LoRA adaptation; its ablations report substantial degradation under full-parameter training. E0.5 instead unfreezes the geometric backbone and jointly optimizes it for future 3D prediction and action generation. Our experiments demonstrate that backbone optimization is effective in this formulation, allowing pretrained geometric representations to adapt to predictive world-action modeling. Thus, the distinction concerns both what the backbone predicts and how its representations are learned.

These findings further motivate us to investigate whether a geometry-native foundation can acquire broad robot interaction knowledge while retaining its pretrained geometric representations. The strong performance observed in simulation, achieved without large-scale embodied pretraining, suggests that 3D foundation models provide an effective starting point for robot action learning. Building on this observation, we extend E0.5 to large-scale pretraining on AgiBotWorld-Beta, where robot actions and future geometric states are jointly modeled. Rather than adapting the backbone solely for action prediction, we continue to supervise future geometry throughout pretraining, allowing the geometric foundation to learn manipulation-relevant dynamics under explicit spatial constraints. We subsequently evaluate this pretrained model on distinct physical robot embodiments to examine how large-scale robot knowledge improves real-world manipulation.

Experiments on widely used simulation benchmarks and real-robot tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of E0.5. Predicting future 3D states improves the average success rate by 9.43 percentage points over the variant without geometric reconstruction and by 7.93 percentage points over current-state reconstruction, highlighting the benefits of predictive geometric supervision. The advantage is especially pronounced under distribution shifts: in our evaluated out-of-distribution (OOD) setting, E0.5 achieves approximately 30 times the accuracy of the video-prediction-based WAM baselines. Together, these results establish 3D foundation backbones and future geometry prediction as an effective basis for generalizable world-action modeling.

Our contributions are twofold:

World-action models built on 3D foundations. We introduce E0.5, which adopts 3D foundation models as its primary backbones and develops their geometric representations for joint world modeling and action prediction.

Explicit future 3D state prediction. We jointly learn future geometry and actions while optimizing the geometric backbone, achieving approximately 10-percentage-point improvement over current-state reconstruction and strong OOD generalization relative to video-prediction-based WAMs.

1. World-action models built on 3D foundations. We introduce E0.5, which adopts 3D foundation models as its primary backbones and develops their geometric representations for joint world modeling and action prediction.

2. Explicit future 3D state prediction. We jointly learn future geometry and actions while optimizing the geometric backbone, achieving approximately 10-percentage-point improvement over current-state reconstruction and strong OOD generalization relative to video-prediction-based WAMs.

title: Perceiving and Predicting Dynamic Sports: Spatiotemporal Intelligence in Vision Models for Egocentric Tennis Video
authors: Tudor Braicu,Joseph DelPreto,Jared Boyer,Mónika Farsang,Maximilian Stölzle,Tim Niklas Seyde,Daniela Rus
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Agile robots require spatiotemporal intelligence to interpret scenes, reason about interactions, and anticipate future events. Yet it remains unclear how well foundation vision models support these capabilities, particularly from a moving egocentric camera, which is a natural view for robots. To investigate this, we collect an annotated tennis dataset and train a suite of vision models on spatiotemporal tasks. Our dataset contains egocentric video synchronized with five allocentric videos, estimated global positions, labeled contact times, and annotated stroke types. We then evaluate seven prediction tasks from egocentric images: 2D ego player and 3D ball localization, future player and ball trajectories, forehand or backhand stroke anticipation, time to the next ego player ball contact, and 3D ball position at that contact. We compare image encoders, video encoders, and vision-language models with jointly trained prediction heads. The best performing models achieve mean current-frame localization errors of 0.14 m0.14\text{\,}\mathrm{m} for the ego player and 0.54 m0.54\text{\,}\mathrm{m} for the ball, future forecasting errors of 0.34 m0.34\text{\,}\mathrm{m} for the ego player and 0.91 m0.91\text{\,}\mathrm{m} for the ball over 1.1 s1.1\text{\,}\mathrm{s}, and a mean contact-time prediction error of 0.14 s0.14\text{\,}\mathrm{s}. Auxiliary depth information substantially improves 3D ball localization, suggesting that inferring metric depth remains a challenge.
Longer image histories do not improve ball forecasting, indicating that representations exploit scene context rather than rely solely on inter-frame motion.
Finally, we propose a conditional diffusion model to generate whole-body kinematic tennis motion from vision encoder predictions on egocentric video at real-time rates, adapting movements as predictions are refined.
These results move towards a deeper understanding of how foundation vision models can support real-time dynamic robots using egocentric video.
introduction:
Advances in robot hardware and learned controllers are enabling increasingly agile whole-body movements [1] and athletic behaviors [2, 3, 4], but coordinating these movements with fast objects and other agents requires visual processing to be sufficiently accurate and timely to guide immediate action. This motivates spatial intelligence that supports both estimating the current state of the environment and anticipating its evolution [5, 6, 7].

Spatial intelligence of vision-language models has been studied with question-answering techniques that probe their understanding of where objects and agents are located and how they are oriented [6, 8].
Accounting for how these relations evolve over time extends the scope to spatiotemporal intelligence [7].
We further distinguish understanding from forecasting [9] – understanding seeks to infer current spatial configurations, motions, and action cues from observed inputs, while forecasting aims to predict future states or actions using current and past observations. Representations that expose this information can support downstream visuomotor control and embodied planning [10, 11], while learned world models can predict future representations to guide action [12, 13]. These applications motivate evaluating what information is accessible in large-scale pretrained visual representations and how adaptation affects their usefulness [14].

We use tennis as a concrete setting to explore perceptual demands of highly dynamic sports: localizing players and fast-moving objects, anticipating trajectories, and coordinating body motion for imminent contacts [5, 15, 16]. Returning a tennis ball couples these capabilities – spatial accuracy and timing are crucial since the players and ball continue moving during perception, planning, and execution [17, 4].

There have been three main data modalities used by robots tackling these challenges. First, dedicated spatial sensing uses  mocap (mocap) sensors or calibrated camera systems to directly estimate player and ball positions for trajectory forecasting and control [3, 4, 5, 17]. Second, allocentric videos, recorded by external cameras at fixed court locations, support ball tracking and trajectory analysis [18, 19], player behavior modeling, simulated skill learning [20, 21], and spatial question-answering with foundation vision-language models [22]. Third, egocentric perception, recorded from a player-worn camera, has addressed image-space instance segmentation, forehand action phases, and pose estimation of other players [23, 24, 25]. Egocentric cues such as gaze [26] and head orientation may also reveal aspects of attention and strategy that are less apparent from allocentric views.

For autonomous dynamic robots, egocentric video is especially relevant because it relies solely on a body-mounted camera rather than external sensors – it thus removes workspace limitations and infrastructure demands. However, this viewpoint presents a demanding test of perception: body and head motion mix camera and object motion, court landmarks and relevant objects leave the field of view, and dynamic objects such as a ball can appear small, blurred, or partially occluded.
The joint ability of foundation visual representations to support metric player and object state estimation and causal forecasting throughout such egocentric video of dynamic tasks remains insufficiently characterized.

We therefore ask: How well do foundation vision models support spatial understanding and forecasting from dynamic egocentric video?

To support this evaluation, we collect a tennis dataset with synchronized video from a head-worn egocentric camera and five allocentric cameras. We annotate this data with segmentations and localization information via a custom pipeline that fuses automated inferences and manual labeling.

We then use the egocentric frames as model inputs and evaluate seven spatiotemporal understanding and forecasting tasks split into four groups. Spatial state estimation predicts the current 2D ego player position and 3D ball position. Spatial state forecasting predicts the future 2D ego motion and 3D ball motion. Stroke anticipation predicts whether the ego player’s next stroke will be forehand or backhand. Contact anticipation predicts the remaining time until the ego player’s racket-ball contact and the 3D ball position at contact. Together, these tasks probe the spatial and temporal understanding of pre-trained visual representations.

We select 13 vision encoders spanning image encoders, video encoders, and vision-language models (VLMs). We attach lightweight prediction heads to each encoder’s output visual token stream, train the encoder and probes jointly on all tasks, and evaluate prediction accuracy on held-out rallies. We consistently observe 3D ball prediction errors and 2D ego player localization errors that are on par with expected ball motion across 1–2 frames and expected player motion across 3–7 frames, indicating promising dynamic performance.

We perform ablations to investigate representations, dynamic information, and horizon lengths. Ball prediction errors reduce significantly with supplementary depth information, indicating that metric depth estimation is weakly encoded in the visual representations. Longer conditioning histories do not improve 3D position inference; in fact, image encoders achieve identical ball forecasting performance with only one conditioning frame, relying instead on other spatial correlations to predict future motion. We study the impact of rally phase and horizon length, finding that higher temporal proximity to ego–ball contact time reduces ball localization error but increases ego player localization error, and that ball prediction error increases with the forecasting horizon.

Finally, we connect egocentric video understanding to whole-body tennis motion generation through a conditional motion diffusion model [27]. Trained on our dataset, the diffusion model uses the above vision-based predictions of racket–ball contact position, time remaining until contact, and whether the ball is approaching or departing (derived from ball forecasting) as conditioning information. As new visual observations refine contact time and position estimates, the model adaptively re-plans its whole-body kinematic motion. The planning system is instantiated with a finetuned vision-only variant of the LFM2.5-VL-450M [28], which is the fastest of our evaluated VLM-derived models and capable of 100 Hz100\text{\,}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z} inference on modern desktop GPUs. This pipeline demonstrates the utility of pre-trained spatiotemporal representations for downstream real-time robot applications.

Key contributions are as follows:

A tennis video dataset of 8585 rallies with 53,15553,155 egocentric frames and five synchronized allocentric views, annotated with 3D ball trajectories, 2D court-frame player trajectories, stroke type labels, and contact times, to be released upon acceptance of the paper.

A systematic evaluation of foundation vision model representations for seven tasks of spatiotemporal understanding and forecasting from egocentric tennis videos.

Empirical findings that (i) spatiotemporal task performance is comparable across image encoders and VLMs, but not the video encoder; (ii) supplementary depth information reduces ball localization error by 50–60%; (iii) longer conditioning histories yield little benefit.

A conditional diffusion model that generates whole-body kinematic tennis motion conditioned on predictions from a vision encoder trained on egocentric video.

1. A tennis video dataset of 8585 rallies with 53,15553,155 egocentric frames and five synchronized allocentric views, annotated with 3D ball trajectories, 2D court-frame player trajectories, stroke type labels, and contact times, to be released upon acceptance of the paper.

2. A systematic evaluation of foundation vision model representations for seven tasks of spatiotemporal understanding and forecasting from egocentric tennis videos.

3. Empirical findings that (i) spatiotemporal task performance is comparable across image encoders and VLMs, but not the video encoder; (ii) supplementary depth information reduces ball localization error by 50–60%; (iii) longer conditioning histories yield little benefit.

4. A conditional diffusion model that generates whole-body kinematic tennis motion conditioned on predictions from a vision encoder trained on egocentric video.

title: Understanding Human-Robot Collaboration through Joint Action
authors: Chengwen Zhang,Jianyang Wang,Chang Liu,Yukun Wang,Yuan Xu,Zhoutong Ye,Jie Cai,Chun Yu,Yuanchun Shi
abstract:
Human–robot collaboration requires partners to coordinate interdependent contributions toward a shared goal.
Joint Action theory provides concepts for understanding this coordination, but how these concepts are instantiated and combined across empirical research remains fragmented.
We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA 2020, identifying 83 empirical papers published between 2021 and 2026.
Through theory-driven framework analysis, we organized the literature into nine constructs across three capacities: Representation, Prediction, and Integration.
We analyze how these constructs are distributed and co-occur across studies, revealing where empirical evidence concentrates and where it is absent.
By mapping empirical HRC research onto a unified Joint Action framework, this review offers a coherent overview of HRC studies, identifies gaps in current evidence, and provides guidelines for future research.
introduction:
Human–robot collaboration (HRC) brings humans and robots together to accomplish tasks through interdependent contributions (Hoffman and Breazeal, 2004; Bauer et al., 2008). In activities such as handing over an object, transporting a load, or creating an artifact together, each partner’s actions shape what the other can do next. Partners need to establish what they are acting on, anticipate one another’s contributions, and coordinate when and how to act. When expectations fail, they must also restore the conditions for continuing together. Understanding HRC therefore requires examining the processes that connect individual actions into a shared activity.

Joint Action theory provides a basis for examining these processes. Research on human joint action identifies three functionally related capacities: sharing representations, predicting actions, and integrating the predicted effects of one’s own and others’ actions (Sebanz et al., 2006). These capacities direct attention to how partners establish a common basis for action, form expectations about one another, and organize complementary contributions in space and time (Vesper et al., 2010). Related accounts of grounding explain how partners establish sufficient evidence of understanding and repair communication when that understanding breaks down (Clark and Brennan, 1991). Together, these perspectives offer concepts for examining how collaboration is established, maintained, and restored across different tasks and robot systems.

Applying these concepts to HRC requires attention to what the available evidence actually establishes. Recognizing a partner’s intention does not by itself establish shared intention, and providing information does not establish that the information has been understood. Similarly, coordinated task performance leaves open whether partners hold compatible task representations and how the human experiences control over the joint outcome. Prior work has connected Joint Action theory to interactive robot design, coordination, and the psychological and philosophical challenges of acting with robots (Curioni et al., 2019; Iqbal and Riek, 2019; Belhassein et al., 2022). Building on this work requires distinguishing the collaborative mechanisms implemented in a system from the stronger claims about shared understanding, commitment, or agency that its behavior may invite.

Existing reviews provide complementary perspectives on HRC, including industrial safety and interfaces (Villani et al., 2018), robot learning (Mukherjee et al., 2022), and the broader organization of collaboration, communication, and cognition (Singh et al., 2026). More focused reviews examine communication, intention-based systems, and human autonomy and agency (Salehzadeh et al., 2022; Zhang and Doyle, 2023; Glawe et al., 2026), while Joint Action reviews connect theoretical mechanisms to HRI and compare interaction with human and robot partners (Belhassein et al., 2022; Navare et al., 2026). These contributions establish a foundation for a further question: how do empirical HRC studies instantiate distinct Joint Action constructs, and which constructs are studied together? Addressing this question requires bringing together studies that use different terminology while preserving distinctions among mechanisms that may appear similar in system descriptions. It also requires including relevant studies that investigate collaborative mechanisms without explicitly adopting the term joint action.

To address this question, we conducted a systematic review following PRISMA 2020 (Page et al., 2021). Our review includes 83 empirical papers published between 2021 and August 10, 2026, in which humans and robots contribute to a shared task through interdependent or coordinated actions and collaborative mechanisms are a central focus. We combined theory-driven coding with open coding of how each construct was operationalized. The resulting framework comprises nine constructs organized across Representation, Prediction, and Integration, with 29 subcodes describing their implementation in the reviewed studies. These capacities provide complementary perspectives on joint activity and can operate concurrently. Our investigation addresses three research questions:

RQ1: How are Joint Action constructs instantiated in empirical human–robot collaboration research?

RQ1: How are Joint Action constructs instantiated in empirical human–robot collaboration research?

RQ2: How is research attention distributed across these constructs, and how do their operationalizations co-occur within studies?

RQ3: What evidence gaps and research directions emerge from examining human–robot collaboration through Joint Action?

Our synthesis shows that the reviewed literature concentrates on a common execution architecture of partner-action processing, task sharing, and action coordination, while shared intention and cooperative commitment are less frequently addressed. Co-occurrence analysis reveals asymmetric dependencies among subcodes: task division, monitoring, and action prediction function as structural prerequisites that most other collaborative mechanisms presuppose. Human adaptation to robot limitations emerges as a recurring enabler of smooth execution, yet whether it reflects genuine preference or temporary accommodation remains largely unexamined. These findings motivate closer examination of whether successful execution is accompanied by compatible task understanding, experienced agency, and manageable demands on the human partner. We use this synthesis to identify directions for partner modeling, agency evaluation, learning through repair, transfer in co-training, and the management of pauses, handoffs, and withdrawal. This paper makes three contributions:

A theory-driven synthesis of 83 empirical HRC papers that distinguishes nine Joint Action constructs and characterizes their operationalizations across Representation, Prediction, and Integration.

A theory-driven synthesis of 83 empirical HRC papers that distinguishes nine Joint Action constructs and characterizes their operationalizations across Representation, Prediction, and Integration.

An analysis of construct coverage and subcode co-occurrence that maps the distribution and combinations of collaborative mechanisms investigated in the reviewed literature.

An evidence-grounded research agenda that connects gaps in current implementations and evaluations to questions about human understanding, agency, adaptation, and the sustained organization of joint activity.

1. RQ1: How are Joint Action constructs instantiated in empirical human–robot collaboration research?

2. RQ2: How is research attention distributed across these constructs, and how do their operationalizations co-occur within studies?

3. RQ3: What evidence gaps and research directions emerge from examining human–robot collaboration through Joint Action?

title: Vision-Language-Action or World-Action? Just Action Models
authors: Yonghao Yu,Lang Huang,Runyi Li,Toshihiko Yamasaki
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
The vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action model (WAM) communities debate whether control policies should inherit pretrained knowledge from vision-language models or from visual generators. The debate, however, bundles three separable choices: backbone initialization, the objective applied to future observations, and whether the machinery for that future loss is kept at inference. A gap between a VLA and a WAM therefore cannot simply be attributed to any one of them. We show that decoupling these choices yields a common framework for both families, which we term Just Action Model (JAM): a pretrained visual backbone with an action expert, trained with an action loss and a foresight loss. The foresight loss trains current-observation features to predict frozen encodings of the recorded future through a prediction head discarded after training, so no visual generation is involved in either training or inference, and the backbone can be chosen freely.
We first compare objectives within fixed policy architectures, then evaluate the foresight recipe across backbone families.
The resulting JAM policies outperform their matched FastWAM and ImageWAM counterparts on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and achieve similar or slightly higher success rates on RoboTwin. Compared with FastWAM, JAM improves the success rates from 97.0%/55.3%/91.2% to 98.2%/64.5%/91.4%, respectively. With cached foresight targets, JAM reduces estimated online training FLOPs per sample per update by 73% relative to FastWAM.
Our results show that future supervision improves control without visual generation or additional inference machinery, and strong foresight performance is attainable with either generator-initialized or vision-language backbones.
Project Page: https://y0uroy.github.io/JAM
introduction:
Pretrained visual models provide a starting point for robot control. Standard vision-language-action models (VLAs) adapt vision-language representations to predict actions (Kim et al., 2025b; Black et al., 2025a; Black et al., 2025b). World-action models (WAMs) start from image or video generators and learn actions together with future visual prediction (Ye et al., 2026b; Yuan et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Bi et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). These approaches differ, as depicted in Figure 1, in both their pretrained knowledge and how they use the robot trajectories: most VLAs learn only the actions in a trajectory, whereas a WAM also learns to generate the observations that follow. Comparing their success rates alone does not identify which difference matters.

We separate three choices: backbone initialization, the objective on recorded future observations, and the modules used at inference. Recent attempts such as FastWAM (Yuan et al., 2026) and ImageWAM (Zhang et al., 2026a) remove test-time video or image generation and suggest that visual generative objectives at training time are the key to WAMs. We ask a more basic question: does learning from recorded future observations require a visual generative objective at all? If not, can backbones without visual generative pretraining learn from future observations in the same way?

We show that predicting future representations can replace visual generative supervision in policy training.
We introduce Just Action Model (JAM), a common recipe for a pretrained visual backbone and an action expert. The policy is trained with an action loss and a foresight loss: a prediction head maps current-observation features to targets supplied by a frozen future anchor. Future observations provide targets for the foresight loss, never inputs to the action path. The anchor branch and prediction head are used only during training, and fixed targets can be cached. At deployment, the backbone encodes the current context and the action expert predicts the action chunk. JAM requires no image or video generation during policy fine-tuning or deployment. The backbone may still come from generative pretraining, and the action expert still uses flow matching.

We evaluate the recipe in two stages. First, we replace the generative objectives of FastWAM and ImageWAM while keeping each policy’s architecture, data, optimizer, training budget, and deployment path fixed. Predicting future representations preserves or improves success, and targets at future positions are more effective than those at the current position. Backbone and future anchor pretraining play different roles: a pretrained FastWAM backbone remains effective with a randomly initialized, frozen future anchor, and direct VAE features give its strongest result. JAM (Ovis-U1) performs best with targets from the pretrained Yak backbone, so the preferred target is architecture-dependent. With the best target for each architecture, LIBERO-Plus success rises from 55.31%55.31\% to 64.54%64.54\% for FastWAM and from 65.27%65.27\% to 79.95%79.95\% for ImageWAM. With cached targets, this recipe reduces estimated online FLOPs per sample per update by 73.0%73.0\% for FastWAM and 36.8%36.8\% for ImageWAM.

Second, we retain the common foresight objective and instantiate it with generative, self-supervised, and vision-language backbones. On LIBERO-Plus, JAM (Ovis-U1), JAM (DINOv2-L), and JAM (Qwen3.5-2B) reach 79.95%79.95\%, 70.39%70.39\%, and 81.14%81.14\%, against 65.27%65.27\% for ImageWAM (Ovis-U1), which is trained with the generation loss ℒG\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{G}}. These results establish the recipe’s applicability across all three families: generative backbones can learn from future observations without a visual generative loss, and the same supervision applies to non-generative backbones.

Our contributions are:

title: FastBEVFusion: Simple Multi-Modal Fusion for 3D Object Detection at 50 FPS
authors: Tom Sanitz,Emre Gülsoylu,Simone Frintrop,Christian Wilms
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Reliable real-time 3D object detection based on LiDAR and camera data is critical for safety in autonomous driving, where systems must accurately perceive their surroundings with minimal latency. Many state-of-the-art systems achieve high-quality detection results but fail to meet real-time constraints, limiting their practical use. To address this challenge, we propose FastBEVFusion, a simple, fast, and robust fusion system for 3D object detection. Based on modality-specific features, FastBEVFusion projects these features into semi-aligned modality-specific BEV spaces, without relying on a computationally intensive and potentially error-prone depth estimation. Given these BEV spaces, we propose a light-weight, soft, and dynamic fusion module based on cross-attention, which adapts dynamically to the scene context and enables feature fusion across the entire BEV spaces. Experiments on the complex nuScenes dataset show that FastBEVFusion outperforms state-of-the-art real-time systems, and achieves over 50 FPS without deployment libraries. Additionally, our system shows strong robustness to calibration errors, making FastBEVFusion a powerful 3D object detection system for real-world applications.
introduction:
3D object detection is an important task in autonomous driving and other robotics applications. In such real-world settings, robustness and low latency are essential to ensure safe operation. For instance, low latency allows rapid reaction to potentially dangerous situations in autonomous driving. Consider an autonomous vehicle driving at 120 km/h. In an emergency brake, it requires 72 m to stop. A 333 ms latency of the recognition system adds 10 m to the braking distance, while reducing the latency to 20 ms (50 FPS) limits this extra distance to only 66 cm – potentially preventing a fatal outcome.

Systems for 3D object detection are typically based on point clouds from LiDAR sensors [46, 11, 43, 40], images [37, 18, 36, 35], or a fusion of both [26, 30, 14, 1, 21]. Single modality systems usually exhibit lower latency [13, 16], whereas fusion-based systems produce high-quality detections by leveraging the strengths of both modalities [10, 45, 42]. While LiDAR offers natural depth information, camera-based systems improve the detection of small or distant objects. Hence, the modalities are complementary, leading to a strong interest in fusion-based systems.

Fusion-based systems combine modalities on various levels. Shallow fusion methods augment LiDAR features with semantic information derived from images [30, 39] or transform detections between modalities [26, 25, 3]. These approaches do not fully exploit the complementary nature of the modalities by only using modality-specific detection results. Instead, several methods combine aligned bird’s eye view (BEV) spaces [21, 42, 10, 29] to generate detections based on fused features. However, this requires depth estimation per pixel for accurate alignment, which can be time-consuming and error-prone [29, 3]. Omitting depth estimation, several recent approaches learn the fusion between modalities on the level of unaligned features [41, 14, 45] or queries [45, 1]. While the above methods offer high-quality detection results, they mostly exhibit high latency of 100 ms to 500 ms, due to complex processing, including multiple attention blocks [45, 41]. This is impractical for real-world robotics applications like autonomous driving, which require low latency.

In this paper, we propose FastBEVFusion, a fast, simple, and robust fusion approach for 3D object detection leveraging LiDAR point clouds and multi-view images. The approach is based on cross-attention of semi-aligned modality-specific BEV spaces and learns to fuse the modalities in a fast, soft, and dynamic fashion, incorporating the scene context. Hence, it combines ideas from BEV-based fusion and feature-level fusion. This combination is computationally very efficient, since we apply a fast uniform depth distribution when projecting image features into a BEV space and exploit the semi-aligned nature of the BEV spaces to introduce a light-weight fusion module. To compensate for the missing depth information leading to semi-aligned BEV spaces, our fusion module learns to attend to the relevant parts of the image BEV space, given a feature from the LiDAR BEV space. This enables soft associations between LiDAR and image features. As the fusion is data-driven, it dynamically adapts to the scene context. Due to its simple design in all components, including the fusion, FastBEVFusion achieves up to 50 FPS while outperforming real-time11
1
            
            
          We argue that real-time on the used nuScenes dataset is 12 FPS (83 ms) due to sensor imaging frequency. 3D object detection systems on the nuScenes dataset (see results in Fig. 1). At the same time, FastBEVFusion is robust to calibration errors and sensor misalignment, common challenges in practice.

Overall, our contributions are threefold:

We propose FastBEVFusion, a new and light-weight fusion system for multi-modal 3D object detection.

Our fusion combines BEV-based and feature-level fusion in a purely learned fashion leading to a robust and fast (50 FPS) system.

In our evaluation, FastBEVFusion substantially outperforms state-of-the-art real-time systems.

1. We propose FastBEVFusion, a new and light-weight fusion system for multi-modal 3D object detection.

2. Our fusion combines BEV-based and feature-level fusion in a purely learned fashion leading to a robust and fast (50 FPS) system.

3. In our evaluation, FastBEVFusion substantially outperforms state-of-the-art real-time systems.

title: MCP-Net: Real-Time Coronary Perception Network and Topological Analysis for Robotic Guidewire Navigation
authors: Sahar Nasirihaghighi,Tianyuan Wang,Kenan Niu,Stefano Stramigioli
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Coronary guidewire navigation during percutaneous coronary intervention requires continuous interpretation of vessel anatomy, guidewire position, and target stenosis under two-dimensional X-ray fluoroscopy. While existing approaches commonly address vessel segmentation or device localization as separate tasks, a robotic system requires a more structured perception of the coronary scene to support downstream navigation. In this work, we present a simulation-driven framework centered on a Multi-Task Coronary Perception Network (MCP-Net) for robotic guidewire navigation, integrating coronary vessel segmentation, vascular topology extraction, and roadmap generation. Starting from three-dimensional coronary CT angiography, we generate simulated fluoroscopy images containing vascular structures, simulated guidewires, stenotic lesions with varying severity, and diverse vascular geometries, together with simulation-derived ground truth. MCP-Net jointly performs coronary vessel segmentation, guidewire-tip localization, and stenosis localization from a single fluoroscopic frame. These predictions are subsequently converted into a structured vascular graph containing centerlines, bifurcations, endpoints, branch directions, and branch angles. By associating the predicted stenosis with this graph, the framework generates a roadmap from the automatically selected graph root toward the target lesion. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework can jointly recover coronary perception targets and transform them into an interpretable vascular representation suitable for downstream robotic navigation.
introduction:
Coronary artery disease remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is one of the primary procedures used to restore blood flow through stenotic coronary arteries [1, 2]. During PCI, the interventionalist must advance a thin guidewire through a complex, branching coronary vasculature toward the target lesion under two-dimensional X-ray fluoroscopic guidance. This task requires continuous interpretation of vessel geometry, identification of the lesion, and selection of the appropriate branch at successive bifurcations. The difficulty is compounded by vessel overlap, low image contrast, respiratory and cardiac motion, and the loss of depth information inherent to projection imaging [3, 4]. These challenges have also motivated the development of robotic-assisted PCI (RA-PCI), which enables remote manipulation of coronary guidewires and devices and has demonstrated clinical feasibility while reducing operator radiation exposure [5, 6, 7]. However, increasing the level of robotic assistance requires reliable intraoperative perception capable of extracting actionable vascular information directly from fluoroscopic images.

For robotic guidewire navigation, however, vessel segmentation alone is not sufficient. A navigation system must reason about both the device and its surrounding anatomy: where the guidewire tip is located, where the target stenosis lies, how the coronary tree branches, and which sequence of vessel segments connects the coronary root to the target. Such information must also be available at interactive rates if it is to support intraoperative robotic decision-making. Existing work has investigated coronary vessel segmentation, guidewire or catheter localization, and vascular analysis [8, 9, 10], but these components are commonly considered as separate problems. Consequently, even an accurate segmentation mask does not directly provide the structured anatomical representation required for downstream navigation, including vessel connectivity, bifurcation structure, branch orientation, and a path toward the target lesion.

A second challenge is the availability of suitable training and evaluation data. Dense annotation of coronary fluoroscopy is difficult and time-consuming, particularly for thin or overlapping vessels. Precise annotation of guidewire tips, stenosis location, and stenosis severity introduces additional ambiguity, while annotations of centerlines and vascular topology require further expert effort. More importantly, the ground-truth geometry underlying a two-dimensional projection is generally unavailable in real fluoroscopic data. These limitations make it difficult to jointly train and quantitatively evaluate all of the perception and geometric components required by a robotic navigation pipeline.

In this work, we address these challenges through a simulation-driven, multi-task framework for coronary perception, topological analysis, and real-time roadmap generation. Starting from three-dimensional coronary CT angiography, we generate fluoroscopy-like projections containing coronary vessels, simulated guidewires, and stenotic lesions with different severity levels across diverse vascular geometries. Since the underlying scene geometry is known, task-specific ground truth can be generated automatically for vessel segmentation, guidewire-tip localization, stenosis localization, and geometric analysis. These data are used to train the proposed Multi-Task Coronary Perception Network (MCP-Net), which jointly predicts the vessel mask, guidewire-tip location, and stenosis landmarks from a single fluoroscopy frame. The predicted vasculature is subsequently converted into a structured centerline graph containing bifurcations, endpoints, vessel geometry, and branch information, from which a target-oriented vascular roadmap is generated.

This design deliberately separates learned image perception from geometric vascular reasoning. MCP-Net performs the image-dependent tasks jointly in a single forward pass, while centerline extraction, graph construction, and roadmap generation operate directly on the resulting vascular representation. The combination provides not only pixel-level predictions, but also a compact and interpretable description of the coronary anatomy that can serve as a perception interface for downstream robotic planning.

The main contributions of this work are:

We develop a CT-based coronary fluoroscopy simulation framework that generates synthetic intervention scenes containing coronary vasculature, simulated guidewires, and stenotic lesions with varying severity, together with automatically generated task-specific ground truth.

We propose MCP-Net, a multi-task coronary perception network that jointly performs coronary vessel segmentation, guidewire-tip localization, and stenosis localization within a unified architecture.

We introduce a real-time vascular topology and roadmap generation framework that converts the predicted vasculature into a structured graph containing centerlines, vessel calibers, bifurcations, endpoints, and branch geometry, and generates a navigation-oriented path toward the detected stenosis.

We provide a comprehensive evaluation on the simulated fluoroscopy dataset, including comparisons with established segmentation architectures, vessel segmentation and connectivity, guidewire-tip and stenosis localization, lesion geometry, vascular topology, roadmap generation, and end-to-end computational performance.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work, and Section III presents the proposed framework. Sections IV and V describe the experimental setup and results, respectively. Section VI discusses the findings, limitations, and future directions, and Section VII concludes the paper.

1. We develop a CT-based coronary fluoroscopy simulation framework that generates synthetic intervention scenes containing coronary vasculature, simulated guidewires, and stenotic lesions with varying severity, together with automatically generated task-specific ground truth.

2. We propose MCP-Net, a multi-task coronary perception network that jointly performs coronary vessel segmentation, guidewire-tip localization, and stenosis localization within a unified architecture.

3. We introduce a real-time vascular topology and roadmap generation framework that converts the predicted vasculature into a structured graph containing centerlines, vessel calibers, bifurcations, endpoints, and branch geometry, and generates a navigation-oriented path toward the detected stenosis.

4. We provide a comprehensive evaluation on the simulated fluoroscopy dataset, including comparisons with established segmentation architectures, vessel segmentation and connectivity, guidewire-tip and stenosis localization, lesion geometry, vascular topology, roadmap generation, and end-to-end computational performance.

title: Polarity--Time Interaction and Multi-Level Reliability for Event-Based Spacecraft Pose Estimation
authors: Yonglong Zhang,Zongwu Xie,Yang Liu
abstract: Sparse event responses produce uneven keypoint errors whose effects on spacecraft pose depend on correspondence geometry and the reliability of successive observations. We present a reliability-aware framework connecting polarity–time localization, geometric recovery, event–CAD refinement, and trajectory optimization. A three-branch representation combines positive events, negative events, and recent-event timing through cross-branch attention and gating, followed by spatiotemporal aggregation. An ordered semantic-point head estimates relative correspondence precision for geometrically constrained pose recovery. Event-edge and CAD-projection agreement then guide local pose refinement under keypoint-geometry safeguards. At the sequence level, a ten-dimensional descriptor combines heatmap shape, reprojection consistency, and geometric conditioning to set time-aligned observation scales. On the official SPADES challenge test set, the complete system achieves a combined pose score of 0.0474, approximately 5.4% below PASAN+IRIS. Validation ablations reduce the score from 0.0772 for base localization with uniform PnP to 0.0514 for the complete cascade; on identical single-frame observations, quality weighting reduces the score from 0.0549 with constant-weight optimization to 0.0514.
introduction:
Non-cooperative spacecraft pose estimation provides relative geometric information for rendezvous and docking, on-orbit inspection, and space servicing. Given a target CAD model, a vision system can localize semantic keypoints and recover rotation and translation from two-dimensional-to-three-dimensional correspondences. Illumination changes, shadows, and missing local structure make the quality of these observations spatially nonuniform. An event camera asynchronously reports the location, polarity, and time of brightness changes, providing fine-grained temporal measurements for dynamic targets [1]. Pose-estimation methods must therefore operate on sparse spatial responses whose distribution changes with motion.

Research on event-based spacecraft pose estimation has addressed event representation, geometric recovery, and temporal processing. SPADES established a dataset and evaluation baselines [2]. Polarity decoupling and spatiotemporal aggregation organize localization evidence across adjacent event windows [3], while keypoint-based initialization can be connected to model-projection matching and kinematic smoothing [4]. Other work has studied compact event representations and neuromorphic deployment [5]. Together, these studies show that event-based localization can establish semantic correspondences through learned features and constrain pose through known geometry and temporal relationships.

The central challenge is to assign influence to measurements according to their effect on pose recovery. A sharp heatmap response describes local concentration, while the pose error induced by that correspondence also depends on its camera ray and configuration relative to the other CAD points. At refinement time, agreement with sparse event edges must be assessed together with keypoint geometry and sensitivity to projection sampling. At the sequence level, refinement changes reprojection residuals and geometric conditioning, so the quality used for temporal fusion must describe the final observation. These issues connect correspondence weighting, candidate acceptance, and trajectory weighting through the reliability of the measurements entering each stage.

We address these issues through reliability-aware pose initialization (RPI), event–CAD consistency refinement (ECR), and multi-source quality-aware kinematic smoothing (MQKS). Polarity–time interaction supplies semantic keypoint observations; the proposed reliability mechanisms determine how those observations influence geometric recovery, which refined candidates are accepted, and how the resulting poses contribute to trajectory optimization. The contributions are:

Geometry-aware correspondence reliability. An ordered CAD11 context combines local heatmap shape, camera rays, and semantic geometry to predict relative point precision. A local pose-error propagation proxy complements localization-error likelihood, linking the learned weights to their effect on translation and rotation rather than heatmap concentration alone.

Geometry-aware correspondence reliability. An ordered CAD11 context combines local heatmap shape, camera rays, and semantic geometry to predict relative point precision. A local pose-error propagation proxy complements localization-error likelihood, linking the learned weights to their effect on translation and rotation rather than heatmap concentration alone.

Geometrically safeguarded event–CAD refinement. A direction-reversal-invariant orientation moment and unit-mass overlap score compare event and CAD structure. Candidate acceptance combines improvement over a same-pool geometric reference with keypoint-geometry bounds and agreement across two projection-integration resolutions, addressing event support and sampling sensitivity within the refinement decision.

Quality weighting of final pose observations. A ten-dimensional descriptor combines heatmap shape, reprojection consistency, and geometric conditioning. Pose-dependent terms are recomputed after refinement, and separate translation and rotation scales weight the corresponding observations at their physical timestamps, adapting temporal fusion to variations in observation quality.

Validation experiments examine correspondence weighting on fixed coordinates, the aggregate contribution of ECR within the cascade, and quality weighting on identical pose observations. The complete system achieves a combined score of 0.0474 on the official SPADES challenge test set; on the validation set, MQKS reduces the score from 0.0549 with constant weighting to 0.0514.

title: Bridging Exploration and Loss of Plasticity in On-Policy Reinforcement Learning
authors: Andrea Vasco Grieco,Evelyn D'Elia,Edoardo Caldarelli,Raffaello Camoriano
abstract:
Deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms have been observed to lose the ability to adaptively learn from new data, a phenomenon termed Loss of Plasticity (LoP).
While many metrics have been shown to correlate with it, the causal mechanisms and the geometric conditions from which it can arise have not been clearly identified.
We analyze LoP in Proximal Policy Optimization with isotropic Gaussian policies, the state-of-the-art formulation for many continuous action spaces in RL.
We report multiple metrics which characterize the effect that the policy standard deviation σ\sigma has on LoP, and we also suggest related explanations for the effectiveness of widely adopted LoP mitigation techniques.
We observe a significant effect of σ\sigma on the extent of LoP, and accompany this with both theoretical and experimental supporting arguments.
Our experimental validation consists of LoP benchmark evaluations against standard baselines as well as real-world policy deployment on a 7-DoF robotic arm.
introduction:
In the last decade, reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved impressive results in a broad set of domains, ranging from natural language processing [34, 13] to robotics  [33, 14].
A popular class of RL algorithms are policy gradient (PG) methods, originating with REINFORCE [48] and achieving improved success rates by integrating natural gradients [3, 2, 23].
A relevant RL subclass are on-policy gradient methods, in which the samples used for training are obtained by collecting rollouts with the current policy.
The development of Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [43] represents a landmark in this field, due to its relative simplicity, stability, and sample efficiency.
PPO is used to solve complex robotics tasks [19, 39, 28] and is considered the state-of-the-art technique for on-policy RL.
To model problems in which the agent acts in a continuous action space, a typical approach is to adopt Gaussian policies [6, 37], even though alternative exploration strategies, such as Policy Gradients with
Parameter-based Exploration (PGPE) [44] or natural evolution strategies [47, 40] have also been proposed.

Despite its success, PPO is not well studied theoretically, and its use is accompanied by a proliferation of heuristics [11, 4, 18] and known technical issues, such as the premature collapse of the Gaussian policy’s standard deviation σ\sigma [15].
In fact, most of the theoretical research focuses on vanilla PG methods such as REINFORCE, either deriving the optimal learning rate and batch size for safe PG [38, 36, 35], or showing that PG’s gradients with Gaussian policies suffer from increased variance as σ→0\sigma\to 0 [49].
However, results for PPO are very limited, with [17] only informally mentioning that gradients scale inversely with respect to σ\sigma, yielding large updates and instability.

Another issue observed in deep RL is the diminished ability of neural networks to learn new objectives after being trained, commonly referred to as Loss of Plasticity (LoP).
Indeed, [9, 8] observe that PPO asymptotically collapses and that this process is accelerated under non-stationarity.
Some explanations include the lack of feature representation richness
[20, 26, 30], the sharpening of the loss landscape  [31, 29], or dormant neurons [45]. Additionally, [33, 32] study gradient norms correlated with this phenomenon. Finally, [22] studies LoP in PPO specifically, but only focuses on discrete actions.

To mitigate LoP, multiple strategies have been proposed.  [31, 5, 10, 8] show that tweaking the Adam optimizer [24], either by setting the first and second moment coefficients β1\beta_{1} and β2\beta_{2} to the same value, or by partially resetting the optimizer parameters, is effective in reducing LoP.
Furthermore, [46] shows that increasing the strength of entropy regularization under non-stationarity is effective in improving task adaptation. Finally, [21] proposes formalized mathematical conditions that could explain LoP, showing that there exist LoP manifolds in which the weights of a neural network would be trapped after entering, with any gradient descent method regardless of the objective.

While LoP has been thoroughly studied in recent years, there is no consensus on its causes. Furthermore, for many of the proposed causes, there exist counter-examples. For this reason, we focus on a specific setting, PPO with Gaussian policies, and show formally and experimentally a novel link between the policy’s standard deviation σ\sigma and LoP. In summary, our contributions are:

The derivation of bounds linking multiple LoP metrics to σ→0\sigma\to 0, formally proving and numerically verifying that under mild integrability assumptions the gradient norm and the Hessian sharpness diverge, while the Hessian approximate rank collapses, as σ→0\sigma\to 0;

Experiments on an established benchmark showing that σ\sigma is related to the observed LoP phenomenon and that the effectiveness of existing techniques counteracting LoP is explained by their indirect influence on σ\sigma;

Task-adaptation experiments with real-world robotic deployment demonstrating that our results also apply to a complex scenario with a continuous action space.

title: Compatibility and future-proof testing for multi-agent systems
authors: Yueshan Li,Lorenzo Fiaschi,Andrea Censi,Emilio Frazzoli
abstract:
Independently developed autonomous agents, such as autonomous vehicles, must guarantee joint compatibility, such as safety and task-completion requirements, when they operate in a shared environment.
Existing methods require a centrally designed specification, or interaction mechanism before any agent is deployed.
However, such centralized design is unrealistic when agent designs are confidential to their developers, and it is not flexible enough to accommodate future agent designs.
We study a bi-level structure in which a regulator coordinates developers by publishing seed agents,
and each developer independently tests its agent to ensure that it is compatible with every seed-compatible agent, a property we call future-proofness.
Under this structure, joint compatibility is guaranteed for any agents that are designed and tested independently, without any coordination with each other.
In this work, we first formulate compatibility for general multi-agent systems
and show why it is not trivially implied by seed-compatibility.
We then characterize the future-proof agents as the closure of the seed and show that this closure is monotone in the seed.
Finally, we study a class of executable tests that involve interaction with the seed alone, and we ask to what extent such tests can distinguish the future-proof agents.
introduction:
Autonomous agents increasingly take part in daily life and share their environment with human beings and with other autonomous agents.
These agents serve different purposes, come from different vendors, and are designed independently. Guaranteeing compatibility among them is therefore a challenge.
For instance, as many as 26 companies have obtained permits to test automated vehicles on public roads in California [1],
and drone operators fly through overlapping airspace [2].
Beyond robotics, large-language-model (LLM) agents are expected to cooperate with human beings and with each other [3].
In all these cases, a population of autonomous agents is deployed by different developers without direct coordination.
Nevertheless, their joint behavior must remain acceptable, so that safety and efficient task completion are guaranteed.
In short, they must be compatible.

Compatibility is typically certified through centralized design.
For instance, in aviation a conflict-resolution protocol is imposed on every participant [4],
and safety is guaranteed as long as all participants follow the protocol.
However, centralized design is unrealistic when agent designs are confidential to their developers
and regulators have no right to pre-approve them [5].
Moreover, agents can be updated over the air after deployment, and a single update can change two million vehicles overnight [6].
As a result, new testing concepts are needed that rely neither on the implementation details of the agents nor on coordination between developers.

We propose future-proof testing, illustrated in Figure 1.
A regulator publishes a set of agents that serves as the common reference for all developers, which we call the seed.
The seed is the set of agents that the regulator want to be compatible with all the future ones. For instance, this set can contain the agents already deployed, or represent the conventions that the regulator wants to see in their system.
Each developer then tests its agent independently against the seed, without coordination with other developers.
Once an agent passes the test, it is compatible with the seed and with every other passing agent, even though the passing agents are never tested against each other.

Seed-based coordination of this kind is already practiced.
For example, UN Regulation 157 scripts a family of cut-in manoeuvres that an automated lane-keeping system must survive [7].
However, designing the passing criterion of such a test is non-trivial.
Section III-A gives a simple counterexample in which passing against the seed does not imply that the certified agents are safe together.

This paper establishes the theoretical foundations of future-proof testing with safety guarantees.
We propose a general formulation of multi-agent systems and acceptance criteria.
On this basis, we define a compatible set as a set of agent designs of which any combination can be deployed without violating the acceptance criteria.
Within this framework, we first show, both by example and in theory, that seed compatibility does not in general imply mutual compatibility.
We then characterize the future-proof agents, which are the target of future-proof testing and provide the desired safety guarantees.
Surprisingly, the set of future-proof agents grows with the seed, so a more demanding reference admits more future-proof agents.
Finally, we ask what a developer can establish from testing against the seed alone.
We answer with a lower bound on the testing loss of seed-based testing, that is, the future-proof agents that no such test can identify.

This paper makes three contributions.

We provide theoretical foundations for seed-based coordination and explain why testing against the seed alone does not naturally lead to compatibility among agents.

We characterize the target of correct seed-based testing, namely the future-proof agents, and bound the testing loss of seed-based testing from below.

We showcase the theory in two case studies: a chain of braking vehicles and a decentralized path finding in a grid-world warehouse.

A world model calibrated for the collection policy is not calibrated for the deployment policy.
A model trained under one pattern of action selection is assessed under another once a
planner, controller, or downstream policy starts choosing actions from its predictions. The
transition mechanism may remain stable, yet the distribution of state–action queries can move
into regions where the model’s residuals follow a different marginal law. Calibration under the
collection policy is then a statement about the wrong measure. Shifting deployment mass toward
state–action pairs with larger residuals lowers the target coverage of unweighted source quantiles.
